It was taught long ago by the wise bodhisattva
and by the supreme Sage.

Then again the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara said to the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, "Lord of Secrets, these mantra words carry great secrecy and are supremely secret.

"My son, for your benefit, the utmost of the fierce,
renowned as the family of the Unbearable:
whatever mantras there are, all of them,
the wise should accomplish.
The vajra and lotus families as well,
renowned as the bracelet on the crown,
in order surely to destroy them,
I properly proclaim this vidyā:"

namaḥ sarba buddha bodhisatvānāṃ apratihata śāsanānāṃ oṃ kara kara kuru kuru mama kāryāṃ jaṃbha jaṃbha sarba sarba daha daha sarba bajra bināśaka mārdha ḍāka jībantāṃ takarā mahā bitri tarā piṇe paca paca sarba duṣḍaṃ mahā gaṇapati jībantāṃ takara bandha bandha sarba grahāṃ ṣaḍ mukha ṭha ḍa bhuja ṣa ḍa caraṇa rudra mānaya brahma tyaṃ debanānaya mābilamba mābilamba bhuṣa hrī maṇḍala madhye prabeśaya samayamanusmara hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā

"Lord of Secrets, this supremely secret one of great diligence, called the Six-Faced One, a limb of Tārā, is the great king of wrathful ones who vanquishes all. If merely by reciting it even the lords who dwell on the ten bodhisattva grounds are destroyed, what need is there to speak of savage obstructors? Merely by reciting it, great protection is accomplished. Here the mudrā is called the Great Family; it destroys obstructors.

"The heart mantra of this king of wrathful ones is:

oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭṝḥ bikṛtānana hūṃ sarba śatruṃ stambhaya phaṭ phaṭ svāhā

"Through this mantra all enemies will be seized by a disease of great stabbing pains, or else by a one-day fever. Through constant recitation, for as long as it lasts, they will not turn to loving-kindness, nor will they attain a mind of compassion; until the recitation is completed there will be neither release nor binding. This is to be done against those who harm the Three Jewels, not against others who have peaceful minds. One should also apply the Great Spear mudrā.

"Here what serves as the near-heart mantra is:

oṃ hrīḥ kālarūpaṃ hūṃ khaṃ svāhā

"One should apply the Great Spear described before as well. It will do whatever one wishes to all malicious beings.

"The supreme heart mantra, blessed by all the buddhas, called the Single Syllable, is hūṃ. It performs all rites; one should also apply the Great Spear mudrā. It turns back all calamities and brings all bhūtas under control. In short, this king of wrathful ones should be applied to all rites, and when accomplishment comes through recitation in the center of the maṇḍala, something extraordinary will occur.

"Here what serves as the mantra of dismissal is:

namaḥ sarba buddhānāṃ apratihata śāsanānāṃ tadyathā jaya jaya sujaya mahākāruṇika biśvarūpini gaccha gaccha svabhābanāṃ sarba buddhaṃ svabisarjāya saparibāraṃ svabhabānāṃ cā prabeśaya samayamanusmara sarbārtha sva me sidhyaṃtu bidhya sadāḥ mnorathaṃ ca me paripūraya svāhā

"This is the mantra of dismissal, and it should be applied in all rites. Its mudrā is renowned as the Excellent Seat, and with it one should also offer a seat. By reciting it mentally seven times, one dismisses them all. It should also be applied to the worldly and transworldly maṇḍalas, and, for the mantras themselves, to the accomplishments of mantra, the pledges, the recitation, the times, and the definitive vows."

Then again the great being once more gazed all around at the divine sons of the Pure Abodes and spoke to the great maṇḍala of the assembly the Extensive Chapters of the mantras of his own host of vidyās.

namaḥ sarba buddhānāṃ apratihata gatīnāṃ oṃ niṭi svāhā

This is the vidyā called Keśinī, who follows Noble Tārā, and it performs all rites. It is the heart of the mudrā of the great pledge, and it is applied in all rites concerning poison.

namaḥ smanta buddhānāṃ apratihata śāsanānāṃ oṃ niṭi

This is the vidyā called Keśinī the Close Attendant, and it performs all rites. Its mudrā, called the Opened, should be applied in all rites concerning the planets.

namaḥ smanta buddhānāṃ apratihata śāsanānāṃ oṃ ni

This vidyā, called She of the Stalk, performs all the virtuous rites of conduct. Its mudrā, the Excellent Seat, is applied to summoning yakṣiṇīs.

namaḥ smanta buddhānāṃ acintyaddhātarūpiṇāṃ oṃ ṣṭai svāhā

Join properly the Hollow mudrā
of her who vanquishes all ḍākinīs.
Explained by the bodhisattva,
this vidyā-mantra is called Kapālinī.
She is the very lotus of all buddhas,
highly praised, possessing a goddess's form.

namaḥ smanta buddhanāṃ apratihata gati cāraṇaṃ tadyathā oṃ barade sāhā

The Utpala mudrā itself
is applied to the Eye, glorious by nature.
The goddess who holds many forms
swiftly brings about wealth.

namaḥ smanta buddhānāṃ acintyaddhūtarūpiṇāṃ oṃ suri svāhā

Joined with the Spear mudrā,
she destroys all fevers.

namaḥ smanta buddhānāṃ acintaddhātarūpiṇāṃ oṃ ture svāhā

She is called Tārā Endowed with Intention,
highly praised, performing all rites.
Joined with the Staff mudrā,
apply it to her who destroys obstructors.

namaḥ smanta buddhānāṃ acintyaddhūtarūpiṇāṃ tadyathā oṃ bilokini svāhā

The vidyā called the Radiant One
brings the whole world under control
and bestows every happiness;
it should be applied with the Lotus mudrā.

namaḥ smanta buddhānāṃ acintyaddhūtarūpiṇāṃ tadyathā oṃ biśva biśva saṃbhabe biśarūpiṇāṃ kaha kaha ābiśa ābiśa samayamanusmara ruru tiṣṭha svāhā

The vidyā Great Diligence
was taught by the Guide of the World.
Her heart mantra and mudrā are equality itself;
she makes all beings descend into possession, and is virtuous.
She is proclaimed as the Manifold One.

namaḥ smanta buddhānāṃ oṃ cintyadbhutarūpiṇāṃ tadyathā oṃ śvete prābasu hvāhā

Arrange it with the form of the Lotus Seat;
it performs all rites.

namaḥ samanta buddhānāṃ apratihata gati prātiriṇāṃ tadyathā oṃ śrīḥ

This vidyā is the Great Glorious Lady,
taught by the Protector of the World.
Joined with the Joining of the Mouths mudrā,
she bestows a great kingdom.

namaḥ smanta buddhānāṃ sarba satvābhaya pradāyikā tadyathā oṃ ajite kumāra rūpiṇī oṃ hi agaccha mama karyaṃ kuru svāhā

She who is renowned as Ajitā,
youthful, born of nectar,
joined with the Full mudrā,
turns back all enemies.

namaḥ smanta buddhānāṃ acintyadbhutarūpiṇāṃ tadyathā oṃ jaye svāhā bijaye svāhā ajite svāhā

Renowned as the Four Sisters,
they follow the bodhisattva.
They roam all the lands entirely
and take care of sentient beings.
Their brother is renowned as Tumburu,
and they attend upon him.
Riding together on a boat as their mount,
they dwell upon the ocean.
Arrange them with the Fist mudrā;
it fulfills all wishes.

namaḥ samanta buddhānāṃ lokāgrādhibatināṃ tadyathā oṃ kumāri mahākumāri krīḍa krīḍa mahārākṣasi bodhisatvānujñāta mayurāsane pāśa parśūpāṇi raktāṃgī raktagandddhānulepana priye priye kha kha khāhi khāhi hūṃ nritya rakta puṣpārcita mūrtti samanusmara bhrama bhrama bhramaya bhramaya hulu hulu mābilamba sarba karmāṇi me kuru kuru picitra rūpa dhāriṇi tiṣṭha tiṣṭha hūṃ hūṃ sarba buddhānujñāte svāhā

When the bodhisattva who cares for beings
had spoken it,
all the lands without exception
quaked in six ways.
For the benefit of all beings
and to turn back malicious beings,
my vidyā is ever renowned,
renowned everywhere as ever protecting.
That very protection on which beings rely
is well marked with the signs of the world.

Then the bodhisattva,
his heart moist with compassion, spoke:
"The great-souled bodhisattva,
for the benefit of the childish,
has taught what beings are to practice,
possessed of conduct toward all who wander.
Joined with the Staff and Life-Pole mudrā,
when the great-souled one applies it,
if it summons even Brahmā and the rest,
what need to speak of results for humans?
Having gathered the whole of this ritual system
into the mind of the Maiden,
this vidyā-mantra, renowned among the rākṣasas,
has been properly taught."

Thus the bodhisattva spoke,
wishing to care for sentient beings.
This heart mantra called the Three Syllables,
this vidyā-mantra, has been properly explained:
for the benefit of all sentient beings,
supreme for summoning enjoyments.
The Staff and Life-Pole mudrā
is arranged for all rites.

oṃ hūṃ jaḥ

This vidyā-mantra, in brief,
brings results for humans.

namaḥ smanta buddhānāṃ samantotyotita mūrttināṃ abikṛta graha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā

This near-heart mantra, too,
is joined with the Axe mudrā.
Likewise it summons the bhūtas,
and likewise the planets together with the mātṛkās.
When all are sealed with the mudrā
and arranged, it will bear fruit.
It terrifies the bhūtas,
and frees those whom malicious beings have entered.

This is the great messenger of the Blessed Lady Noble Tārā, who performs all rites, the attendant called Ekajaṭī, who performs all rites. By mere recitation alone she performs all rites. She terrifies all bhūtas, summons them, and brings them under control, and she fulfills everything that the vidyādhara wishes.

namaḥ smanta buddhānāṃ apratihata śāsanānāṃ tadyathā oṃ prahmā suprahmā prahmā barcase śāntiṃ kuru svāhā

This mantra is Mahābrahmā,
explained by the bodhisattva.
The bhūtas fully attain peace,
and in an instant they become cool.
Joined with the Lotus mudrā,
one swiftly attains well-being.
For the acts of fierce rites,
the Veda of the Guardian of Existence is wanted.
This has been spoken in brief;
this rite is the abridged one.

namaḥ smanta buddhānāṃ apratihata śāsanānāṃ tadyathā oṃ garuḍa bahana cakra pāni catur bhuja hūṃ hūṃ samayamanusmara bodhisatva ājñāpayati svāhā

The bodhisattva declared it.
It swiftly accomplishes the aim of pacification,
and it destroys the bhūtas.
It has a body in the form of Viṣṇu.
Joined with the Wheel mudrā,
it properly accomplishes the aim of stability.
This, in the tantra of Viṣṇu,
is a rite taught at length;
it brings accomplishment to all beings,
and the bodhisattva explained it.

namaḥ smanta buddhānāṃ apratihata śāsanānāṃ tadyathā mahā maheśvara bhutādhipati bṛṣabha dhvaje pralaṃba jaṭa mukuṭa dhāriṇī sita bhasma dhusarata mūrti sa aṃ phaṭ phaṭ bodhisatva ājñāpayati svāhā

Wishing to benefit sentient beings,
I proclaim this mantra.
Joined with the Spear mudrā,
it destroys all the bhūtas.
This rite that has been taught here
was taught long ago in the Śiva tantra
for beings who dwell upon the earth.
Its vast and various qualities
are declared by the Śiva tantra as well.

namaḥ smanta buddhānāṃ apratihata śāsanānaṃ tadyathā oṃ śakuni patata pakṣiṇa śaka khakha khāhi khāhi samayamanusmara hūṃ tiṣṭha bodhisatva ājñāpayati svāhā

This mantra is of great diligence,
renowned as Garuḍa,
supreme among those who tame the hard to tame.
It destroys the poisons of hooded serpents.
Joined with the Great mudrā,
it destroys them together with unbearable calamities.
The poisons of things stationary and moving
it heals beyond doubt.
Out of love for the beings to be tamed,
this is the bodhisattva's true word:
he acts in the form of a garuḍa,
king of birds, possessed of great light.
All the extensive rites
that are taught in the garuḍa tantras,
tantras that benefit all beings,
I too have proclaimed.
If in the tantra that names the garuḍa
the king of wrathful ones has not been taught,
then, to destroy the poison of hooded serpents,
he moves about in the form of a bird.
Whatever worldly mantras there are,
the rites stated by way of example,
for the sake of beings to be tamed,
he employs in such and such ways.
And whatever tathāgata mantras there are,
and those of the vajra and lotus families,
their rites here in these Extensive Chapters
are as they were spoken before.
Just as nurses of many kinds
take pains to protect a child,
so for those whose minds are utterly childish
I am the cause of the vidyā-mantra forms.
What the One with the Ten Powers taught long ago,
I too now teach.
The meaning of the mantra tantras without remainder
the one of great light has proclaimed through realization.
What the supreme Victor taught
the son of the One with the Ten Powers has taught:
Avalokiteśvara, of marvelous and inconceivable form,
has spoken it.

Then again the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara gazed all around at that entire world system and at that great maṇḍala of the assembly, and entered into the samādhi called Properly Urging All Pledges. Through his abiding in that samādhi, the mind of the conduct of accomplishment of all beings without exception came to abide firmly in all sentient beings.

As soon as the bodhisattva mahāsattva had entered into it, there appeared for the great assembly gathered from everywhere a maṇḍala, the Array of Ornaments of the Jewel Essence in the Hand, set in a place of brilliant variety, an inconceivable and marvelous magical display. If even all the pratyekabuddhas, the noble śrāvakas, the bodhisattvas engaged in conduct, and those possessing the ten grounds who abide as lords of the ten grounds were unable to draw that maṇḍala or have it drawn, what need is there to speak of sentient beings who are ordinary people?

The great bodhisattva gazed upon those who abide in the place of accomplishing the pledges of that excellent noble maṇḍala. Then all the buddhas, the blessed ones, all the pratyekabuddhas, all the noble śrāvakas, all the bodhisattvas abiding on the ten grounds who have been consecrated as regents and have obtained the pledge, those engaged in conduct, and all sentient beings with defilements and without defilements, through the blessing of Avalokiteśvara, through a cause concordant with the inconceivable conduct of buddhas and bodhisattvas and through the distinction of samādhi, came to know properly for themselves that they had entered the maṇḍala arisen from his heart. If no ordinary person can even conceive of it in the mind, what need is there to speak of drawing it or having it drawn?

Then again the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara said to those sentient beings who had properly entered into the pledge of the great maṇḍala, "Friends, listen! If this is a pledge that not even the tathāgatas and bodhisattvas may transgress, what need is there to speak of sentient beings and other noble ones?"

Then again the great being said to Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, "O Son of the Victors, the mind-born pledge that transcends humans has been definitively taught. For humans, I shall explain how, when the tathāgatas have passed into parinirvāṇa, sentient beings will properly enter and accomplish all the accomplishments of worldly and transworldly vidyā and mantra."

Then again Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, said to the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, "O Son of the Victors, if you know that the time has now come, speak, speak!

"When Śākyasiṃha, Protector of the World,
has passed into parinirvāṇa,
in this supreme buddha field of humans
the beings upon the earth, through your maṇḍala,
by merely seeing it in the world,
will fully give rise to the accomplishments of mantra.
If one is ignorant and the rite is impaired,
or if one has not become a master of the pledge,
then even for great-souled Brahmā
the accomplishment of vidyā-mantra will not occur.
If one does not strive earnestly at mantra
and does not see the teaching of the pledge,
then even though one strives in many ways,
the accomplishment of vidyā will not occur."

When the application of the pledge is impaired,
if even Śakra (Indra), though he strives hard,
does not gain the accomplishment of vidyā,
what need is there to speak of humans on earth?
One who knows that very treatise of the pledge
and accomplishes the actions of the conduct
will accomplish both mundane and noble mantras
merely by reciting them.
Having fully entered the maṇḍala of the bodhisattva,
one performs all the rites.
Within the bodhisattva's teaching,
one's accomplishment of vidyā is constant.

Then again the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi, made a request to that great being: "O being, O great being!" And the noble Avalokiteśvara spoke the maṇḍala rite for the sake of sentient beings.

First of all, in the fortnight of miracles, or in the month of Caitra, or in the bright half of the month of Vaiśākha, on a highly praised day, having looked for a favorable planet, on the first day of the bright fortnight joined with an auspicious lunar mansion, or on the full moon, or at another time, avoiding the months of the rainy season, one should consecrate the ground in the morning.

Near a great city, or wherever the maṇḍala master himself dwells, where a river enters the ocean, or beside a river, or close to the shore of the ocean, in the northeastern quarter of the great city, neither too far nor too near, the maṇḍala master should go, and for seven days or a fortnight, keeping a strict fast or observing the fasting vow, he should dwell there apart. In whatever places he dwells, in a clean spot free of stones, potsherds, ashes, charcoal, husks, skulls, bones, and places where bones lie, a spot that has been very thoroughly cleansed, with water free of living creatures mixed with the five products of the cow, and with water of sandalwood, camphor, and saffron, empowered eight thousand times with the king of wrathful ones, Tārā's Subjugator, and joined with the great mudrā of the Blessed Lady, one should sprinkle that spot in the four directions, and sprinkle it all around, above, below, level across, and in the intermediate directions.

Then at that spot one should make it square on all sides, sixteen cubits, or twelve cubits, or eight cubits. Of these, the large one is sixteen cubits, the medium twelve cubits, and the small eight cubits.

These three kinds of maṇḍala
were taught by the All-Seeing One.
The large is for one who desires kingship;
the medium makes wealth increase;
the small, the pledge of mantra,
performs all rites and is pacifying.

There one should draw whichever maṇḍala one wishes in one's mind. At that spot one should dig down about two cubits, and if one sees there stones, charcoal, ashes, bones, hair and the like, or various kinds of living creatures, one should dig at another spot. There it will be free of harm and free of injury. On mountain peaks, too, and on the banks of great rivers that flow into the ocean, wherever it may be, having examined it very carefully with great effort and having made it very clean and free of living creatures, one should draw it.

At that spot, again, one should fill the pit with clean earth from a riverbank, or with earth from an anthill, or with earth from any place free of living creatures, mixed with water free of living creatures into which the five products of the cow have been blended. Having filled it, one should pound it well and make it level all around, and then make whichever of the three kinds of maṇḍala one wishes.

Four pegs of khadira wood should be empowered seven times with the king of wrathful ones himself and driven in at the four directions. A thread of five colors should be empowered seven times with the king of wrathful ones and wound all around in the form of a square maṇḍala. In the same way, in the central area inside, it should also be made with four corners. The maṇḍala master, staying within the center, should recite the root vidyā or the root heart mantra eight thousand times. Having bound the crown knot with the great mudrā and the root mantra, and having protected his companions with the root mantra of the wrathful one and protected himself, he should go outside while continuing the recitation, circumambulate the maṇḍala clockwise, and sitting facing east on a mat of kuśa grass, bearing in mind all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, he should wind the thread around that maṇḍala in a square form. Outside it, keeping a one-day fast, he should consecrate it.

Then, having performed here the preliminary practices of the maṇḍala master, the preceptor, skilled in his own vidyā, in mantra and in tantra, for the sake of all sentient beings, with special devotion to the Great Vehicle, keeping a one-day fast, accompanied by good companions, and having seen the procedures of the various treatises, should thoroughly purify fine, brilliant powders of five colors, and should place in the center of the maṇḍala the powder empowered with the mantra and heart of the root vidyā.

Outside as well, it should be proclaimed in a place adorned with banners, raised flags, and four gateways, with plantain trees swaying with clusters of fruit and hanging all around with clusters of fruit, and resounding with the sound of great drums, clay drums, and conches. On the four sides, one should listen to the Dharma with the sound of praises in harmony throughout. In the four directions one should recite volumes of the sūtras of the Great Vehicle, namely: the Perfection of Wisdom should be recited in the south; the noble Samādhi of the Moon Lamp in the west; the noble Gaṇḍavyūha in the north; and the noble Sublime Golden Light in the east. If there is no one to recite the volumes in this way, one should request a person, a Dharma teacher who knows how to recite the four sūtras, so that the Dharma may be heard.

Then the maṇḍala master should rise, recite the root vidyā over fragrant white flowers mixed with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron, and spread them as a carpet over the whole maṇḍala.

Having strewn them, he should go outside. Then two or three painters, who for seven days have partaken of the food they wish, who have given rise to the awakening mind, and who abide in keeping the fasting observance of the poṣadha, those companions or disciples who have given their promise, should be admitted.

One whose crown knot has been bound with the root vidyā itself should then take, each separately, fine powders of gold, of silver, of the brilliant substance of various precious gems, and of shining, beautiful copper; and great kings who are possessed of great wealth and who are righteous should be admitted here. From merely seeing the maṇḍala, one is certainly inclined toward awakening; what need is there to speak of one who accomplishes mantra?

The supreme being of the Śākyas has passed into nirvāṇa.
For sentient beings of little merit,
how could there be such wealth as this?
This rite shall therefore be taught.
The bodhisattva endowed with great light,
having seen people in poverty,
taught in condensed form
a maṇḍala that is small and brief.

Powders of śāli rice and of coarse grain, very fine and brilliant, of five colors, should be tinted to the hues of white, yellow, red, black, and green. The maṇḍala master should take the powder set down earlier, bind the great mudrā of the Blessed Lady, and seal the powder with the root vidyā.

Another master, one who accomplishes pacification, having seen the ritual for the rites, should make a fire pit outside the maṇḍala, in the southeast. It should measure two cubits, with a depth of about one cubit, with a rim all around in the form of lotus petals. Having kindled the fire with kindling sticks of palāśa wood, he should invite the fire god, Agni, with fuel sticks of bilva wood about a span long, still moist and smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, using the root heart mantra, or the mudrā and the root vidyā-mantra. Having invited him, he should again make one hundred and eight fire offerings with the vidyā of the Single Syllable stated earlier, or with the heart of the root vidyā.

Then the maṇḍala master, having purified his crown knot and gathered the requisites, should set himself and a very skilled painter, or a disciple, to the work. Then the maṇḍala master, bearing in mind the buddhas and bodhisattvas, should burn incense with the incense vidyā stated earlier. Joining his palms, he should pay homage to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas and to the bodhisattva, the great being, noble Avalokiteśvara, then take up the powder and lay out the forms, and the skilled painter should complete them.

By these rites, first of all, one should draw the Buddha, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, endowed with the supreme of all aspects, seated on a jeweled lion throne, teaching the Dharma in the abode of the Pure Abodes. When the maṇḍala master has drawn this, the assistant practitioner should perform the rite of self-protection and the vidyā, and then give a torma to all the bhūtas, scattering it in the four directions outside the maṇḍala, and above and below.

Then, having bathed, he should go near the fire pit, put on clean clothes, perform the rites of cleanliness and protection, and with the root vidyā make eight thousand fire offerings of oblations of ghee mixed with saffron. Then, sitting on a mat of kuśa grass, he should recite right there and remain right there. White mustard seed should be empowered one hundred and eight times with the mantra of the king of wrathful ones, Tārā's Subjugator, and having been empowered, it should be placed in a bowl closed with another bowl turned over it. If one sees the many transformed forms of obstructors coming, or fierce roars, wind, rain, or any other ill omens of whatever kind, one should wrathfully make fire offerings of mustard-seed oblations seven times. Then the obstructors will be terrified. As for human obstructors, if one makes fire offerings of barley five times, that person will become paralyzed, or will become powerless, or will die, or in that very instant will be seized by nonhuman beings.

Then the assistant practitioner should sit right there on the mat of kuśa grass and remain, reciting the king of wrathful ones, Tārā's Subjugator.

Then the maṇḍala master should place, on the right side of the image of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, two pratyekabuddhas seated cross-legged on lotus seats. Below them should be two great śrāvakas listening to the Dharma. To their right should be the Blessed One, noble Avalokiteśvara, adorned with all ornaments, white like the color of an autumn cloud, seated on a lotus seat, holding a lotus in his left hand, his right hand granting the supreme boon. To his right in turn should be the Blessed Lady Pāṇḍaravāsinī, holding a lotus in her hand, with her right hand paying homage to the Blessed One Śākyamuni, seated on a lotus seat, wearing a crown of matted locks, wearing a lower garment of white silk, wearing an upper shawl of silk, and marked with three dots of black ash. In the same way the Steadfast One and Bhṛkuṭī should also be drawn, each seated on her own seat in her own posture. To their right one should also draw the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā, the Tathāgata Locanā, and the Uṣṇīṣa Queen.

Likewise, sixteen bodhisattvas are to be drawn, namely: Samantabhadra, Kṣitigarbha, Gaganagañja, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Sarvāpāyajaha, Maitreya holding a yak-tail fly whisk in his hand and gazing at the Buddha, the Blessed One, Vimalamati, Vimalaketu, Sudhana, Candraprabha, Vimalakīrti, Healer of All Illnesses, King Lord of All Dharmas, World Goer, Mahāmati, and the one called Upholder. These sixteen great bodhisattvas should be drawn with utterly peaceful bodies, adorned with all ornaments. The chief vidyā kings, the vidyā queens, the forms of the lotus family, and the mudrās should be drawn as explained in scripture and in their proper places.

At the outer edge, too, the places should be set out in square form. Well-made lotus flowers, and whichever vidyā deities come to mind, should also be placed in those positions. Likewise, on the right side of the Blessed One Śākyamuni there should also be the two pratyekabuddhas called Gagana and Completely. Likewise, the gates of entry should be made facing east in every maṇḍala. On the left side of the Blessed One Śākyamuni one should also draw two other pratyekabuddhas, called Candana and Siddha. Below them one should draw two great śrāvakas, Mahākāśyapa and Kātyāyana.

At their side should be the noble Vajrapāṇi, appearing dark blue like an utpala lotus, in an utterly peaceful form adorned with all ornaments, holding a yak-tail fly whisk in his right hand, his left hand placed on the head of the wrathful one. Vajramuṣṭi, Vajrāṅkuśa, Vajraśṛṅkhalā, Subāhu, and Vajrasena should be shown with their proper attire and their proper emblems, destroying the obstructors. All the vidyā kings and queens together with their retinues, and their forms, mudrās and so forth, should be drawn as they come to mind. To their left, two vajra mudrās should be drawn in square form. Having drawn them, one should say: "Whatever hosts of vidyās have not been called to mind in their places, may they dwell in this place!"

Above them one should draw the six perfections and the Blessed Lady Māmakī, adorned with all ornaments, with utterly peaceful bodies. Above them in turn one should draw the eight uṣṇīṣa kings, ablaze with garlands of flame all around, binding their mudrās, each in the form of a great universal monarch: golden in color, with calm faculties, adorned with all ornaments, casting a slight glance toward the image of the Tathāgata. They are Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, Abhyudgatoṣṇīṣa, Sitātapatroṣṇīṣa, Jayoṣṇīṣa, Padmoṣṇīṣa, Vijayoṣṇīṣa, Tejorāśi, and Unnatoṣṇīṣa. These eight uṣṇīṣas should be drawn.

At the gate on the side of entry, two bodhisattvas should be made. On the right side one should draw the one called Going Beyond the World, with an utterly peaceful body, wearing a crown of matted locks, holding a rosary with his right hand in the gesture of granting the supreme boon, holding a water flask with his left hand, facing the gate, his face slightly frowning. On the left side of the gate of entry one should draw the great bodhisattva Victor over the Unvanquished, with an utterly peaceful body, wearing a crown of matted locks, holding a staff and a water flask in his left hand, holding a counting rosary with his right hand while granting the supreme boon, his face slightly frowning, facing the gate of entry.

Beneath the lion throne should be a wheel of Dharma ablaze with garlands of flame all around. Beneath it, dwelling in that jeweled palace, one should draw the Blessed Lady, the great vidyā queen, with a body neither too thin nor too stout, utterly peaceful in form, beautiful, her face slightly smiling, holding a blue utpala lotus in her left hand and a bilva fruit in her right hand, adorned with all the ornaments of a young girl, wearing a jeweled crown, with a garland of pearls worn as a sacred thread, wearing an upper garment of silk, her lower body clad in a silk garment, ablaze with garlands of flame all around, seated on a lotus seat, gazing at the king of wrathful ones, Tārā's Subjugator, facing the gate of entry into the maṇḍala, lovely to behold in every way, and bearing a form made like that of the rākṣasī Ekajaṭā.

On her right side, beneath the lotus, one should draw the king of wrathful ones, Tārā's Subjugator, of a greatly transformed form, ablaze with garlands of flame all around, as if receiving commands, and gazing at the one who is a great bodhisattva. On the left side, beneath the lotus, five bodhisattvas in the form of gods of the class of the Pure Abodes should be drawn, namely: Utterly Stainless, Utterly Tamed, Pure, Dispeller of Darkness, and All-Illuminating. All of them dwell in the abode of the Pure Abodes, on a ground like a floor of stone made of many blazing jewels, carpeted with brilliant, many-colored flowers ablaze all around, and they should be drawn with beautiful forms.

The surrounding outer enclosure should be square, with four gateways, bright with brilliant colors of five kinds; and with very straight and not low lines one should make the inner maṇḍala. In the east, above the Blessed One Śākyamuni, in the center of the drawing, one should make the Lord of Flower Kings seated on a lotus seat, a Tathāgata form drawn very small, ablaze with garlands of flame all around, granting the supreme boon with his hand, and residing at the uṣṇīṣa of the body. To his right one should draw the mudrā of Uṣṇīṣacakravartin. To his left one should draw the mudrā of Tejorāśi. Above the Tathāgata Locanā one should draw Prajñāpāramitā. Above the Blessed noble Avalokiteśvara, to the right of Prajñāpāramitā, one should make the Blessed One Amitābha in the form of a Tathāgata, granting the supreme boon with his hand, seated on a lotus seat, ablaze with garlands of flame all around. To his right in turn are the mudrās of the begging bowl and the Dharma robe. Likewise, in sequence, at the place of entry the lotus mudrā should be made. To the left of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarāja, one should draw the mudrā of the uṣṇīṣa Tejorāśi, ablaze all around.

To his left in turn one should draw the Tathāgata Ratnaketu, seated on a mountain of jewels, teaching the Dharma, emitting the blazing light of blue beryl, emerald, and rubies of many kinds, radiant on every side. To his left in turn one should draw the mudrā of Jayoṣṇīṣa, ablaze all around. To his left in turn one should draw the mudrā of the wheel of Dharma, ablaze all around. To his left in turn one should draw the mudrās of the water flask, the counting rosary, and the auspicious seat. At the place of the gate, on both sides, one should draw three-pronged vajras, ablaze all around. Below the Blessed One Avalokiteśvara one should draw the great mudrā the Staff-Bearer and the mudrā of the utpala lotus, ablaze all around, without their touching one another.

The outer maṇḍala, surrounding the drawn form of the maṇḍala, should also blaze with the five colors, brilliant and lovely to behold, beautified by four corners, with four gateways in the four directions.

Outside the inner maṇḍala, at a distance of about two cubits, in the east, one should draw Mahābrahmā: four-faced, clad in a white garment, with a white upper garment and a white sacred thread, golden in color, wearing a crown of matted locks, holding a staff and a water flask in his left hand, with a vajra in his hand. To his right in turn one should make a son of the gods of the Ābhāsvara heaven, his body clad in silk, with an upper garment of silk, his face utterly peaceful, wearing a crown of matted locks, with a white sacred thread, seated cross-legged, his right hand granting the supreme boon. To his right in turn one should make a son of the gods of the Akaniṣṭha heaven, adorned with all ornaments, his body utterly peaceful, his mind dwelling in meditative concentration, clad in silk, with an upper garment of silk, seated cross-legged, granting the supreme boon with his right hand, with a white sacred thread. In sequence after him one should draw the sons of the gods of Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Yāma, Śakra, and the rest, in their proper order, with their proper attire and shapes. Below Śakra, the class of the Four Great Kings, the sons of the gods Sadāmatta, Mālādhara, Karoṭapāṇi, the Two-Lute ones, and the earth-dwelling gods, should be drawn in their proper order and with their proper attire.

Likewise, in the south, one should draw the sons of the gods Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, Parīttaśubha, Puṇyaprasava, and the rest, with their proper attire and shapes. Likewise in the western quarter, and likewise in the northern quarter too. In the western quarter, below them, they should be drawn in two rows. Beyond the two maṇḍalas there will be a third maṇḍala, and in its four directions one should draw the Four Great Kings in their order.

In the north, on the right side of the entrance, is Dhanada, dwelling near his treasure, adorned with all ornaments, his crown slightly bent, in the form of a yakṣa. To his right one should draw the yakṣa generals Maṇibhadra and Pūrṇabhadra. Likewise, in sequence, one should draw the great yakṣiṇī Hārītī, with the boy Priyaṅkara seated on her lap, gazing intently at the maṇḍala. One should also draw Pāñcika, reddish yellow and terrifying, and near them one should draw the mudrās of the yakṣas.

Likewise, in sequence, in the western quarter one should draw the god who holds a noose in his hand, and the eight great kings: the nāgas Nanda, Upananda, Takṣaka, the son of Vāsuki, and the rest. Likewise, in the second row, in their order, one should draw the yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, sages, siddhas, pretas, piśācas, garuḍas, humans, nonhumans, and the rest; and the medicines, the varieties of precious jewels, the mountains, the rivers, and the continents, in their order, all those renowned as chief and all the supreme chiefs.

In the south one should draw Yama together with his retinue of seven mātṛkās. In the east is Agni, ablaze with garlands of flame all around, holding a staff, a water flask, and a counting rosary in his hands, wearing a crown of matted locks, clad in a white garment, with an upper garment of silk and a white sacred thread, golden in color, marked with three dots of ash. Their various ornaments, weapons, attire, shapes, and colors should be drawn in the second row.

In the great maṇḍala entered from all sides is the Lord of Umā, riding a bull, holding a trident in his right hand; and the goddess Umā, adorned with all ornaments; and the son of the Kṛttikās, riding a peacock, holding a short spear in his hand, in the form of a youth, six-faced, his body appearing red, clad in a yellow garment with a yellow upper garment, holding a bell in his left hand and holding a red banner. In their order one should clearly draw Bhṛṅgiriṭi in a very emaciated form, the great Gaṇapati, Nandikeśvara, Mahākāla, and the seven mātṛkās, with their proper ornaments, attire, and shapes. There are the eight Vasus, the seven sages, and Viṣṇu, four-armed, holding in his hands a discus, a club, a spear, and a sword, with the garuḍa as his mount, adorned with all ornaments. One should also draw the eight planets, the twenty-seven lunar mansions, and the eight secondary planets that move through the sphere of the earth; and in their order the fifteen days of the bright and of the dark fortnights, the twelve houses of the zodiac, the six seasons, the twelve months, the junctures of the year, the Four Sisters riding in a boat, and their brother, the fifth, dwelling in the water. In brief, they should be set out as mudrās. The gods should be placed in two rows, in their order.

In brief, the third maṇḍala too should be clearly drawn on the basis of the three maṇḍalas, and in all three maṇḍalas the places should be set out in squares. These are the Blessed One's. To summarize, the Buddha, the Blessed One, the chief of all beings, must certainly be clearly drawn.

The noble Avalokiteśvara of the lotus family must be drawn on the right. The noble Vajrapāṇi of the vajra family must be drawn on the left. The noble Samantabhadra, chief of the bodhisattvas, must also be drawn. Mañjuśrī in youthful form must be drawn. The rest must be drawn as mudrās, as they have been set out. These make up the inner maṇḍala.

In the middle maṇḍala, in the eastern quarter, Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, must be clearly drawn. Likewise, in the southern quarter, the Ābhāsvara gods. Akaniṣṭha and the formless ones are in the form of a maṇḍala of gods. The gods of the sphere of neither perception nor nonperception, who are not manifest, are not drawn. In the northern quarter, the sons of the gods, Śakra king of the gods, Suyāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Parīttābha, and the rest, each one a king of the gods, must be clearly drawn. The rest are to be clearly drawn as mudrās, as they have been set out.

Likewise, in the third maṇḍala, in the northern quarter, Īśāna, lord of the bhūtas, together with Umā, must be clearly drawn. Near the second gate is the youthful son of the Kṛttikās on a peacock seat, holding a short spear in his hand, his body appearing red, wearing an upper garment of yellow cloth, holding a bell and a red banner in his right hand, in the form of a youth, gazing intently at the maṇḍala. In the eastern quarter, the garuḍa in the form of a bird and the sage Mārkaṇḍa must be clearly drawn; the rest, too, as mudrās as they have been set out. In the southeast, the four maidens, together with their youthful brother, abiding in a boat as their vehicle and journeying across the great ocean, and the king of the fire gods, must also be clearly drawn. Likewise, in the southern quarter, one must clearly draw the utterly terrifying lord of the rākṣasas of the city of Laṅkā, dwelling there in a picumarda tree, and the bodhisattva in the form of a yakṣa called Jambhala Jalendra. The rest too are to be set out as mudrās. Likewise, in the southwestern quarter, the nāga chiefs Nanda and Upananda must be drawn, and also the sun, chief of the planets. In the western quarter, the supreme sage called the Muni Kapila and the bull among the naked tīrthikas, in naked form, are to be set out in order as mudrās. In the northwestern quarter, Dhanada, king of the yakṣas, Pañcaśikha, king of the gandharvas, and Druma, king of the kinnaras, these must be drawn. The rest too are to be clearly drawn as mudrās, in order, according to the shapes in which they abide.

"One should clearly draw four maṇḍalas" means this: the fourth, outer maṇḍala is decorated with five lines, beautified with a garland of mudrās, square, in the form of four gateways, adorned with the Four Great Kings, each abiding in its proper order, as follows. At the gate of entry, as its mudrā, one should draw a blue utpala lotus. To the right and left, a lotus, a vajra, an axe, a conch, a trident, a club, a discus, a svastika, a vase, a fish, a conch, a bracelet, a water flask, a victory banner, a flag, a noose, a bell, a knife, a hammer, a bow, and an iron arrow: with these mudrās of the finest weapons of many kinds one should fill the surrounding enclosure on its four corners as a garland.

Then, in the four outer directions, four great mudrās should be placed. In the north, having made a maṇḍala in square form, a vajra with three prongs at both ends, ablaze all around. In the east, one should place a maṇḍala in triangular form, ablaze all around. In the south, having made a maṇḍala in the form of a bow, one should place a begging bowl, ablaze all around. In the west, having made a maṇḍala in the form of the sun, a blue utpala with its own stalk and leaves, ablaze all around. In the intermediate directions there will be four mudrās. In the northwest, having made a maṇḍala in round form, a noose, ablaze all around. In the southwest, having made a maṇḍala in long form, a staff, ablaze all around. In the southeast, having made a maṇḍala in triangular form, an axe, ablaze all around. In the northeast, one should place a sword, ablaze all around.

Having clearly drawn everything, above, below, and level across, three mudrās are to be drawn with the powder itself near the gate of the outer maṇḍala, namely: a garment, a fan, and sandals, ablaze all around. These one should clearly draw." Thus it was said.

By the wise bodhisattva
Who desires the benefit of beings,
These rites of the maṇḍala
Have been taught here in brief.

Then the master of the maṇḍala should first of all accept disciples. They are brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas and śūdras whose faculties are not deficient and all of whose limbs are beautiful; who have generated the mind set on awakening and are followers of the Great Vehicle; great beings whose disposition is not to want any other vehicle; who are faithful and of virtuous character; who strongly desire great kingship, who disdain small wealth, and who strongly desire great wealth. They are monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen who are excellent, disciplined and endowed with moral discipline, who abide in their vows, who observe the restoration ceremony and abide in their vows, and who bear no hatred toward the great bodhisattvas. They are of great standing and of good family, by nature practicing the Dharma, keeping a fast day and night, wearing clean clothes, with fragrant hair, having bathed three times, and keeping silent. On that day they are perfumed with fragrant camphor, saffron and Malaya sandalwood, and have always performed the ritual rinsing. Seated on mats of kuśa grass, having had the rite of protection performed, chaste, truthful, and with their minds set on the Victor, they should be placed in that very outer maṇḍala, neither too near nor too far.

They should be pure and should have performed the purifications, in number from one up to eight, and no more. They should also all be devoted to one another. Great kings of the kṣatriya caste who have been anointed on the crown of the head, and their sons and young daughters who do not know the ways of the village, may be accepted, because the Blessed One, the great bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, who has the form of a youth, awakens childlike people and delights the young. Therefore, first of all, such ones who do not know the ways of the village should be made to enter. This is for the increase of the great king, for the increase of life and health, of power and great wealth, and above all because, through moral discipline, the accomplishment of the vidyā becomes firmly established.

Having first placed them in this way, the master, accompanied by a good companion, should burn camphor incense and go outside without turning his back. Having gone out, he should bathe, as is convenient, in water that is thoroughly clean and free of living creatures, over which the root vidyā has been recited eight hundred times and which has been sealed with the great mudrā. Having performed the ritual rinsing, clean and wearing clean clothes, he should go to the fire hearth, sit on a mat of kuśa grass facing the northeast, and perform a fire offering of eight thousand oblations of ghee mixed with camphor, saffron and sandalwood. By the rite stated before, he invites the deities and requests them to depart. Then he should enter the maṇḍala again.

Having entered, he should offer eight full vases, furnished with clean cloth, adorned with leafy branches and fruits of the sahakāra mango tree, with gold, silver, jewels and grain placed inside. These should be offered one each: the first to the Blessed One Śākyamuni; the second to all the buddhas; the third to the whole Saṅgha of noble śrāvakas; the fourth to all the bodhisattvas; the fifth to the great bodhisattva, noble Avalokiteśvara; and the sixth to all the gods. The seventh and the eighth should be placed in the gatehouse of the second maṇḍala, and one of them should be placed after dedicating it as shared in common with all sentient beings.

Then, by the very rite stated before, he should burn incense, bind the utpala mudrā, and again invite the deities: all the buddhas, all the pratyekabuddhas, the noble śrāvakas, the great bodhisattvas, and all the bhūtas; and Avalokiteśvara too should be invited by the very rite stated before. Likewise flowers, incense, scents, lamps and food offerings should be presented, by the procedure already shown, with all the food offerings, to all of them, in proper sequence. Since lamps are mentioned, lamps of ghee should be offered. Since food offerings are mentioned for all, noble and not noble: boiled śāli rice with curd and honey, oil cakes fried in ghee and prepared with a special milk porridge, aśoka coils, sugar candy and the like should all be offered to the tathāgatas. Filled pastries, sandalwood infusion, honey and milk, and dishes cooked with milk porridge are for all the pratyekabuddhas, the noble śrāvakas, the great bodhisattvas and the noble gods, and fragrant flowers too should be offered to them. Laḍḍu sweets, special garbhatkvā cakes and the provisions mentioned before should be offered to all the gods, the hosts of bhūtas and all sentient beings.

Likewise jasmine, tagara flowers, punnāga and the rest, as specifically taught before, should be offered to the buddhas, the pratyekabuddhas, the noble śrāvakas, the great bodhisattvas, and all the gods, noble and not noble. In particular, jasmine flowers are for the Tathāgata family, lotuses for the Lotus family, and likewise blue lotuses for the family of Vajrapāṇi; for the others, it is done with ordinary mantras. Camphor incense is for the Tathāgata family; sandalwood for the Lotus family; and likewise guggulu should be known to belong to the Lord of Secrets, the Vajra Holder himself. To all other mantra deities ordinary incense should be offered.

To all the noble ones
Lamps of ghee should be offered.
To the mantra deities who are not noble
Let fragrant sesame oil be offered.
In keeping with the sequence of the rite,
Incense is given by reason of what has been seen.
The scents stated in just that way
Are always for all the mantra deities.
Whatever is stated for the Tathāgata,
And whatever is stated for Vajrapāṇi
In their own respective tantras,
The practitioner, for the sake of mantra practice,
Should regard here as the rite.
It is to be followed throughout.

Thus it was said.

Then the master of the maṇḍala, following the rite as seen before, performs the subsequent acts of inviting the deities, worshipping them, offering incense and the rest, and presenting the food offerings. After that, together with a supreme companion in practice who is skilled and quick, he should loudly sound the tones of drums, paṭaha drums and conches, and, adorned with incense, flowers, lamps and garlands, circumambulate the outer maṇḍala in the four directions, the intermediate directions, above, below and all around, and then cast an abundant torma for all the bhūtas, all of it without meat.

Then, having bathed, he should again perform eight thousand fire offerings of śāli rice mixed with curd, honey and ghee, and of thick porridge, with the root vidyā or the heart mantra.

Having performed the fire offering, the master of the maṇḍala, who has carried out the rites of protection for the great beings who are to enter the maṇḍala arranged before, shows the maṇḍala to those he has accepted as disciples: those who have generated the mind set on awakening, who have kept the restoration ceremony, who have offered their own bodies to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas for the sake of accomplishment, who have become a shared resource for the enjoyment of all sentient beings, who will take their place at the unsurpassed seat of awakening, and who through their virtues wish to attain buddhahood, the wisdom of omniscience. By the very showing of the maṇḍala they are freed from all evil; even people who commit the deeds of immediate retribution are freed in that instant.

Then the master of the maṇḍala should cover the faces of those who wish to enter the maṇḍala with a cloth of silk freshly woven by a weaver, free of hairs, consecrated seven times with the root vidyā, and perfumed with fragrant sandalwood and saffron; and the practitioner should first lead them in before the Blessed Lady. A prince who has been anointed on the crown of the head, or a son of the kṣatriya caste, or others of great zeal who desire great kingship, should also be led in. While they stand in the second maṇḍala with their faces covered, they should be given fragrant flowers mixed with sandalwood and saffron and made to cast the flowers with thoroughly cleansed hands. Wherever a person's flower falls, the vidyā mantra of that deity should be given to him. It is universally known that in other lives that deity and this person were bound together. That very deity is his spiritual friend, and accomplishes for him his taking his place at the seat of awakening and his perfecting of great awakening, the wisdom of omniscience. That very deity is the one he is to accomplish, and accomplishes for him great wealth, great kingship, persons renowned for great power, and this companionship. In this very life, by applying himself intensely to whatever practice he takes up, all his rites will succeed. In this way, one after another, such persons may be led in, up to eight, and no others. Thus it is said. Others who wish to practice may also enter as they wish, for the sake of exhausting their evil deeds, but for them it amounts only to the pledge. Thus it is said.

If the master of the maṇḍala is to confer consecration, first of all, outside the maṇḍala, neither too far nor too near, in the northeastern quarter, he should bless a piece of ground with the root mantra and purify it with mantras. Then, regarding it just like the consecration of a king, he should consecrate such persons as these, up to five: those with wholehearted, clear faith in the Buddha, the Dharma and the Saṅgha; of great zeal; never apart from the awakening mind; who have entered the Great Vehicle; who serve the Three Jewels; whose faculties are complete and who are not of despised standing; who wish to accomplish vidyās and mantras in this very life; of good intention; whose minds delight in the conduct of mantra; who by nature seek auspicious signs; and who, as a cause of awakening, have no doubt about the meaning of the vidyā and keep their minds fixed upon it. The rest should be set aside. Thus it is said. This is by the distinction of being wise and unconfused in conduct; others are not to be admitted.

Then, just as at the consecration of any king, all the requisites should be gathered, and the master and the preceptor should be pleased. Then a canopy is stretched out, banners and flags and a white parasol are held over the head, white yak-tail whisks are waved, and with great honor the joyful sounds of conches, great drums and clay drums are loudly sounded, with cries of victory. While he is praised with verses of auspiciousness and extolled with the verses of well-being spoken by the Victor, the circumambulation is made. Having performed that auspicious rite and bowed to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, he should speak these words: "Master, in order to follow rightly in the accomplishment of the mantra conduct of all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, to enter rightly into the maṇḍala of liberation, the great secret beyond all that is worldly, and because I wish to realize buddhahood through the whole kingdom of the Dharma, in short, so that buddhahood may come about, I shall apply myself with zeal." Thus it is said.

Then, while he sits on a mat of kuśa grass facing the east, seeing and understanding the maṇḍala, the master should first confer on him the consecration of the vidyā and recite the great mudrā and the root vidyā. Then whatever vidyās and mantras there are should be written with gorocana on a leaf of birch bark. Having written them, one should wash one's hands and a pair of bowls joined mouth to mouth with sandalwood and saffron, then place the birch bark inside the joined bowls and set it within the maṇḍala at the feet of the bodhisattva, the great being Avalokiteśvara. Then, sitting there, one should first recite the root vidyā mantra one hundred and eight times. Then the one seated there on the mat of kuśa grass should be consecrated.

In the outer maṇḍala, the master should take up the full vase that was earlier placed near the gate, the one shared in common with all, and, reciting the root vidyā, consecrate the disciple on the crown of the head. He should consecrate the disciple on the crown of the head with the water, as the disciple wishes. Thus it is said. Then the pair of joined bowls should be given to him as his own. He should be made to read the writing by the light of a lamp. If what he has thereby received is a vidyā or mantra of the Blessed One, it performs its rites through the reading alone. Otherwise it becomes effective when it is accomplished step by step and with effort. Others become accomplished through mantra recitation alone. After that the mantra will be fully grasped. At first it is accomplished through practice alone. This is said for one who is free of doubt. That very mantra written earlier will certainly be accomplished through the master's three accomplishments, without effort.

In this same way the consecration of the vidyā should be given first. As for the consecration in the second maṇḍala: if in the second maṇḍala one consecrates the disciple on the crown of the head with the full vase that was presented to all the maṇḍalas and all the deities, by exactly the rite given before, he is freed from all evil and receives the permission of all the buddhas. He will also have a special longing to accomplish the pledges, maṇḍalas, mantras and mudrās of all that is worldly and beyond the world. All the bodhisattvas confer on him the consecration of a master.

In the third maṇḍala, with that same rite, one should consecrate him on the crown of the head with the full vase offered to all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. One should say: "All the buddhas and bodhisattvas, endowed with great miraculous power, grant you permission to teach the vidyā mantras of all that is worldly and beyond the world, to draw maṇḍalas, to explain them, to teach the tantras, the mudrās of the tantras and their conduct with certainty, and to teach their own rites with certainty." In this very life, or in other lives that follow, he will certainly attain buddhahood.

Likewise, for the consecration of victory and complete victory, with the rite taught before, one consecrates him in exactly the same way with the full vase offered earlier to the Blessed One and the full vase offered to the bodhisattvas. Likewise one should say: "The buddhas, the blessed ones, the great bodhisattvas and the śrāvakas grant you permission: be unassailable by all bhūtas, invincible by all embodied beings, and completely victorious. Accomplish all the mantras just as you wish!"

Then the master of the maṇḍala should give consecration to each of the five beings, according to each one's wish. Then, having led them into the maṇḍala one after another, he should present them to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, circumambulate the maṇḍala three times, and request the deities to depart. Then, on another day, they should gradually be trained in the conduct of vidyā and secret mantra and set to its practice.

At that same moment one should go and take up the full vase of water offered earlier as a support, the one offered earlier to the great bodhisattva, and have those who have entered the maṇḍala face the east and drink three handfuls of the water. One should say this: "O great bodhisattvas, whoever transgresses the secret pledge will generate much demerit."

In whatever maṇḍala it may be, those of low caste who have come into the maṇḍala there should also be helped: the master of the maṇḍala, having roused the mind of great compassion, has them, at the hands of an assistant, with a clean white cloth bound over the head by another, or standing wholly covered with cloth, bind the mudrā of the pledge, and the low-caste persons should then cast the flowers. Then, through those assistants as well, all the beings who have entered should bathe. For them too, only the pledge comes about. And their practice will also be accomplished.

Then one goes to the place where the fire rite was performed before, with kuśa grass whose tips are unbroken. There, too, three kinds of fire hearth are taught: for pacifying, for increasing, and for fierce rites. For pacifying, it is lotus-shaped. Or, by gratifying, it serves also for subjugating. For fierce rites it is triangular. In every procedure of the fire rite kuśa grass is spread out. Having bowed to all the buddhas, one should set the fire rite at the eastern tip. Having bowed to the bodhisattvas, the great beings, who later perform the fire rite, at the southern tip. Having bowed to all the bodhisattvas, one should give it at the northern tip. Likewise the tasks are performed by assistants of steady character: the fire rite with the kuśa grass. First, it is done with the root vidyā. First one should offer twenty-one oblations of parched rice mixed with curd, honey and ghee. For pacifying, it is with pure ghee. For increasing, it is a fire offering of three apāmārga sticks. For fierce rites, it is with kaṭake. This procedure of the fire rite is also common to all practices everywhere, and to the ancillary practices of all the maṇḍalas.

Then the master of the maṇḍala, having shown the principal god of the Pure Abodes and performed the fire rite, should say these words to those who have entered all the maṇḍalas. Then, with recitation of the root vidyā, the guest water is offered.

"May the buddhas, the blessed ones, the bodhisattvas, and also the eminent gods of great miraculous power, and the śrāvakas of the Blessed One, please listen! Whoever in this maṇḍala of the pledge has acted with reverence, even if going beyond the rite, and whoever else has in some way let himself fall short, may they, through this root of virtue, attain the consecration of all the maṇḍalas, and never be parted from the domain of all the tathāgatas and the domain of all the bodhisattvas! May they swiftly attain happiness!" These words should be spoken.

To all the beings who have entered the maṇḍala one should say: "In short, you must never be parted from the awakening mind. Be devoted to giving, abide in loving-kindness and the rest, worship all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, and, in short, study the scriptures, the vidyās and the secret mantras spoken by the buddhas and bodhisattvas. You must never be parted from the awakening mind."

Then the master of the maṇḍala, having offered guest water with fragrant flowers to all of them, the bodhisattvas and the rest, or else having offered the guest water mentally, recites the root vidyā with gaccha gaccha, or simply recites svāhā, looks out in the four directions, binds the root mudrā of the Blessed Lady, and, gazing steadily upward, should request the deities to depart. Thus it is said.

This completes the second chapter, the extensive chapter on the rite of the maṇḍala, from the Root Rite of the Blessed Lady, Noble Tārā Ūrdhvajaṭā, of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.

Then that great being, again surveying the maṇḍala of the assembly complete in every respect, spoke to all the sons of the gods: "Listen! What is the Tārā that is the supreme accomplishment, the supremely secret, the rite of all sādhanas, that performs all the rites of vidyā and performs the excellent rites of vidyā, that is greatness itself and brings about great aims, that averts all calamities and accomplishes all aims, the supremely auspicious, auspicious in every way, spoken by all the buddhas, that has truly become my own supremely secret essence, to be applied in all minor rites, and that brings accomplishment in all the great rites of the great queen of vidyās? It is this: namo ratnatrayāya nama āryābalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā tāre tuttāre ture svāhā.

"Friends, this is Noble Tārā, who performs all great rites and who is accomplished by recitation in all minor rites. This vidyā, supremely secret, utterly secret, supremely accomplished, which destroys all rites applied by others, also serves as the rite and sādhana of the second maṇḍala. Through Noble Tārā it is to be applied to all great rites in summary and to all minor rites, and also to the rites and sādhanas of all the maṇḍalas.

"Whether by day or by night, it should be drawn in a clean place. The master of the maṇḍala, himself free of faults and alone, should first make a maṇḍala that is square and even, with four gates, measuring four cubits. In the center is the mudrā of a lotus. To its right are a blue utpala, the mudrā of a staff, and the mudrā of a water pot. To the left are the mudrā of a three-pronged vajra, the mudrā of Pāṇḍaravāsinī, and the mudrās of Hayagrīva and Mahāśrī. At the eastern gate is a lotus; in the north an utpala; in the south a vajra; in the west, apart from the order of entry; and above, the mudrā of a noose in coiled form. After that, having performed the fire rite outside and done the worship and the rest by the rite stated before, one should enter the maṇḍala.

"For this, one who desires kingship does it at a haḍpya tree. One who desires wealth does it at the shrine of the god of his own house. One who desires horses does it in a horse stable. One who desires elephants does it in an elephant stable. One who desires a son does it at the foot of a bodeci tree. For one seized by a brahmarākṣasa, it is done at a place protected by Brahmā. For one seized by a nāga, near a nāga tree. For one seized by a ḍākinī, at a crossroads. For one seized by a yakṣa, at the foot of a banyan tree. For one seized by a pūtana, near a well. Other places too may be used as one wishes; wherever it is done, there is no fault.

"Friends, in short, this vidyā serves for the maṇḍala and for all rites; it is to be applied to all rites. It should be applied together with this great secret. This maṇḍala bears the fruit of the wish to benefit beings. The vidyā of the Tārā maṇḍala increases all wealth; for the benefit of practitioners it increases all prosperity. In short, it is renowned as having become the master of all embodied beings who will come in the future.

"Then this great maṇḍala, once obtained, destroys misfortune and brings peace, and carries off disease and enemies. Whoever sees and hears of such a maṇḍala, which brings about the splendor and strength of all beings, and then gives rise to clear faith in the rite, I prophesy, without doubt, to the awakening of all the buddhas. They will become buddhas of the future, and those guides of the world will also rejoice.

"The maṇḍala on the ground, it is said,
Performs all the rites of pacifying.
Through it the destitute gain benefit.
Beings without protector and in suffering
Should make use of the maṇḍala.
With powder of sapphire and the like
One should draw the maṇḍala in full.
If there is no sapphire or the like,
One should draw it with powder of śāli rice.
If there is no rice powder or the like,
One should draw it with powdered brick and the like.
If there is no powdered brick or the like,
One should draw it with sand.
Thus the wondrous maṇḍala of Tārā,
Which gathers all good qualities,
Is the true word of the Protector of the World,
Spoken by the bodhisattva." Thus it was said.

This completes the third chapter, the extensive chapter on the rite of the sādhana and the rite of the maṇḍala, from the Root Rite of the Blessed Lady, Noble Tārā Ūrdhvajaṭā, a Great Vehicle sūtra belonging to the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.

Then the great being, again surveying that great maṇḍala and contemplating the noble true nature that is without entity, taught the rite of the painted cloth, the supreme rite of accomplishment of the Blessed Lady, the great sovereign of vidyās, which all the tathāgatas have taught and in which they rejoice.

First of all, on an auspicious day, one should take cotton bought at the hero's price and have it prepared into cotton by the hands of a brahmin girl. Then that cotton should be blessed: taking the thread bought at the hero's price, with the root vidyā, one should say these words: "May all the buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas bless it! May the Blessed Ones and the great bodhisattvas grant that all goes well, that my life bears fruit, and bless the accomplishment of the mantra!"

At that time one may hear the sounds of paṭaha drums, great drums, conches, vīṇās, flutes, staff drums and muraja drums; or kṣatriya men, kṣatriya women, women, boys, girls or other people may suddenly utter words such as "Victory!", "Accomplished!", "Bestowing accomplishment!", "Given!", "Take it!", "Glory!", "With fruit!", "The wheel of action!", "Many!", or other such words of good omen; or the sound of bells may arise, or sounds of joy. The vidyādhara should know these to be the blessing of the buddhas, the blessed ones, and the bodhisattvas. For it is said that otherwise accomplishment has no fruit.

If at that time those people give out harsh sounds, uttering such things as "Take it!", "Eat it!", "Seize it!", "Ruined!", "Destroy it!", "Alas!", "Not for long!"; or if men, buffaloes, jackals, donkeys, cats, or lowly animals, two-footed or four-footed, give out their cries, then the practitioner should know that there will be no supreme accomplishment for him, and in this very life he should discipline himself thoroughly. Having done everything again as before, he should begin anew. In this way, through seven attempts, even one who has committed the five deeds of immediate retribution will succeed through applying the rite the seventh time. Thus it is said.

Then the practitioner, having performed protection for that girl, should have her sit on a mat of kuśa grass, placed facing the east or facing the north. He himself should eat a feast of caru, and should also have the girl eat a feast of caru. On the mat of kuśa grass examined before, by that same rite, he should have her spin the cotton. The thread, soft and well twisted, should be properly taken up by the girl blessed before, and the girl should make it in counts from one, five, eight and so on up to about sixteen, duly reckoned by weight in kārṣas.

Of these, the best is to make sixteen;
Likewise the middling is eight;
For accomplishing the minor rites,
Five and one are the least.
For all the mantras, the knower of mantras
Should do as he is able.
From that time onward, whatever
Evil deeds were done before
Are destroyed in that very instant
By the mind fixed upon the thread.
Having taken up this thread,
One should put it in a clean vessel.
Having set it in its proper place,
One should fumigate it with camphor incense.
With scents that do not come from the bodies of living creatures,
Or with saffron, sandalwood and the like,
Or with campaka, mālikā and the like,
It should be perfumed with fragrant flowers.
Having placed it in a clean place
And performed the rite of protection,
The knower of mantras, who understands all rites,
Should recite in deep meditative composure.

Then one should go to a weaver
And give him whatever wage he wants.
He should not lack any limb, nor be emaciated;
He should always delight in the white Dharma;
He should not be tormented by illness, nor be old;
He should be free of phlegm and of troubled breathing;
He should be neither a eunuch nor of both sexes,
And he should not be of low standing;
Having given up evil transgressions,
He should be fully endowed with good marks,
Highly praised and pleasant to look upon,
Virtuous in all his conduct through understanding,
And versed in the ways of the world.
For one who desires accomplishment,
To weave the supreme cloth
Is one praised, endowed with the strength of virtue,
Or an intelligent craftsman, highly skilled.
By the supreme weaver of cloth,
Who excels in great skill,
The best cloth is made.
A middling one produces the middling;
The lowest serves for the minor rites,
Being inferior in every respect.
Whatever the craftsman asks,
Give him the price accordingly.
At the very first word
The craftsman speaks, the knower of mantras
Should quickly give the price.
This is called the hero's purchase.
Haggling over it, and over its price,
Reverses the effect.
The cloth of one who swiftly gains accomplishment
Is unsurpassed and supreme,
Most worthy of veneration in the rites,
The very happiness of gods and humans,
And the glory of all bhūtas:
So taught the perfectly awakened Buddha.

Then the vidyādhara, having given the restoration vows to the weaver, chooses a very pure lunar mansion, or the fortnight of miracles, or a bright day, having carefully observed a bright planet; or it may be in another bright fortnight. In springtime, when the sahakāra mango has put forth its shoots and blossoms, and the flowers and branches of the trees are flourishing, at that best of seasons, in the morning at sunrise, together with the favorable conditions taught before, the weaver should eat a meal of caru, put on white clothes, and bind a crest upon his head. He should be well washed, well anointed with white sandalwood or saffron, whichever is available, with his body anointed, his mouth perfumed with the scent of camphor, glad of mind, and freed from hunger and thirst.

Then all the parts of the loom, the shuttle and the rest, should be washed with earth and cow dung, and even new ones should again be washed with the five products of the cow. Then they should be washed with water free of living creatures, and sprinkled with white sandalwood and saffron. In a clean place, free of noise, free of local people, a secluded spot with a canopy, in secret, one makes offerings of flowers, incense and the rest.

Then, afterward, the practitioner should empower white mustard seed one hundred and eight times with that same mantra of thorough purification, and scatter it in the four directions, above and below, and in the intermediate directions. Then, having struck the weaver with white mustard seed, one binds the fivefold crest with the great mudrā; when the binding of the topknot has been done, great protection will have been made. If the cloth is to be of the best kind, the weaver should weave it to this measure: four cubits in width and eight cubits in length. If it is to be middling, it is two cubits in width and five cubits in length. The least is of the measure of one span of the Sugata in width, and in length one cubit of the Buddha. Of these, one span of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is one cubit of a man of the Middle Country who is of proper proportions. This is proclaimed to be the span of the Sugata, and by this measure all measures are explained.

This is for the accomplishment of the ritual dagger,
As the Supreme Person has taught.
After the Sage has passed from sight,
The middling is for one who desires kingship.
For persons who seek great wealth,
And over gods, asuras and hooded nāgas,
The least is taught to bring success.
With the middling, the accomplishment is middling.
The middling cloth at all times
Accomplishes the rites for all sentient beings.
For accomplishing minor rites,
The least cloth at all times
Accomplishes all the rites.
With all substances, at all times,
It accomplishes all the rites.
People who seek the glory of the accomplishments
Set forth definitively by the three kinds of cloth painting,
Even Śakra and the other lords of bliss,
Will not succeed if the rite is impaired.
But if the rite is properly complete,
Then even for ordinary human beings,
Through effort, all the rites
Will be accomplished very swiftly.
The Victors and the Victors' supreme heirs
Have rightly taught this practice.
For sentient beings, wretched and without protector,
Tormented by suffering, it is the glory of all;
This, which lies on the path to awakening,
Has been taught by those who see reality.
That this Dharma is the cause of awakening
Is taught by way of the path of mantra.
Through the maṇḍala that has been rightly taught,
All the worldly maṇḍalas
And the transcendent ones too will be accomplished,
And the mantras accomplished without effort.
Whoever wishes it as a cause of awakening
Will always gain accomplishment.
For others, who never benefit beings,
It is said there is no accomplishment.
For all who engage for the sake of awakening,
All the cloth paintings are said to succeed.
This pledge of the Lord Avalokiteśvara
In particular, so that the aims to be achieved are swiftly accomplished,
Has been taught here by the Blessed One
So that everything may be attained.

Then, in due order, the artisan
Should weave the cloth with effort.
In five days and nights, or in eight,
In sixteen, in two or in four,
Swiftly, working day and night,
When the weaving of the cloth is complete,
The artisan who has supremely succeeded
Is virtuous by day and by night.
Perfect in the conduct of cleanliness,
The artisan, always blessed,
Should go to a distant place
And there void excrement and urine.
Taking off the clothes he came in,
He should put on other, fresh clothes;
Wearing white garments and wearing a garland,
He should rinse himself again and again.
Anointing his body with white sandalwood,
He should make the tools and the rest clean.
Always gentle and well purified,
He should once again weave with effort.
By such practices as these,
Taught by the other Victors,
Or with effort, through careful examination and proper method,
The cloth should be woven in its entirety.
When the weaving of the cloth is complete,
Well produced by the procedure given before,
It should be made of proper measure and even.
On an auspicious day,
The threads should be set evenly, line by line.
In the beauty of the bright fortnight,
On a bamboo staff four cubits long
The cloth is taken up, and then one goes.
Having made the artisan content
By bestowing wealth lavishly,
The mantra practitioner of good vows and good conduct
Goes wherever he wishes,
Worships it with fragrant flowers,
And sets it down in a clean place.
With this very mantra
One performs the rite of protection.
With the mantra by which the cotton was earlier
Purified again, thoroughly, in many ways,
With that same mantra one should protect
Oneself and the cloth itself.
The bodhisattva, the great hero,
Has taught it through mantra recitation;
It was taught by many buddhas,
And by me too it is taught again.
That very form of mantra
Practiced through all the secret mantras,
Of great diligence and great splendor,
Accomplishing all the aims of mantra,
Becomes the cause of protection of every kind
And acts in various ways.
The sentient beings who dwell in Jambudvīpa
Are wholly deluded in the conduct of their minds,
Without faith and perverse,
Greedy for wrong conduct,
And they do not accomplish mantras.
For that very reason it is taught again:
They wander in the dark prison of saṃsāra.
But whoever is always pure in mind,
Faithful, delighting in festivity and auspiciousness,
Always applying himself to all the mantras,
Great-souled and desiring accomplishment,
Always holding and keeping them,
Of great enthusiasm and great splendor,
For him, whatever mantras the Victor has taught
Are perfectly accomplished without effort.
In people who have no faith
White qualities do not arise,
Just as seed sown in salty ground
Yields no sprout and no fruit.
Faith is always the root of the Dharma,
So the One Who Sees All Things has said.
For those whose nature accords with the meaning of the Dharma,
Accomplishment through mantra is always declared.

Then the practitioner, with the artisan,
Who is a painter, or else himself,
Being skilled in painting,
Takes pigments that are unmixed and clear in color,
And colored paints,
And just as was done for the weaver,
By that same rite as before,
Complete with the proper characteristics,
It should be done in full for the painter, as above.

Just as before for the weaver,
By that same rite he
Should paint the picture on the cloth,
Or else one paints the picture oneself.
With camphor, saffron and sandalwood
The pigments in their clay dishes should be charged.
Burning incense, and with the mantra itself
Reciting one hundred and eight times,
Flowers of nāgakesara, punnāga,
Bakula and campaka,
Vāriṣika, dhānasku,
Mālatī and the rest
Should be scattered upon that cloth.
Facing toward the east,
Seated on a mat of kuśa grass, with a mind of faith
Toward all the buddhas and bodhisattvas,
Being resolute, he takes this fine brush
In hand, and with an undisturbed
Mind paints the picture on the cloth.

First of all, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni should be painted, endowed with the supreme of all aspects, marked with the thirty-two marks of a great person, his body beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, seated on a precious lotus, blazing with light on all sides, his body beautified by a fathom-wide aura on all sides, in the act of teaching the Dharma, his body utterly serene, endowed with the supreme of all aspects. The lotus in the center has a stem of beryl. Below, the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda should be painted, firmly holding the stem of that lotus, the great seat, gazing at the Tathāgata and paying homage with their right hands, white, adorned with all ornaments, the halves of their bodies in human form. All around that lotus pond, it should be painted in a beautiful manner, filled with lotus petals and flowers, some slightly open and some in full bloom, with water birds, fish and the like, laid out in full.
