From the lotus stem at the base of the Blessed One, and from those very leaves, many lotus flowers spread out, rising in gradual tiers. On the left side there are eight lotus flowers, and upon them, seated on the lotuses, the bodies of eight great bodhisattvas should be painted.

First of all, the noble Avalokiteśvara, colored like saffron slightly pale, like the filaments of a lotus, and golden, his head adorned with a diadem bearing Amitābha, holding a blue utpala lotus in his hand, and with his right hand paying homage to the Tathāgata. His body is beautiful, he gazes at the Tathāgata with a peaceful air, his face slightly smiling, and enveloped in blazing light on all sides he stands at the center of the circle. On another lotus, the noble Candraprabha, the youthful one, should be painted in the same way. On the third, Sudhana. On the fourth, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin. On the fifth, Gaganagañja. On the sixth, Kṣitigarbha. On the seventh, Mañjuśrī. On the eighth, Fair Eyes. All of these should be painted in the guise of youths, adorned with youthful ornaments.

On the right side of the Blessed One are eight great bodhisattvas, all adorned with every ornament except Maitreya. Close beside the Blessed One is the noble Maitreya in the guise of a celibate brahmin, his matted hair bound up as a crown on his head, wearing robes of golden and red saffron, with an upper garment of red silk, bearing the mark of the three tufts, beautiful in form, with a staff and a water flask placed in his left hand, the skin of a black antelope (kṛṣṇasāra) worn over his left shoulder, holding a rosary in his right hand and paying homage to the Tathāgata, his gaze fixed upon him, his mind engaged in focus on meditative concentration.

On the second lotus the noble Samantabhadra, dark blue like priyaṅgu, his body adorned with all ornaments, holding a precious wish-fulfilling jewel in his left hand and, with his right hand holding a bilva fruit, granting the supreme gift, beautiful in form, should likewise be painted.

On the third, the noble Avalokiteśvara, white like an autumn cloud, adorned with golden ornaments, wearing a crown of matted locks, with a white sacred thread, bearing the Omniscient One on his head: the noble Amitābha, possessed of the ten powers, seated within his matted locks. He is beautiful in form, holds a lotus in his left hand, grants the supreme gift with his right hand, his mind engaged in focus on meditative concentration, his body radiant on all sides.

On the fourth, the noble Vajrapāṇi, holding a vajra in his left hand and, holding in his right hand the plant called "near-cessation" together with its fruit, granting the supreme gift, golden in color, adorned with all ornaments, beautiful in form and of peaceful gaze, his body wound about with a half-necklace, with a sacred thread made of a pearl necklace, radiant with a blazing jeweled crown, wearing a lower garment of fine silk and an upper garment of white silk. The lower and upper garments of the noble Avalokiteśvara and of Samantabhadra are the same. The form of the body is as taught before.

On the fifth of the Tathāgata's lotuses is the noble Mahāmati; on the sixth, Śāntamati; on the seventh, Vairocanagarbha; on the eighth, the one called Apāyajaha. These bodhisattvas hold fruits and books in their hands, beautiful in every way, with upper garments of silk, adorned with all ornaments, their bodies in movement, wearing red saffron robes, seated with legs crossed upon slabs of jewel, of peaceful appearance, enveloped in garlands blazing on all sides. They should be painted while the cloth is being strewn all over with a carpet of fragrant flowers, namely mālatī, vārṣikā, dhanuṣkārikā, punnāga, nāgakesara and other flowers.

On the left side of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, above where the noble Mañjuśrī is, there is a circle of celestial palaces of very tall form, adorned with many jewels. A king of rocky mountains, beautiful, covered with slabs of jewel, should be painted in the form of a mountain.

Eight buddhas, blessed ones, dwelling there should be painted, as follows. The Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin should be painted: radiating the light of precious beryl, with a fathom-wide aura on all sides, blazing brilliantly on all sides with special great jewels such as ruby, sapphire, emerald and the like, beryl, diamond and the rest, colored somewhat like the rising sun, his Tathāgata body wearing a yellow Dharma robe as an upper garment, seated with legs crossed, in the act of teaching the Dharma, wearing a yellow lower garment, his body clad in the armor of the marks of a great person, his body beautified by the eighty excellent minor marks, with a gaze of perfect peace, endowed with the supreme of all aspects.

On the second, the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarājendra should be painted, golden in color. He should be painted strewn with flowers of the finest nāgakesara, bakula and the like. He gazes at the noble Mañjuśrī, full of light on all sides, the radiance of jewels streaming out to the farthest limit.

On the third, the Tathāgata Śālendrarāja should be painted, appearing the color of lotus filaments, in the act of teaching the Dharma. On the fourth, the Tathāgata Fair Eyes should be painted. On the fifth, Duṣprasaha. On the sixth, the Victor Vairocana. On the seventh, Bhaiṣajyaguru, King of Beryl Light. On the eighth, the Tathāgata, the Victor, Lord Who Utterly Pacifies All Suffering, should be painted. All are golden in color, in the form of tathāgata bodies, granting fearlessness.

Above the tathāgatas, at both corners of the painting, two sons of the gods of the Pure Abodes, dwelling in openings among the clouds, should be painted letting fall a rain of flowers. Dwelling in the sky, they should be painted paying homage to all the buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas and noble śrāvakas.

To the north of the pratyekabuddhas, above the bodhisattvas, leaving free the space at their heads, the eight great noble śrāvakas should be painted, namely the elder Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Subhūti, Rāhula, Nanda, Bhadrika and Kapphiṇa. The pratyekabuddhas are these: Fragrant One, Candana, Upāriṣṭa, White One, Sika, Indra, Nemi and Sunemi. All are supremely and exceedingly beautiful, peaceful in demeanor, peaceful in nature, utterly disciplined in aspect. The great śrāvakas, their palms joined, are gazing intently at the Buddha, the Blessed One Śākyamuni.

On the upper side too, gods of the Pure Abodes and two other sons of the attendant gods should be painted, holding a silk canopy, very long on every side and exceedingly beautiful, above all the buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas and noble śrāvakas; they are sons of the gods wearing divine garlands and garments.

Above the Blessed One Śākyamuni, over his head, there should be painted a silk canopy well arranged upon a network of jeweled strings, pearl necklaces and jeweled threads strung with ruby, sapphire and the like, beautiful with pearl necklaces hanging down all around it.

Below the lotus seat of the Buddha, the Blessed One, near the great bodhisattva, at the side of the nāga king Upananda, there is a mountain of jewels rising up out of the lotus pond: a mountain with jeweled shoots, caves and ravines, jeweled trees wound about with coral creepers, and inhabited and frequented by great sages. Upon it the wrathful king Tārā's Subjugator, of greatly fierce form, holding a noose in his left hand and a club in his right, with a wrathful, frowning face, gazing at the great bodhisattva and receiving his command, with a protruding belly and hair standing on end, black like collyrium and like a storm cloud, with tawny beard, long hair and long nails, red eyes, his neck adorned with snakes, wearing a tiger-skin lower garment, the destroyer of all obstructors, exceedingly terrible, the great king of wrathful ones, blazing on all sides: the wrathful kings Tārā's Subjugator should be painted in exactly this way. Below him are the various matted-haired ascetics.

Below that mountain, seated upon a rock, with body bowed and knees on the ground, holding a censer in the hand, with dress, shape, manner and conduct rendered just as they are, gazing at the noble Mañjuśrī, one should be painted correctly.

Below the Blessed One Śākyamuni, on the right side, the lordly nāga king Nanda should be painted, and beside him another king of lordly jeweled mountains rising up out of the lotus pond, just as described; the wrathful king Tārā's Subjugator should be painted likewise, with a carpet of divine flowers strewn about. That mountain is painted below Avalokiteśvara.

That mountain should be painted very high, in the form of slabs of ruby, with shoots of the same, and with peaks made of beryl. Resting upon it is the goddess who is the compassion of Avalokiteśvara, the noble Tārā, her body adorned with all ornaments, with an upper garment of red silk and a lower garment of multicolored silk, adorned with all the ornaments of a woman, holding a blue utpala lotus in her left hand, golden in color, not too stout and not too old, her mind abiding in meditative concentration, sitting as she receives the command, with her right hand wishing to grant the supreme gift, her body slightly bowed, seated with legs crossed, gazing slightly toward the noble Avalokiteśvara, surrounded by garlands blazing on all sides.

There too, on that very peak of precious beryl, it is surrounded by punnāga trees, every branch adorned all over with flowers, which, having opened, overspread the Blessed Lady Tārā. With those same bending branches, and with clusters of vividly bright coral shoots, of brightly varied form, in blazing colors, the face of the goddess Tārā should be painted, appearing clearly on all sides.

The goddess who destroys all obstructors,
Supreme in destroying fear,
Granting the supreme gift, virtuous,
Should be painted for the practitioner's protection.
The goddess who bears a woman's form,
Child of the compassion of the one with the ten powers,
Is the glory of all beings;
She who grants the supreme gift should be painted.
The goddess who performs great deeds,
The bodhisattva of great light,
Is desired by the practitioner always
For the destruction of all obstructors.
For the protection of lords of men
And for the sake of glory she is renowned.
The lordly wrathful king
Who wishes to dwell on the mountain's peak,
For the sake of destroying all obstructors,
Was taught by the supreme heirs of the Victor.
Greatly fierce, of great diligence,
Greatly violent, of great rays of light,
He should be conceived as being expressly
For subduing beings who hate the teaching.
For the practitioner's protection,
And for destroying all the obstructors,
He, of terrible and wrathful nature,
Summons the deities of the mantras.
Exceedingly fierce, of fierce form,
Without pity, he decisively restrains.
Those who commit violent evil deeds,
Who have not been brought under control, he brings under control.
Those who move in the sky and move on the earth,
And those who move everywhere beneath the earth,
All the malignant ones who oppose
The teaching of the Sage, he destroys.

The cloth should be painted square all round
And at its four corners.
Along the lower edges of the cloth
A broad river is to be made.
A nāga marked by a serpent hood,
One alone, is to be made throughout,
With white and handsome limbs,
Half his body formed in human shape,
Always joining his palms
And placing them upon his head.
That nāga of seven hoods, of great diligence,
Possessing great power,
Is called by the name Ananta.
He gazes intently at the Tathāgata.
Beautiful with precious jewels,
Exceedingly beautiful and of beautiful form,
Adorned with precious ornaments,
With blazing garlands, he should be painted all over.
Renowned as a great lord of nāgas,
Devoted to the teaching of the Sage,
Striving to benefit all the world,
For the destruction of all obstructors,
He should be painted resting in the river.

This rite of the cloth painting
Has been taught by the Victor in brief;
At length, the tathāgatas
Have explained it fully before.
Whatever wise one paints it,
His merit is endless.
Whatever most terrible evil deeds
Were done over ten million eons
Are destroyed in that very instant
By seeing the painting on the earth.
Those who commit the five deeds of immediate retribution,
Those of corrupt moral discipline and those who are reviled,
Those deeply engaged in every evil,
Beings who wander throughout saṃsāra,
Of low birth:
Those should not be allowed to hold the cloth painting.
Yet the Lord of Sages has said that by seeing
The cloth painting they gain a fruit.
Therefore, through merely seeing it,
In that instant evil is destroyed.
What need to mention the people who attain accomplishment:
Those who enter it with purity,
Those who enter into reciting it after,
And those diligent in listening to the mantra?
Whatever merit there is in offering
To all the buddhas for ten million eons,
The mantra practitioner who paints
The cloth painting on earth will obtain that merit.
Whatever fruit is gained
By one who, in the world, again and again, many times,
Offers feasts to buddhas
As many as are counted the sands of the Ganges,
And to the Victors' heirs, the rhinoceros-like solitary victors,
And to the śrāvakas,
That fruit belongs to the mantra practitioner who paints the cloth painting,
Who sees it and reads the rite,
Who rejoices in it,
And who thoroughly examines all the rites.
Through that accomplishment of his mantra,
As many worldly mantras as there are,
And all the mantras spoken
By the Victor, the supreme being,
By his disciples, the rhinoceros-like ones, and the gods,
And by the great-souled bodhisattvas,
Are accomplished in the presence of this cloth painting.

From the Great Vehicle sūtra collection of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, the Avataṃsaka, the first painting of the extensive root rite of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā of the Upswept Locks, is complete.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, looking upon the entire assembly, said to the bodhisattva, the great being Avalokiteśvara, "Great being, there is moreover an intermediate rite of the cloth painting for you. I shall explain it. Listen well and keep it well in mind. I shall explain.

"First of all, using the colors taught before, the very rite stated before, the artisan examined before, and the intermediate measure given before, with cloth that is exceedingly clean, soft, thoroughly purified, with its selvage, with unmixed colors, free of any mixture of hair and so forth, one should have the later cloth painting painted exactly as the first, except for the measure and the figures.

"First of all, the abode of the Pure Abodes, beautiful in every way, as if made of precious crystal, adorned with necklaces of white pearls. In its center one should have the Blessed One Śākyamuni painted, seated upon a precious lion throne, in the act of teaching the Dharma, endowed with the supreme of all aspects.

"On his right side, the noble Avalokiteśvara, appearing the color of lotus filaments, or of saffron, or of the sun, holding a lotus at his left shoulder, palms joined, gazing intently at the Blessed One Śākyamuni, his face slightly smiling, the great bodhisattva, with a crown bearing an auspicious emblem at its center, with a white sacred thread, his right knee on the ground and his head bowed.

"On the left side of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, Vajrapāṇi, dark blue like priyaṅgu, should be painted just as taught before, except that he is waving a yak-tail fan over the Blessed One."

"At his side the noble Maitreya, Samantabhadra, Vajrapāṇi, Mahāmati, Śāntamati, Gaganagañja and Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin should be painted in order; one should have them painted adorned with all ornaments, just as in the first.

"Above them one should have eight buddhas, blessed ones, painted, seated, the right hand granting fearlessness, their bodies wearing upper robes of yellow Dharma cloth, the left hand holding the edge of the Dharma robe, wearing lower garments of saffron cloth appearing slightly red, radiant on all sides, endowed with the supreme of all aspects. One should have these buddhas, blessed ones, painted, namely the Tathāgata Saṃkusumitarāja, Ratnaśikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa and Fair Eyes.

"On the right side of the Blessed One one should have the noble Avalokiteśvara painted, together with the great circle of his close retinue. One should have the eight great śrāvakas and the eight pratyekabuddhas painted just as taught before, except that the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana and Śāriputra should be painted in the form of attendants, waving yak-tail fans over the Blessed One Śākyamuni.

"In the same way the sons of the gods of the Pure Abodes should be painted. Śakra, lord of the gods, Suyāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Pure, Stainless, Sudarśana, Ābhāsvara, Brahmā lord of the Sahā world, and Akaniṣṭha: such sons of the gods who move in the form realm, and the sons of the gods who move in the desire realm, should be painted in order.

"One should lay out the circle of the retinue that attends on Avalokiteśvara, richly adorned, and have each painted bearing his own form and attire.

"Below the lion throne of the Blessed One one should have painted a mountain made entirely of jewels, rising from the great ocean, as far as the edge of the cloth. In one corner at the edge of the cloth one should have the practitioner painted, in the form of his actual attire and shape, with knee and head bowed, holding a censer in the hand.

"On that jeweled mountain, below the noble Avalokiteśvara, the wrathful king Tārā's Subjugator should be painted just as definitively taught before.

"Below the lion throne, on the left side of the Blessed One, near the feet of the noble Avalokiteśvara, the goddess Tārā should be painted, seated on a jeweled mountain; one should have her painted just as definitively taught before.

"All around that cloth loose flowers should be scattered: one should strew a carpet all round about with flowers of campaka, blue utpala, lotus, saugandhika, mālatī, varṣika, dhānuskārṣikā, punnāga, nāgakesara and the like.

"At the top of the cloth, in the two corners at the edge of the cloth, two sons of the gods should be painted scattering masses of flowers, of brightly varied form, hovering within rain clouds in the sky, white in color.

"This is declared the intermediate cloth painting.
It always brings about virtue and well-being,
And grants middling accomplishments
To the people on the face of the earth.
Whatever slight evil one did before
While wandering through saṃsāra,
By seeing the painting here
It is destroyed in that very instant.
Sentient beings, deluded and unknowing,
Wander in the five destinies.
Whoever sees the intermediate painting
Of the bodhisattva, even one
Who comes to commit evil,
Who commits the five deeds of immediate retribution,
And even one of corrupt discipline, will succeed.
Even the mantras that were taught in various kinds
Bring accomplishment exceedingly swiftly;
It is gained by doing the recitation.
The sick are freed from sickness,
The poor find wealth,
Women obtain sons.
When one looks at the intermediate painting,
At that time, by merely seeing it,
One gains a great increase of merit.
That person will surely come to share
In the happiness of gods and humans,
And in another birth of his
He will surely attain buddhahood.
Through painting it and reading it,
Worshiping the deity and having it painted,
And likewise through seeing and touching it,
One is freed from all evil.
Thus, from seeking after, supplicating,
And rejoicing in the painting of the one of great light,
One swiftly gains a birth together with its fruit.
Even through supreme eons as numerous as particles of dust,
The merit that a person gains
Cannot be expressed in words:
Seeing the painting comes with its fruit."

So it is said. From the extensive root rite of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā of the Upswept Locks, from the Great Vehicle Vaipulya sūtra collection of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, the Avataṃsaka, the third chapter is complete.

Then again the Blessed One Śākyamuni once more said to that great being, "Great being, there is also another, third rite of your cloth painting, called the small one, through which accomplishment is achieved without effort. With the very rite taught before, one should have the artisan paint a cloth painting just one span of the Sugata in measure across, and likewise square on all sides, as before, with the pigments taught before.

"First of all, one should have the great bodhisattva painted, seated with legs crossed on a lion seat, as a young boy, teaching the Dharma as before, radiating rays of light on all sides, beautiful in form."

On the left side one should paint the noble Samantabhadra, standing on a jeweled slab of stone, holding a yak-tail fan in his hand and holding a wish-fulfilling jewel in his left, his color a deep blue-green like the priyaṅgu flower. On the right side, too, one should paint the noble Avalokiteśvara, standing on a jeweled slab of stone, holding a yak-tail fan in his hand and bearing a lotus in his left hand, his body radiant with light on all sides; the noble Avalokiteśvara should be painted as before. Beneath the lion throne one should paint a golden mountain, reaching all the way to the edge of the cloth. At the corner of the edge of the painting, below the lion seat of the noble Avalokiteśvara, on the right side, one should paint the king of wrathful ones, Tārā's Subjugator, as before. Below him one should paint the practitioner holding a censer in his hand, as before. All of this is just as it was before.

Then above the noble Avalokiteśvara one should paint the Tathāgata Amitābha, seated in a cave of a jewel mountain, sixteen finger-widths in size, and one should paint a high overhang of the mountain resembling a many-storied house. All around the painting, in a ring of mountains, one should draw it encircled by the forms of mountains. At the upper corners of the painting, as if hovering and joined to the mountain's overhang, one should paint two sons of the gods of the Pure Abodes, called Pure and Thoroughly Pure, scattering various flowers. One should paint the cloth strewn with various flowers, as if spread with a carpet.

The defining marks of the three kinds of painting
Have all been taught here.
This one is called the small one;
This painting is auspicious for minor rites.
Evil deeds most terrible,
Done over thousands of koṭis of eons,
Are freed by seeing the painting;
By merely seeing the painting
One is freed in a single instant.
Though a wise one, for thousands of koṭis of eons,
Has served and honored the buddhas,
That is not equal even to a sixteenth part
Of seeing this last painting.
Whatever merit there is in making offerings
To all the buddhas, the protectors,
By seeing the small painting
The learned one gains that very merit.
For rites of charm and beauty,
And as a cause of wealth, it is also used.
All the vidyās and secret mantras there are,
Those spoken by Brahmā, Indra, and the sages,
And whatever the garuḍas have spoken,
And Varuṇa, the Sun, Kubera,
Dhanada and the rest, and the rākṣasas,
And all the lords of the asuras,
The great mahoragas and the Moon,
The Wind, Yama, and the rest,
And the mantras spoken by the Lion, the Seizer, and others,
All these mantras are drawn in here,
And are accomplished in the presence of the painting.
Rites of pacifying and likewise
Rites of increase are to be performed;
But likewise here the terrible ones,
Censured by the supreme Victor, are to be abandoned.

Thus concludes the fourth root rite of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā, the extensive chapters on the rite of the cloth painting, from the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, the Avataṃsaka, a sūtra of the Great Vehicle of vast scope.

Then once again the bodhisattva, the great being Avalokiteśvara, rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One Śākyamuni three times, bowed at the Blessed One's feet, and said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it is excellent, excellent, that the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, has spoken this Dharma discourse. For the sake of examining all the observances of vidyā, for benefit, for happiness, and out of compassion for the world, it teaches the skillful means of the bodhisattvas; together with the remaining teachings that lead to the city of nirvāṇa, it is constantly and supremely directed with certainty toward awakening. This great secret vidyā of mine accomplishes, for the bodhisattvas, the aims of all the conduct of vidyā and mantra, and it will make all people flourish.

"In a future time, when the guru of the world has passed into nirvāṇa, when the sun lineage of the Tathāgata has set, abandoned by all buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and noble śrāvakas, all of them forsaking it so that it has become dark, when the vessel of the world has fallen to ruin, bereft of the noble path, of vidyās, of mantras, of medicines, and of all precious jewels, there will arise a realm of beings without the light of being cared for by good people. Those who are lazy, whose mindfulness has lapsed, who are faithless, unruly, in the grip of nonvirtuous friends, given to deceit, guile, lies, and crooked conduct, will be terrified on hearing this Dharma discourse. Delighting in laziness and sloth, they will be without faith. They will seek sensual pleasures and will not seek secret mantras. Delighting in wrong views, they will engage in much that is not merit, and there will arise those who reject the true Dharma.

"For the sake of those who are bent upon Avīci, who go to the fiercest of the fierce, tormented by suffering; in order to bring under control those not under control, and to grant fearlessness to those who have been brought under control; for the knowledge of the practice of gathering beings through skill in means; and for the rite of the cloth painting: if the Blessed One deems that the time has come to speak of it now, may the Blessed One please speak."

When he had made this request, the Blessed One said: "The extensive rite of the observance of the supremely secret vidyā, supremely secret, fulfilling every wished-for aim, of great purpose and perfect abundance, the supreme essence of all seventy vidyās, will be accomplished at that time without conceptual thought. Moreover, it has been spoken by seventy-six koṭis of buddhas, who, through skill in means for the sake of training beings, protect those who wander in saṃsāra and cause them to be supremely directed with certainty toward awakening. Its vidyā is this: namo ratnatrayāya nama āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya tārendra tāre tuttāre ture svāhā. This is called Noble Tārā the Fully Flourishing.

"namo ratnatrayāya nama āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya tāre ture ture svāhā. This is called Noble Tārā Sumukhī, the Fair-Faced."

namo ratnatrayāya nama āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya tāre tuttāre ture svāhā. This is called Noble Tārā the Excellent Center.

namo ratnatrayāya nama āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya tadyathā tāre tuttare ture svāhā. This is called Noble Tārā of Good Conduct.

namo ratnatrayāya nama āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya tāre tuttāre ture svāhā. This is called Noble Tārā of Excellent Marks.

namo ratnatrayāya nama āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya tare ture ture svāhā. This is called Noble Tārā the Little Southern One.

namo ratnatrayāya nama āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya tāre tuttāre ture ture svāhā. This is called Noble Tārā the Well-Abiding.

namo ratnatāyāya nama āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya tāre tuttāre ture ture svāhā. This is called Noble Tārā the One Who Bows Close.

"Blessed One, this great vidyā of mine is equal to the great supreme essence. It supremely accomplishes every task. It has arisen for all sentient beings like a buddha. All the buddhas rejoice in it. It protects from the eight great fears. It performs every rite. It is a teacher of the path to awakening. It is the vidyā of the lotus family. It is properly applied for those of superior, middling, and lesser capacity. It grants the ripened fruit of most excellent deeds, and it will be accomplished even in the time when the teaching has declined. For the sake of guarding the way of the true Dharma, they will enter into equipoise and attain accomplishment. Through only a small practice, they will accomplish their aims of a great kingdom and of lordship over great wealth. Very swiftly, at that time and on that occasion, they will attain accomplishment.

"This rite of the cloth painting has been condensed because at that time, on that occasion, there will be great fear, and beings of the five degenerations, of little merit, will appear. Known to be of little power, short-lived, and weak in diligence, they will be unable to exert themselves in such tasks as accomplishing the rite of the cloth painting in its fully extensive form. It is for their sake that it is taught in this most condensed way.

"First of all, one should buy the material at a hero's price, about one srang in weight or about half a srang, and have a weaver weave a cloth, with its fringe, about one cubit long and about half a cubit wide. Or else, again, one should take a new piece of cloth free of hairs, very white, as long from top to bottom as one wishes, two, four, six, five, ten, or eight cubits, and have the artist paint it as one wishes. The pigments should be unmixed, scented with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron. As for the cloth, combine sandalwood, saffron, and camphor, mix them with clear water free of living creatures, put the cloth into a new vessel to soak, and leave it well pressed down for three days.

"Having made a protection in a clean place and having made oneself clean as well, on the full moon of the bright fortnight, in front of the vessel holding the cloth, facing east, one should sit on a mat of kuśa grass and recite these mantra words eight thousand times: tadyathā oṃ he he bhagabāna bahurūpadhara dibyacakṣuṣa avalokaya avalokaya māṃ samayamanusmara kumārarūpadharaṇa mahābodhisatva kiñcarayasi hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.

"Having recited this mantra, one should lie down to sleep right there. In a dream it will be shown whether there will be success or not. Then, on rising, if one has seen a dream with signs of success, one should paint the cloth painting without delay. If one has not seen a dream with signs of success, one should take the cloth out of that vessel and dry it in the sun. Once it is dry, one should again conceal it well in another new vessel, make a protection, and set it aside. Then again, taking any one mantra one wishes from among those supreme essences, of the six-syllable ones, one should again recite its syllables a hundred thousand times. Then the cloth painting will be accomplished very swiftly.

"First of all, taking that cloth, in the fortnight of miracles, or else on a day of the bright fortnight, under a virtuous lunar mansion in proper conjunction, on the day of a planet's turn falling on a virtuous date of the bright fortnight, at the hour of midnight on a night of most beautiful auspicious signs and perfect good fortune, the artist, keeping the poṣadha fast, should paint that cloth painting.

"In a clean place, burning camphor incense, first of all one should paint the noble Avalokiteśvara adorned with all bodily ornaments, his head crowned with a topknot, adorned with the marks of a great being, golden in color, wearing a lower garment of fluttering blue silk and an upper robe entirely of blue silk, seated on a lion throne in the half-crossed posture, teaching the Dharma, his right foot placed on a jeweled footstool, seated on the lion throne, endowed with the supreme of all aspects, lovely to behold, his face slightly smiling, gazing at the practitioner.

"On the right side is the noble Samantabhadra, deep blue-green like the priyaṅgu flower, waving a white yak-tail fan, holding a wish-fulfilling jewel in his left hand, beautiful in his whole body, adorned with all ornaments, wearing a lower garment with fluttering blue silk, bearing a pearl necklace as an offering, holding a white lotus in his left hand, and with his right hand holding a white yak-tail fan with a golden handle and waving it, peaceful in aspect, gazing at Avalokiteśvara. Likewise the noble Samantabhadra is seated on a seat of a white lotus. Both of them should be drawn in this way.

"Of three lotuses rising from a single lotus stalk, on the anthers of the middle, root lotus are the lion throne and the jeweled footstool of the great bodhisattva. On another lotus is the noble Samantabhadra. On the third lotus is the noble Mahāsthāmaprāpta."

"That lotus stalk is beautiful, in the form of precious emerald, bearing many lotus flowers in full bloom, half in bloom, and flowers not yet opened. One should paint the two nāga kings Nanda and Upananda, who come from the great lake Anavatapta, holding the lotus stalk that grows from the great lake. Those two nāga kings are white in color, adorned with seven serpent hoods, beautiful with every ornament, half of the body a human body marked with serpent hoods, the other half a serpent's body, gazing intently at the noble Avalokiteśvara, half submerged in the water, and beautified with precious jewels and garments.

"Below, around the great lake, at the corner of the edge of the cloth painting, on the right side, one should draw the practitioner gazing intently at the circle of the feet of the noble Avalokiteśvara, holding a censer in his hand, bowing with body and knees, with dress and color just as they are.

"Above the noble Avalokiteśvara, at the two edges of the cloth, one should draw two very beautiful sons of the gods, garland bearers, holding garlands of flowers, hovering in the sky, scattering great masses of flowers. All around the painting one should draw nāgakesara and other flowers strewn about. The three figures, as one wishes, should be established or drawn. One should paint the noble Avalokiteśvara teaching the Dharma, and the noble Samantabhadra and the noble Vajrapāṇi holding yak-tail fans in their hands. The practitioner should without fail have the three figures painted as he wishes, in the aspect he wishes and with their shapes just as they are; or one should paint them in whatever way the practitioner wishes. In the center the bodhisattva, the great being, and on the two sides Vajrapāṇi and Samantabhadra should without fail be painted, as one wishes.

"On a piece of cloth obtained in whatever way, a span or about a cubit in size, the artist should paint it, whether it be oneself or another, an artist who does not keep the poṣadha or one who has faith, one who is clean or unclean, one who has moral discipline or one whose discipline is broken: any of these is acceptable. But the practitioner himself must without fail have done the preliminary practice, and must without fail have generated, with faith, the mind set on awakening. In that way the mantra will be accomplished, but otherwise, through one who does evil, never.

Thus by one who has come to faith
The deities of mantra are to be accomplished;
Through that faith the king of secret mantras
Is accomplished here, and not otherwise.
For faith is the supreme vehicle
By which the Guide leads beings on.
In people who lack faith
Bright qualities do not arise,
Just as a green sprout does not
Come from a seed burned by fire.
For people endowed with faith
The deeds of the buddhas will be accomplished.
All the deities, and especially
All secret mantras, every one,
Are not accomplished without faith.
The deities of the world
And likewise those beyond the world
Are accomplished by one who is said to have faith
And who is free of turbidity.
Because their minds have reached that awakening,
They will surely accomplish awakening.
Accomplishment by other means has not been taught;
That would run contrary to this teaching.
The small, the large,
And the middling cloth paintings have been proclaimed.
That which accomplishes all rites
I shall now thoroughly explain."

Thus concludes the fifth extensive chapter, on the rite of the cloth painting, from the rite of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā Ūrdhvajaṭā, in the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, the Avataṃsaka, a sūtra of the Great Vehicle of vast scope.

Then once again the Blessed One Śākyamuni addressed the bodhisattva, the great being Avalokiteśvara: "Great being, the teaching you have given for the sake of those beings, this explanation of the extensive rite of the cloth painting, will be accomplished with only a few means. For their sake I shall explain, in proper accord, the distinctions drawn by classifying the means of accomplishment and its expanded qualities. Listen well and keep it well in mind; I shall explain it for the sake of all sentient beings."

Then once again the bodhisattva said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it is excellent that you have spoken well to us, showing the abundance and making clear the power to accomplish the qualities of the conduct of mantra. Blessed One, if you deem that the time for it has now come, please speak, out of compassion for us."

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni looked upon the maṇḍala of the entire assembly and smiled. Then from the mouth of the Blessed One Śākyamuni came forth rays of light, blue, yellow, white, crimson, crystal-colored, and others. As soon as those rays had come forth, they illuminated the maṇḍala of the entire assembly and outshone every place in the great trichiliocosm, the world system of a billion worlds. They outshone the light of the lunar mansions, the light of the hosts of mountain gods, and even the light of the moon and sun, mighty and of great miraculous power as they are, so that these became dim and lightless and no longer shone forth. Outshining them, and having extinguished all the light of jewels, mantras, medicines, and precious things, the rays sank back once more into the mouth of the Blessed One Śākyamuni.

Then once again the bodhisattva, the great being Vajrapāṇi, who had gathered and was seated in that very maṇḍala of the assembly, rose from his seat, swiftly bowed at the Blessed One's two feet, and said this to the Blessed One: "The buddhas, the blessed ones, do not smile without cause and without condition. Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, of your smile?"

When he had asked this, the Blessed One said to the bodhisattva, the great being Vajrapāṇi: "Vajrapāṇi, so it is, so it is. Just as you have said, the Tathāgata does not smile without cause and without condition. There is a cause; there is a condition.

"There are those who are rightly devoted to the means of accomplishment through following the practice of vidyā in the root rite of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā, the lord of sūtras, who rely on the cloud of Dharma and rightly follow and pursue it; who hold it, who read it, who have faith in it; who have it written in a volume and honor it with sandalwood, powders, unguents, incense, garlands, parasols, victory banners, and flags of many kinds, or with special kinds of cymbals, or with various music and the clapping of hands; or who even continually attain a mind endowed with rejoicing; or in whom the hair stands on end; or in whom joy arises on hearing of the power and potency of the vidyā; or who rejoice in it; or who carry out its practices one by one. I prophesy all of them to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening: all of them will become buddhas, blessed ones. It is for this very reason that the Victor smiled, and not for any other.

"First of all, one who has seen the samaya, has done the preliminary practices, and has received consecration should take, from this king of rites, the root vidyā, or the heart mantra, or the near-heart mantra, or any other mantra, whether of a single syllable or whatever one wishes, go to a great wilderness, and recite it for seven years, eating fruits, foods from the water, roots, and leaves. Then the preliminary practice will have been done.

"Then one should climb to the summit of a mountain, place the principal cloth painting facing west, and oneself face east. Sitting on a mat of kuśa grass, one should offer a hundred thousand white lotuses, dyed with white sandalwood and saffron, below the cloth painting, to the Blessed One Śākyamuni, to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, to the pratyekabuddhas, and to the noble śrāvakas. One should also burn camphor incense, as much as one can afford. One should make offerings to the sons of the gods with whatever flowers one can find.

"Then on the bright full moon of the fortnight of miracles, or on any full moon, at the hour of midnight, one should make a hearth shaped like a lotus in front of the cloth painting and kindle a fire of white sandalwood wood. Combining saffron and camphor, with as much oblation as one can afford, one should perform a fire offering eight thousand times. Then one should make a protection.

"Then rays of light will come forth from the Blessed One Śākyamuni, and all around the cloth painting there will arise a single blaze. Then the practitioner should offer a guest-water offering with white lotus flowers dyed with sandalwood and saffron. Then the practitioner should swiftly circumambulate the cloth painting three times, bow to the buddhas, to all the bodhisattvas, to the pratyekabuddhas, and to the noble śrāvakas, and then fearlessly take hold of the cloth painting at the edge of the cloth on the side where the practitioner was painted before.

"Then, merely by taking hold of it, he will fly up. In the mere snap of a finger he will pass beyond the world of Brahmā and come to dwell in the world system of Sukhāvatī, where the Blessed One, the Tathāgata King Mighty through Perfectly Arisen Flowers, dwells, lives, abides, and teaches the Dharma. There he will enjoy himself for a thousand great eons, without old age and without death. The very place where the painted image remains will be blessed by all the buddhas and bodhisattvas. He will know their blessings. He will pass through thousands of buddha fields. He will display thousands of bodies. He will bring forth many powers of miraculous display. The noble Avalokiteśvara will become his spiritual friend. He will be certainly directed toward awakening."

From the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, the Avataṃsaka, the piṭaka of the Great Vehicle of vast scope, from the extensive chapters on the painted image in the root rite of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā Ūrdhvajaṭā, the sixth, on the rite of the means of supreme accomplishment and the fruits of the rites, is complete.

Then once again the great being addressed the hosts of gods present in the maṇḍala of the entire assembly: "Friends, listen! This is the rite of action for accomplishing the maṇḍala of the practice of the vidyā of the noble Tārā, together with its great rites; for the sake of protecting the practitioner, it is the supreme heart, the ultimate secret, spoken by all the tathāgatas, the great queen of vidyās, by reciting which all mantras are recited.

"O, O hosts of gods! This is the queen of vidyās that cannot be transgressed. If even a bodhisattva who is lord of the ten grounds is summoned by this vidyā, brought under its power, and made to long for it, what need is there to mention other bodhisattvas, and those of the world and beyond the world? It destroys all mantras and all obstructors. It is of great diligence and great might, uniquely heroic. Among all vidyās it alone is declared supreme over all mantras, and it alone, the queen of vidyās, is declared supreme among the great terrors. What is it? It performs all great rites, accomplishes all aims, does all tasks, cuts off all mantras, utterly destroys all malicious rites and all evils, brings each and every mantra to completion, and makes things virtuous. It penetrates ever higher above all the vidyās and mantras of the world and beyond the world; it is unobstructed; it is the true heart of all the tathāgatas; it fulfills every wish. What is it?

namo ratnatrayāya nama āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā tāre tāre tuttāre ture svāhā

"Friends, this is the supreme, ultimate secret that performs all great rites, the great queen of vidyās that no being can transgress, that no bhūta can withstand, that all buddhas declare auspicious, accomplished by all vidyās and mantras, sovereign of all the world, lord of all lords of vidyā, the very nature of loving-kindness toward all who are hostile, compassionate toward people, and destroyer of all obstructors. In short, in whatever way it is applied, in that way it acts. Even without having been accomplished, it performs rites.

"Whatever one touches after reciting the vidyā comes under one's power. If one consecrates a garment and wears it, one will have good fortune. If one consecrates a tooth stick and chews it, tooth disease will be cured. If one consecrates white karavīra seven times and eats it, food will come even without one's seeking it.

"For eye disease, consecrate powdered rock salt seven times and fill the eyes with it, and the eye disease will be cured.

"For ear disease, take the chidhrika that comes forth from the back of an elephant and appears when the thunder roars, wrap it in kabuka leaves, and cook it over a small fire. Once it is cooked, cook it further, combine it with lukewarm water and rock salt, consecrate it seven times, and cleanse the ears with it; in that very instant the disease will be pacified.

"If, when a woman is giving birth, the womb is blocked and she is overwhelmed by stabbing pain, grind the root of aṭarūṣaka in water free of living creatures and smear it around the navel, and she will give birth easily.

"For a man harmed by a thorn, or with a weapon lodged inside his body, consecrate old ghee one hundred and eight times and give it to him to drink, or smear it on that place, and in that very instant he will be free of the thorn.

"For indigestion, distension, and feverish illness, consecrate black salt, rock salt, or any other salt and have it eaten; one will be freed from that illness and be at ease that very day.

"For fever from a chronic illness or an acute fever, grind the root of the mātuluṅga citron and give it to drink with water free of living creatures; one will be freed from it without harm, by reciting seven times, or twice.

"If a barren woman wishes to bring forth what has not been born, boil the root of aśvagandhā together with ghee, mix it with cow's milk, recite over it twenty-five times, and have her drink it at the time of her menses. After she has bathed, if she avoids other men and the householder also entirely gives up sexual misconduct out of desire, a son of her own man, her own husband, will be born.

"For a woman for whom more than three or five years have passed since giving birth, or who has not conceived for many years; or who has been sealed by another's mantras or medicines, or harmed by another; or whose womb has been made unable to hold; or in whom illness has arisen; or who has abandoned other remedies; or whose womb has been made unable to hold by some slight illness of any other kind; or into whom poisons, whether stationary, moving, artificial, or natural, have entered; or upon whom practices of roots, mantras, medicines, love, and enmity have been worked: combine old ghee and the eyes of peacock feathers and grind them, mix with sugar, consecrate it twenty-seven times, and have her eat a portion the size of a myrobalan. For seven days and nights she should drink boiled milk with sugar, and one should recite the mantra again and again.

"For pain in the head, consecrate a crow's wing seven times and fan the person with it, and he will be at ease.

"For diseases such as those from excessive intercourse with women, grind the root of alambuṣā with milk, add the root of nīlikā, recite over it one hundred and eight times, make it into a gruel with milk, and drink it.

"Likewise, for quartan fever, daily fever, fever every second day, fever every third day, continuous fever, chronic fever, violent fever, and the like, mix milk porridge with ghee, consecrate it one hundred and eight times, and give it to drink, and the person will be at ease.

"Likewise, for one seized by a ḍākinī graha, consecrate one's own face one hundred and eight times and look at the person, and he will be at ease. Likewise, for the grahas of mātṛkās, of children, of pūtanas, of vetālas, of kumbhāṇḍas, and the like, and for all people seized by violent malicious beings, consecrate one's own hand one hundred and eight times and touch the head of the one seized, and he will be at ease.

"By reciting it once, one protects oneself. By reciting it twice, one protects one's friends. By reciting it three times, one protects the house. By reciting it four times, one protects the village. By reciting it five times, one protects the area that is the village's range. Likewise, by reciting it up to a thousand times, one will have protected an army.

These, or other minor rites as well, can be performed even without having accomplished the practice.

Then, if one wishes to accomplish the practice, one should not perform the minor rites. Going into single-minded solitude, one should resort to a secluded place: where a river that flows to the ocean comes down, the shore of the ocean, the bank of the Ganges, or the bank of some other great river. Having swept a clean spot, one should bathe three times and change one's clothes three times, keep silence, and eat alms food. Eating leaves, barley meal, milk and fruit, one should recite one million one hundred thousand times.

When the signs of accomplishment are seen, one should then begin the practice. In that very place one should set up the principal painted scroll and make a great offering to it. Then, in lamp vessels made of gold or silver, or of copper or clay, filled with turuṣka oil, or filled with fragrant oil, or filled with cow's ghee, one should offer to the scroll one hundred thousand lamps with wicks made from strips of new cloth.

As soon as the garlands of lamps have been offered all around it, rays of light will issue from the scroll, and as soon as they issue, the scroll will become a garland blazing on every side. In the sky above the sound of great drums will resound, and the word "Excellent!" will also be heard. Then, with the swiftness of a vidyādhara, the practitioner, who was drawn earlier at the edge of the corner of the scroll, should offer a welcoming water offering to the one present in the scroll, circumambulate, pay homage to all the buddhas, and take hold of it. Then, merely by taking hold of it, he will fly up together with all those lamp bearers. He will travel even to a hundred and one celestial palaces. Those vidyādharīs, each holding divine cymbals, singing sweet songs and dancing, will be seen filling the space all around, and they will consecrate the practitioner as a great king of vidyādharas. Together with those lamp bearers he will sport, free from aging and free from death. He will live for a great eon, like the rising sun, beautiful with divine ornaments and adorned with brilliant garments. He will bring them under his power and they will do his bidding. He will enjoy himself with them, and all the divine vidyādharas too will attend upon him as his servants. He will become a great king of vidyādharas, will live long, and will be invincible to all the siddhas. In a single instant he will go to the world of Brahmā. If even Śakra (Indra) cannot rival him, what need is there to mention other vidyādharas? And in the end he will attain buddhahood. The noble Avalokiteśvara, too, will become his spiritual friend.

There is yet another means of accomplishing the rite. Having practiced severe austerities, one then goes into single-minded solitude and dwells apart, entering a great hermitage without bustle and free from bustle. In a place where there is a great lotus lake with water, one climbs to the summit of a mountain that stands beside another mountain. Having offered scents, flowers and so forth to the vidyā mantras, eating as one wishes milk or barley meal, lotus roots and fruit, and eating what comes from milk, one should recite the vidyā one million times.

At the end of the recitation, by that very rite taught before, one should set up the principal painted scroll, anoint lotus flowers with white sandalwood and saffron, kindle a fire of khadira wood, and perform the fire offering with thirty-six thousand of the lotuses anointed before. Then, at the end of the fire offering, rays of light will issue from the painted scroll of the Blessed One Śākyamuni. They will illuminate the practitioner completely and then sink into the crown of his head. As soon as they touch him, the practitioner will possess the five superknowledges. He will attain a bodhisattva ground. He will roam about in a divine form as he wishes, and will live for thirty-six eons. He will pass through thirty-six buddhafields, and he will also clearly behold their powers. He will please thirty-six buddhas, and they too will rejoice at his offerings and veneration. And in the end he will be wholly devoted to awakening. He will be cared for by a great bodhisattva as his spiritual friend, all the way until he reaches nirvāṇa in awakening.

This completes the seventh extensive chapter, the rite of the means for accomplishing the supreme rite, from the Root Ritual of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā of the Upswept Locks, a Great Vehicle sūtra of great extent belonging to the Avataṃsaka of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.

Then once again the Blessed One Śākyamuni taught the supreme rite of accomplishment. Having taken up the root vidyā mantra of this king of ritual manuals, one should go onto the Ganges river and stay on a boat. In the middle of the Ganges, drinking milk and water, one should perform the recitation thirty thousand times, over as many days and nights as one wishes. Then, at the end of the recitation, one will see all the nāgas.

Then, beginning the practice, one should make a lotus-shaped hearth in the very middle of the boat. Then one should make a great offering to the painted scroll with flowers such as nāgakesara. Placing the principal scroll facing west, and oneself facing east, seated on a mat of kuśa grass, one should consecrate each nāgakesara flower seven times, kindle a fire with khadira wood, and perform the fire offering with nāgakesara flowers mixed with white sandalwood and saffron, up to ten thousand times. When other nāgas are seen, one should not, out of craving, accept the substances of accomplishment they hold out. For at the end of the fire offering one will fly up together with a nāga mount. One will become a king of the vidyādharas. All the lords of the nāgas and their kings will follow one and remain like servants. One will live for thirty intermediate eons. One will act with full freedom, and one's movement will be unobstructed. One will directly see the noble Avalokiteśvara, who will touch the crown of one's head. Merely by that touch one will possess the five superknowledges. One will certainly go on to buddhahood.

Further, there is what serves as the means of accomplishment for the rite of supreme accomplishment. As before, one goes onto the Ganges river. Having made a boat from a single piece of bilva wood, made very sturdy and well built, one climbs aboard it, and with an oar made of bilva wood the practitioner, very skilled and clear-headed, should row that boat along. Never leaving the great river Ganges, one should row everywhere straight ahead or swiftly with the current.

Then, having taken up the root vidyā, or the heart mantra, or the near-heart mantra, or the single-syllable mantra, or the mantra of the wrathful one, or of the messenger, or of the far-following attendant, or any other mantra at all, one should place the principal painted scroll facing west, and oneself face east at first, and afterward as one wishes. Eating milk, barley meal and fruit, or water, or eating lotus roots and fruit, keeping silence, bathing at the three times of day and changing one's clothes three times, always engaging in utterly pure deeds and possessed of an utterly pure mind, one should first of all, before the scroll, as was explained, according to the rite seen before, recite the vidyā one million times. Then, if it is the root vidyā, at the end of reciting it sixty thousand times the boat will go to the great ocean.

Then one should gather up the implements of the practice and leave them in that same place as before. Then, when the boat goes out to the great ocean, one should not be afraid and should not turn it back. Nor can it be turned back, except by the power of the practitioner. Then in a mere moment it will enter even a great ocean that lies a thousand yojanas away, so what need is there to speak of a short way? Having entered it, one should begin the work of accomplishment on the water.

Then, in a hearth of the shape described before, or in an earthen vessel made by a potter, one should kindle a fire of khadira wood. With burnt offerings of nāgakesara stamens and flowers, white sandalwood and camphor mixed together, whether in very small or very large quantity, one should, as before, perform the fire offering six million times with the root vidyā.

While one is performing the fire offering, the rākṣasas who live in the city of Laṅkā, taking on various forms, will cry out "Hā hā!" And the nāga kings who live in the nāga city of Bhogavatī, bearing forms of many kinds, some very peaceful and some very wrathful, will rise up, and the nāgas and rākṣasas will say, "Rise up, rise up! Be our lord!" Likewise asuras, yakṣas, gods, mahoragas, siddhas and all the nonhumans will greatly entice one, but one should not rise. Then the vidyādhara, reciting the mantra, should threaten them with the threatening forefinger of the left hand. Then they will scatter, flee in every direction, and be terrified.

Then, at the end of the fire offering, the boat will carry the practitioner off and in an instant go to the realm of Akaniṣṭha. He will travel to other world systems as well, and come back. He will come to know the minds of bodhisattvas. He will possess the five superknowledges, great miraculous power and great might. He will always see the noble Avalokiteśvara. All nāgas, all rākṣasas, all yakṣas, all gods, all asuras and all sentient beings will come under his power. Once they are set to doing his bidding, all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, the pratyekabuddhas and the noble śrāvakas, and those who have accomplished this mantra, will be loving-kindness itself toward him and will favor him. He will be invincible to all beings.

Further, there is a supreme means of accomplishment of the rite. One should have a large boat made of bilva wood, either a craft from a single trunk or one assembled from parts, and make on it a great dwelling. On that boat, stationed at an island in the middle of the Ganges, one hundred and twenty men holding lamps in their hands should board the boat. Wearing white clothes and with protection performed, they should be placed before the principal painted scroll, set up according to the rite given before. Then, having made a great offering to the scroll, one should perform a fire offering of thirty-six thousand oblations of powdered nāgakesara mixed with saffron, white sandalwood and camphor, together with khadira. Then, at the end of the fire offering, the boat will go to the world of Brahmā and come back in a mere instant, and he will roam about as he wishes. He will see the noble Avalokiteśvara. From merely seeing him he will attain the five superknowledges, and he will live long and remain for a great eon. He will become a great vidyādhara king, a universal monarch. Those lamp bearers too will be accomplished as his vidyādharas. Together with those companions he will roam about as he wishes and go wherever he pleases. The buddhas, the blessed ones, will be delighted by his offerings and veneration. And in the end he will certainly attain buddhahood.

Further, there is the excellent means of accomplishment of the rite:

On a riverbank or on the ocean's shore,
likewise on the Snowy Mountains,
on Vindhya, the king of mountains,
there one should accomplish the supreme rite.
On Sahya and on Malaya,
on Mount Gandhamādana,
on Vulture Peak, the king of mountains,
the supreme rite should be accomplished.
On the cliffs of the great ocean,
and where there are trees, flowers and the like:
the mantras spoken by the Victor
should be accomplished in these places.
In a clean place, wholly secluded,
at the village outskirts, for the four acts,
keeping silent and avoiding contact,
one should always pass water.
For the body, at the abode of the gods, and in defecating,
those who keep the vows should observe cleanliness.
For touching, soft earths are wanted.
Earths free of living creatures,
three portions taken in the proper way,
are always for the anus alone.

Likewise, at the end of both, the hands.
The mantrin, always taking up the earths
that were described before,
the reciter, always the feet:
the right one and the other,
having placed them each against the other,
should carefully wash the feet,
just as was described at length before.
The cleanliness of one who recites mantra
is a cleanliness free of foul smell;
so the Sage himself has always taught.
These are taught in brief;
"They are seen in all the tantras,"
so said the Lord, the Sage himself.
Then the reciter should sip water,
disciplined, delighting in the work of accomplishment,
by the rite described before;
this is the inner purity of mind.
Cleanliness is declared to be of five kinds.
For the mantrin, in all the mantras,
cleanliness of body, and likewise
of speech and of mind are proclaimed.
The fourth is the cleanliness of truth,
and water is declared the fifth.
The way of truth: anger subdued,
knowing the tantras, having studied the treatises,
skilled in the subtle reality and its meaning,
knowing mantras, renowned in the rites,
and skilled inwardly through reasoning:
for such a one accomplishment is not hard to find.
Words of falsehood, which forsake
the way of truth, should not be spoken.
Forsaking all truth,
vicious, utterly vicious,
hateful and quarrelsome,
harsh and striking at the vitals,
fallen away from the way of truth,
tormenting other beings,
slander, an afflicted mind,
the forsaking of all good dharmas,
likewise a nature bent on harm,
always immoral, practicing what is not Dharma:
these the reciter of mantra should give up.
Likewise the ways of the village,
from which anger and covetousness arise,
and the terrors of the world beyond,
the wise ones, the rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddhas,
and the buddhas of the past have condemned,
as well as the ever-recurring afflictions.
Likewise one who always speaks lies,
pursuing worldly accomplishments for the ends he desires,
who utters lies upon the earth,
falls into a great and unbearable hell.
Likewise, because of his former misdeeds
and his delight in them, in the world of Yama
he dwells there again and again, forever.
One who makes his living by constant lying
will fall into unbearable lower realms:
Kālasūtra, Pratāpana,
Saṃjīva, the forest of sword leaves,
and likewise the śālmali forest;
there he dwells for many eons.
A person who speaks falsely,
who speaks wrongly of the secret mantra,
who out of delusion misrepresents it,
and who deceives the bhūtas:
how could he have accomplishment?
Therefore one who out of delusion,
not having seen the accomplishments of mantra,
says, "There are no accomplishments for mantrins,"
speaking words like these,
one who has utterly forsaken
the Buddha's teaching here upon the earth:
even in many tens of millions of eons
how could he become accomplished?
Therefore he will be cooked
in the unbearable, greatly terrifying Avīci,
in Saṃjīva and Kālasūtra,
and cooked in Pratāpana.
A place free of creatures
such as scorpions and snakes should be sought,
well supplied with fruit and flowers,
with clear water, highly praised:
there the knower of mantra should do the approach of the mantra.
Other places are not proclaimed for this.
At a temple, or in a charnel ground,
at a single firm landmark,
at a single sign, and likewise at the outskirts,
the knower of mantra should do the approach of the mantra.
Having protected himself and his companions,
and endowed with the secret mantra practiced before,
the mantrin should always recite the mantra.
In a great and excellent forest with great trees,
where flowers, fruits and the like grow,
on mountain peaks and in caves,
with clean watering places,
on the delightful banks of great rivers,
the knower of mantra should do the approach of the mantra.
Knowing the mantra, he gains certain realization.
In the east too, the great river,
the auspicious bank of the Lohita,
and likewise the land of Kāmarūpa,
and the excellent town that brings prosperity,
the lowlands where this excellent one flows,
dwelling places and excellent rivers:
in those places the reciter, always
pure and intelligent, should stay.
Do the preliminary approach there!
At Gaṅgādvāra, all the rites;
likewise always where the Ganges
meets the Venomous River,
all the applications,
and the recitation with the mantra of the pure.
Great charnel grounds and others too:
there the reciter should always recite.
Where there are clear waters and streams
free of living creatures,
for that very reason, intently,
in meditative equipoise, one should recite the mantra.
If there, by the world's way of thinking,
some slight lack of merit is seen,
still, since the mantra has indicated it,
one should stay there for a little while
and then go elsewhere.
At the time when the moon is eclipsed,
even if it is not the proper time, for a short while
one should stay there, and not otherwise.
Otherwise the knower of mantra, as best he can,
should then quickly depart.
In places on the earth
where stūpas of the Sugata stand, one should always dwell.
All the worldly tīrthikas,
fallen into bad views,
and the places of other tīrthikas
the knower of mantra always avoids;
the one who knows mantra does not stay there.
Where the best of beings, of vast intelligence,
the supreme Victor, has dwelt,
and the rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddhas,
the bodhisattvas of great fortune,
the sons of the supreme Victor, and the śrāvakas:
in all the lands upon the earth
where all of these have dwelt, the knower of mantra
should diligently do the preliminary approach.
In meditative equipoise, the secret mantra
should be recited in that place.
In these places that have been taught,
all the rites that have been taught,
and the means of accomplishment of the rites, are to be done.
If these places cannot be found,
then in any place whatsoever
one who is pure should do the preliminary approach.
With faith and devotion, the work
of the supreme rite of the sādhana is begun.

First of all, one should set up the principal painted image facing west, and oneself face east. Taking earth from an anthill or earth from the bank of the Ganges, one should mix it with pushel tsé, white sandalwood, saffron and camphor, and make the figure of a peacock. Having placed it before the painted image, one should make a wheel-shaped diagram from pure kuśa grass with uncut tips, gathered from a clean place, and holding it before the painted image with the right hand, and the peacock with the left hand, at midnight on the full-moon day of the bright fortnight, one should make a great offering to the painted image and, with the fragrance of burning camphor incense, recite until dawn breaks. Then, at the time of sunrise, it will become a king of peacocks, and the wheel too will blaze.

Then, wearing divine garlands and clothes and fully adorned, in whatever form one wishes, like the rising sun, one should pay homage to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, circumambulate the painted scroll, and take up the scroll. If one then sits on that peacock seat, in a mere moment one will pass beyond the world of Brahmā. One will become a vidyādhara king, a universal monarch, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of niyutas of vidyādharas. One will live for sixty eons. One will go wherever one wishes and enjoy oneself fully. One will travel without obstruction. One will be endowed with the riches of the gods. One will directly see the noble Avalokiteśvara, and he himself will become one's spiritual friend. And in the end one will attain buddhahood.

Likewise, there are a staff, a water pot with a spout, an implement carried for worship, realgar, bezoar, a sword, an iron arrow, a single-pointed spear, a battle-axe, and weapons of various special kinds; special things made of earth: two-footed creatures, four-footed creatures, birds, and special mounts such as lions, tigers and leopards, made from anthill earth mixed with sweet-smelling fragrances. Or seats, mounts, bedding, a white parasol, a diadem, every kind of ornament, every kind of jewel, and every kind of the requisites of one who has gone forth: a rosary, sandals, an alms bowl, Dharma robes, a needle, a knife and the like, made of fine iron; or anything else at all, the implements of beings, vessels and the like, made of fine iron, or made of anthill earth or river earth. All of these one should wash with the five products of the cow, sprinkle and purify, and consecrate them one hundred and eight times, as before, with the mantra of application, or the single-syllable mantra, or any other mantra, using, apart from what is taught in this king of ritual manuals, whatever vidyā of the rite of accomplishment one wishes and delights in. One who protects himself and fully guards his companions, who is well able to keep secrets and knows the mantras and tantras, should set up the painted image facing west in the place described before, and position himself as before.

Having made a great offering to the painted image, burning chiefly camphor incense, and having made the special weapons, implements and creatures described before as replicas, as described before, on the night of the full moon of the waxing fortnight one should take up any one of those articles and recite for the whole night. Then at the time of sunrise, at that juncture, great garlands of light rays will be seen all over the painted image.

If the practitioner has taken up a special mount, then, riding it, he will go wherever he wishes. If he has taken up or held a special ornament or a special weapon, he will become a great king of vidyādharas. He will go wherever he wishes, with a divine body like the risen sun, endowed with garlands of great light rays, a body radiant like lightning, the lord of all vidyādharas, long-lived and remaining for a great eon, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of niyutas of vidyādharas, and enjoying himself in a celestial palace of divine jewels.

The mount made of earth, fashioned before, by which he gained accomplishment will become greatly powerful. It will be his mount and his companion; it will avert the mantra accomplishments of others and bring about every accomplishment of his own mantra; it will be loving-kindness itself, wishing him well and ever devoted to him. Whatever his weapons, ornaments, jewels of various kinds, seats, bedding, creatures and the like may be, they will always remain bound to him as his protection, his guard, and his great shelter. He will become one of great might, great diligence and great body.

He will directly see the noble Avalokiteśvara, who will grant him the words "Excellent!" and anoint the crown of his head, and will act as his spiritual friend until he attains the seat of awakening. He will certainly gain the ten powers in full and become worthy of offerings. He will not be overwhelmed by beings and will be invincible to all the bhūtas. He will not break the lineage of the true limit, and he will attain the grounds. He will become certain of the ten powers and of bodhisattvahood, and will attain samādhi.

In brief, dwelling in an excellent place, before the excellent painted scroll, delighting in excellent offerings, one should perform all the supreme rites, and the other supreme rites as well.

For the sake of becoming a vidyādhara who travels through the sky, following the bodhisattvas, gaining the five superknowledges and attaining the grounds, traveling to every world system in this very body, and bringing to perfection the continuum of the ten powers; for the sake of directly seeing the noble Maitreya; for the sake of making the teaching of the Dharma meaningful; for the sake of not cutting the lineage of the buddhas; for the sake of surpassing all and attaining the wisdom of omniscience; for the sake of entering into the abundance of the Dharma cloud; for the sake of being free from the torment of the afflictions and fully pacified by a stream of nectar rain; for the sake of engaging in caring for the world and doing so earnestly; for the sake of guarding the Tathāgata's way of Dharma; for the sake of making the Tathāgata's words meaningful; for the sake of cultivating the rite of the means of accomplishment of mantra practice; and for the sake of the arising of buddhas, all bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas and great noble śrāvakas, one should accomplish this king of ritual manuals.

Endowed with the vast power of mantra, sitting close before the principal painted scroll, one should accomplish this king of scrolls with the mantra rites of all the mundane and supramundane, with the various paths found in all the tantras, in short, even with the rites taught in other ritual manuals. They will quickly become accomplishments, and what I have taught will without doubt be accomplished.

This completes the eighth chapter, on the accomplishment of the supreme painted scroll, from the Root Ritual of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā Ūrdhvajaṭā, a Great Vehicle sūtra of great extent belonging to the Avataṃsaka of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni again looked upon the great circle of the assembly and spoke to the great bodhisattva: "Great being, there is the intermediate rite of your painted scroll, the intermediate means of accomplishment of the rite. I shall explain it in brief, so pay close attention, and I shall explain it."

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Avalokiteśvara, said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, Teacher, compassionate toward the world, delighting in benefiting all sentient beings, out of compassion for us, and with regard for the people of the future, please speak whatever you consider to be timely."

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the bodhisattva, the great being Avalokiteśvara: "Great being, listen. First of all, what are the moral discipline, the observances, the practice of cleanliness, the restraint, the recitation, the fire offering, the meditative concentration, the rite, and the place to dwell, through which the work of accomplishing the conduct of all beings is fruitful and not in vain, and the accomplishments of the application of all mantras are achieved? I shall explain it: great being, listen.

"First of all, having first properly undertaken the observances of the vidyā and properly taken up moral discipline, one should first of all properly follow the commitments explained by the maṇḍala master. He should be one who has expounded your king of ritual manuals, clear about what was definitively taught before, conscientious, who has received empowerment as a master, who knows the rite you have taught, learned, clear-minded, endowed with the Dharma, truthful, of great enthusiasm, grateful, steadfast, good-hearted, neither too old nor too young, free of desire for any gain or honor, living a celibate life, and compassionate. He would not tell a lie even for mere gain, or for the sake of enjoyment, or out of attachment, so what need is there to speak of something utterly trifling, of gain, or of the forms of delusion? He should be firm in his pledges, possessed of compassion equally toward all beings, of generosity and moral discipline; one who has done the earlier practice of your secret vidyā, the repetition of the mantra and the preliminary approach of the vidyā; who has properly entered your maṇḍala; who knows the world; who properly cares for others; fruitful and skilled; thoroughly engaged in what is good; fearless and harmless; unattached; heroic; firm in diligence; and free of illness, that is, not of a constitution made unfit for the work by any illness; and born into a great and high family. One endowed with these qualities becomes a maṇḍala master. The practitioner too should be like him, or lacking only slightly in some of these qualities.

"Having made offerings to such a maṇḍala master, one should make this request for the purpose: 'Master, since we wish to follow the vidyā and mantra of the bodhisattva, the great being, and the commitments of the maṇḍala of that Blessed Lady, out of compassion for us, and having given rise to a beneficial intention, master, please teach it.'

"Then the maṇḍala master, by the rite taught before, should examine the disciples one by one as is proper and admit them, and having conferred empowerment as before, should give them the vidyā and the mantra and teach the commitments in their proper order. The great secret, the mudrās, the tantras, the mantras and the rites, too, he should examine over a long time; once he knows their dispositions, he should teach the tantras, the mantras and so forth, and all the rites. This rite, that it is not to be done otherwise, has been proclaimed.

"Then the disciple should offer to the maṇḍala master, as far as he is able, whatever pleases the master, or even his own person and his wealth. Then the maṇḍala master should regard him as a son. He should look after him like a son, and like a mother support him with provisions.

Then that practitioner should take up any vidyā or mantra whatsoever and go to a solitary place. Applying in full, as above, the site taught earlier, he should, with those very vidyās and so forth, perform the invitation, the request to depart, and the lamps, scents, incense, tormas and food offerings in full, by the very rite taught for the maṇḍala. Having invited the deities and offered them seats, he should bathe three times at the three junctures of the day, change his clothes three times, and do the mantra recitation every day.

Here, as for what is called the time of the junctures: the period from the end of the night until about the time the sun rises is explained as the first. Midday is this: after the sun has risen, at the juncture measured by a period of time, when the disk of the sun stands fully in the sky, one who knows the rite should know it as the midday juncture. At the time of sunset, too, about the remaining quarter is to be called the third juncture.

A master who is learned and has good friends,
Who is perfectly endowed with moral discipline and vows,
Who is born in a great family,
And steadfast in diligence in every way,
Perfectly endowed with mantras, tantras and so forth,
Clear-minded in all activities,
Subtle, learned, and knowing the right measure,
Who always holds to the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu),
Of great enthusiasm and endowed with splendor,
Without regard for worldly concerns,
With faith in the Dharma of the supreme Sage,
Who has abandoned worldly people,
Who does recitation and keeps to solitude,
Who has relied on approach beforehand,
Who knows the secret mantras of the bodhisattvas,
And sees the conditions other than these,
Who knows the secret mantras spoken by the Buddha
And the applications of the worldly ones,
Who has made protection and is steadfast in power,
Always delighting in the conduct of cleanliness,
Who follows in every way
The path the buddhas have taught,
