And the secret mantras the Victor has spoken,
Always diligent in reciting secret mantras,
Always mindful of the fruit in this very life
And likewise in the world beyond,
Fearful of every wrongdoing,
And likewise even of the slightest,
Pure, learned and without laziness,
Honest in mind and lovely to behold,
Who in whatever mantras the One with Ten Powers has taught,
And likewise in those of the Victor's heirs,
And in whatever mantras belong to the worldly ones,
And in those of the vajra and lotus families too,
Has always labored,
Who holds the meaning of scriptures and treatises,
Healthy and not lacking in capacity,
Free from old age and sickness,
Likewise having good friends, accomplished in mantra,
Quick in everything he does,
And likewise not overly tall,
Living in celibacy and great in wisdom,
Especially knowledgeable,
Alone and free of bustle,
Brave, and one who has received empowerment,
Who here has reached the far shore of awakening,
Diligent in bringing existence to peace,
Who likewise practices the spells,
Of great power and knowing the world,
Caring for beings, for sentient beings,
And fully endowed with glory,
Delighting in giving and in benefiting the bhūtas:
To such an exceptional master
One should always make supplication.
He bestows the accomplishment of the mantras
Of the maṇḍala that has been drawn;
Through the empowerment he gives,
The great fruit will be granted.
The disciple who desires accomplishment
Should always honor him like the Sage.
Not to transgress his words
Is what the disciple must strive to do.
As far as his means and possessions allow,
He should offer his goods to him,
Whether a little or a great deal,
Whatever will please him.
Just as, for the sake of sustaining the body,
One gives wealth to one's father,
So the disciple who knows the Dharma
Should offer wealth to the master.
He will gain the accomplishment of ultimate lordship,
Long life and likewise health,
And will attain a flourishing destiny.
If the disciple honors that guru,
His mantras will succeed.
Through seeing the path and the rite,
Through relying on approach,
And likewise through worship made with paintings,
All the buddhas will be pleased,
And likewise the heirs of the supreme Victor,
And all the gods will be pleased.
If one always attends on and honors the guru,
Then through seeing the guru and the mantras
All of these will become stable.
The practitioner, beforehand and at the very start,
Should follow the commitments.
Whether the guru is lesser than he or his equal,
Or even if he is far more eminent,
Out of delusion or excessive anger
One should never despise the guru.
He in turn, in this tantra,
Should always give him the instructions.
When he has bestowed the accomplishment of mantra,
He has not been miserly in this.
To the disciple described before
He should always give the instructions.
When he has bestowed the accomplishment of mantra,
The one who has an eye
That increases the affection of embodied beings
Is the one he should make his disciple.
Where master and disciple, for each other's sake,
Follow one another in turn,
Where a continuity of affection is maintained,
And a gentle disposition is upheld,
To such a one mantras should be given.
The master, and likewise the disciple:
When the disciple looks upon the guru,
He will always be glad,
Or both will perfectly attain accomplishment.
To him one should always teach
The path itself and the conduct of mantra.
Since both know each other as father and son,
They follow the mantras together with their fruit,
And likewise attain stability and joy.
The disciple should always
Protect the guru with great effort.
Sons who are great beings
Keep the stream of the Buddha's Dharma unbroken.
To those who lack this, who have no protector,
Give the mantras as they have been taught,
Even to destitute beings and to eunuchs.
For all, and above all,
The conduct of mantra is supremely excellent.
For the lowest, the highest and the middling,
It is to be practiced at all times.
Toward the teachings that have been fully received,
One should keep up the continuity of upholding them.

To beings of settled understanding
One should give fully, even what they desire.
Therefore the mantra that he desires
The disciple himself should take up.
Since it has been shown to him by that master,
That is the path, and no other.
The one who desires accomplishment,
When he is to go far from that father,
Bows his head to him as to a father,
And then goes wherever he wishes.
Then, having gone to this place,
In meditative equipoise he recites the secret mantra.
Following the practice of begging for alms,
And keeping silence, he recites at the three times.
In this way it comes about just as taught.
Fully entering the path as it is,
At that time he cuts off all wavering.
Empty houses and great wildernesses,
Great mountains and the banks of rivers,
Clean places, cow pens and great lakes,
Secluded places that people have abandoned: these he should frequent;
Temples and the foot of trees,
A solitary high mountain,
The delightful shore of the great ocean,
River islands or islands,
And the many kinds of place taught before,
Various lands that please the mind;
And in other quarters besides these
He should recite the mantra in meditative equipoise.
A companion who has the right characteristics
Is a reasoner certain of the meaning of the mantras,
Who knows the very kinds of omens,
Brave and victorious in battle,
Courageous and patient,
Perfectly endowed with faith and moral discipline.
In this domain taught by the Victor,
With a companion who has the highly praised characteristics
And is endowed with patience,
The rites will be accomplished victoriously, without effort.
Rising from his bed at dawn,
In water from a stream or a great lake,
Free of living creatures and free of impurity,
In that water he bathes;
Then with earth and powdered cow dung
The knower of mantra should rub his body.
Then in water purified with mantra,
Exceedingly stainless,
The diligent reciter should bathe.
He should not bathe too long.
Then, rising, he should wash
His hands with earth as well.
Seven times, and seven, and seven times again,
Twenty-one times he should rinse.
There, again, he uses a tooth stick;
Having cleaned his teeth, he should throw it away.
Then, bowing to the Protector,
And having bowed to the Lord of the World,
The knower of mantra makes pleasing offerings.
With various acts of praise and offering
He praises him perfectly again and again.
Likewise, with fragrant flowers,
He offers water to the Teacher, the Protector,
And bows his head to the buddhas.
Then those who have become disciples
Confess their wrongdoing
In the very presence of those lords of the world.
Having offered themselves as well,
They should sit before the painted cloth.
He sits upon a mat of kuśa grass.
When the knowers of mantra have both sat down,
In accordance with the characteristics,
There, with a rosary,
He should recite with great effort.
At that time he does not recite other mantras.
A deficient rite is to be avoided,
And likewise one that is excessive.
For rites of the middling kind
Those who keep the vows should recite the mantra.
Reciting too loudly is to be avoided,
And the words should not be too faint either.
For rites of the middling kind
The Victor has highly praised this.
Neither too loud nor too soft,
One should always recite at a middling pitch.
All the buddhas of the past
Have said such words are glorious.
He should not recite in the presence of others,
And should always keep his course of practice secret from others.
He recites within range of his own hearing.
Likewise, with the mantra at a middling pitch,
Through recitation he will greatly prosper.
Some who have heard the mantra well
And desire the middling accomplishment
Should recite the mantra virtuously.
Therefore, apart from people,
Having heard well the true meaning of the mantra,
Free from crowds and in seclusion,
The reciter should recite the mantra.
A quarter of the night,
And half of its half:
About the time of the red dawn,
When the disk of the sun rises,
Is the first session, as is fitting;
So the Sage, the supreme being, has said.
The measure of the time is four,
And it is proclaimed as the middle.
Then, when the sun has half set,
At that time one leaves off the mantra recitation.
At the time the mantra recitation is set aside,
He offers water and requests the deities to depart.
The one who keeps the vows avoids other ways.
If, when he has then set it aside, some of the day remains,
He should do virtue within the Sage's teaching:
Reading the sublime Dharma,
Such as the Perfection of Wisdom,
And always honoring and reading
The volume of the Ten Grounds.
Then, when the time has come,
Having bowed to his own mantra, the lord of mantras,
And to the Sage, the supreme being,
He then goes out for his livelihood,
And likewise keeps to conduct at the proper time.
He eats at the proper time and subdues his senses.
The practitioner who is endowed with the Dharma
Has deep faith in the Buddha's teaching and is diligent.
When he enters another village,
He keeps silent and delights in clean conduct.
He goes for alms to the houses
Of beings who always keep the Dharma.
The reciter regards as pure
Water free of living creatures and food that is properly cooked.
Those perfectly endowed with right view,
Who have deep faith in the Buddha's teaching:
At such houses he should always
Accept alms for the sake of his alms food.
Just as one who is valiant, clad in armor,
Enters a perilous land,
Always vanquishes his enemies,
And cannot be overcome by enemies,
So the mantra practitioner lives by alms.
When he always enters the village,
Likewise, if he sees forms and hears sounds
That are apt to arouse attachment, which is unwholesome,
For the sake of calming desire
He should meditate on the wholesome contemplation of the unattractive.
Even when he sees a woman's body
Adorned with the features of youth,
He should meditate on bodies despised and rotting,
Eaten by worms, lying in the charnel ground,
On the body as impermanent and suffering,
Impure and foul-smelling.
Because of it, the childish and deluded
Go and circle among the five destinies,
And, strung on the thread of karma,
Grieve for a long time.
Those deluded by the obscuration of ignorance
Are blind, and have suffering as their cause.

Where the mind is inverted,
Through attachment people come to ruin.
By the various paths of karma,
Attached in many different ways,
Going crookedly for a long time,
They engage in going and coming.
Clinging as though things were permanent,
They act in every way out of grasping.
Where beings delight in what is unwholesome,
They wander long upon the road.
Like the circling of a water wheel,
Those born in the little lake of existence,
Those beings, are tossed about everywhere
By the unbearable river of suffering.
Likewise, that women are
The very root of suffering
Has been declared by the buddhas and bodhisattvas,
And likewise by the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
And by the sages.
The ocean of existence, never stilled:
These great lakes are hard to dry up.
Where beings sink,
Deceived by thoughts of women, is this:
They go to the hells, the world of animals,
The world of pretas, the asuras,
And likewise the human world itself,
And the destiny of the gods,
Always circling round and round.
Those deceived by attachment to women
Sink into the great mire
Of the prison of the ocean of saṃsāra.
A foolish man attached to women
Is like a jackal attached to a corpse.
In that which beings always delight in,
They endure unbearable suffering,
And surely fall away from the white Dharma.
One who dwells firmly in the Buddha's teaching
Turns back all the suffering
Of the ocean of existence.
Those who delight and strive in reciting mantra,
Renowned for great power and possessed of a steady mind,
Endowed with splendor and capable in mantra:
For them there is no suffering.
Those who know true restraint, measure and truth,
Who honor the guru and the gods,
And who are respectful to mother and father:
For these three there is no suffering.
One should attend to impermanence, suffering and emptiness,
And to the benefit of others.
A woman's body is a ghostly form,
Likewise a boil and a thorn.
Seized by the hook of the aggregates of bad understanding,
One does not pass beyond saṃsāra.
For one always attached to women
There is no accomplishment.
For him there is no supreme destiny,
Nor is there even a middling one,
Nor is there even a minor accomplishment.
Here, if the reciter breaks his discipline,
To one of broken moral discipline the Lord of Sages
Has not taught the accomplishment of mantra.
He has no path to go to the city of nirvāṇa,
And is bereft of any direction.
Here, for the despicable childish one,
How could there be accomplishment of mantra?
For this person of broken discipline
Not even a good destiny will come,
Nor is he even inclined toward happiness;
Likewise, what need is there to say
That the mantras spoken by the Victor will not succeed for him?
When the crown of a palm tree
Has once been cut off,
It does not turn green again;
When would a shoot ever come again?
Likewise the deluded one seeking accomplishment in mantra,
Of broken discipline and sinful deeds,
Always attached to women again and again,
And keeping company with bad friends:
How could the king of mantras succeed for him?
Therefore, when a reciter
Indulges in the faults of women
That the Sugata has rejected,
And yet seeks to gain accomplishment,
The childish one deluded about women
Has not been taught by any other to succeed.
Then, first of all, the intelligent,
Clean, delighting in freedom from bustle,
Of good family, steadfast and brave,
Of good mind and pleasing to behold,
Who know how to discern Dharma and what is not Dharma:
For them accomplishment is not hard to find.
The knower of mantra who has entered upon this
Thus enters the village for alms.
Having gone as he wishes,
In places examined beforehand,
The wise one, with a pure mind, sets the food aside,
And, having set aside the food,
Goes outside and washes his feet.
Then, back at that place again,
With waters free of living creatures,
First he draws the water;
Second, with the left hand,
He scrubs below the waist.
Then, applying the right hand again,
He should wash with his hands.
With the pure earth set down beforehand,
Clean, seven times,
And with pure water, he makes himself clean.
Yellow dung from a tawny cow
He takes in a clean, stainless vessel,
Mixes it with water free of living creatures,
And first, for the supreme one,
The Teacher, the Sage, he makes a maṇḍala,
In particular about a cubit across.
The second is for the lord of his own mantra,
The third for the goddess of the family:
These the mantra practitioner who recites
Should always make again and again.
The fourth is known to be
For the enjoyment of all sentient beings.
On the right, for the Lord of the World,
He should always make this maṇḍala.
For the sake of the Three Jewels
That maṇḍala is square.
The second is for the pratyekabuddhas,
The third for the heirs of the One with Ten Powers.
These seven maṇḍalas
Are all square.
A cubit or half a cubit is acceptable,
And they are to be made every day.
At that time the reciter, in a hidden spot,
Destroys his wrongdoing every day.
Then the mantra practitioner, the sage, rises,
Carefully washes both hands,
And rinses with clean water.
Pure water, free of living creatures,
Stainless and clean,
He carefully takes up in a clean vessel.
From a great lake or a stream,
Or from a spring or a river,
Coming from a clean place,
Strained by hand so it is clean of creatures,
The mantra practitioner rinses again,
Always two or three times.
Then he should touch his mouth,
And likewise the openings of the ears,
The eyes and the nostrils,
And touch the crown of the head and the region of the navel.
The one who does virtue, five or seven times,
Should do everything according to the rite.
Perfect in the conduct of cleanliness,
The reciter, having become clean,
Takes up his alms bowl
And goes into the water.
Where a river stands,
Or likewise where it runs low,
Or where streams flow, and so on,
As a means of caring for the human world,
Likewise he should always recite mantra.
For that very reason the Chief of Sages,
With great diligence, has taught this.

By the one whose name is Kāśyapa, Long ago, at that time, upon that earth, In this king of Tārā's ritual manuals, For the welfare of the bhūtas, This mantra was fully proclaimed. The whole world, fallen into suffering, Poor, weary and emaciated, Those who were most deeply afflicted: It was spoken for their sake. Welfare itself for the bhūtas, For those who rely on it again and everywhere, For the sake of food for all the bhūtas, This secret mantra was supremely spoken: "I shall utter this secret mantra. All who rely upon the bodhisattvas, And you śrāvakas, listen! It vanquishes the grip of illness. Those tormented by the sickness of hunger, Whatever beings suffer from thirst, For the pacifying of all suffering, You who desire prosperity, listen!" Kāśyapa, the great light, The Chief of Sages, spoke thus. The afflicted ones, their minds gladdened, Made supplication to that all-pervading lord: "Great Sage, King of Dharma, Knower of Dharma, please explain the secret mantra. Be compassionate toward beings Who abide by the supreme commitment." When they had made this request, the Sage Proclaims the supreme mantra in full, With the voice of the kalaviṅka bird, The great drum and the thunder of clouds, With the voice of Brahmā, of great diligence, He who is the son of Brahmā, the supreme Victor: "Whatever beings have come here at all, The footless and the many-footed, The two-footed and the four-footed, All you hosts of bhūtas, listen! In short, for the benefit of all beings, I shall explain the mantra from which happiness arises. For beings and others of past, future and present Who have gathered here, I shall explain it concisely. You who desire prosperity, listen! namaḥ samanta buddhānāṃ apratihata śāsanānāṃ tadyathā oṃ gagane gagana gañjo ānaya sarva lahu lahu samaya manu smara ākarṣaṇe mā vilamba yathe pitaṃ saṃpādāya svāhā"

When the Blessed One Kāśyapa had spoken thus, he fell silent. In the interval during which the Perfectly Complete Buddha Kāśyapa proclaimed these words of the vidyā-mantra in full, the whole of the great sky became completely filled with clouds of food fit for the great. The whole expanse of the sky in all the worlds of the great trichiliocosm appeared to be completely covered with clouds of food. In accordance with one's intention, for the sake of what one desires, one should take it up and wash.

Then, rising once again,
He goes to the monastery or his dwelling.
Wherever he has properly stayed before,
Wherever he lives, there he should go.
Having gone there, the reciter, in that spot,
Should set down his alms bowl.
Then he should quickly rinse,
And likewise take up the bowl again.
The alms bowl may be of earth or of leaves,
Or of silver, or likewise of gold,
Or of copper, or even of bark.
He offers a food offering to the Teacher.
Having offered food to the Teacher,
Then again he offers to the king of vidyā-mantras.
If a single guest has come,
Or to one who is suffering, he gives what he can.
The food itself, in every case,
Is certainly to be eaten.
He should not give away too much.
Here the knower of mantra should not torment himself;
He should be fully endowed with awareness.
Keeping just the measure of the stomach,
The rest of the food is always for others.
One oppressed by hunger and thirst
Cannot accomplish the aim of the mantra;
If one eats too little or too much,
One cannot perform the approach for the mantra's aim.
For that very reason the Lord of Victors
Said to all embodied beings,
"Beings subsist by food."
That by which humans live,
And gods, asuras, gandharvas,
Nāgas, yakṣas, kinnaras,
Rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas,
Bhūtas, stars and planets:
Any that do not depend on food
Do not exist at all.
The coarse food that is always eaten
Is known as morsel food.
Beings whose food is subtle are set apart.
As the Tathāgata has taught,
Those who always have meditative concentration as their food
Move in form and stir;
And the gods of the formless realm as well
Feed on the fruit of absorption.
The beings of the intermediate existence, too,
Are well known as eaters of smells.
Likewise the beings of the desire realm
Eat food of many different kinds;
The gods and humans who are possessed of desire
Eat morsel food.
For that very reason the Lord of Sages
Taught, as a cause of the Dharma,
That "beings subsist by food."
These things are well known.
The reciter who is always diligent
Should know the right measure of food,
Because the approach of the vidyā
Rests upon this food.
For one whose conduct is unerring and pure,
Who is virtuous and lives in celibacy,
And who knows the right measure of food,
Accomplishment is not hard to find.
Just as, so that it can pull its load,
And so that the cart may last a long time,
One greases the hub of the cart's wheel,
So the mantra practitioner who knows mantra
Takes food for the sake of sustaining himself.
For the sake of nourishing the body,
The reciter should always nourish it,
For the sake of accomplishing the mantras,
And as a cause of the accumulations for awakening.
All food and,

and whatever foods they craved, those rained down upon them. With whatever foods they craved, for the act of eating and for the pacifying of the suffering of hunger; and for the thirsty, drink like the current of a river of water endowed with the eight qualities, to be drunk, also rained down there just as their minds desired. In that instant all beings had every sickness of hunger completely pacified and all thirst removed. The whole assembly, endowed with everything, was filled with wonder and satisfaction; they rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said and delighted in it, bowed their heads at the Blessed One's feet, and vanished right there. The Blessed One Kāśyapa, too, remained in the abode of the tathāgatas.

"I, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, also at that time rejoiced in what was taught in this rite of the king of ritual manuals, for the benefit of all beings, for the removal of hunger and thirst, and especially for the sake of all who recite mantra. First of all, the reciter should accomplish this mantra."

If he has no wish to go for alms, he should climb to the summit of a mountain and do seven hundred thousand recitations. Then he should eat the three white substances or drink milk. On that very mountain summit he should set up a middle-sized painted cloth of the noble Tārā as before, make a great offering, and make tormas and food offerings on a vast scale. Then, with this very secret mantra spoken by the Perfectly Complete Buddha Kāśyapa, he should kindle a fire with sticks of khadira wood and perform eight thousand fire offerings with moist udumbara sticks smeared with curd, honey and butter, or else with sticks of bilva wood.

Then, at midnight, a great black cloud and a whirlwind will come; he should not be afraid, and if he rises he should not go away. He should protect himself with the heart mantra of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā, seal the maṇḍala, and protect his companions too, as before. Then the black whirlwind will vanish, and a woman adorned with every ornament, with a garland of light illuminating all the directions, will sit before the practitioner and say, "O great being, rise! You have succeeded!" Then the practitioner should offer her water for the feet, scented water mixed with jasmine flowers. Then she will vanish right there. From that day on, she gives him, or twenty-five of his companions, whatever foods they desire, and she also provides every requisite they wish for. Then the practitioner should offer water for the feet and request her to depart. He should circumambulate the painted cloth three times, take up the painted cloth, bow to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, and then go to a mountain summit or an uninhabited place. There, once he himself or his companion has swept it, he should spread out what is to be spread out, and in that place perform the rites of traveling through the sky and the like.

Then the practitioner, as before, should sit upon a mat of kuśa grass, invite the middle-sized painted cloth to be present as before, kindle a fire with khadira wood, and for twenty-one days, in three sessions, with white lotus flowers smeared with curd, honey and butter, perform eight thousand fire offerings with the root vidyā, the heart mantra or the near-heart mantra, for the sake of any great rite, or for the sake of the one-syllable mantra. Then at midnight, at the close of the fire offering, he will see the Blessed Lady Tārā directly, and she will grant the supreme boon he desires: traveling through the sky, invisibility, the ground of a bodhisattva, the state of a pratyekabuddha, the five higher knowledges, long life, great kingship and great wealth, the favor of a great king, or the course of practice that follows the noble Avalokiteśvara. In short, she grants everything the mind desires. Whatever he asks for, she grants accordingly, and he obtains all the substances of accomplishment. She summons great beings; in short, she does everything just as it is requested. She also thoroughly purifies even the faults of karma that have heaped up. So spoke the Blessed One Śākyamuni.

Another rite of activity, which serves as the middling sādhana, is this. First of all, in a special place, a clean spot, a riverbank, or the shore of a river island, he should do everything as before, set up the painted cloth facing west, and himself face east. Sitting upon a mat of kuśa grass, he should apply everything in full as above and do six hundred thousand recitations in three sessions. When the recitation is complete, he should kindle the fire exactly as before and perform eight thousand fire offerings with cassia flowers mixed with white sandalwood or with saffron. If, at the close of the fire offering, the painted cloth moves, he will become a minister. If a radiance of light appears on the painted cloth, through that light comes kingship. If the painted cloth is stirred all over by garlands of flame, it is kingship of the family of the Four Great Kings. If fire appears on the painted cloth, it is lordship over the Thirty-Three, that is, the state of Śakra. If the painted cloth appears to teach the Dharma, it is the lordship of the three bodhisattvas. If the hand of the figure on the painted cloth touches the crown of his head, he will gradually attain the five higher knowledges, the realization of the seven grounds, and the certainty of the ten powers.

Then the practitioner, having accomplished the mantra spoken by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, should, by that very attainment of the means of dispelling hunger and thirst, and by that very rite, apply himself diligently to the procedures of the rite that is the means of accomplishing the aims of the vidyā conduct concerning requisites; otherwise he will not succeed. Following in this way, step by step, the conduct of mantra, in short he diligently and definitely accomplishes it, and accomplishes the special substances, medicines and requisites, and the precious jewels, just as was definitively taught before.

The knower of mantra, the reciter of mantra,
Intent upon the rite that has been explained,
The mantra practitioner, at that time, in that place,
Having eaten food from pure people,
With a joyful mind
And with his senses fully satisfied,
Always takes up what remains in his bowl,
And with a good mind goes to a clean river.
Having set it down in a solitary spot,
The one who keeps the vows gives it to the animals.
Having given suitably to the animals,
He carefully washes his bowl.
What is to be done with the bowl's remainder:
Food without leavings and free of odor
The Sage has called the bowl's remainder.
In the vessel used for begging
One does not eat the food there;
Food, fruits and substances
Should never be eaten there.
Nor should one eat from lotus petals,
Or from what comes from the blue lotus;
Those with sweet fragrance are rejected,
And the mantra practitioner does not eat from them.

Nor should the mantra practitioner eat from the kumuda,
Or from what comes from the plakṣa or the udumbara,
Nor yet from the leaves of the pāṭī,
Nor from what comes from thorny branches in the mountain wilds,
Nor on the leaves of the mango either;
Likewise from what comes from the sāṭala,
From sāla leaves, from the śirīṣa,
And from what comes from the bodhi tree;
The tree beneath which the Blessed One, the Buddha,
The Lion of the Śākyas, sat:
That tree should be carefully avoided.
Nor on the branches of that tree,
Nor on the nāgakesara tree either:
On these one should never eat at all.
The wise avoid all of them by every means.
A hut of leaves of the Sage
Should never be trodden on out of folly;
The mantra practitioner's pledge would be broken.
Food should be eaten on leaves
Other than those leaves.
Earthenware and copper are prescribed,
Likewise what is made of gold and silver,
And what is made of crystal and of stone;
Having likewise taken one's food,
The mantra practitioner should always eat from these.
One should not eat on the back of a leaf,
Nor likewise in the palm of the hand.
The sons of the One with Ten Powers,
The pratyekabuddhas who are like the rhinoceros,
The chief śrāvakas of the Tathāgata:
Other leaves, and the food offered to them,
The reciter should avoid.
Nor should he tread on written letters with his feet.
Various foods and oil cakes,
And likewise drinks and foods,
The mantra practitioner should take with care.
All the food offerings
Offered to the Victors and the supreme Victors,
And likewise to the śrāvakas, the supreme persons,
And to the Three Jewels,
The reciter should always avoid.
For an embodied being who takes even a little,
His mantras will not succeed because of it,
Let alone every kind of good fortune
And lasting glory.
One who eats the food offerings and tormas
Of the Victor's followers and of Śiva's followers,
Then none of his rites will succeed.
One who is pure, learned and endowed with moral discipline,
Compassionate and engaged in compassionate deeds,
Delighting in the conduct of cleanliness,
Accomplishes vidyā-mantras in every way.
Food that has been given to other beings
The reciter should not eat.
Nor should he eat other food
That has not been carefully examined by others.
Food that is given to oneself
Should be accepted, even if it is only a little.
For the knower of mantra who proceeds in this way,
His accomplishment, the enemy of evil,
Comes to be brought to full completion.
The reciter who by this rite
Keeps the observance of taking food
Is well praised by the sages.
In accomplishing all mantras,
In brief, by seeing the rite,
It applies to all eating and to all actions.

Then I shall explain still more.
The mantra purifies everything.
Then the reciter should rinse with water,
And at that time recite this mantra.
Then the mantra practitioner, having recited
The body-purifying mantra seven times, says:
"Hosts of bhūtas and gods, here
Listen to its meaning in full!"
Having touched the whole body with water,
The sage should recite this mantra:

namaḥ sarva buddhānāṃ aprahihata śāsanānāṃ tadyathā oṃ sarva kilbiṣa nāśani nāśaya sarva duṣṭa prayuktaṃ samaya manusmara hūṃ jaḥ svāhā

When partaking of any other food allowed by the training, one should first consecrate it by reciting this mantra over it seven times, and then partake of it. Having eaten, one should rinse with water as before and smear it on the whole body, beginning with the crown of the head, and then one should rest. One rests for half a moment or for one watch.

Then, having bowed to the painted image and to all the buddhas, one should read the volumes of the true Dharma: the noble Perfection of Wisdom, the noble Samādhi of the Moon Lamp, the noble Ten Grounds, the noble Sublime Golden Light, the noble Great Peacock, and the noble Ratnaketu Dhāraṇī; one should read any one of these or of others besides. This is for about a quarter of the length of the day. Then, having become fully calm, one may read as one wishes. Having folded up the volume, one should put on clean clothes and bow to the true Dharma. Then, for the sake of bathing, one goes to the bank of a river or to a large pool that can be entered. Having drawn water free of living creatures and consecrated it by reciting over it seven times, one should cast it into the water with this vidyā. What is it?

namaḥ samanta buddhānāṃ apratihata śāsanānāṃ tadyathā oṃ sarva duṣṭa staṃbhaya hūṃ nadī vara dhariṇe samaya manusmara phaṭ phaṭ svāhā

Having made protection with this, it serves for binding the directions, for the companions, for binding the maṇḍala, for binding the mouth, and for summoning all the wicked and the extremely wicked. For binding obstructors too, one recites it seven times over a thread and ties it around the waist, and thereby everything is completely bound. At all times of recitation and all times of bathing, in order to destroy wicked obstructors and for complete pacification, this mantra should be recited one thousand times. Then all the rites are performed. One should be set upon a lotus seat, endowed with the great mudrā. In all the rites, nothing whatever will turn out otherwise.

Then the practitioner should take powders made of earth and the like and bathe as is comfortable, bathing with water free of living creatures. In everything, in all actions, it should be done only with what is free of living creatures. Then, having bathed, one should anoint oneself with an earthen substance or with other perfumes of pleasant fragrance, and with special requisites. One should not throw spittle, excrement, urine and the like into the water. Nor should one play in it.

Endowed with compassion, one should contemplate oneself and all sentient beings individually: as selfless, as empty, as possessed of suffering, as choked by suffering, as overwhelmed by feelings, as beings possessed of the suffering of bondage that arises like waves. Seeing these beings, who are thus without practice, as the ones whose mass of suffering from poison, cutting, falling, scattering, terror and the like the knower of mantra is to bring to cessation in just that way, as dwelling in the dense ocean of saṃsāra, and considering them as without a resting place, without a protector, without a refuge, and of extremely lowly mind, the meditator, standing in water up to the neck or up to the navel, should hold the mind one-pointedly within that very water.

First of all, one should imagine a great lotus on whose petals are great flowers, beautified by the leaves of a great lotus and lovely to behold. It has a stalk made of precious beryl, lotus filaments made of the precious madaka, and a well-opened stem made of crystal, and it is beautified by the crystal and ruby flowers that grow along it. Upon it is a lion throne beautified by many jewels and covered with a pair of fine cloths.

One should imagine the Blessed One, the Buddha, seated upon it. He is seated teaching the Dharma, golden in color, adorned with a maṇḍala of light pervaded all around by garlands of blazing light, vast like the sky, as if supremely painted, seated with legs crossed. On his right is the noble Avalokiteśvara, endowed with the supreme of all aspects, seated on a great lotus seat and holding a yak-tail whisk, placed at the side where the Blessed One sits; his body is reddish yellow, like the color of ground saffron. On the left is the noble Mahāsthāmaprāpta, white like an autumn cloud, holding a yak-tail whisk in his hand.

Likewise there are the eight bodhisattvas: the noble Maitreya, Samantabhadra, Kṣitigarbha, Gaganagañja, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, the noble Mañjuśrī, the noble Vajrapāṇi, and the one called Sudhana. To the right of these ten bodhisattvas one should imagine eight pratyekabuddhas: Candana, Gandhamādana, Ketu, Sitaketu, Desire, Near Desire, Nemi, and Nemi; these are the eight. In that same place are eight great śrāvakas, namely the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the noble Śāriputra, Gavāṃpati, Bharadvāja Piṇḍola, Pilindavatsa, the noble Rāhula, the noble Mahākāśyapa, and the noble Ānanda. Near these great śrāvakas one should visualize an infinite saṅgha of monks. Near the pratyekabuddhas one should visualize infinite pratyekabuddhas. At the place of the eight bodhisattvas, too, one should visualize an infinite saṅgha of bodhisattvas. Likewise, all around, one should visualize the maṇḍala of the retinue as possessed of a great maṇḍala of retinue.

The great bodhisattva himself, while standing in water up to the navel, should make offering to the Blessed One with a shower of flowers as large as Mount Meru, lying in vast, great heaps, of many kinds of divine and human flowers: māndārava flowers and great māndārava flowers, lotuses and great lotuses, dhānuskārika, parṣika, and indravara flowers of many kinds. And to all the noble śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and to the bodhisattvas he should make offerings of powders, robes, parasols, victory banners and pennants, and of many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of niyutas of delightful divine and human lamps. Likewise he should present tormas, incense, food offerings, offerings, honors and the like, the requisites needed by gods and humans.

One should visualize rays of light streaming forth from the ūrṇā hair between the eyebrows of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, illuminating oneself and all the directions. As soon as the meditator enters this meditative concentration, he obtains the fruit of Brahmā's merit. He will certainly become directed toward supreme awakening.

Meditative concentrations such as this
Were taught by the supreme beings of the world.
For the well-being of all bhūtas,
And for the benefit of mantra practitioners,
At that time the chief of the first concentrations,
For the benefit of all mantra practitioners,
Was taught for the sake of sentient beings.
Then the maṇḍala of the seventh supreme Sage
Shall be explained in detail.
The Sage taught it as the first,
And the maṇḍala of the second,
And the third, other than these.
In the first is the supreme accomplishment;
In the middling, likewise, others;
In the lesser, minor things are accomplished:
So the supreme Sage has definitively taught.
Likewise the meditations on the painted image
Are superior, middling and lesser,
And all of them destroy evil.
Besides these, the wise
Should practice the kinds of meditative concentration.
If one abides firmly in that concentration,
The mantras will succeed for him.
The rite has been explained as one wishes.
The reciter, having cultivated meditative concentration,
Having offered there the mantra's guest water,
Requests the deities to depart as they please.
Having come out of that body of water,
He then goes as is comfortable.
In the place prescribed before,
Well calmed by seeing the rite,
The mantra practitioner recites the secret mantra there,
Just as was stated earlier.
His own deity, who was invited,
He there requests with mantra to depart.
Then, having protected himself
And likewise his companions,
He knows that very thing through wholesome action,
And delights in and bows to the acts of the rite.
With many kinds of praise and offering,
Having praised in every way the supreme persons,
With his own mantra he praises the Protector,
The śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas like the rhinoceros,
And the bodhisattvas, the great beings,
Able to care for the three worlds.
Then the reciter of secret mantra
Rises again from that seat,
And having gone to a distant place,
Avoiding the direction of the outer wind,
He casts away mucus and spittle,
And likewise excrement and urine.
By day he faces the north,
And at night he faces the south.
There the reciter of mantra
Should never think about his aims.
There he should not do the recitation
Of the mantras said to perform his rites.
Having gone, by night or at other times,
The good mantra practitioner then sits on the ground,
And rinses with pure water.
He should put the hem of a clean cloth into the water.
With seven lumps of earth
He carefully washes his feet;
Having taken seven applications thoroughly,
For excrement there are thirty applications;
For the hands, at both ends,
And likewise for spitting,
And for mucus, two each in the same way.

Then one should carefully rinse with water.
In a spot that has gone far from the dwelling,
Having likewise gone as far as a sound carries,
In an open space, by a road or the like,
Then elsewhere, as one wishes,
Outside, at the southern edge,
Where there is no water and no precipice,
And likewise where it is covered with sand,
Avoiding rivers and avoiding their banks too,
Carefully avoiding unclean water,
Hidden and thoroughly cleansed,
And avoiding the outlying regions,
Having gone to a spot that is utterly secluded,
The mantra practitioner should discard the impurities.
The reciter, knowing the proper time,
Does not follow his urges as he pleases.
Then, going to a clean spot,
Likewise at the outskirts, having done
The business of excrement
And of urine,
There, with his body at ease,
With both parts covered and hidden,
In a spot where there are no people,
He should accomplish the king of secret mantras.
Likewise, in all such places,
On mountains and in thickets,
In delightful dwellings at the outskirts,
And likewise free of the vicious beings
Whom the Victor rejected,
One accomplishes all the kings of secret mantra.
In a land whose king is righteous,
Where people delight in clean conduct
And are respectful to mother and father,
Where the twice-born castes have left,
The accomplishment of the deities will be attained.
It is in that place, and not elsewhere.
The delightful, fortunate banks of the Bhagīrathī,
The very beautiful Yamunā,
The Sindhu, the Narmadā, the Vakṣu,
The pure banks of the Candrabhāgā,
The Kāverī and the Sarasvatī,
And the great river Śītā:
These are fields of accomplishment, and no others,
So the sons of the One with Ten Powers have explained.
The fields that the One with Ten Powers spoke of:
The pathless mountains of the north,
Kashmir and China,
Nepal, and likewise Mangyul,
Great China and Khotan:
All of these without exception are fields of accomplishment.
Whatever mountains and rivers
Lie in the northern direction
Are declared to be lands of merit,
Where barley and wheat are eaten.
Wherever sentient beings are compassionate,
There accomplishment always comes.
Śrīparvata, the great rocky mountain,
Which lies in the southern land,
And the glorious stūpa of Dhānyakaṭaka,
Which holds the relics of the Victor on earth:
There one should accomplish mantras,
Swiftly, every rite and every rite.
The Vajrāsana and the great stūpa,
The beautiful place of the wheel of Dharma,
And where the chief of Sages passed into peace:
There too one should look for accomplishment.
The stūpa of the descent from the gods,
Sāpakṣe, and the place of the great miracle,
The supreme town called Kapilavastu,
And there in the Lumbinī grove where he was born:
The king of secret mantras will succeed there.
On Vulture Peak, which the Victor
Praised and greatly lauded,
And likewise the rock and the Cool Grove,
The supreme town called Kusuma,
Likewise ever the city of Kāśī,
Mathurā and Kanyakubja,
The city of Ujjayinī on earth,
Likewise the stūpa at Vaiśālī,
Ever Mithilā on earth,
The chief towns and cities,
And other places where Victors appear:
In these lands of merit, highly praised,
In them one accomplishes siddhi.
Lands other than these,
Villages, regions and mountains,
Sites and chief towns,
That lie by milk or by flowing water:
There, keeping to solitude,
One will delight in recitation and fire offering.
In places without a roof,
And always in empty houses,
One should first perform the approach.
The rites that accord with the mantras,
The mantra practitioner, always in the central land,
Should properly be intent on mantra recitation.
Fully engaged in recitation, always diligent,
Accustomed to mantra, knowledge and giving,
Practicing moral discipline, very steadfast,
Delighting in benefiting all beings,
With faith in the conduct of mantra,
The one who keeps the observances recites as before.
In a clean land, being cleanly,
Free of barbarians and thieves.
There one remains for a great eon,
Because of being parted from the light of the pledge;
In the unbearable darkness of hell
Childish people are cooked.
Those who disparage the true Dharma,
Who are obscured by the darkness of ignorance,
Or who are childish in wisdom,
Deluded and with perverse pride,
Who despise the king of vidyās,
Will fall into unbearable hell.
Therefore one should not do evil;
Speaking falsely is also reprehensible.
Contempt for the true Dharma
And wrong views are reprehensible.
Therefore, always having faith,
Always rely on the rites of secret mantra.
Speaking the truth and knowing the Dharma,
Always benefiting sentient beings,
The knower of mantra relies on mantra,
And his accomplishment is certain.
With the supreme, the middling and the lowest,
One performs rites of many kinds.
Rites are performed through actions.
Through actions that are always beneficial,
Being properly endowed with the rites of action,
One will always succeed in them.
For the aim of the task and for every aim,
One should perform rites of many kinds.
Whatever, for the task's sake, is not a task
Should be applied to the work of the task.
The purpose of acts that bear fruit
Should always be carried out as an act.
Action, rite and fruit:
From action, rite and fruit always come.
What lacks fruit becomes fruit,
And fruit itself always bears fruit.
What lacks fruit is itself fruitful;
All things, indeed, bear fruit.
The yogin's mantra is to be accomplished:
Even one lacking proper application,
The one who lacks it and the one endowed with it both accomplish.
Without what is to be accomplished and one who accomplishes,
There is no accomplishment in it.
All substances of accomplishment
Are contrary to the cause of accomplishment.
When the mantra's accomplishment is not accomplished,
The mantra is the cause that accomplishes it.
From the wish to act
The desired rite becomes clear.
In all rites that are not rites,
One should not perform the tantra of rites.
Rites endowed with the meaning of mantra and tantra
Should all be undertaken.
A rite driven by eagerness for what is begun and for beginning
Should not be undertaken.

Mantras whose work has not been undertaken
Will not succeed for any embodied being.
This was taught of old by the Chief of Sages,
Who cares for all sentient beings:
The true vow of the Victor's sons,
Taught by the speaker of secret mantra.
The practitioner knows all the mantras,
And in this king of ritual manuals the words
Are taught in the manner of mantra.
The path that has become the cause of awakening
Accomplishes all mantras themselves;
It becomes equal to knowledge.
Before long, then,
The wise one will gain accomplishment.
For the pacification of all bhūtas
It was proclaimed by all the buddhas.
By this path of the way of secret mantra,
Which goes to the city of nirvāṇa,
And likewise ever the path of awakening,
All the aims of the Dharma are perfected.
Its ultimate ally
Is first to abide as the Buddha himself.
Likewise, here, spontaneously,
One gains accomplishment together with its fruit.
Knowing the various rites and teachings,
One will put the mantras to work.
Moral discipline, meditative concentration and the liberations:
These are obtained in brief.
That it accomplishes siddhi and every aim
Was taught by the chief Victor.
The person who gains the aim of the feet
And abides in an excellent destiny,
And likewise ever the chief of yakṣas;
The lowest is the cause of kingship.
Of the worlds of the asuras and the gods,
And likewise lordship over them:
The mantra practitioner will obtain them all.
He will perform acts that bear fruit.
Properly endowed with the conduct of cleanliness,
Always delighting in moral discipline and meditative concentration:
So the mantras have been taught in full.
Then the mantra practitioner should recite the mantras.
The mantra practitioner who wishes for wealth
Performs rites of many kinds,
And likewise the supreme, the middling
And the lowest are to be done.
By the lowest, enjoyments increase;
By the middling, a higher embodiment;
And by the supreme, ascent:
These the reciter always obtains.
At the end of recitation the mantra practitioner rests,
And should observe for as long as the time lasts.
When the time for recitation comes,
Then the practice is to be done there,
And likewise one accomplishes the rites.

By constantly reciting in this way, a person exhausts his own evil. Whatever rite of former karma the mantra practitioner has performed, which remains to be accomplished over a succession of births, and likewise what will be found in his collection of karma, when it arises, through reciting mantra it serves again to exhaust the evil of the reciter of mantra; that karma is destroyed and the mantra becomes accomplished. Likewise, through supreme, middling and lowest worldly offerings and recitation, evil is exhausted without remainder, and all the evil that has filled the succession of births is destroyed. Through reciting the mantras of the tathāgatas, one becomes adorned with ornaments of many kinds on one's body, delighted by the presence of the sages, and renowned for every good quality; one becomes the king who dwells in the abode of the yakṣas, and is always endowed with the attainment of the siddhi of every aim.

From the Root Ritual Manual of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā, Ūrdhvajaṭā, from the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, the Avataṃsaka, a Great Vehicle sūtra of vast extent: the ninth chapter, the rite of the middling painting, is complete.

Then again the Blessed One Śākyamuni looked upon the maṇḍala of the entire assembly and spoke to the bodhisattva, the great being, the noble Avalokiteśvara: "Great bodhisattva, listen! Your followers of vidyā-mantra strive for the benefit of all sentient beings. Listen well to the vidyā-mantra that sentient beings are to recite, the rite of the rosary with which they are to count it, the rite of the means of accomplishment common to all the tantras, the rite for all mantras, and hold it well in mind. I shall explain it."

When he had spoken thus, the great being said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, excellent, excellent! Blessed One, out of compassion for us, please take this up and teach it, for the sake of the sentient beings who have fully entered into the conduct and the pledges of all vidyā-mantras, and for the benefit of all sentient beings."

When he had made this request, the Blessed One said this to the bodhisattva, the great being Avalokiteśvara: "Great being, I shall explain its divisions in detail. Listen! What is it by which one strives earnestly in the conduct of all mantras and accomplishes every aim of sentient beings? First of all, what becomes the mantra is:

namaḥ sarva budhānāṃ acintyaddhūta rūpināṃ acintyaddhuta rūpināṃ tadyathā oṃ kuru kuru sarva artha sādhāya sarva duṣṭa vimohani gaganābalaṃbe viśodhāya svāhā

With this vidyā one should perform the rites for all rosaries. One should perform the rites of purifying, enlivening, taking, setting in motion and the like.

First, at the tree for the rosary,
Having consecrated it with this
Thirty-seven times,
The one who keeps the observances should make protection.
Having slept one night there,
One should examine one's dreams.
A nonhuman, complete in form,
Ugly, baring its fangs fiercely,
Says to the mantra practitioner,
'Blessed one, take it as you wish.'
The practitioner, rising at dawn,
Goes to that tree.
If even in a dream one does not see
That ugly form baring its great fangs,
The mantra practitioner should leave that tree
And go somewhere else.
First is the rudrākṣa;
Other than that, the Indra tree;
The bodetse is also desirable.
Moreover, one should climb a fruit-bearing tree
Together with a companion
Accomplished and skilled in climbing trees.
If one has no companion,
One should climb it oneself.
Having climbed to where the fruit is on the upper branches,
The one of excellent observances,
Always heedful there,
Takes the fruit from the upper branches.
One should apply it well to the upper level.
The upper is for supreme accomplishment,
So the supreme person has taught;
The middle is for middling accomplishment,
And the lowest is for the lower."

Fruits that creatures have not spoiled:
These one should properly take.
Those gained from the western branch
Should be employed as the cause of substances.
The yakṣiṇīs of the north and the like:
These summon the gods together.
The act of summoning that is explained
Is for pacification, for the sake of all.
War between the gods and the asuras,
Kinnaras and rākṣasas,
Bring about desires of many kinds.
For the flourishing of all bhūtas,
The rites that bear fruit
Accomplish the whole of conduct.
The branches on the eastern side
And the fruits that grow there,
If likewise taken with care,
Are the cause of the aim of long life;
Through mantra they always produce
The fruits of accomplishment of many kinds.
Whatever branch grows toward the south,
Full of leaves,
Steals the life of sentient beings;
The reciter should carefully avoid it.
Wherever fruit is declared
On branches that lean to the south,
In that direction lies the destruction
Of enemies' lives and the splitting of lineages,
The cause of much that is without merit;
The reciter carefully avoids it.
Whatever fruits are proclaimed
To grow on branches that hang down below:
Through them one goes beneath the earth,
Where the asuras dwell.
Having taken those fruit-bearing garlands,
Which are well proclaimed,
On a creeper that goes downward,
One then goes beneath the earth.
Having entered there, the reciter
Attains there the very bliss of the gods.
Joined with the daughters of the asuras,
He remains there for an eon.
Having taken all the fruits for the rosary,
The reciter then performs recitation.
Having made protection together with it,
He then goes as is comfortable.
In that distant place,
In that clean spot, the mantra practitioner
Should likewise always stay,
And should arrange the rosary that has been produced.
With diligence he takes the rosary fruits,
And then thoroughly purifies them.
That is known as enlivening the rosary.
Three, seven, eight and one,
And twenty-one times,
The knower of mantra should purify it there.
Always with the previous mantra,
Recited eight or seven times:
After that it is considered pure.
With a well-praised lotus fiber,
And thread spun by a girl,
Threefold and with five strands,
The one who keeps the observances makes the rosary cord.
The one who knows the reality of mantra strings it.
The fruits are small and round,
Always without holes made by creatures,
Their parts unimpaired and unspoiled,
Beautiful and of pleasing color,
Without holes and without cracks,
Round beads just as they should be:
Likewise rudrākṣa,
Bodetse and intrakṣa,
The fruits always even and beautiful.
When there is excellent fruit,
The mantra practitioner, supremely diligent,
Should carefully string the rosary.
Of gold, or else of silver,
Or made of gems and crystal,
Of pearl, of conch, of musāra,
And of coral one may make them too:
Rosaries of many kinds are to be made.
Moreover, fine rosaries
Made of precious substances are to be made,
And those with rosaries of beads
Of herbs that grow from the earth
Should string the thread in meditative equipoise.
Moreover, some beads,
Or those made of fruits or of minerals,
Strung with the tip of kuśa grass,
The reciter should also make with care.
One hundred and eight, or twenty-five,
Or fifty: these are middling.
The mantra practitioner, in meditative equipoise,
Should string the measures of fruits.
One thousand and eight is also to be made;
This rosary is the superior one.
These four kinds of rosary
The mantra practitioner should always string.
Then, having strung it, the mantras,
With three or two marker beads,
And with rings made of brass,
And likewise of gold and of silver,
And then with rings made of copper,
One should string the rosary throughout.
Then at the end one should make an eyelet,
And arrange them on it in order.
One should carefully wind it beautifully.
Having made it clearly
The abode of all the buddhas without exception,
It is then seen as like a maṇḍala.
Like the shape of a snake's hood,
It is adorned by being wound around.
It is like strings of pearls,
Fashioned as a necklace.
Then, at the edge of a wholesome stream,
Having bathed in the stainless water,
Having bathed in due order,
One should rise from the place of water.
Likewise one should diligently rinse.
Having taken the rosary thread,
One washes it thoroughly with the five products of the cow;
Having washed it thoroughly with powdered earth,
On a clean cloth, with fragrant scent,
One anoints it thereafter,
And with a highly praised color,
White sandalwood and saffron,
One should carefully wash it with warm water.
Likewise both will go.
Having gone to the appropriate place,
Where there is the middling painting,
Of the supreme Victor, the Chief of Sages,
The Lion of the Śākyas, supreme among humans,
Or likewise an image of the Teacher,
Or one that holds the relics of the Victor on earth,
One places it before that object of offering.
Having set it down near it,
Then, in its presence,
Abiding in the pledge, one recites
One thousand and eight times,
Or else one hundred
Together with eight.
Having observed a fast for a day and a night,
One offers the rosary to the seventh Sage.
One should recite as before,
Making the amount equal to that.
Then one recites fully on the rosary.
Staying there that very night,
On ground strewn with kuśa grass,
The knower of mantra should sleep there.
Whatever dreams one sees,
If one sees an auspicious dream,
The dream is a definite indication,
And one should accomplish siddhi by it.
If in a dream one sees
Buddhas, śrāvakas, or those like the rhinoceros,
The mantra practitioner will succeed, with its fruit;
One should certainly perform its rite.
One sees the form of a monk,
Or various beautiful images of brahmins:
If one sees that dream,
One should likewise offer the rosary.
The one who accomplishes all the aims of mantra
Will likewise succeed without doubt.

From the Root Ritual Manual of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā, Ūrdhvajaṭā, from the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, the Avataṃsaka, a Great Vehicle sūtra of vast extent: from the chapter on the rite of the middling painting, the tenth chapter, the chapter on the rite of the rosary, is complete.

Then once again the Blessed One Śākyamuni looked out over the great maṇḍala of the assembly, complete in every respect, and said to the great bodhisattva, the noble Avalokiteśvara: "Great being, there is the special rite that completes your chapter on the knowledge mantras (vidyāmantras), and the accomplishment of the knowledge mantra that applies the work of the fire offering. Within the special rite for making use of the fire, what is it that beings who strive in the conduct of the knowledge mantras apply and abide in? The great secret of the collection of knowledge mantras is this: tadyathā oṃ tiṣṭha hari piṅgale hi rakṣa di hi da dā dī pā ya hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. Avalokiteśvara, this supreme heart mantra performs every action and grants every desire. First of all, the practitioner, reciting this heart mantra of the fire once, should offer three oblations of ghee into the fire as a fire offering; thereby the fire god will have been invited. Applying it in the same way, for pacifying, increasing, and fierce rites, there are three kinds of kindling sticks.

For pacifying, wood of the aśoka tree,
Especially when it is still moist,
A span or about a cubit long,
Or a span with three finger-widths more:
Know well the proper form of the sticks.
This is the rite to be performed.
Without holes and without cracks,
Likewise resembling a parrot's wing,
Green or white in color;
Black in color should be avoided.
Avoid those eaten by worms;
Offer those that have no holes.
Further, those not of the finest color,
And those of inferior quality, are rejected.
They may be dry or moist;
At that time one should begin.
Not rotten and not crooked,
And those too long should be avoided.

Then, when making the hearth,
Square on every side,
Dig carefully downward
To a measure of four cubits,
Or three cubits, or two,
Or likewise just one cubit;
Always free of living creatures,
And well filled with sand.
Then a rim shaped like a lotus,
Circular all around;
Or else, carefully, a square one
Made with three tiers.
For pacifying and increasing rites
This too has been rightly proclaimed.
For fierce rites, in the center of the ground
Make a vajra, two-pronged
Or three-pronged.
The hearth is two cubits across.
In a clean place smooth it likewise.
Likewise practice on a riverbank,
In places by a solitary tree,
In charnel grounds and empty houses:
There one should properly begin the fire offering.
Likewise on mountain peaks,
In empty temples,
And likewise in great wildernesses:
Whatever places of practice
The supreme person has taught,
For all the rites of fire offering
These have been taught as the sites.
Seated on a mat of kuśa grass
A cubit in size,
There the knower of mantra in particular
Should perform the work of the fire offering.
By abiding firmly in that very place,
Accomplishment comes swiftly, without doubt.
Facing east or north,
Perform the pacifying and the increasing rites.
The south is for the ways of fierce rites;
The mantra practitioner should avoid it.
Facing east brings the accomplishment of pacifying;
For increasing, too, face north.
Thus at all times one should
Undertake the recitation of the knowledge mantra.
With bilva, arka, plakṣa,
And nyagrodha, perform the increasing rites.
The wood of fierce rites, which is dry,
And the hot, the sour, and the sharp:
All these should be avoided;
The sages have always forbidden them.
For pacifying and increasing rites,
Moist wood is most auspicious.
Likewise for fierce rites, dry wood,
And the hot, the sour, and the sharp.
If those kindling sticks are not to be had,
One should always regard other wood as them.
They should be examined for two tips.

Green and glossy and even,
Like the neck of a peacock:
With kuśa grass of such a kind,
Kuśa all around the perimeter
Should always be spread;
For pacifying and increasing rites,
With grass the color of emerald.
Likewise, it is with dry grass always
That evil deeds are done;
Here the supreme Victor has forbidden it.
With stainless, pure water,
Always free of insects,
Then sprinkle all around.
Circling to the right,
One should diligently kindle the fire.
Perform the ablution according to the rite.
With the roots of clean grass
Make a lamp of proper measure;
Then, forming a fist,
Carefully kindle the fire.
Not with the breath of the mouth,
Nor ever with the hem of a garment;
The lower robe and upper robe are to be avoided.
Fanning with another cloth,
Or with the wind of the hand,
Is not approved.
With a clean fan, likewise with a cloth,
Or with a jeweled fan, one should fan it.
When by this the wind rightly arises
And the fire has been made even,
The knower of mantra should kindle the fire.
Composed in equipoise for the fire offering,
Then, with the left hand,
Having sprinkled there,
There, with the ghee of a cow,
One should offer three oblations.
Then, after that, pay homage
To all the buddhas, the protectors,
And to one's own mantra, the lord of mantra;
Then pay homage as one wishes.
At that time, reciting the mantra
Of the heart of the fire a hundred times,
The diligent one, with fragrant flowers,
Should always invite the fire.
Having always invited it, the knower of mantra,
Skilled in the rite of the site, offers seat and abode
With that mantra, and with no other.
Kindling sticks mixed with curd and ghee
And smeared with honey:
Of these, make the fire offering three times.
For increase, with mantra and action,
With garlands of flame blazing all around,
Where it is stirred up, apply them without fail;
Imagine the thirsty one satisfied.
In pacifying and increasing rites,
By the one who knows the secret mantra,
The form of the deity is delighted.

For fierce rites, one should visualize a form
Other than the common deities
That are certain to appear.
In due order, here in the hearth,
With whatever flowers are to be found,
And reciting seven times over the ghee,
Then invite the deity in that manner.
When it has been invited once again,
By firm establishment both remain.
Kindling sticks mixed with the substances,
Ghee and honey in equal measure as taught,
And likewise mixed with curd:
To the count of a thousand or a hundred thousand,
Or a hundred and eight, one should always offer.
Likewise the mantra practitioner, holding the knowledge mantra,
Recites it once for each and casts it into the fire.
With garlands of blazing fire,
And likewise with flames become one,
Perform the fire offering of the pacifying rite.
When it is smokeless, the increasing rite.
Fierce rites with smoke
Have been censured and rejected by the Victor.
When the fire takes on its proper color,
Apply the work of the fire offering.
For pacifying, the color white
Is always praised by the supreme Victor.
If one makes the fire offering with white fire,
The mantras will succeed for that one.
Likewise the color white is always
Wished for by one who seeks the accomplishment of increase.
Black, the color of smoke,
And tawny too are inauspicious.
Through the changing of the three colors,
These are the three kinds of accomplishment.
Another color, the color of clouds,
Or again, if it stays fixed on the ground there,
For that mantra practitioner there is no accomplishment.
If one sees colors like these,
Or a fire of many varied colors
Blazing, then
One should begin the rites over again,
And the recitation is to be done once more.
If the mantra has succeeded,
Having seen this in the rite,
Engage again in the fire offering.
For both the dismissal and the invitation
One should recite the mantra of the fire.
And having examined it carefully beforehand,
Request this maṇḍala to depart.
The acts of invitation,
And the other acts done there as well,
Are to be performed with that same mantra.
The practice of the fire, and likewise the image,
Should be undertaken in the presence of the painting.
That the mantras succeed there
Was taught by the tathāgatas of the past.
The rites praised by the Victor
Are all to be performed right there.
The other rites that are done,
Evil rites in particular,
Are those the supreme Victor reviles,
That go against the world and are censured.

Rising aloft, universal sovereignty, The grounds of the bodhisattvas, Likewise the five superknowledges, And the possession of worldly godhood are accomplished. One always diligent with the painting, Skilled in the work of the fire offering, Becomes a lord of the underworld, Or else moves through the sky. The gods above the earth and the yakṣas, And the yakṣiṇīs, one always summons; Lordship of a kingdom, Of a country, or of a town; Vidyādharas and asuras: One brings all beings under one's power And summons all the bhūtas. If the great beings, the great-souled, The bodhisattvas, the great beings, Who rest firmly on the ten grounds, Are summoned by the work of the fire offering, What need is there to speak of humans on the earth? Likewise chieftains and lords, And above all the lords of the world, And all the bhūtas, one brings fully under one's power. Likewise lords of men, For the sake of power over all the bhūtas, Or one becomes equal to a king upon the earth. Likewise, always, in all rites, Do everything by means of the fire offering. The one who is diligent in every way Should rightly practice all the rites; For that purpose one should surely accomplish them. The rite for glory is supreme; It accomplishes the middling as well, And the lesser too. Likewise all the substances Are said to be accomplished in the same way. By engaging in the work of the fire offering, One sees accomplishment together with its fruit. Binding the mudrā, and the knowledge mantra, Should always be done in all the rites. By engaging in the work of the fire offering, One comes to be protected. Then one should recite this mantra; In the rites it is always Recited seven times or eight: namaḥ sarva buddha bodhi satvā nāṃ a pra ti ha ta ga ti ma ga tā nāṃ tadya thā oṃ jvā la tiṣ tha hūṃ ru ru bi śva sambha be svā hā

With this application of the mantra,
One should recite it again over the wood,
Twice or seven times,
And that knower of mantra makes the fire offering into the fire.
Flowers, incense, and perfumes,
In short, everything,
With waters over which the secret mantra has been recited,
With this very mantra, one should sprinkle.
Then, for all the rites,
One should begin the ritual by this means.
For all the rites,
Proceed with the same application as before.
Having bound the earlier mudrā, the one with tresses,
The renowned great mudrā,
Protection will have been made; then
The reciter, with the single knowledge mantra,
Should begin all the rites.
For one skilled in the causes of accomplishment,
If auspicious signs are seen,
If auspicious sounds are always heard,
Then the fruit of the mantra
Will grant the supreme, just as one wishes.
First, by applying oneself to the rite
And engaging in the causes of the mantra,
Whether fruitless or bearing fruit,
That accomplishment shall be told.
If the sound of victory, or of the paṭaha drum,
Or the sound of the great drum is heard,
O diligent one, it is the all-pervading accomplishment;
Rely rightly on the work of the fire offering.
Further, auspicious signs and splendor,
The pleasant sound of birds,
Or melodies of many kinds,
Praised and highly praised by the Victor,
Auspicious, excellent, and delightful,
And sounds of many kinds;
Parasols, victory banners, and flags,
Women adorned with ornaments,
Likewise full vases,
And offering water: if these are seen, they are causes of accomplishment.
Colors of many kinds,
And monks and nuns
Highly praised and honored by the world:
On seeing and looking upon them,
The various modes of secret mantra conduct succeed.

From the Root Ritual Manual of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā, Ūrdhvajaṭā, from the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, the Avataṃsaka, a Great Vehicle sūtra of vast extent: the eleventh chapter, the chapter on the rite of the rosary thread, is complete.

Then once again the Blessed One Śākyamuni looked out over the great maṇḍala of the assembly and said to the bodhisattva, the great being, the noble Avalokiteśvara: "Great being, there is your great secret of knowledge.

It knows the commitments of the rites for the means of accomplishment of all mantras; it has arisen from the Dharma treasury of all the tathāgatas; it has fully entered into accord with the cloud of Dharma; its nature is space; and it has become the foremost sovereign of mantras, both worldly and beyond the world. Great being, just as, for example, the Tathāgata is the chief of all beings, and the one who is foremost among gods and humans, the bull among men, is the Blessed One, the Buddha, so too, bodhisattva, this king of knowledge is taught to be supreme among all mantras and is the sacred chief. It was spoken before by the countless blessed buddhas, tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges. It is the supreme heart of the tathāgata Ratnaketu, supremely secret, held to be auspicious in every way, rightly extolled and highly praised by all the buddhas. It brings relief to all beings, fully pacifies all evil, grants every desire, and fulfills every hope. What is it?"

At that moment there came forth from the ūrṇā hair between the eyebrows of the Blessed One Śākyamuni a ray of light called Fully Urging All the Buddhas. It shone throughout the buddha fields of all ten directions, above and below, and satisfied the minds of all beings, and then it sank back into the crown protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) of the Blessed One Śākyamuni. From the Blessed One's crown protuberance there arose a great light, with a body blazing all around and radiating, which no being whatever could bear to look upon, its body adorned with a maṇḍala of light, of many and various forms, having the form of a great universal monarch: it became the king of knowledge called the Single Syllable. Having come forth, it illuminated the whole expanse of the sky. It was surrounded by all the kings of knowledge, and worshipped by many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of niyutas of vidyādharas arrayed before it. It was being extolled by the king who is the universal monarch of knowledge, the guru of all the world. It held sway over all the buddhas, and with great intelligence it was serving the buddhas and the bodhisattvas who abide on the ten grounds. It adorned the whole expanse of the sky with the jewels of the gods and filled it entirely with what had been made into precious gems. Of beautiful form and supremely luminous, an emanator sending forth hundreds of thousands of koṭis of niyutas of forms of every kind, uttering the sound of the single syllable, radiating great blazing rays of light, it came to rest in the region of the sky. Turning toward the Blessed One Śākyamuni, it gazed upon him, and it gazed upon and illuminated the whole great maṇḍala of the assembly of the Pure Abodes, complete in every respect.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke this great king of ritual manuals of the Single Syllable: namaḥ sarva buddhā nāṃ bhruṃ. The moment he spoke it, all the world systems, all the buddha fields, quaked in six ways. No being whatever experienced suffering such as hunger and thirst.

Then once again the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke this ritual manual of the great king of knowledge: in order to fully display the miraculous power of the samādhi of all the tathāgatas; in order to destroy all evil; in order to purify all suffering; in order that this king of ritual manuals may fully protect all beings; in order to pacify all the sufferings of the hells; in order to display fully the bringing about of inconceivable miracles; and in order to display fully the inconceivable miraculous power of all the buddhas and all the bodhisattvas.

"Great being, for whoever wishes to accomplish this king of mantras, this is the rite for that purpose. First of all, with the power that is said to come from being free of discursive thought, from keeping silence, and from fasting; being earnestly devoted to taming through mantra; with great love for all the bhūtas; endowed with the wisdom that rightly sees the suffering of others as one's own suffering; keeping the senses well restrained; in order to check thoroughly a distracted mind, pride, and the avarice that clings to the hand, giving away one's goods in full measure; not bowing to other gods; with the wealth of faith, a vivid clear confidence in the Three Jewels, having clear faith in the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā; with a nature of great compassion and a well-resolved intention, one generates the mind set on awakening. In short, having made the aspiration for great awakening, one should practice continuously.

"Here, first of all, there is the rite of the painted image. On cloth of good color, undamaged, and not a leftover remnant, one should have the image of the Blessed One drawn as the universal monarch, lord of all kings. It is a golden-yellow figure teaching the Dharma, seated on a lion throne, endowed with the supreme of all aspects, its whole body blazing all around, wearing a necklace. Above it, on a mountain peak, there should be clouds with lightning. Below it, a lotus lake should be made. The Blessed One's crown protuberance should be shown emitting rays of light. The practitioner too, true to his place, dress, and shape, holding a censer in his hand, should be shown gazing at the Blessed One. Having painted the cloth painting in that way, the practitioner should bathe three times a day and put on clean clothes. In a solitary place, away from people, he should install the painting for a long period, and, in every way, with body, speech, and mind, tirelessly make vast offerings to the Blessed One, the Buddha. Then on the day of the full moon he should keep a fast, day and night, and begin the practice. He should eat leaves, gruel, milk, alms food obtained by begging, water, and flour; or else he should eat milk and barley meal.

Burning agaru incense, he should perform the recitation ten hundred thousand times. Thereby the preliminary approach will have been done and the preliminary practice performed.

Then, if he wishes to accomplish the eye ointment, he should take one measure of sauvīra eye ointment bought at the hero's price, and have a brahmin girl, facing north, grind it with the five products of the cow. With the ring finger he should make four pills, cover them with lotus petals, and leave them to dry. Kindling the fire according to the rite of the Blessed One, the Buddha, he should perform the fire offering until a full thousand is complete. Then he should install the painting at a stūpa that contains relics and make vast, vast offerings. Kindling fires of palāśa wood in the eight directions, he should perform the fire offering for the vināyakas with sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. Then he should make maṇḍalas in the four directions and set the guardians of the directions in them. In the second maṇḍala is the one who awakens, holding white mustard seed in his hand. In the third maṇḍala there should be a good companion, though it is also permissible to be without a companion. Having made a great offering of the mantra, he should perform the protection. Sitting facing east, having spread out and strewn kuśa grass, he should cover the pills with three leaves of the aśvattha tree above and four below, press them with his hand, and recite until they grow warm, give off smoke, and blaze.

The first accomplishment is that by this one gains the eye whose nature is that of the Victor: whatever one looks upon, and whoever sees it, all come under one's power. The second accomplishment is that one gains the strength of nine elephants, is swift as the wind, lives five hundred years, and can carry off ten elephants. One cannot be overpowered by any of the vidyādharas; one is like the blazing rising sun, one's body adorned with jewels; one lives for an intermediate eon and leads others; one becomes a universal monarch of the vidyādharas who cannot be overpowered, ever renewed, roaming through the seven paths of the wind. Applying the ointment to the ears, and the hand with orpiment: these too are the three kinds of accomplishment.

Then, if he wishes to accomplish the vajra, he should take wood struck by lightning and make it into the shape of a vajra sixteen finger-widths in length. He should make a round stūpa about a cubit in size and, in front of it, observing this rite, keep a fast for three nights at the full moon. Having made vast offerings to the Blessed One, the Buddha, and gazing at the vajra with his mind fixed on it, he should take up the vajra and go to the charnel ground. He should make a channel following a stream that flows to the east. Taking earth from both banks of the river, he should make a round base with the five products of the cow. Having made the round base, he should make a stūpa about a cubit in size and, in front of it, observing this rite, make offerings. Then, in the charnel ground, he should set the vajra near the painting, place his hand upon it, press it down, and recite until it falls into the hole beneath the mound. Then, having bathed, he should take up the vajra in his hand right there and enter. Taking the alms food he has begged, he should worship the Blessed One with a torma. Having bathed, he should set it down apart, smearing the vajra with ash from the charnel ground until it is covered. By this rite he should recite over flesh from the charnel ground.
