One should offer three hundred thousand white lotuses before the painting; one will obtain a kingdom. If one does not succeed, one will obtain a province.

This completes the great king of vidyās called Releasing the Tether of Saṃsāra, arisen from the samādhi Endowed with Vastness, of the root ritual manual of Ūrdhvajaṭā of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Avalokiteśvara, meditating on the king of samādhis Endowed with Vastness, spoke this great king of vidyās called the Eleven-Syllable, within the Blessed Lady's great king of ritual manuals.

namo ratnatrayāya nama ārya avalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā daśani karaṇi bikaraṇi bidhuli bīlaya svāhā

This, together with the great power it has attained, is the king of vidyās called the Eleven-Syllable, which I taught in the past, constantly, even to eleven buddhas. By reciting it constantly one obtains gold.

Next, the rite for its means of accomplishment, for the sake of accomplishment. One should paint the painting described before with powdered nāgakesara mixed with pālika: Avalokiteśvara seated on a lotus seat, meditating in concentration, holding a lotus in his hand and a rosary in his right hand, white in color. The practitioner, too, is as before. Having set up the painting in the first place, one should recite five hundred thousand times. This will constitute the preliminary approach. On a mountain peak, going without food for three days, one should recite twenty thousand times; one will obtain a thousand pieces of gold.

With white sandalwood pigment one should paint the noble Avalokiteśvara as described before. If, before him, one makes a fire offering of three hundred thousand, together with white sandalwood chips, one will obtain a kingdom. If one does not succeed, one will obtain a village. This is for one who is meditating on the king of samādhis Endowed with Vastness.

This fully completes the great king of vidyās that bestows what one desires and seeks, of the root ritual manual of Ūrdhvajaṭā of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being, the noble Avalokiteśvara, meditating on the king of samādhis Endowed with Vastness, spoke the great king of vidyās called Abode of the Painting, within the great king of ritual manuals, Ūrdhvajaṭā of the Blessed Lady Tārā.

namo ratnatrayāya nama ārya avalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā kaṭeni kaṭe kaṭāṃ kaṭe jyoti tiṣmatī bipule svāhā

This, which has attained great power, is the great king of vidyās called Abode of the Painting. Recited constantly, it grants one's aims, destroys all wrongdoing, and also brings accomplishment.

Again, its rite. On the cloth described before, one should paint Amitābha seated in the cross-legged posture, absorbed in samādhi. At the Blessed One's right is the noble Avalokiteśvara, wearing a crown of matted locks and an upper garment of white silk, joining his palms toward the Blessed One. At his left is the noble Mahāsthāmaprāpta, dark blue like the priyaṅgu flower, seated on a lotus seat, joining his palms toward the Blessed One. Having painted such a painting, one should set it up in a clean place, each figure separately, on a frame of paṭa wood, and, offering scents, flowers and so forth with this very mantra, recite seven hundred thousand times. This will constitute the preliminary approach.

At the end, fasting for three nights, one should recite over each of eight thousand white flowers and offer them before Avalokiteśvara. The sign of accomplishment is that those one thousand and eight lotuses come together in one place; this is the sign of accomplishment.

Having ground these into powder and mixed it with other meat, whoever it is given to, whether a king or a king's minister, will come under one's control. If it is given to someone tormented by illness, all illnesses will be pacified. If one sprinkles that powder on a woman who bears the signs, one will obtain a son. If at dawn one sprinkles that powder on the crown of one's own head, all people will be delighted. In this way that powder does whatever one wishes.

To bring release, for an illness that has been inflicted, or for bleeding, or for a discharge from the private parts, and likewise for poison and all such things, one should give it to drink or give a little as an ointment, and all illnesses will be pacified.

Further, here is the rite of the powder of the Abode of the Painting. Nāgakesara, sandalwood, damanaka, tamāla leaves, pushel tsé, costus and the hundred-petaled flower: these should be combined in equal parts and made into powder. This is the powder of the Abode of the Painting. Having consecrated it with eight hundred recitations, whoever it is given to, in a drink or the like, will come under one's control: that person will remain near as a servant, and one will be free of the fear of weapons; both of these are obtained together and take effect.

Likewise, in time of fear one should offer three hundred thousand white lotuses before the painting; one will obtain a great province. If one kindles a fire with arka wood and makes a fire offering of seven hundred thousand red lotuses, one will obtain a great kingdom. If one does not succeed, one will obtain a great city. If one makes a fire offering of a hundred thousand sesame seeds, one will obtain a village. If one makes five hundred thousand fire offerings, it bestows wealth and grants boons, and brings that under one's control. Merely by reciting a hundred times over a conch, one will attain all one's aims.

This fully completes the Abode of the Painting, the great tantra of the root ritual manual of Ūrdhvajaṭā of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā.

Once again the bodhisattva, the great being, the noble Avalokiteśvara, meditating on the king of samādhis Endowed with Vastness, spoke the great king of vidyās called Lotus Edge.

namo ratnatrayāya nama ārya avalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā byajani bejani bejahate padmaṣaṇḍani pāsīnibuddhe buddhāya paraṃparāya sarbagatibijayāya svāhā

This, which has attained great power, is the great vidyā called Lotus Edge. By reciting it constantly, harm is turned back and one is freed from all illnesses.

Next comes the rite for its means of accomplishment. On a leaf of birch bark one should paint the noble Avalokiteśvara with gorocanā: seated on a lotus, entirely white, his matted locks piled high, holding a lotus in his left hand and a water flask in his right. Then, having installed the painting in a clean place, one should perform everything, scents, incense and so forth, with this very mantra, and recite three hundred thousand times.

At the end, fasting day and night, beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight, one should recite once over each of eight thousand flowers for the Blessed One and touch them to the Blessed One's feet. Continuing in this way until eighty thousand are complete, at the end one should make vast offerings and recite, beginning at dusk. Then the words "It is accomplished!" will come from the sky, and one will obtain whatever one desires.

If one wishes to bring a king or anyone else under control, one should take a garland of jasmine, consecrate each of its flowers, and offer them before the painting. If one offers them for seven days and nights in three sessions, that person will come under one's control.

If one wishes to bring a brahmin under control, one should make a fire offering of the skin of a black antelope into a fire of palāśa wood before the painting, for seven days and nights in three sessions; he will come under one's control. If one makes a fire offering of udumbara flowers into a fire of bilva wood before the painting, he will come under one's control within three days.

If one wishes to bring a śūdra under control, one should make a fire offering of salt into a fire of arka wood before the painting; within three days he will come under one's control. If one wishes to bring an ordinary woman under control, one should make a fire offering of barley into that same fire.

If one wishes to bring a monk or a brahmin under control, one should make a fire offering of dūrvā grass into a fire of khadira wood before the painting, in three sessions for seven days; on the seventh day he will come under one's control. By reciting for one month toward whomever one would bring under control, that person will come under one's control.

This fully completes the great king of mantras called Lotus Edge, arisen from the samādhi Endowed with Vastness, of the root ritual manual of Ūrdhvajaṭā of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being, the noble Avalokiteśvara, meditating on the king of samādhis Endowed with Vastness, spoke the great king of mantras called Lotus Splendor, within the king of ritual manuals of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā.

namo ratnatrayāya nama ārya avalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā damane damane śānte śānte mānase bijaye jayebahe anghe aṇarge darśane apratihihata sāsane tiṣṭha tiṣṭha bijayabahe mababaraṃ śobhane ru ru ru ru ru ru ru rāya svāhā

This, together with the great power it has attained, is the great king of mantras called Lotus Splendor. By reciting it constantly, all illness will disappear.

Next comes the rite for its means of accomplishment. With pigment mixed with the juice of legen dye, one should paint a painting of the noble Avalokiteśvara: white, his matted locks piled high, holding a lotus in his hand, seated on a lotus seat, encircled by a garland of light blazing on all sides. Then, having installed it in a clean place, one should burn scents, flowers and incense with this very mantra and recite five hundred thousand times.

Then one should make three hundred thousand fire offerings of white sandalwood smeared with curd, honey and ghee. One will immediately obtain a kingdom. If one does not succeed, one will obtain a village. If one makes a fire offering of palāśa or of aloeswood smeared with ghee before the painting, one will obtain a hundred koṭis of garments. If one makes a hundred thousand oblations of legen dye, one will see a treasure. If one recites for a month toward whatever has been indicated, one will obtain that aim, except for what has been set up out of mere desire.

This fully completes the great king of mantras called Lotus Splendor, arisen from the samādhi Endowed with Vastness, of the root ritual manual of Ūrdhvajaṭā of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Avalokiteśvara, spoke the great king of vidyās called Śrīvatsa, within the Blessed Lady's king of ritual manuals.

namo ratnatrayāya nama ārya avalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā basura mara bana ghughu naṃparaṃ pārayanaṃ ehi ehi budhya budhya bodhyaye svāhā

This, together with the great power it has attained, is the great king of vidyās called Śrīvatsa, which, merely by being remembered, destroys all harm.

Its rite: with pigment mixed with saffron one should paint the noble Avalokiteśvara, his matted locks piled high, seated on a lotus, holding a lotus in his left hand, his right hand granting boons, adorned at his heart with the mark of the śrīvatsa. On his right one should draw a śrīvatsa in saffron. At a stūpa containing relics, one should install the painting facing west, burn incense at that same stūpa, and recite three hundred thousand times. At the end, fasting day and night, one should recite over each nāgakesara blossom and touch it to the heart of the noble Avalokiteśvara. If one completes this for a month, one will be shown a great treasure. In seven days one will obtain a thousand pieces of gold. One will obtain a regional province.

This fully completes the great king of vidyās called Śrīvatsa, arisen from the samādhi Endowed with Vastness, of the root ritual manual of Ūrdhvajaṭā of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Avalokiteśvara, once again meditating on the king of samādhis Endowed with Vastness, spoke the king of mantras called Bestowal of Fearlessness, within the Blessed Lady's king of ritual manuals.

namo ratnatrayāya nama ārya avalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā gopatibati carapatipati śasani śasini bhūbhū cili cili cilpaya svāhā

This, together with the great power it has attained, is the great king of mantras called Bestowal of Fearlessness. By reciting it constantly one will become a king of the earth.

The rite for its means of accomplishment is as follows. On cloth, with pigment mixed with powdered red lead, one should paint the noble Avalokiteśvara: his matted locks piled high, holding a water flask in his hand, resting at his side, seated on a lotus seat, perfectly bestowing fearlessness. Then one should install that painting at a stūpa containing relics, on the north side of the stūpa, make offerings with this very mantra as one's means allow, and recite a hundred thousand times. At the end, fasting day and night, one should make vast offerings and recite, beginning at dusk. One will hear a voice from the sky saying, "It is accomplished!", and rain will fall wherever the offerings were made. If one does not succeed, one will obtain a province. If, before it, one makes a hundred thousand fire offerings of nāgakesara flowers smeared with ghee into a fire of palāśa wood, one will obtain a hundred thousand pieces of silver; one will obtain a hundred coins.

This fully completes the great king of vidyās called Bestowal of Fearlessness, arisen from the samādhi Endowed with Vastness, of the root ritual manual of Ūrdhvajaṭā of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā.

This completes the thirteenth extensive chapter, the vidyā mantras arisen from the samādhi Endowed with Vastness, from the root ritual manual of Ūrdhvajaṭā of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā, a Mahāyāna sūtra of the vast collection of the bodhisattva piṭaka.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being, the noble Avalokiteśvara, once again entered into the samādhi called Radiating and Destroying the Pure Domain of the Bodhisattvas' Samādhi in the World Systems Endowed with All. Having entered into it, he said:

"Since I am explaining, in this great king of ritual manuals, how the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā, is to be accomplished, and since the intention of the tathāgatas, which wards off all the gods, will be transmitted, I shall explain the perfect bestowal of fearlessness against all that terrifies sentient beings. O hosts of gods, all hosts of bhūtas, obstructors and vināyakas, all lords of the yakṣas, and whatever other chiefs of the vidyās there may be, listen! I shall teach the great king of vidyās called Bhṛkuṭī, spoken by the Blessed Lady Tārā, queen of all vidyās; the sovereign of all vidyās, who has gained mastery, spoken by the Tathāgata; which, in keeping with the very act of supplication, seizes, dries up and slays all great terrors.

"In this king of ritual manuals, the ritual procedure of the means of accomplishment of the Blessed Lady, the noble Tārā, is this. Rising in the morning and having become clean, one should look all around, to the east and the other directions, recite over the palm of one's hand, then gaze at the disk of the sun and recite there over the palm of one's hand. All obstructors will be paralyzed. Moreover, for those of malicious intent, if one does the same each day, all the rites of pacification will be accomplished, without long delay. For increase, one should likewise perform the rite with that same mantra at the time of sunset."

For fierce rites, at midnight, in a solitary place, one should untie one's topknot, recite seven times, gaze up at the zenith of the sky, and meditate with a one-pointed mind. Then that person's fierce rites will be accomplished. Whoever, even among the hosts of gods, all the hosts of bhūtas, and the hosts of vināyakas, performs the practice of the great secret of secrets, the king of knowledge mantras (vidyās) that I have spoken in this way, will without doubt gain accomplishment; and the practitioner of the Blessed Lady, the practitioner taught here in this mantra ritual, will without doubt bring it about. It should be understood in this way and not otherwise.

O hosts of gods, listen to the great vidyā, the great secret of secrets of the mātṛkās! I shall also explain the vidyā of the rite that brings it to happiness.

Then the bodhisattva great being Avalokiteśvara entered into the bodhisattva meditative absorption called Illuminating All Extremes. Through his entering into that absorption, all sentient beings changed their births and came to possess strength, diligence, power, and the five consciousnesses. Rising from that absorption, endowed with action and power, he approached the place where the Blessed One was. Having approached, he bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side.

Then the bodhisattva great being Vajrapāṇi arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Blessed One, bowed, and said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how is it that the vidyā comes or goes?"

When he had said this, the Blessed One said this to the bodhisattva great being Vajrapāṇi: "Vajrapāṇi, excellent, excellent that you have asked about such a thing for the sake of sentient beings! Therefore, son of noble family, listen, and I shall explain.

"In the east, in a buddha field eighty-four thousand buddha fields away, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, the Blessed One called Akṣobhya, taught this very queen of vidyās in his own buddha field. In the south, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, the Blessed One called All-Illuminating Gold, also spoke this very vidyā of Tārā. In the west, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, the Blessed One called Amitāyus, also spoke this vidyā in his own buddha field. In the north, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, the Blessed One called Beautiful Body, also spoke this very queen of vidyās. In this way, in the ten directions too, it has been spoken by all such tathāgatas and others; son of noble family, all those tathāgatas proclaim this very heart mantra.

"Son of noble family, in the east, beyond countless buddha fields, there is a world called Vimalā. There, in the buddha field of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha called Vimalaprabha, there is a bodhisattva great being called Ratnākara, and that Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly complete Buddha, Blessed One, taught this vidyā to the bodhisattva Ratnākara. Beyond that, past further buddha fields, there is a world called Ratnavatī. There dwells the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, the Blessed One called Jewel Radiance, and there is a bodhisattva great being called Ratnaśrī.

"Then the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, the Blessed One Jewel Radiance, said to the bodhisattva great being Ratnaśrī: 'Son of noble family, I have explained this vidyā for the benefit of sentient beings; hold it supremely!' Then the bodhisattva great being Ratnaśrī, through the blessing of the Tathāgata, held the vidyā supremely.

"Then, in the world Vimalā, in the buddha field of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, the Blessed One called Vimalaprabha, the bodhisattva great being called Ratnākara took his place. Then the Blessed One said to the bodhisattva great being Ratnākara: 'Son of noble family, this is the heart mantra of all the tathāgatas. For the benefit, welfare, and happiness of sentient beings, in order to care for gods and humans as well, and for the sake of all sentient beings, it should be explained to all sentient beings. Hold it supremely!' Then the bodhisattva great being Ratnākara bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet and held the vidyā supremely.

"Son of noble family, the bodhisattva great being called Ratnākara was none other than this bodhisattva great being Avalokiteśvara, who at that time, on that occasion, was in that buddha field. And the one called the bodhisattva great being Ratnaśrī in the buddha field of the Tathāgata Jewel Radiance is the goddess Pāṇḍaravāsinī. In the place that became the buddha field of the Tathāgata Amitābha, son of noble family, this is the very going and coming of this vidyā; son of noble family, she teaches the king of vidyās."

Then the bodhisattva great being, the noble Avalokiteśvara, approached the place where the Blessed One was, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, and said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, I shall give the vidyā to Vajrapāṇi for the sake of accomplishment." Then the bodhisattva great being Avalokiteśvara said this to the bodhisattva great being Vajrapāṇi:

"Vajrapāṇi, I too shall give the heart vidyā of Pāṇḍaravāsinī."

Then the bodhisattva great being Vajrapāṇi said this to the bodhisattva great being Avalokiteśvara: "Bodhisattva, you who are wholly compassionate toward sentient beings, exceedingly compassionate, grant fearlessness to sentient beings! Teach the vidyā spoken by the Sage!"

Then the bodhisattva great being Avalokiteśvara, with a slightly smiling face, entered into the meditative absorption called Blazing Like the Fire of Destruction. All the buddha fields were stirred by its light rays: a third eye appeared on the bodhisattva's forehead, and from that eye there arose light rays that bring all manner of things under control. Those light rays illuminated all the buddha fields. In all the buddha fields, too, these words were heard: "Son of noble family, excellent, excellent that you have spoken such a vidyā!" All the buddhas and bodhisattvas were showered with lotuses, utpalas, kumudas, puṇḍarīkas, saugandhikas, kaṭoras, mañjūṣakas, and great mañjūṣaka flowers. "Son of noble family, speak the king of vidyās!"

Then the bodhisattva great being Avalokiteśvara, through the blessing of the Buddha, spoke the vidyā:

namaḥ sarva tathagatebhyaḥ arhatebhyaḥ samyaka saṃbuddhebhyaḥ oṃ bhaya nāśani trāsani trāsa trāsaya bhṛkuṭi taṭi vaitaṭi vaitaṭi svete jaṭini svāhā

As soon as this vidyā had been spoken, the great trichiliocosm, the world system of a billion worlds, rose in the west and sank in the east, rose in the south and sank in the north, rose in the north and sank in the south, rose in the east and sank in the west. Thus the great trichiliocosm shook in six ways. The gods dwelling in their celestial palaces were moved from their seats. The gandharvas were thrown face down. The voices of the asuras failed, the speed of the garuḍas slackened, the rākṣasas cried out "truṭatatara," and the malevolent ones drew near. The hosts of mātṛkās uttered wretched sounds of wailing and a clamor of lamentation. Likewise the yakṣas, the kinnaras, and the great mahoragas were left without refuge and without ally, and even the divine realms as far as Akaniṣṭha were burning. All the gods hurried in haste into the presence of the Tathāgata.

Then Vajrapāṇi too, delighted by the light rays of the ornament of the Tathāgata's miraculous display, moved from his seat and came into the presence of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha. Then the Blessed One comforted all the gods and bodhisattvas: "Do not be afraid! Friends, do not be afraid!" Then the Blessed One said this to the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi: "Vajrapāṇi, enter!" The moment that great being entered the crown protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) of the Tathāgata, the great trichiliocosm shook in six ways.

Then again the Blessed One said to all the gods: "Sons of noble family, sing praises to the heart of the Tathāgata and to the bodhisattva great being Avalokiteśvara!" Then all those gods, the gandharvas, yakṣas, and others, and the bodhisattvas, paid homage to the heart of the Tathāgata and to the bodhisattva great being Avalokiteśvara. Then the whole assembly, filled with wonder, came to where the Blessed One was. Having come, they bowed their heads at the Blessed One's feet and said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it is wondrous that a bodhisattva has spoken such a secret mantra! Sugata, it is supremely wondrous!"

Then the bodhisattva great being Vajrapāṇi spoke. The bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi came forth from the crown protuberance, bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, and said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it is wondrous that the power of the great bodhisattva has been proclaimed, which the gods have never heard before. Sugata, it is wondrous!"

The Blessed One said: "Son of noble family, so it is. In times past, in the east, in the buddha field of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha called Padmanetra, eighty-four koṭis of vidyādharas dwelt, each in their own place. In that buddha field the word 'woman' is not even designated; all of them are flawless vidyādharas and do not pass beyond the state of a vidyādhara. Son of noble family, all the gods, all the bodhisattvas, all the lords of the yakṣas, the gandharvas, bhūtas, piśācas, kinnaras, great mahoragas, and the rest, in short, son of noble family, do not pass beyond the order of all the tathāgatas."

Then the bodhisattva great being Vajrapāṇi went to where the bodhisattva great being Avalokiteśvara was. Having approached, he joyfully spoke the secret mantra:

namo ratna trayāya namaś caṇḍa vajra pāṇaye mahā yakṣa senā pataye oṃ ṭakki hūṃ phaṭ

This too, which is the heart of the bodhisattva great being and of all the hosts of vidyās, the heart of the king of supreme vidyās, the king of vidyās, should be recited a thousand times.

This concludes the first chapter of the subsequent tantra, called "Generation."

Then all the bodhisattvas, the gods, gandharvas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, skandas, unmādas, oppressing spirits, and all the vināyakas, the kings from every land, the gods together with the gods of the earth, the rivers and the oceans, and the great medicine deities came to where the Blessed One was. Having come, they bowed their heads in homage at the Blessed One's feet and sat down to one side.

Then all of them said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, we wish to put some questions to the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha." When they had said this, the Blessed One said this to the bodhisattvas and the gods: "Fair-faced ones, excellent! Ask whatever you wish."

They said this to the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha: "Blessed One, how is the rising or the setting of the vidyās defined, and at what time are the vidyās accomplished?"

When the gods had said this, the Blessed One said this: "O gods, sons of noble family, when tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas appear in the world, at that time the vidyās arise. There are those endowed with diligence, those whose diligence is slack and sluggish, those with courage, the lazy, liars, those of harsh speech, killers, the violent, the craving, and the greedy. Those of them who never know this side and never know the far side, people such as these, do not find accomplishment in the vidyā.

"Son of noble family, in times past, in this very Fortunate Eon, eighteen kings of the vidyādharas passed away. Possessed of great miraculous powers and great might, they became renowned by the name of vidyādharas. All of them, through being vidyādharas and through the might of the vidyā, sported, rejoiced, and took their delight.

"Son of noble family, in the east was the king of the vidyādharas called Sinless, lord of four koṭis of vidyādharas. In the north was the king of the vidyādharas called Sumeru, lord of ten koṭis of vidyādharas. Near Sumeru, king of mountains, were the king of the vidyādharas called Elephant Host, the king of the vidyādharas called Lord of the Asuras, the king of the vidyādharas called White Mount, the king of the vidyādharas called Fine Attire, the king of the vidyādharas called Golden Limbs, the king of the vidyādharas called Ornament of the Lotus Array, the king of the vidyādharas called Vajra Hand, the king of the vidyādharas called All-Illuminating Jewel, the king of the vidyādharas called Noose Mudrā, the king of the vidyādharas called Light of Blazing Flames, the king of the vidyādharas called Displayer of All Illusions, and the king of the vidyādharas called Ever Joyful. These eighteen kings of the vidyādharas, each surrounded by fourteen thousand vidyādharas and possessed of great might, all sport, rejoice, and take their delight together with women.

"Son of noble family, these vidyādharas follow the vidyā within seven lives: wherever they are born, there, by the power of this vidyā, each of them regains their memory. Son of noble family, by abiding in such a state the vidyā is accomplished."

Then that assembly of gods and bodhisattvas, filled with wonder, showered the Blessed One with flowers of many kinds. Then, so that all the gods, the bodhisattvas, and the rest might rejoice with delighted minds in the vidyā, the rite was taught. Then that bodhisattva spoke the vidyā-mantras:

oṃ padma vajri hūṃ

This is the heart mantra.

gagana vidāriṇi

This is the near-heart mantra.

oṃ bhaya nasani phaṭ

This is for the head.

oṃ trapani hūṃ

This is for the crown protuberance.

oṃ taṭi hūṃ

This is the armor.

oṃ vaitaṭi hūṃ

This is the canopy.

oṃ svete jaṭini phaṭ

This is the fence.

These are the remaining mantras of the vidyā's retinue. With the root vidyā itself one offers scent, flowers, incense, and so forth.

Then the bodhisattva great being Avalokiteśvara taught the rite of the painted scroll of the Blessed Lady. First of all, a cloth of no fixed size and free of hairs should be washed. It should be washed seven times with white sandalwood and aguru leaves mixed with spikenard, consecrated seven times with the mantra of the Blessed Lady. Once washed, it should also be anointed. It should be fumigated with bhūtakeśī, gajāhva, śatrughnī, and priyaṅgu; these betoken the accomplishment of whatever one desires. Having kept a one-night fast, an intelligent person should attend to it. Then, at dawn and at night, one should kindle a fire and perform a hundred thousand fire offerings of white mustard seed mixed with one's own blood. By this very rite, no obstructors will arise while the scroll is being painted. It should be anointed further still, for otherwise, through the influence of the vināyakas, it will not be accomplished.

Then the vidyādhara himself, reciting the vidyā-mantra, should have the painter bathe. After he has bathed, one should also give him fine clothing, for as long as the painting lasts. The painter should keep the poṣadha vows, and while he is painting, tormas of many kinds should be offered at the edge of the cloth and four full vases should be set out. In the center a square maṇḍala should be made, and a full vase set there as well. All the vases should be adorned with flowers. Garlands of lamps are also offered. The vidyādhara, keeping the vidyā in mind, should burn incense.

Then the painter, having paid homage to all the tathāgatas and all the bodhisattvas, should lay down the Brahmā lines. Then again the vidyādhara, facing east, should approach and, before the painted scroll, perform eight thousand fire offerings with kindling sticks of apāmārga.

Then the painter, having eaten the feast offered to the deity, should, with unmixed colors, paint the image of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha Amitābha. He is golden in color and seated on a white lotus seat. On his right is the noble Avalokiteśvara, white like an autumn cloud, with a hanging crown of matted locks, three-eyed, with light rays streaming from his forehead, seated on a lotus. Behind him should be painted the goddess of the vidyā, clad in white garments, scattering lotuses. Right next to her should be painted Bhṛkuṭī, wearing white garments. On the right should be painted the Blessed Lady Great Compassion, blue-green like priyaṅgu, holding a jewel in her hand. All of them should be made one span of the Sugata in size, each seated on her own lotus.

On the left side is Vajrapāṇi, blue-green, adorned with every ornament, holding a vajra in his hand. On the left side the supreme king of vidyās sits beside a peacock. Beside the king of vidyās should be painted the Golden One and Vajrāṅkuśī. Vajramuṣṭi should be painted, blue-green, fully adorned with every ornament, holding a vajra. Vajradaṇḍa should be painted, holding a staff. Behind Vajradaṇḍa should be painted Vajramati, Vajrī, and the Goddess of Meteoric Iron. On the left should be painted the Terrifier of the Gods. Vajrāṭṭahāsa, wearing a serpent as his sacred thread, should be painted, and beside Vajrapāṇi should be painted Vajrasena, with a hanging crest, fully adorned with every ornament. All of them are each seated on a lotus.

The Four Great Kings should be made, and below them the four classes of vināyakas should be drawn in distorted forms, fleeing. Below them a lotus lake should be made. A nāga holding a lotus in his hand should be painted. All the hosts of gods should be painted scattering flowers. The great drums of the gods should be painted. Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and the rest should also be painted with their weapons. The king of the vidyādharas, Anaṅga, should be painted. Beside the nāga king, the practitioner should be painted holding a censer in his hand.

Merely by painting this scroll one is freed from all evil deeds. Thereafter one accomplishes the deities with ease. Then the vidyādhara, living on alms food before that supreme king of scrolls, should recite the vidyā one million two hundred thousand times. Then the vidyādhara Anaṅga will appear to him in a dream, saying, "Son of noble family, accomplish it! Accomplish it!"

Then the vidyādhara should have a lotus made of the three metals, with a center of gold, petals of copper, and veins of silver, with a thousand petals. It is surrounded by four lotuses, and these four he should have made with a hundred petals each. Thereafter the practitioner, eating milk and gruel, should recite the vidyā.

Then, on the full moon, having kept a fast for three nights, with the scroll set up facing east, one should invite all the deities of the Blessed Lady onto the right side of the lotus. One should offer torma with great care. White flowers, agaru, costus, and saffron should be offered, and a hundred butter lamps lit. To the asuras, torma; to the yakṣas, white torma and butter lamps; to the gandharvas, torma and butter lamps; to the piśācas, torma, red flowers, and butter lamps. To the garuḍas, yakṣas, kinnaras, great mahoragas, rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, vetālas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, unmādas, oppressing spirits, and the hosts of mātṛkās, together with the vināyakas: meat, jambulika, svatika, and the like. To the yakṣas: meat, blood, stalks, fruit, and the three sweet substances. To the nāgas: parched rice, mung-bean sweets, and fruits. Foods of many kinds, lamps, and incense are offered to each separately. As the deity's awareness grows, one should make the offering seven times.

Then on the seventh day one should appoint a companion. After careful consideration, one should appoint someone who is grateful, always compassionate by nature, and free from illness. Then the wise one, having properly begun the rite, sitting on a consecrated mat of kuśa grass, pressing the stamens of the lotus with his right hand, should perform eight thousand fire offerings. The scroll will shake violently. The nāgas too will roar, but one should not be afraid. Again one recites eight hundred times. In the directions and the intermediate directions the sound of great drums resounds. The vināyakas flee in all directions, and the vidyādharas who travel together through the world systems come. The daughters of the asuras gather. The clouds rumble and roar. The gods too will come. All the yakṣas and all the kings of the vidyādharas gather. The earth quakes in six ways, and all the hosts of vidyās lose their potency.

Then the vidyādhara should quickly perform eight fire offerings with kindling sticks from the bodhi tree. Then the noble Avalokiteśvara will come together with the gods. When he has come with the gods, one offers him an arghya offering. As soon as he arrives, all the gods and all the kings of vidyās send down a rain of flowers. Then the vidyādhara, pressing the lotus, should recite the vidyā seven times. From each lotus, four koṭis of lotuses will arise.

All sixteen thousand vidyādharas, every one of them, appear seated on lotus seats. Then the vidyādhara should recite once. Then from the body of the Blessed Lady rays of light of many colors stream forth; they anoint the practitioner and then sink into the stamens of the lotus. Then again eighty-four koṭis of vidyādharas, seated upon lotuses, will appear. That lotus array appears adorned with the seven kinds of precious substances, pervading eighty-four thousand leagues on every side. There he becomes worthy of homage from all the tathāgatas and all the bodhisattvas, praised by the gods and honored by the kings of the vidyādharas. Surrounded by a hundred koṭis of vidyādharas he goes forth, and in an instant, a moment, a mere flash, he passes beyond seven buddha fields to the world system of Sukhāvatī. He takes birth at will and dies at will. In the time of the perfectly complete Buddha Kāśyapa there was a king of the vidyādharas called Overpowerer, and he accomplished this rite.

This completes the first chapter of the Blessed Lady, the great queen of vidyās.

Then the bodhisattva great being Vajrapāṇi, out of joy, told Avalokiteśvara the rite. A painter who keeps the poṣadha vows should paint the image of the Blessed One, yellow like gold, teaching the Dharma. On the right is the noble Avalokiteśvara, white like an autumn cloud, made in sublime form, with a white sacred thread over reddish-yellow, wearing an upper garment and lower garment of silk, holding a wooden staff in his hand. On the left is Vajradhara, blue-green, adorned with ornaments, brandishing a wrathful vajra in his left hand. Beside Vajradhara should be painted Vajrāṅkuśī and Vajramuṣṭi. Beside the noble Avalokiteśvara should be painted the heart of the Blessed Lady, She Who Goes in Equality, blue-green like priyaṅgu and adorned with every ornament. Beside the Blessed Lady should be painted the supreme heart, white in color, holding a kurba in her left hand. Above should be painted the sons of the gods of the Pure Abodes, holding garlands of flowers in their hands. The great drums of the gods should be painted. Below should be painted one holding a censer in his hand.

Living on the three white substances, one should recite the vidyā seven hundred thousand times before the scroll. In this way the preliminary practice will have been done. Then, properly beginning the rite, one first takes realgar and washes it with milk inside a cloth. On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, having made vast offerings to the scroll, one should set four full vases at the four doors. All of them should be adorned with flowers. All the rites are to be done with this very Blessed Lady. Then, seated on a mat of kuśa grass, one should wrap the realgar in seven leaves of the aśvattha tree, set it down, and recite until the noble Vajrapāṇi moves. Then the vidyādhara should offer arghya mentally. One should recite again until it smokes and bursts into flame. When it has flamed and one takes it up, one becomes like a sixteen-year-old with curled, coiling hair, surrounded by sixteen vidyādharas, and will live for eighty thousand years. When he dies he will be born in the vajra family.

No lunar date is required, no constellation is required, no fast is required. Take the corpse of a man who has died with his head laid toward the east on the shore of the ocean, and adorn it with scents, flowers, and so forth. The practitioner, facing east, with his mind focused on each part in turn, should recite the vidyā over fresh butter from a cow of like stock and pour it into the mouth of the corpse, and should recite the vidyā until the corpse stirs all over and rises. Then the vidyādhara should enter the ocean and stay in the water until the sun rises. By that alone he becomes like an eight-year-old with curled, coiling hair, and by merely forming the wish, all his requisites will appear. He will live for sixty thousand years. He will fly eleven thousand leagues.

One should have a Vajrapāṇi made from the wood of a lightning-struck tree, and a figure of the Blessed Lady She Who Goes in Equality, the heart mantra, made from priyaṅgu wood together with medicinal herbs. One should have an Avalokiteśvara made from nimba wood. All of them should be placed, each separately, on a pankan fruit. One should have the practitioner made kneeling, holding a censer in his hand. Then, wearing clean clothes and keeping a vow of silence, one should recite She Who Goes in Equality one million one hundred thousand times. In this way the preliminary practice will have been done. Then on the fifteenth day, having fasted for three nights, eating maṇḍalaka, one should offer a feast to the Saṅgha. Then at night, having made vast offerings to the Buddha, the Blessed One, one should afterward offer tormas of many kinds together with fruits and light a thousand lamps. Then, having performed the protection, seated on a mat of kuśa grass, one should make twenty garlands of utpala flowers, offer them into the right hand of the noble Avalokiteśvara, and recite until all is seen. Without being afraid, one should recite the vidyā again. When they move and one takes them up, one gains a vajra body blue-green like the petals of a blue utpala, becomes the good fortune of all the vidyādharas, and will live for eighty thousand years. He will soar eighty-four thousand leagues. When he dies he will be born in the vajra family.

On an even cloth a painter who keeps the poṣadha vows should paint the Blessed Lady Bhṛkuṭī: the goddess should be painted blue-green and three-eyed, with her attire and ornaments complete. Below, the practitioner should be shown holding a censer in his hand.

Then the practitioner should recite the vidyā three hundred thousand times before the painting. Then, going at night to a charnel ground, he should set up the painting facing east and offer scent, flowers and incense, and to all the bhūtas on the ground. Then the vidyādhara, sitting alone upon a mat of kuśa grass, should take the soot of the great fat in a skull cup and recite the vidyā of She Who Goes in Equality. Then the vidyādhara should again recite the vidyā until it gives off smoke and blazes. He becomes like a second eye of the Victor, and like the weapon that is the spear of Maheśvara; all the great lords of the earth come under his power through the vidyā.

Then, if one wishes to accomplish eye ointment, one should go to the shore of the ocean. First, as the approach, one should bathe with water and milk and, keeping silent, recite the vidyā eight thousand times. Then the vidyādhara, clean and wearing clean clothes, should smear a patch of ground the size of a cowhide and have an image of the noble Vajrapāṇi consecrated there. Then he should take five skull cups, light them well with fragrant sesame oil, and make them smokeless. Then he should make tormas of various kinds and offer butter lamps; then he should place the ointment separately in the skull cups, and, having performed the protection before Vajrapāṇi, sit upon a mat of kuśa grass and recite eight thousand times. That eye ointment becomes warm. Then the vidyādhara should quickly recite the vidyā seven times in full. It gives off smoke and blazes. When it blazes, he takes the skull cup and goes to the abode of Vajrapāṇi. He becomes like a flax flower, an unprecedented lord of ninety million.

Then, if one wishes to accomplish the vajra, a painter who keeps the poṣadha vows should paint with unmixed colors the Blessed Lady Bhṛkuṭī and the Blessed Lady's heart essence, She Who Goes in Equality, blue-green like priyaṅgu and adorned with every ornament; the heart essence, moreover, holds a vajra in her right hand. Then the practitioner should climb to the summit of a mountain and, keeping silent, even without a companion, recite one million six hundred thousand times. Then on the fifteenth day, clean and wearing clean clothes, he should make a vast offering to the painting and light butter lamps. Then the practitioner, having performed the rite of protection, should sit upon a mat of kuśa grass and have a three-pronged vajra, eight finger-widths in size, made of kuśa grass whose tips have not been cut. Pressing that vajra with his right hand, he should recite for as long as it takes for light rays to come from the Blessed Lady. Hearing the sound "ciṭi ciṭi" from the vajra, he should not be afraid but should recite the vidyā again for a moment. When he hears the sound of a great drum, he should again recite the vidyā for a moment. The vidyādhara should quickly perform eight hundred fire offerings with kindling sticks of the bodhi tree smeared with butter and honey. Even after the fire offering is complete, he should recite until light rays come from the vajra. Having bathed at the three times of day, he comes to have hair that is curled and coiled, the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, like a second Vajrapāṇi, and a clear blue-green body, and he lives for an eon. When he dies, he will be born in the vajra family.

Then, if one wishes to accomplish the hook, the practitioner should do the preliminary practice as before. Eating milk and barley meal and keeping silent, in a cow pen, on a bed spread with kuśa grass, clean and wearing clean clothes, bathing at the three times of day, he should recite She Who Goes in Equality. Then he should go to a river that flows to the ocean and, living on alms, enter water up to his waist and recite one hundred thousand times. He should offer food to the Saṅgha. Then a painter who keeps the poṣadha vows should paint an image: on the right, the noble Avalokiteśvara, yellow like gold and three-eyed; beside him should be painted the Blessed Lady Bhṛkuṭī. The Vajra Holder too should be painted, entering into the uṣṇīṣa of the Tathāgata. All should be well placed upon lotus seats. Then the practitioner, having made a vast offering, should sit upon a mat of kuśa grass, as the Blessed Lady has commended. Then the vidyādhara should make a hook of kuśa grass whose tips have not been cut, take it in his right hand, and recite countless times until light rays come from the hook. Those light rays circle the practitioner and vanish, and by holding it he becomes a vidyādhara, and all the vidyādharas follow him. Holding the hook in his hand, he becomes the lord of a thousand vidyādharas. He lives for an eon, travels like the wind, has a divine body, and knows his own death. When he dies, he will be born in Sukhāvatī.

This concludes the fourth chapter, on the Blessed Lady, the Great Queen of Vidyās, spoken by the great bodhisattva, the noble Vajrapāṇi.

Then again Great Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, approached where the bodhisattva mahāsattva, the noble Avalokiteśvara, was. Having approached, he bowed his head to the bodhisattva mahāsattva, circumambulated him, and sat to one side. Then again Great Brahmā said this to the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: "I shall explain the rite of my queen of vidyās."

The bodhisattva said, "Excellent, Great Brahmā, excellent! For the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, speak the rite of the great queen of vidyās."

Then again Great Brahmā spoke the rite: "Whatever son of good family recites or holds the queen of vidyās, him I shall always follow. Wherever he is born, I shall grant him the recollection of the Buddha, and he will always remember his births. He will not be born into a low caste. By reading it, his activities will be accomplished. When he goes into the midst of bandits, he should bring it to mind.

In fear of snakes, and when thunderbolts fall, one should recite it once. If one brings it to mind in the presence of someone who is angry, it bestows great glory. If one wishes to heal someone afflicted by a graha, one should consecrate it seven times and burn a measure of it; the person will be freed. If one wishes to break a seal, one should consecrate one's face seven times and then look; the seal will be broken. With white mustard seed the maṇḍala is bound. With the kīla the mansion is purified. With the kīla itself the boundary is bound. Wherever a vajra is present, in that place one should recite the heart mantra of the Blessed Lady, She Who Goes in Equality, eight hundred times; the vajras will be bound. If one wishes to split a vajra, one should take poison, liṅga, karavīra flowers, and a ram's horn, in equal portions, consecrate them with the vidyā eight hundred times, and then smear this on the fire of the vajra; the vajra will be split apart.

If one wishes to accomplish wealth, after doing the preliminary practice as before, a painter who keeps the poṣadha should paint, on an unspoiled cloth free of hair, an image of the Buddha, the Blessed One, teaching the Dharma. On his right should be the noble Avalokiteśvara, white like an autumn cloud, wearing a crown of matted locks, with Amitābha seated on his head, adorned with every ornament. On his left should be the Vajra Holder, dark blue, adorned with every ornament, holding a vajra in his hand. Beside the noble Avalokiteśvara one should paint the Blessed Lady Bhṛkuṭī, dark blue like the priyaṅgu flower. Beside the Blessed Lady one should paint the Great Queen of Vidyās. Brahmā too should hold a water flask in his hand. Below, one should paint vināyakas of various forms. All the deities should be placed on lotus seats. The practitioner is as before.

Then, on the fifteenth day, the practitioner should make a protective cord from thread spun by a maiden and twisted, as before, under the constellation Puṣya. Then he should make vast offerings to the painted cloth, present tormas of many kinds, and light butter lamps as well. Then the vidyādhara, seated on a mat of kuśa grass, should consecrate the protective cord seven times and offer it into the right hand of the noble Avalokiteśvara. The vidyādharas also touch it with their eight right hands. One should recite the vidyā until it becomes warm, or gives off smoke, or blazes. When it blazes, one offers water for honoring with the mind. Then the vidyādhara should bring Brahmā to mind; by merely recollecting him, it becomes a wooden staff. One should strike it with white mustard seed over which the mantra has been recited a hundred times, and it becomes the protective cord. Then, recollecting the Blessed Lady, one should take it up. As soon as one has taken it up, one becomes a vidyādhara with curling ringlets of hair, having the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, with a body white and clear, a lord over the twelve lands. One goes to the world of Brahmā. When one passes from there, one will again experience the vidyā.

Another accomplishment: as before, the vidyādhara should recite the heart mantra of the Blessed Lady, She Who Goes in Equality, in a charnel ground. Then, living on alms food, he should take a shroud from the dead and wash it with these substances: sandalwood, tagara, phushel tsé, bālaka, and rājahā. Having combined these substances, he should wash it. When an intelligent person has washed it, he should offer incense to it for seven days. Then on the fifteenth day the vidyādhara should go to the charnel ground, smear a patch of ground the size of a cowhide, and make offerings of scents, flowers and so on. Having made a torma for all the bhūtas, the practitioner should then sit on a skull, wrap himself completely in that cloth, make protection, and recite the vidyā until it becomes warm, or gives off smoke, or blazes. When it becomes warm, one brings beings under one's power. When it gives off smoke, one becomes invisible. When it blazes, one becomes a lord of sixty vidyādharas, with curling ringlets of hair and a white body. Moreover, merely by wrapping oneself in that cloth in any way at all, one makes it one's own. At that time one will also give a share to the vidyādharas. When one dies, one will be born in Sukhāvatī.

Then, if one wishes to accomplish a rosary, as before one should recite five hundred thousand times at the ocean. Then one should make a rosary of kuśa grass and tie twenty-five knots. Then one should go to a charnel ground and smear a square maṇḍala. Then the vidyādhara should set down a corpse and a kyibung, and place the rosary between them. Having made offerings of scents, flowers and so on, one presents a great torma. Then the practitioner should sit on the corpse's chest and recite the heart mantra of the Blessed Lady, She Who Goes in Equality. One should not be afraid of the various kinds of obstructors, which come like rain. As long as it becomes heated, one offers water for honoring with the mind, and then one should recite again until it becomes a true rosary. Again, the practitioner, while expounding, should recite the Blessed Lady seven times. Then light rays will issue all around, and one should seize the vidyā with mindfulness. As soon as one seizes it, one has curling ringlets of hair, the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, whatever form one wishes, and the radiance of the rising sun, and is surrounded by thousands of vidyādharas. In an instant, a moment, a split second, one goes to the world of Brahmā and becomes Brahmā himself. When one dies, one will be born in the world Vimalā.

Then, if one wishes to enjoy the daughter of an asura, one should live on alms food and recite the vidyā, She Who Goes in Equality, five hundred thousand times on a mountain peak. Then a painter who keeps the poṣadha should paint an image of the Blessed One teaching the Dharma. If, before it, one relies on all the mantras with the mind, the treasures of the asuras will come under one's power.

This concludes the fifth chapter, the Blessed Lady, the Great Queen of Vidyās, spoken by Brahmā.

Then the king of elephants, Three Pegs, approached the place where the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara was.

Having approached, he circumambulated the bodhisattva mahāsattva, bowed his head at his feet, and spoke to the great bodhisattva as follows: "Great bodhisattva, I shall explain the rite of this king of vidyās."

Then the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara spoke to the king of elephants, Three Pegs, as follows: "King of elephants, it is excellent, excellent, that you explain the rite for the sake of sentient beings. Therefore, speak whatever you have to say."

The king of elephants, Three Pegs, said: "The practice should be done without regard to the date of the month, without regard to the constellation, and without keeping a fast. One should take the corpse of a woman, and in a charnel ground smear a patch of ground the size of a cowhide. Placing the corpse with its head to the east, one should worship it with offerings of scents, flowers and so on. Then, having put eye ointment into her bhaga, one should recite until it moves. Through this one will have eyes like those of the Victor, and will live for four thousand years.

"On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should take the limb-born part of a man who has died, dry it, and wash it with an astringent. Having worshiped it with scents, flowers and so on, on the fourteenth day of the following dark fortnight one should go to a shrine of Maheśvara and make a torma for all the bhūtas. Placing it on the right side of the body of Maheśvara, one should put that limb-born part between two bowls joined mouth to mouth, and recite the vidyā eight thousand times. Then, as a sign of accomplishment, the joined bowls will move, and one should take them up while recollecting the vidyā. As soon as one takes them up, one becomes invisible. One travels a thousand yojanas and lives for five thousand years.

"On the eighth or the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should go to a charnel ground, take the five sense organs of a child who died before it was born, and make them into a pill. Having wrapped it all around with the three metals, one should then smear a maṇḍala, place the pill inside a skull cup, and recite the vidyā, She Who Goes in Equality, eight thousand times. By putting the pill in one's mouth, one becomes invisible. One will live for six thousand years and will travel a hundred yojanas.

"On an unspoiled cloth, a painter who keeps the poṣadha should paint the Blessed Lady, She Who Goes in Equality. He should paint the king of elephants, Three Pegs. He should paint the forms of obstructors facing downward, in distorted shapes. Below should be the practitioner, holding a censer in his hand. Then, before the painted cloth, one should recite three hundred thousand times.

"Then the vidyādhara should take the corpse of one who was of good birth. In the charnel ground he should worship the Blessed Lady with scents, flowers and so on, and make a torma for all the bhūtas. Guarded by a good companion, pure, and wearing clean clothes, he should stand with his feet placed on the corpse's forehead and recite the vidyā. At some point the corpse will rise up; one should not be afraid. Then the vidyādhara should recite over white mustard seed seven times and strike it with the seed, and it will be subdued. Then the vidyādhara should recite the vidyā and touch it with his right hand. As soon as he touches it, he will see a kharusta. He should recite the vidyā and take it up. As soon as he takes it up, he will have curling ringlets of hair and the appearance of a sixteen-year-old; he will be four-armed, an elephant vidyādhara surrounded by six vidyādharas, moving like the wind, and he will live for an eon. When he dies, he will be born in Sukhāvatī."

This concludes the sixth chapter, the Blessed Lady, the Queen of Vidyās, as explained by Three Pegs.

Then Īśāna, lord of the bhūtas, delighted by her vidyā, spoke a rite: "A painter who keeps the poṣadha should paint an image of the Buddha, the Blessed One. He should paint the noble Avalokiteśvara holding a lotus in his hand. On the left he should paint the noble Vajrapāṇi, resembling a flax flower. Beside the noble Avalokiteśvara he should paint the Blessed Lady, dark blue like the priyaṅgu flower, adorned with every ornament. He should also paint the sons of the gods scattering flowers. Below, he should paint the practitioner holding a censer in his hand.

"Then for one month the vidyādhara should eat milk and barley meal and recite the vidyā before the painted cloth. Then he should take the skulls of five heads, use three of them to make a hearth of three stones, and fill one skull with fat. Then the vidyādhara should make a torma for all the bhūtas. Sitting by the fifth skull, he should consecrate each white mustard seed seven times and perform eight hundred fire offerings. When that fire offering is complete, bubbles will arise. Pressing them down with his right hand, he should recite eight hundred times. Then he will hear the sound of weeping; he should not be afraid. Then the vidyādhara should quickly strike with white mustard seed consecrated seven times, and it will turn into a man. Recollecting the vidyā, he should say, 'Rise up! Rise up!' It becomes a svatika. Then the vidyādhara should consecrate realgar seven times and make a tilaka mark on it with that, and it becomes a lord of elephants. He should mount it. As soon as he mounts it, he will have curling ringlets of hair, the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, and a body white and clear; riding the great elephant, he will live for eight thousand years and fly eighteen thousand yojanas. When he dies, he will be born in the abode of the gods of Tuṣita.

"The practice should be done without regard to the date of the month, without regard to the constellation, and without keeping a fast. One should take the corpse of a man who has died, bathe it with scented water on the bank of a river, adorn it with new clothes of various kinds and with ornaments, and lay it with its head to the east. The practitioner, having a good companion keep guard, should sit on a mat of kuśa grass, consecrate white mustard seed seven times, put it into the corpse's mouth, and recite the vidyā. At some point the corpse's mouth will open. Then the practitioner, being fearless, should press down on its chest with his left foot and recite the vidyā until it lets out a fierce cry.

At some point it will give off smoke. Fearlessly, one should strike its forehead with white mustard seed recited over seven times. A snake will then be seen coming from its mouth. Without fear, one should touch it while recollecting the vidyā; as soon as one touches it, it turns into a sword. One should seize it while recollecting the heart mantra. As soon as one seizes it, one has curling ringlets of hair and the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, and becomes the unobstructed lord of all the elephant vidyādharas, living for sixty thousand years.

There is also the accomplishment of the short spear. As before, eating milk and barley meal, one should climb to the summit of a mountain and recite three hundred thousand times. Then the vidyādhara should mix ash from a charnel ground and earth from an anthill with milk; as before, eating milk and barley meal, he should climb to the summit of a mountain and recite three hundred thousand times. Then the vidyādhara should mix ash from a charnel ground and earth from an anthill with milk and make the figure of a peacock, measuring one span of the Sugata, and paint it with unmixed colors. Then he should go to a charnel ground, smear a maṇḍala with cow dung, worship with scents, flowers, incense and so on, and make a torma for the bhūtas. Then, pure and wearing clean clothes, he should sit on a skull, place the peacock on a second skull, and recite until the peacock moves. Then the vidyādhara should present water for honoring with flowers that have not fallen to the ground, consecrated seven times. Again he should recite the vidyā. Then they will come all together from the directions. Without fear, he should touch the peacock while recollecting the heart mantra, and it will turn into a woman. She will say, "Son, what shall I do?" He should say to her, "Dwell in my body." Then she will vanish into the palm of the vidyādhara's hand. In that very instant he has curling ringlets of hair and the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, holding a short spear in his hand, and all the vidyādharas come under his power, except those cakravartins who see him and gaze upon him. He flies together with them and roams through the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. He lives for an eon, and when he dies he will be born among the sons of the gods of Akaniṣṭha.

If one wishes to accomplish a lion, the vidyādhara, as before, eating only milk and keeping a vow of silence, should recite the vidyā five hundred thousand times as the practice of the vidyā. Then he should put wood struck by lightning in milk for seven days. He should knead white earth with sandalwood water, using the lightning-struck wood. Then, under the constellation Puṣya, the vidyādhara should make two lions. Afterward he should make vast offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and offer tormas of many kinds. Then the vidyādhara, pure and wearing clean clothes, should sit on a mat of kuśa grass, press the lion with his right hand, and recite the vidyā, She Who Goes in Equality, until the lion moves. As soon as it moves, it shakes greatly. He should recite correctly and, without fear, keep reciting the vidyā until the sound of the great drum of the gods resounds. Then the vidyādhara should strike the lion with flowers consecrated seven times. When it is struck all over, the lion roars a lion's roar, and other practitioners will surely take heed. Then he should recite the vidyā again, mount the lion, and go. As soon as he has mounted, all the vidyādharas scatter flowers. Riding the lion, he travels like the wind. When the lion roars, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three fall from their seats, and the daughters of the asuras also come under his power. Surrounded by ten million vidyādharas, he lives for an eon. When he dies, he will be born in the world realm Vimalā.

A painter who keeps the poṣadha should, under the constellation Puṣya, paint with unmixed colors an image of the Blessed Lady Bhṛkuṭī made of priyaṅgu wood. Before it, the vidyādhara, keeping silence, should recite the vidyā six hundred thousand times. Then he should take a corpse obtained from a charnel ground, bathe it with fine fragrant scents, bind it well, and set it facing east. Then the practitioner should worship it with flowers and so on, present a great torma, and sit on a mat of kuśa grass. Having covered it with a jewel and consecrated it seven times with the Blessed Lady's mantra, he should perform a fire offering of twenty-eight ladlefuls into the mouth of the vetāla. The corpse's mouth will open. The practitioner should quickly drive a khadira-wood kīla eight finger-widths long, consecrated seven times with the Blessed Lady's mantra, into its big toe. Again the practitioner should recite the vidyā until its tongue has stretched out a cubit long. Even if the sound of thunder roars, he should not be afraid. Then the vidyādhara should recite quickly and strike the vetāla's forehead with white karavīra flowers, and it will be subdued. On the tip of its tongue he will see a jewel, beautiful, wreathed in a garland of flames; he should recite the vidyā and take it. As soon as he takes it, he has curling ringlets of hair and becomes a sixteen-year-old cakravartin of the vidyādharas. Whatever he thinks of all comes about, except for birth and the exhaustion of the defilements. He lives for an eon, and the jewel adorning his head illuminates eight million yojanas all around. All the vidyādharas also come completely under his power. When the time comes for him to pass from this life, the Blessed Lady herself appears and urges him on. Saying, "Son, those powers of the jewel are exhausted; you should practice again," she vanishes. Afterward he will remember this queen of vidyās. He will not go to or be born in the lower realms, the states of ruin. At all times, this will grant him the recollection of the Buddha.

This completes the chapter of the Blessed Lady, the Queen of Vidyās, as expounded by Īśāna.

The four world guardians spoke the rite of the Blessed Lady: "Merely by recollecting this queen of vidyās, all obstructors are paralyzed. In this world realm there are those who know neither what is near nor what is far: those without Dharma, of sinful mind, of little wisdom, who kill living beings; the fierce, the ill-complexioned, the weak, the crooked, the hunchbacked, the thick-necked, and others with necks like a crow's; those who look like dwarfs, deer, camels or black yaks; those with yellowish-gray hair, bad nails, or the voice of a crow; and likewise the pot-bellied, the filthy, and any others tormented by disease. For these, the vidyā as it has been described will not be accomplished.

"By our words of truth, this is how, having first exhausted their former karma, they may then practice the vidyā: the old, the one-eyed, the blind, the hunchbacked, the crooked, and others like them. Again, one should have a Blessed Lady made of white sandalwood, one cubit of the Sugata in size, and have a painter who keeps the poṣadha paint it with unmixed colors. Then one should invite her to be seated on the shore of the ocean, bathe three times a day, eat alms food, burn guggulu as incense, and offer two million recitations. When the recitation is complete, one should perform eight hundred fire offerings of guggulu and kuñjika with the Blessed Lady's mantra. Then the karma will be exhausted."

Then the Four Great Kings, looking at the vināyaka, said this: "O vināyaka, listen! You must not approach the vidyādhara who holds this queen of vidyās."

The vināyaka said this: "Any vidyādhara who again transgresses the rite and, through conceit, fails in the practice, him we shall approach to obstruct, and we shall destroy even the merit he has gathered over a hundred years."

The king of the gods said: "O, O vicious vināyakas! To destroy you, I shall explain these medicines:

Moon-Bearer, Belly, and Kindly One,
Tiger-Slayer, and Four-Hands too,
Pig's Ear, Elephant-Caller,
Tangled-Conduct, costus, and saffron,
Together with iron filings,
Moistened with an elephant's urine:
Ground, then, just as one wishes,
The wise should make them into pills.
Flowers, lamps, tormas and scents;
After defecating and urinating, wash with clay;
Bed, seat and clothing tied up;
Scents, flowers, and all the rest,
Should all be well prepared with it. Otherwise
The vināyakas will seek an opening."

As soon as this was spoken,
All the vināyakas, their minds
Thrown into confusion, fled
From one another to all quarters, glancing in dread.
They will not cause obstruction again.
Wherever this supreme medicine is,
There they will not draw near;
Even within a hundred yojanas
They will not obstruct this one.
The accomplishment of all of this one's rites
Will come about.
Whatever vidyādhara, again,
Focuses evenly at the three times,
In that practitioner no one at all
Will find an opening.

A painter who keeps the poṣadha should paint an image of the Blessed One, yellow like gold, teaching the Dharma. On his right is the noble Avalokiteśvara, wearing a crown of matted locks, his body dark blue and adorned with a protective cord, holding a lotus in his hand. One should paint Vajrapāṇi, like a flax flower, holding a vajra in his hand and radiating light all around. Beside Vajrapāṇi one should paint the Four Great Kings with their weapons. Beside Avalokiteśvara one should paint the Blessed Lady Bhṛkuṭī, dark blue like the priyaṅgu flower. Below is the practitioner holding a censer in his hand.

Then the practitioner, eating alms food, should recite three hundred thousand times before the painted cloth in a clean place. Then he should take the painted cloth, climb to the summit of a mountain, make a buffalo of black earth, make vast offerings to the painted cloth, and offer a torma to all the bhūtas. Then the practitioner should make protection, put on clean clothes, sit on a mat of kuśa grass, and recite She Who Goes in Equality. He should recite until light rays stream from the buffalo's right horn. Then he offers water for honoring with the mind. Then he should mount the buffalo. As soon as he has mounted it, he takes on the body of a god, surrounded by seventeen vidyādharas. He will fly sixty thousand yojanas. The daughters of the asuras will also come under his power. He will live for five hundred thousand years.

Having purified his body, he should make vast offerings to the painted cloth and tormas of many kinds. Then the practitioner should make a noose of kuśa grass, press it with his right hand, and recite until it blazes. He should touch it while recollecting the vidyā. When he takes it up, he has curling ringlets of hair and the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, holding a noose in his hand, surrounded by sixteen vidyādharas, and he will fly five thousand yojanas. He will live for fourteen thousand years. When he dies, he will be born among the gods of the realm of the Four Great Kings.

If one climbs to the summit of a mountain, eats alms food, and recites She Who Goes in Equality ten million times, one becomes a vidyādhara. Surrounded by five vidyādharas, one goes without obstruction; in an instant, a moment, a split second, one travels to the Sahā world, and having gone there one remains for an eon. When one dies, one will be born in a buddha field.

This concludes the eighth chapter, the Blessed Lady, the Great Queen of Vidyās, spoken by the Four Great Kings.

Then all the kings of the garuḍas spoke the rite of the Blessed Lady. To cure poison: one makes colors with water that has dripped from leafy branches, snaps one's fingers, and, while dancing, recites mentally; by reciting seven times over white flowers, one cures the burning. With a thread one frightens the grahas. With guggulu incense one makes fangs fall out.

With jasmine flowers one drives away. By reciting over white mustard seed mixed with blood, one repels enemies. With cow's flesh one causes withering. With ariṣṭa leaves, dripping blood and nettles, one brings under control. With arka flowers one bestows wealth. With hundred-petaled flowers one makes the piśācas flee in terror. With a creeper one drives away a family or a household. The nāgas are dealt with by flowers of the nāga tree. With chaff one cuts off a vidyā. By this one will accomplish the vidyā of an opponent.

Pure and wearing clean clothes, one should bathe three times a day and change one's clothes three times, eat milk and barley meal, and recite one million times; the body will then be purified. Then, under the constellation Puṣya, the practitioner should paint a garuḍa with yellow earth, cow's urine and green pigment, and place a garland of lotuses on its neck. Having worshiped it with the three precious things, the practitioner should then smear a maṇḍala with the products of the cow and place four full vases at the four doors. On the four full vases he should paint the four nāga kings. Then he should take butter from a cow whose calf is of the same color, place it in a copper vessel, press it with his right hand, and recite the vidyā until it gives off smoke and blazes. If he drinks it when it gives off smoke, he becomes invisible, lives for fourteen thousand years, and travels a thousand yojanas. If it blazes, he attains the body and mind of a god. He brings relief to all. He is surrounded by ten vidyādharas. When he dies, he will be born in Sukhāvatī.

If one goes to a river that flows to the ocean, eats alms food, and performs a hundred thousand fire offerings of nāga-tree flowers mixed with curd, honey and ghee, the nāgas will rise. Then the practitioner, without fear, should place in the center a vase adorned with flowers, and on top of it place a wheel diagram. Then the practitioner should make protection, sit on a nāga seat, and recite the vidyā until light rays stream from the garuḍa. The garuḍa will circle the practitioner and sink into the crown of his head. He should take hold of it by reciting the vidyā. When he mounts it, sixty thousand vidyādharas will approach, and he will travel at will like the wind. Like the light of the rising sun, he puts all the nāga vidyādharas to flight for a thousand yojanas. Free of stain, he lives for eighty thousand years. When he dies, he will be born in the world realm of Sukhāvatī.

Having done the preliminary practice, the vidyādhara should then go to a charnel ground, smear a patch of ground the size of a cowhide with cow dung, worship with scents, flowers and so on, and make a great torma. On the eighth day of the following dark fortnight, he should go to the charnel ground, smear a patch of ground the size of a cowhide, and make vast offerings. If the practitioner then recites the vidyā eight thousand times, it will be accomplished. If he puts it in his mouth, he will become invisible. He will live for five thousand years.

This concludes the ninth chapter, the Blessed Lady, the Queen of Vidyās, as explained by the garuḍa.

Then all the hosts of mātṛkās, together with the yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, pūtanas and kaṭapūtanas, rose from their seats and approached the place where the noble Avalokiteśvara was. Having approached, they bowed their heads at the bodhisattva's feet and spoke a rite of the vidyā:

"It is to be done without regard to the date of the month or the constellation, and without keeping a fast; any vidyā at all is complete for it. In a charnel ground, on the right side of the body of Maheśvara, one recites the vidyā eight hundred times; if one then puts it in one's mouth, one becomes invisible and will seize the six portions of the earth.

"One should take a bamboo that has not been touched and wrap it with the three metals. Then, pure and wearing clean clothes, one should go to a charnel ground, worship with scents, flowers, incense and so on, and also make a torma for all the bhūtas. Then the practitioner should take a skull in his left hand, press it with his right hand, and recite the vidyā until it lets out a clamor. He should take it up while recollecting the vidyā; as soon as he takes it up, he becomes invisible. He seizes the six portions of the earth and lives for a thousand years. He takes his pleasure together with the daughters of the gods and the asuras.

"On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should take the tongue of a woman who has died and wrap it with the three metals; one then travels as swiftly as thought, like the wind. If, while keeping celibacy with this, one turns one's mind toward what one desires, one goes alone to that world realm and remains there for a great eon. One takes birth at will.

"If, pure and wearing clean clothes, one recites the vidyā in a charnel ground for six months, one becomes invisible and lives for five hundred years. One should grind it together with owl's eye ointment, make a pill wrapped with the three metals, and place it between two bowls joined mouth to mouth on the right side of the body of Maheśvara. Pressing it with the right hand, one should recite the supreme, immeasurable vidyā, and keep reciting until one hears a splitting sound. If one takes the pill while recollecting the vidyā and puts it in one's mouth, one becomes invisible and will live for two thousand years.

"One should take eye ointment, realgar, milk and lotus filaments in equal amounts and wrap them with the three metals. One should understand the procedure for the constellation Puṣya, and then practice.

"One who wishes to accomplish the piśācas should smear a maṇḍala the size of a cowhide in a charnel ground and make a torma of meat, liquor and so on. Facing east, if one performs eight thousand fire offerings of human hair mixed with blood, all the piśācas will come. One should not be afraid and should not make protection, but should say this: 'Come under my power!' When this is said, they will reply, 'So be it,' and vanish. Every day they will give five coins each, and these too must be spent in full.

In a charnel ground, a preta called by its own name, Stainless, comes under one's power. In a charnel ground one should make an effigy and pin its feet with a ritual dagger. Then one should recite the vidyā (the spell). For this, too, one should smear a maṇḍala about the size of a cowhide, make extensive offerings, and recite the vidyā a hundred thousand times. In a charnel ground one should perform eight thousand fire offerings of sesame; for seven days one should perform the fire offering at night. Each day it gives five silver coins. If one performs a hundred thousand fire offerings of kumuda lilies smeared with curd, honey and ghee, one will certainly see it.

Having made an effigy of charnel-ground ash and sitting close beside it, one kindles a fire of arka wood; if one then performs eight thousand fire offerings of jasmine flowers smeared with fragrant sesame oil, one becomes invisible. If, by this very rite, one names them by name, one becomes a king of Lāñja or a minister.

To bring a woman under one's power, one performs a fire offering of atimukta flowers, and she comes under one's power: after seven days, whenever one thinks of her in one's mind, at that moment she comes.

Going to a charnel ground, one smears a maṇḍala and performs a fire offering with human flesh; on the seventh day, those seized by piśācas are freed by one's mere glance.
