Having recited twenty-one times, one should make fire offerings of sesame to bring a young woman of good family under one's power. One who wants clothing should make fire offerings of dūrvā grass and the thorny plant, eight thousand times or for seven nights. Having empowered sweet flag eight thousand times, seven times over, one binds it on the hand. One who wants wealth should make eight thousand fire offerings of guggulu pills for seven nights. One who wants to be master of a household should make fire offerings of perfume for seven nights. Making eight thousand fire offerings of ghee, one obtains a village. For expulsion, one should make fire offerings of nimba leaves smeared with pungent sesame oil. Human flesh is for the rite of expulsion. Husks are for the rite of causing enmity. For driving someone to roam, snake slough and ash are used. For unmanning someone, cow dung and indra.

Husks are for binding water. For pacification, one uses śamī leaves together with milk.

Each day, rising at dawn, having made offerings to the Buddha, the Blessed One, as one can afford, one should recite one hundred thousand times. This accomplishes what has not been accomplished. To destroy what others have accomplished, it seizes them with binding. Making fire offerings of the thorny plant for seven nights destroys the enemy. One who wants clothing should make eight thousand fire offerings of dūrvā grass and the thorny plant. One who wishes to make a house shake violently should take a human bone, make it into a peg eight finger-widths long, and drive it into the house. If one recites eight hundred times over a flower and gives it, the person is brought under one's power.

At the king's gate, with saffron, rgya spos, tamāla leaves, and hundred-petaled flowers with their stalks, wrapped in cloth, by the proper rite, one sprinkles the powder on the clothes: for one beset by human enemies, those human enemies are brought under one's power.

To be victorious in battle, one recites eight thousand times over a banner, and empowers perfume, flowers and incense with the mantra of the Blessed Lady, noble Tārā. Having offered water at the fire hearth seven times, one sends the banner forth and has it displayed to the opposing army. It strikes them as a vajra thunderbolt strikes a tree.

Over black sesame, before an effigy one has made, one recites a thousand times, and, speaking the target's name, one eats it. By reciting eight thousand times, one places all seeds, or all medicines, or all perfumes, or fragrant flowers, or a lotus without black roots, in a vase, and recites a thousand times over it. One should bathe beneath a bodhi tree, or elsewhere. Speaking the target's name, one makes fire offerings of white mustard and lotus, or of the powder of lotus petals, stalks and roots, and of khadira charcoal: the person is brought under one's power. If, inside a bilva fruit, with things mixed with honey, one recites eight thousand times over the smoke and the charcoal, a queen, a minister, or whoever is named is brought under one's power.

Before noble Avalokiteśvara, one offers perfume, flowers and incense and makes offerings to the Blessed Lady. Then whoever one names while making fire offerings of jasmine flowers, blue utpala, or other flowers is brought under one's power. To bring a siddha's beloved under one's power, black sesame; to bring the foremost queen under one's power, priyaṅgu; to bring all beings under one's power, red śāli rice: whoever one names when making the fire offering is brought under one's power. If one speaks the name of a maiden and makes fire offerings of stamen flowers, she is brought under one's power. If one makes eight thousand fire offerings of milk, milk porridge, ghee and honey before the Blessed Lady, it is a rite of increase for whoever one calls by name.

Beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight, one does this at a stūpa containing relics, before an image, or before a painted cloth facing west. At first light, on a mountain peak, one kindles a fire with kuśa grass and bilva sticks and makes eight thousand fire offerings of fully opened lotuses smeared with curd, honey and ghee. One should offer incense of agaru, kunduruka and śrīveṣṭaka, and a torma of milk and curd; and in addition one gives the obstructors a torma for all the bhūtas. Then, on the eighth day, one becomes a sovereign.

Eating milk and barley gruel, if one makes fire offerings of white lotuses in full bloom, one finds a great treasure or a land. One should make fire offerings into the fire of yellow flowers smeared with curd, honey and ghee: one becomes lord of a land. For three nights, subsisting on flour, one should make fire offerings for three nights. Likewise, it is also accomplished by doing seven hundred thousand without interruption. If one makes one hundred thousand fire offerings of those same sticks smeared with curd, honey and ghee, a koṭi of gold appears. Rising early, preceded by bathing, practicing celibacy, and kindling the fire well, one makes eight thousand fire offerings of nāgakesara and priyaṅgu: within three months one experiences an extraordinary accomplishment, and much wealth comes. If one makes fire offerings of beef and khaṇḍa, one obtains a place of cattle. Likewise, if one makes fire offerings with sticks of priyaṅgu and nāgakesara, beings are brought under one's power.

Beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight, one kindles a fire beneath a bilva tree and makes one hundred thousand fire offerings of bilva and āśibilva smeared with ghee: one sees the goddess Tārā. Having become pure, fasting through four meals, one should make ten thousand fire offerings: one sees a great treasure. Likewise, for twenty nights, eating milk and barley gruel, one makes one hundred thousand fire offerings of white mustard seed: one becomes a lord of wealth. Having done the preliminary practice, one makes fire offerings day and night of white mustard seed smeared with ghee: within a month it causes good, steady rain to fall. Fasting through four meals, one makes ten thousand fire offerings: one finds wealth.

When the bright fortnight arrives, the wise one should strike at the three junctures of the day before the painted cloth of the goddess. Within the bright fortnight, this goddess grants him the supreme gift. With this knowledge mantra one should make a fire offering of a thousand oblations of sesame. If one kindles the fire with bilva wood, one sees the goddess, and she makes one a lord of wealth or of grain. Having made extensive offerings to the Blessed Lady, if one makes one hundred thousand fire offerings of hundred-petaled flowers, one finds wealth. In front of a stūpa containing relics, in a clean place, if one kindles a fire for the goddess with palāśa sticks and makes one hundred thousand fire offerings of utpalas, a district is brought under one's power. With this knowledge mantra, offering fragrant incense and eating milk and barley gruel, one makes a thousand fire offerings of lotuses: one obtains a thousand pieces of gold. If with this one makes one hundred thousand fire offerings of flowers, it grants whatever one has in mind.

If one makes a thousand fire offerings before the painted cloth, one sees a treasure. Eating milk and barley gruel, if in a clean place one makes one hundred thousand fire offerings of priyaṅgu smeared with curd, honey and ghee, together with milk, one finds a hundred pieces of gold. A garland of various kinds.

Then, fasting for three nights at the battlefield, one should make eight thousand fire offerings with agaru sticks at the three junctures of the day. Then, reciting throughout the night, if the painted cloth shakes or the bundle of garlands stirs, then it is accomplished, and it grants kingship. It bestows whatever one has in mind: it heals all illnesses, frees from death and bondage, dispels harm, and seals the maṇḍala.

Before noble Avalokiteśvara one should make a thousand fire offerings of flowers: this brings beings under one's power. Or else, placing a painted cloth at the foot of the bodhi tree, by this same rite, eating barley gruel, one should recite one hundred thousand times. Eating a single meal a day and keeping the eight-branched poṣadha, one accomplishes the food rites of noble Avalokiteśvara.

Or else, at the time of an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should have noble Avalokiteśvara painted, white as an autumn cloud and wearing a white upper robe. To one side one should have the goddess Tārā painted, golden in color, seated on a lotus, adorned with every ornament, and gazing all around upon the practitioner. Having made extensive offerings of perfume, flowers, incense and torma, with one's eyes fixed on the moon, one should offer recitation until the moon is released. The goddess Tārā will come, blazing in her own form, the color of the rising sun, holding a blooming lotus in her hand. One should offer her water and request the supreme boon.

Beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight, one should practice eating milk and gruel. One keeping the eight-branched poṣadha, abstaining from cooked food and salt, should make eight thousand fire offerings of guggulu before the painted cloth: one finds eight coins. This is the rite of kunduruka. This is also the rite of bilva. Devadāru should be applied for the sake of accomplishment. Here, with the root knowledge mantra, one should make eight thousand fire offerings of agaru. If one kindles the fire well with wood of a milky-sapped tree, it grants all wealth.

Having made offerings of perfume, flowers and incense to a stūpa containing relics, one rises early, kindles the fire well with ladle in hand, and makes eight hundred fire offerings of nāgakesara and priyaṅgu: within a month one will come to be looked upon. One should make one hundred thousand fire offerings of vikaṅkata sticks smeared with curd, honey and ghee. In a clean place, as in the earlier rite, if one kindles the fire well with palāśa sticks and makes offerings to the Blessed Lady, one finds a hundred pieces of gold. With this knowledge mantra, if one makes eight thousand fire offerings of priyaṅgu sticks smeared with curd, honey and ghee, one finds a thousand pieces of gold. With this knowledge mantra, having offered perfume, flowers and incense before noble Avalokiteśvara, one kindles the fire well with udumbara sticks and should make one hundred thousand fire offerings: this fulfills all desires, together with the supreme. Kindling a fire with aśoka wood, one should make a hundred fire offerings of white mustard seed: she comes in visible form, directly before one.

Having recited one hundred thousand times over incense, one who is clean, wearing clean clothes, eating milk and barley gruel and reciting constantly, obtains every wish one wishes for, and it grants all desires. Having done the preliminary practice, for five nights eating milk and barley gruel, or drinking milk, one should recite one hundred thousand times. At the end, having fasted for three nights, if on the full moon one worships with perfume, flowers and incense, one sees the goddess in her own form. Eating milk and barley gruel, one should make one hundred thousand fire offerings of white mustard seed. Drinking milk for twenty-one days, one kindles the fire well with apāmārga sticks and should make a thousand fire offerings of white mustard seed smeared with curd, honey and ghee. If one kindles the fire well with sticks of a milky-sapped tree, by this one will certainly see a treasure. With this knowledge mantra, eating milk and barley gruel, if one kindles a fire with bilva wood and makes one hundred thousand fire offerings of sesame smeared with curd, honey and ghee, one sees the goddess in her own form.

Having offered perfume, flowers and incense before noble Avalokiteśvara, one kindles the fire well with udumbara wood smeared with curd, honey and ghee, and makes one hundred thousand fire offerings with arka sticks: without striving for it, one finds wealth and grain. Kindling the fire well with deva wood, one should make a thousand fire offerings of devadāru: she comes in her own form. A fire offering of ghee is for pacification. A fire offering of dūrvā grass is for increase. By making eight thousand fire offerings smeared with curd, honey and ghee, one likewise finds all the wealth one wants.

Making twenty-one knots in a thread spun by a maiden, one sends a girl off as a bride. One who wishes to sleep at night should recite the knowledge mantra countless times: one will not see bad dreams. If one recites eight hundred times before an effigy made of black sesame, whoever's name one has in mind is brought under one's power. If one recites eight hundred times over black grain, whoever's name one speaks is brought under one's power.

To bring beings under one's power, before the painted cloth, one should make fire offerings of lotuses into a fire of apāmārga sticks. Kindling the fire well with bilva sticks or with sticks of a milky-sapped tree, one makes one hundred thousand fire offerings of lotuses: one becomes a universal monarch of power. Again, with ten thousand lotuses one gains a kingdom. By a fire offering of one hundred thousand lotuses, one gains great wealth. In all these fire offerings, having worshiped with perfume, flowers and incense, eating milk and barley gruel, whoever one calls by name while offering jasmine flowers is brought under one's power. Kindling the fire well with eight hundred bilva sticks, one should make fire offerings of one hundred thousand lotuses. Whoever one calls by name is brought under one's power.

Having recited twenty-one times over an ointment of gorocanā (bezoar), one should anoint the head with it. Or else one should mark a tilaka on the face. All people will be delighted. One should make eight thousand fire offerings of lotus seeds smeared with curd, honey and ghee. Whoever is named comes under one's power. Through the grace of noble Avalokiteśvara, things will turn out otherwise. If lotuses are not to be found, one should make fire offerings of eight thousand blue utpalas. One should make fire offerings of perfume or flowers; with one hundred thousand, the deities will be accomplished.

For bathing, one should put all the medicinal herbs and all the seeds into a vase that is not blackened at its base, and bathe with water empowered by eight thousand recitations. Those struck by obstructors, or oneself, will be pacified.

Utpala, costus, a portion of aloeswood, nakha perfume, and nard, in portions increasing fourfold: before the painted cloth image, having made vast offerings to noble Avalokiteśvara and lit lamps of cow's ghee, one combines all these substances with flowers, and with this one should have bathed whatever king, royal minister, royal queen or practitioner, or those whose lives are passing away untimely. They will become long-lived. Fortunate ones struck by obstructors are freed from the obstructors.

Remaining in a fast day and night in the presence of noble Avalokiteśvara, one should make a hundred thousand fire offerings of brahmadāri or jitendraya, aloeswood and turuṣka incense; in the same way it will be accomplished. One should make eight thousand fire offerings of black sesame smeared with curd, honey and ghee and mixed with sandalwood powder or dried dung, and it will be accomplished. Another rite: making a hundred thousand fire offerings of sandalwood sticks four finger-widths long, smeared with curd, honey and ghee, it will be accomplished.

Beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight, having kindled a fire beneath a bilva tree, one should make eight million fire offerings of bilva fruits smeared with curd, honey and ghee. One sees the goddess in her own form; she bestows a great kingdom, and she also bestows whatever else one asks for.

To free someone from a bhūta graha, one should touch them with the lotus mudrā; it puts the spirit to flight.

Even without having performed the preliminary practice, one should kindle a fire with wood of a milky-sap tree and make a hundred thousand fire offerings of lotuses smeared with curd, honey and ghee. Likewise one should make a hundred thousand fire offerings of red and blue utpalas, or else a fire offering of jasmine flowers. Before the painted cloth image, eating milk and barley gruel, one should make ever-increasing offerings and should eat food obtained by begging. Having made vast offerings of perfume, flowers and incense, at the end of a fast kept day and night, one should make a fire offering of fragrant flowers. By this, even without the preliminary practice, even one whose moral discipline is utterly broken accomplishes the grounds. Or else one should make a hundred thousand fire offerings of white mustard seed mixed with black sesame and smeared with curd, honey and ghee. It will be accomplished in the same way.

One who desires wealth makes a fire offering of royal mustard or of mustard seed with apāmārga sticks. Or else, to bring a minister under one's power, one makes a fire offering with sesame oil, and this may also be applied in all rites. To bring a maiden under one's power, it is the former fire offering, smeared with curd, honey and ghee. For a royal queen, it is this rite. Having kindled a fire of bodhi-tree wood, one makes a fire offering of articles of enjoyment. To bring under one's power, it is a fire offering of royal mustard. To bring under one's power, one should make a hundred thousand with sticks of the kambojikā flower. Having kindled a fire with bodhi-tree sticks smeared with curd, honey and ghee, in a fire without a hearth, having honored the god and the goddess with perfume, flowers and incense and made vast offerings, eating milk and barley gruel and wearing clean clothes, it grants whatever one has undertaken. Making a fire offering of a hundred vāsaka flowers brings under one's power whoever is named. A fire offering of black pepper destroys the vināyakas.

Beneath the bodhi tree, having made offerings of perfume and flowers, when the moon is seized by the eclipse planet, one should take realgar, place it on seven aśvattha leaves, and meditate until it blazes. By taking it up, one becomes a vidyādhara, unimpeded among all the gods, who goes quickly and swiftly to supremely beautiful divine palaces, with the color and splendor of the rising sun, who travels in the company of all the vidyādharas and is surrounded by hundreds of divine beings. For eye ointment for the ears, it is this very rite.

One who wishes to accomplish gorocanā should first, while eating milk and barley gruel, recite a hundred thousand times. At the time of a lunar eclipse, on seven pippala leaves, or at a stūpa containing relics, one should set out the gorocanā in a hundred portions and perform the rite by encircling it with the vidyā mantra. It is endowed with enjoyments and the rest; making a tilaka with it, one becomes a vidyādhara whose body is adorned with every ornament and who takes whatever form one desires, and one lives for a thousand years.

Taking flakes of the eye ointment that comes from Sauvīra, purifying them well by heating in fire, and steeping them a hundred times, when the moon is seized by the eclipse, one enters the water and should recite until it becomes a kumbhāṇḍa. Merely by being broken for an instant, it disintegrates. Anointed with this, one becomes endowed with splendor, wearing a crest and earrings, one's body adorned with garlands of lotuses, and goes on aspiring even to the very summit of all vidyādharas. Together with one's retinue, one lives for five thousand years. One becomes a vidyādhara who goes like the wind and travels as swiftly as the mind. By a fire offering of a hundred thousand lotuses and utpalas, one obtains a thousand pieces of gold. The rite of palāśa is just this.

Furthermore, here is what becomes the means of accomplishment of the great rite. It may be done in the presence of a Victor, or before the painted cloth image, or even by the ritual taught in other ritual manuals: that ritual of the painted cloth image in which the names of these vidyās are recited three times each. Or, near a stūpa containing relics, in a clean place, eating milk and barley gruel, beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight, one may live on flowers, fruit, caru, and roots, or on a diet of curd, or on water, flour, and gruel, or on a diet of perfume, or a diet of vakra, or a diet of ghee; or else one should practice the vow of silence. First of all, one should do the approach. Fully observing the eightfold poṣadha, one should make offerings, proclaiming them each day. One should eat alms food in accordance with the scriptures. Fully embracing the awakening mind, one should eat only when tormented by suffering. The practitioner, after bathing at the three times of day, should sit on an auspicious kuśa mat, wear clothes that have been cleansed, and recite one hundred thousand times. At the end, observing a fast day and night, having kindled a fire with khadira wood, one should make eight thousand fire offerings at the three times of day of sticks of milky-sap wood or of black aloeswood, four finger-widths or a finger in length, smeared with turuṣka and sesame oil.

Then it will be accomplished. On the fifteenth day, in the four directions, one should set out four vases made of cloth, filled with water, their mouths covered with mango twigs, without defects at the base and without blackening. On the right side, the vase called Fully Victorious, made of clay or of gold, filled completely with jewels and all the seeds, with all the medicinal herbs and roots, the jewel essence, its mouth covered with lotus-net flowers, its neck tied with undamaged dukūla cloth, is to be placed in the center. Likewise in the east is the vase called Rising. In the west is the vase called Haring. Naming the vases in this way and so forth, one should set them in place as in the Perfection of Wisdom.

One should offer twenty fragrant flowers, tormas and garlands, and offer twenty bowls filled with perfume in the four directions. One should set twenty bowls filled with milk in the four directions. One should offer a hundred ghee lamps. One should light four vase lamps. One should offer twelve bowls filled with milk porridge to the nāgas. One should present twelve bowls of sesame soup as torma to the rākṣasas. One gives eight bowls of warm gruel as torma to the bhūtas. One should offer a torma of hwak and other foods to noble Avalokiteśvara. For the others, one should set in the four directions bowls filled with cream and curd, as is fitting and as is suitable. One should offer incense of black aloeswood. One should set in the four directions bowls of incense of camphor, white sandalwood, kunduruka, and śrīvāsa.

Then, beginning the rite in the evening, observing a fast day and night, having kindled a fire with arka sticks or khadira wood, the invitation in this rite is made with this mantra. The mantra is: namo ratna trayāya nama ārya a ba lo ki te śva rā ya bo dhi satvā ya ma hā satvā ya hi ri hi ri su ru su ru ma hā kā ru ṇi kā ā gaccha ā gaccha ārya a ba lo ki te śva rā dhi ri dhi ri ṇi ya thā sa ma ya ma nu sma ra sā hā At the time of requesting departure, one urges him on with fragrant flowers.

Having offered the welcoming water in a vessel made of silver or of clay, one should then, during a lunar eclipse or a solar eclipse, make eight thousand fire offerings of black aloeswood sticks of the size stated, or of the other things mentioned, smeared with sesame oil. Then, in the east or another direction, noble Avalokiteśvara, supremely compassionate, holding in his hands a round water flask and a staff, with a crown of matted locks hanging down, will come. Then, having taken white fragrant flowers by the handful in the vessel described, one should offer the welcoming water. Then noble Avalokiteśvara says, "Whatever boon it may be, I shall grant it." He gives whatever boon one has chosen: going through the sky, or invisibility, or kingship, or all the accomplishments of vidyā, or kingship over the vidyādharas, or weapons, or long life, or bringing all beings under one's power, or accomplishing gorocanā, or accomplishing eye ointment, or transferring treasures, or entering caverns, or the elixir of rejuvenation, or accomplishing realgar, or the five higher knowledges, or the rite for the body one desires for oneself, or the divine eye, or the destruction of disease, or divine knowledge, or hands and feet, or freedom from defects of the eyes, or concealment from Indra, lord of the gods, or the destruction of disease, or, for leprosy or whatever bodily disease is incurable, liberation from each of these, and the retention of what one has heard, and the gaining of wealth: whatever boon one has chosen, he grants it. One also goes to the abode of noble Avalokiteśvara. One will live for an eon.

The practitioner of the Blessed Lady, noble Tārā, having a kuśa mat, should know the udumbara rite: two wooden sandals of udumbara wood, or on potter's clay; from there on, everything is the same.

There follows the rite of the supremely secret near-heart mantra of Tārā: namo ratna trayāya nama ārya a ba lo ki śva rā ya bo dhi satvā ya ma hā satvā ya oṃ ku ru ku ru kulle svā hā This is the supremely secret near-heart mantra of all these vidyās. Merely by reciting it, it suppresses all fears. All diseases are exhausted and destroyed. It destroys all fears. Minor rites too are accomplished by reciting it. Reciting it two million one hundred thousand times makes one travel through the sky. Then one should recite over an eye ointment of realgar placed within seven aśvattha leaves until it becomes warm. When it grows warm, it brings under one's power; when it gives off smoke, one becomes invisible; when it blazes, one goes through the sky. One should make a fire offering of a hundred thousand oblations of sesame.

It grants whatever one desires. One should recite one million one hundred thousand times, until one sees noble Avalokiteśvara. When one sees him, whatever one has undertaken is accomplished. Making a hundred thousand fire offerings with sticks of white sandalwood, each day one obtains a coin. Making a hundred thousand fire offerings with sticks of red sandalwood, each day one obtains six kārṣāpaṇas. One should recite seven hundred thousand times each, and one becomes invisible. One should recite five hundred thousand times, and it destroys disease. By reciting it three times over eight nights, it destroys disease. One should recite one million two hundred thousand times, and one obtains elixir and essence. By eating it, wrinkles and white hair are cast off. With three hundred thousand one removes gṛdhrasī (sciatica): having heated iron, and having smeared the right foot with sesame oil recited over three times, one should burn the foot with that iron and say, "Gṛdhrasī, be cut off!" By reciting two hundred thousand times, one brings a royal queen under one's power. By making oblations of royal mustard one brings under one's power, and in seven nights one becomes a lord of wealth, except for what has been set aside out of desire. If one recites a hundred thousand times over apāmārga and anoints oneself with it, one obtains whatever food and drink one asks for. If one makes a fire offering with arka sticks, one obtains a hundred gold coins. One should make a fire offering with biṇyakaṃ wood, and all people will be delighted. One should make a hundred thousand fire offerings with tāmūla powder, and one will bind on a crown. One should recite ten million times, and one becomes a vidyādhara surrounded by a retinue of a hundred. One should make a fire offering of eight thousand oblations of parched rice, and in seven days the obstructors cease to be. One should recite one million two hundred thousand times, and dry cow dung will be cooked into hwak. If one anoints oneself while saying "without root" or "without poison", one becomes fragrant. Combining all the ingredients of betel properly, one should make a fire offering with a hundred thousand. One will never be without betel. Apāmārga removes eye disease. For one struck by fever, it is done by sweeping with kuśa grass. Having recited eight hundred times over a thread, one should tie it on, and one becomes fortunate. If one makes a fire offering of a hundred thousand of gruel together with curd, for as long as one wishes there will be no lack of food. If one makes a fire offering of a thousand oblations of ghee, one obtains three districts. It is said that beings of little merit should accomplish it by performing the practice three times. One should make a hundred thousand fire offerings of guggulu pills the size of a cowrie shell; each day one obtains sixteen paṇas. One should spend it all, leaving nothing over. One should make a hundred thousand fire offerings of donka flowers, and one obtains a hundred and twenty million new garments of various kinds.

It is accomplished by nothing other than giving prompted by compassion, likewise faith, and the approach to the deity. So it should be understood.

As for this king of ritual manuals, contained within all the teachings, this vidyā contained within all ritual manuals: its rites could not be taught in full even in hundreds of years, nor could they be taught by condensing them into this or that. In other rituals too, all those rites for accomplishing this vidyā should be performed, and likewise one accomplishes the actions that have been specifically stated. It is said that in this king of ritual manuals, those vidyā mantras, and whatever is to be accomplished by mantras, should be accomplished just so, with vast and utterly clear samādhi and the rest, and also by the rituals of other ritual manuals.

The conduct of the means of accomplishment of this king of ritual manuals, giving, the various kinds of rites of the means of accomplishment and so on, the maṇḍala rites, the vidyās of worldly and transworldly aims, the mantras, the ten rites of the great mudrā taught at length in all the ritual manuals, and the eight rites of the great bodhisattvas all become the same. That is to say, the ritual manual of noble Samantabhadra, the ritual manual of the four great bodhisattva youths, the Vast Mountain, the Universal Mountain, and the Tantra of Victory over the Three Worlds: these all come to be the same in the rites of conduct of all the great ritual manuals. Just so, what I have spoken and the king of ritual manuals taught by the infinite buddhas are to be easily accomplished, and one goes to the far shore of infinite awakening.

From the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, the extensive chapter on the vidyā of the rites common to all the root ritual manuals of the Blessed Lady, noble Tārā Ūrdhvajaṭā, is complete.

The chapter on mudrās is to be written.

Then the great being entered into the samādhi that fully delights the mudrās, the rite of drawing the mudrās, common to the rites of all maṇḍalas and contained in all the tantras. With a broadly smiling face, he then spoke the characteristics of the mudrās:

The characteristics of the bindings,
Once known, are here set forth.
Of all the tathāgatas,
The mudrās of the family, in three parts:
A sun disk blazing all around,
The mudrā of the complete uṣṇīṣa.
The disk of the rising sun
Is the mudrā of the wheel-turning monarch.
That same uṣṇīṣa, raised a little,
Is the mudrā of the upward-rising uṣṇīṣa.
Entirely white, with a white parasol,
A blazing wheel, radiating out,
A mass of splendor, a vajra essence,
Invincible to others, wound three times:
The mudrā of the Victor's uṣṇīṣa.
A wheel with eight spokes and a hub
Is the characteristic of the wheel of Dharma.
A lotus with a precious jewel
Is the mudrā of the Jewel Essence.
That same, set within separate circles,
With a ring that performs all actions;
What is set in its center is not the center.
That eye is the eye of the tathāgata.
That same, lowered at its base,
Is the tathāgata's ūrṇā.
The sign of power above and below the tip
Is the power of the tathāgata.
A blazing mass, invincible to others,
Is the circle of the blazing essence.
All the mudrās, the alms bowl and the rest,
Through the distinctions of mantra or of mind,
Are the mudrās of the tathāgata family.

On the outer part of an eight-petaled lotus,
Petaled, complete and full,
The form of the moon with its digits:
The root mudrā, bearing a lotus.
Upon a swaying lotus,
A wish-fulfilling jewel firmly set:
This is the mudrā that brings abundance.
For Hayagrīva and for the one facing forward,
It is the anther of the lotus.
A white lotus is Pāṇḍaravāsinī's (the White-Clad One's);
That same anther is Yaśovatī's.
The utpala itself is Tārā's;
The utpala is also the moon's.
Slightly jeweled, with a wrathful frown,
Together with its stalk, it is Śrī's;
This is the family called "all the female messengers."
Opened and in full bloom, it is the queen of the family.
Common to all the rest
Are ointment, or the round flask and water pitcher;
Those forms, for the remaining ones,
Should be known by those who possess the vidyā.
With flames, they are the mudrās of the lotus family.

A five-pronged vajra,
Two-faced, the goddesses each in place,
With a garland of flames, the supreme vidyā:
This is the vajra of the vidyā king.
The samaya vajra set upright;
Rising up from the middle of a vase is Māmakī.
With one uṣṇīṣa is the Victorious One;
With two uṣṇīṣas, the Fully Victorious One;
With three uṣṇīṣas, the sign of the vajra.
The form of a spear in the middle
Is the sign of the vajra.
Having made a coil in the middle,
Coiled about the spear, it faces forward.
In a disk at the center of a vajra,
A disk blazing all around:
This is the Garlanded Lady.
At the tips of both vajras,
The garland-purifier holds a garland.
Slightly to the side of the crest,
A hook: Vajra Hook, the Hook Lady.
A staff is the Staff Lady; likewise
An axe set at the tip of the middle prong.
A vajra fist, also with a vase.
Then, the definite forms:
A single-pointed vajra with flames,
A vajra blade, the point of a spear;
For the female messengers they are long,
For the wrathful ones, short.
Radiating out is the vidyā king;
With an uṣṇīṣa slightly in the middle,
It is called the vidyā king.
A spear below and a vajra above
Is for the hosts; a spear above
And a vajra below, for all the vināyakas.
In the middle, in the four directions of the vedī,
A three-headed vajra with a vedī
Is for the maṇḍala of the vidyā king.
That same, here too, likewise,
Is with flames everywhere:
Make seven, five or three flames.
For all of the vajra family,
The characteristics of the five vajras,
With mudrās, are for the fierce ones,
Together with a vedī.
As for the others, the worldly ones,
With flames, but not fierce,
They are placed separately, without a vedī.
In accordance with how they are to proceed,
The worldly ones by virtuous conduct,
By knowing the transcendent tantra,
Do all things by the maṇḍala of the ritual manual. So it is said.

oṃ sa ra sa ra vajra prā kā raṃ hūṃ phaṭ svā hā
This is the fence.
oṃ bi phu rad rakṣa vajra pañja ra hūṃ phaṭ svā hā
This is the vajra tent.
oṃ kī li kī li vajra vajri bhu bandha bandha hūṃ phaṭ svā hā
This is the stake.

Thus these are the mudrās for drawing their maṇḍalas.

Then that great being once again entered into the samādhi called Fully Urging On the Mudrās, and said, "Those who engage fully and evenly in the mudrās and in all the vidyās, which are the same in the general rite of all the means of accomplishment, will without any doubt realize accomplishment."

Then, with the palms at the center,
Middle finger against middle finger,
That same placed with the tips of the index fingers looking at each other:
This is proclaimed as the samaya mudrā
Of the tathāgata family, together with its mantra.
First, complete it with the mantra;
Then come recitation and the rest.

Here again the mantra is:
namaḥ sarva ta thā ga te bhyaḥ oṃ ta thā ga tā ud bha vā ya svā hā
This is the samaya mantra of the tathāgata family.

The back of the left hand is turned the other way and bent back, the little finger of the hand is grasped, and with it the two thumbs, slightly extended, are pressed down. As for the fingers, this is the supreme samaya mantra, renowned in the vajra family.

Here again the mantra is:
namaḥ sarva ta thā ga te bhyaḥ oṃ vajra ud bha vā ya svā hā
This is the mantra of the samaya mudrā of the vajra family.

Making middle finger meet middle finger,
One joins the palms together,
The two fingers always without a gap.
First binding it, and likewise afterward,
Once it is complete, recitation and the rest follow.

Here again the mantra:
namaḥ sarva ta thā ga te bhyaḥ
These words are for the samaya mudrās.
oṃ padma ud bha vā ya svā hā
This is the samaya mantra of the mudrā of the lotus family.

These samaya mudrās,
These three, are proclaimed everywhere.
They are of immeasurable qualities,
Of great power, overcoming adversaries.
First, and always again, the practitioner
Should bind them before the deity;
He will obtain its accomplishment,
Swiftly, the pacifying and other rites he desires.
The infinite protectors of the world
And their great-souled heirs
Taught the great mudrās for all embodied beings
For the sake of accomplishment.
Always rising early,
One should bind them each and every day.
Pure, endowed with faith and intelligence,
Through that, accomplishment will arise.
The intelligent one who knows
These three samaya mudrās,
Holding them by the noble one's instruction,
Will gain their accomplishment without doubt.
One who understands these,
Even if the ritual is deficient,
As a practitioner achieves its accomplishment.
For the Mahābalas and the others,
In order to protect the mudrās everywhere,
Then that great comforter said:
"I, through the all-illuminating
Meditation that fully urges on the mudrās,
Always and in every way
Have taught the mudrās,
Common to all the Tārās,
Wherever the eternal is taught.
Whatever vidyās are in other ritual manuals,
These too should be applied."

Here again the characteristics of the mudrā are given.
Again, with the fingers interlaced,
Joined twice and so held,
The two index fingers fully extended,
And likewise the thumbs, O wise one,
With the mind well settled in equipoise,
One binds the root mudrā.
For the purpose of inviting Tārā,
These are joined with the vidyā.
This, the root mudrā of all the Tārās,
Bestows great benefit.
For the practitioner, all aims
Come from applying his own vidyā.
Even if the rite is deficient, through faith
The deities come at once.
That same, with the thumbs bent,
One should offer the welcoming water.
Then it becomes the welcoming-water mudrā,
Bestowing the fruits that people desire.
This is the mudrā of the welcoming water.

Bending the hand back, raise it and extend it;
Carefully set the thumbs as a seat.
That itself, for the sake of the accomplishment one desires,
Fully pleases the deities.
This is the mudrā of the seat.
The tips of the thumbs
Are bent, and whatever becomes separated;
Bathing, one accomplishes one's own excellent aim.
This is the mudrā of bathing.
Close beside the base of the fingers
Set the right thumb;
Wholly avoiding medicines
And the parts of living creatures, offer perfumes.
This is the mudrā of perfume.
Likewise the left thumb too
Is set, placed evenly;
One should offer various flowers
Endowed with supreme divine fragrance.
This is the mudrā of flowers.
The tip of the right index finger
Is bent and comes to rest on the middle finger;
With that, together with the thumb,
One should offer incense.
This is the mudrā of incense.
The left thumb and index finger
Are made to rest upon the middle finger;
Clean, pure, and perfectly endowed,
With that, one makes the offering of torma.
This is the mudrā of torma.
Having set the two thumbs
At the tips of the index fingers,
With excellent ghee of the cow
One should make offering to Tārā.
This is the mudrā of the lamp.
The index finger at the tip of the middle finger
Is joined at its outer tip joint;
The thumb and the ring finger
Hold the thread of the counting rosary.
This is the mudrā of holding the rosary.
Always facing toward the fire,
The ring finger of the right hand
Is placed at the joint of the middle finger;
On the middle fingers of the joined hands
The thumbs are slightly bowed.
This is the mudrā of inviting the fire god.
Having joined the ring finger and thumb,
One applies it together with the mantra;
With that one says, "Please depart."
This is the mudrā of urging on the invited fire god.

This is the mudrā encircled by the assembly of vidyās of all the Tārās. Practitioners who desire unequaled accomplishment should always apply it in common.

Having made the legs crooked,
The mudrā fully extended:
The two hands are extended, and a wheel;
First urging the thumbs,
One binds a fist, and the thumbs,
Lined up evenly, should be extended.
This mudrā with the middle finger raised
Is known as the staff mudrā
Of the wise bodhisattva.
The practitioner should apply it quickly;
It will bring about all accomplishments.
This is the staff mudrā.

Well joined together, the palms become hollow: this is the mudrā of joined palms. Where the thumbs are placed inside, it is the excellent seat: this is the mudrā of the excellent seat. When, from the mudrā of joined palms with hollow palms just described, the ring fingers are properly joined, this, the chief of the mudrās of joined palms, in the form of a lotus, in the form of rays of light, is the lotus mudrā. So the intelligent practitioner should understand. It should be applied for the sake of the seat. This mudrā is of great renown. This is the lotus mudrā. The root mudrā that was described, that utpala, is to be stated here. Opened by about a barley grain, the mudrā's lotus crest is itself a limb. The utpala mudrā is fully proclaimed as the mudrā of the Victory over the Three Worlds and as whatever is the mudrā of all the assemblies of Tārā. Bending it at the three joints is the mudrā of Bhṛkuṭī. That very one, with spaces between the joints, desired just so, is taught as the mudrā of vast samādhi. The mudrā with the index finger and thumb properly joined comes from the crest of Ekajaṭī. The vidyā mantras taught first in the samādhi: the second mudrā is Ekajaṭī's. Joining them together, extending the rest outward in the shape of hair, with the two middle fingers well placed in the form of a spear: this mudrā is explained as the spear. It makes the deity blaze, and it is perfectly the same; merely by showing it, all the wicked are destroyed. This is the spear mudrā.

These great mudrās
Are applied for the sake of the samaya.
Whoever knows them correctly
Will obtain accomplishment.
All the remaining mudrās
Are to be made immeasurable and countless.
The mudrās have been fully proclaimed.
What is said here in brief is this:
Beings whose minds are dull
Cannot perform the great rites;
So it is stated here in brief.

From the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, the extensive chapter on mudrās of the root ritual manual of the Blessed Lady, noble Tārā Ūrdhvajaṭā, is complete.

Then once more the great being, again meditating on the samādhi of the intrinsic nature of things, which accomplishes all rites, taught in this king of ritual manuals the means of accomplishment of the great vidyā of his own family called Pāṇḍaravāsinī, for the sake of protection and for averting obstructors:

namo ratna trayā ya nama ārya a ba lo ki te śva rā ya bo dhi satvā ya ma hā satvā ya darśa na parṣa ṇa bhyo śra ba ṇa sma ra ṇye na bā syā ma haṃ sarva satvā nāṃ sarva byā dhi ci kitpa ka tadya thā oṃ ka ṭe vi ka ṭe ka ṭāṃ ka ṭe ka ṭā vi ka ṭā vi ka ṭe bha ga va ti vi ja ye svā hā

This is the great vidyā of the one called Pāṇḍaravāsinī, which brings accomplishment through all vidyās and mantras. With this family vidyā of the lotus family one protects oneself, protects others, protects one's servants, keeps the painted cloth image in place, and protects the deities; and for this accomplishment of the painted cloth image, too, one should recite it after doing your means of accomplishment three times or seven times. Then one should begin the recitation of one's own deity, and accomplishment will come swiftly. At the end of the recitation, too, the obstructors pass into another existence. By constant recitation one also becomes free of disease. It frees one from all harm and makes one live long. One also finds happiness. It likewise serves for protecting oneself with a thread, for turning back harm, and so on.

Then, its mudrā is the general root mudrā of all the Tārās. That same, with the index fingers bound and made into a coiled shape, and the pair of thumbs also pressed together, is the mudrā of Pāṇḍaravāsinī. This too is the vidyā of the means of accomplishment through the mudrā, which proceeds evenly, without doubt. First, having bowed at her feet, one should then perform all the rites.

Again, in this great lord among kings of ritual manuals, one becomes able to carry out the noble Tārā, and all the splendid accomplishments of all the Tārās, protection, and the averting of all harm that has been done: the thorough application of the ritual procedures of the manual of all the noble Tārās. What is it? namo ratnatrayāya nama ārya avalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya candre candramati sūrye sūryamati ghuni ghuna la la le le sūte sūtani siddhi siddhi parākrame svāhā amitābhāsutā svāhā sarbeṣaṃ ārya avalokiteśvarāya svāhā This is the great vidyā of noble Tārā called the Noble Excellent One, which destroys all harms.

All of this, the vast conduct of the ritual procedures of Tārā's manual, the means of accomplishment, the mudrā rites and the rest, should be accomplished by means of the Moon of noble Tārā. Thus it should be fully understood. One may also accomplish it with the ritual procedure of another manual. Even without a manual one may perform this fierce rite: leaving out the syllables of homage, one should put hūṃ phaṭ in place of the svāhā of the bare vidyā. It may also be done with the ritual procedure of another manual. Whomever one wishes, one will bring under one's power. Or else one will destroy them. In short, one accomplishes whatever one wishes.

Then that great being looked upon the maṇḍala of the entire assembly and, with a pure intention, said to the great beings: "Those who practice this king of ritual manuals, who make offerings to it, and who write it down will attain the accomplishment of every aim. Loving-kindness toward all sentient beings and complete joy toward all sentient beings will also arise. It will protect them. Wherever this king of ritual manuals appears, that place will become a shrine, and that very place will come to be as if in the palm of one's hand.

"In the world with its gods, whatever son of good family or daughter of good family obtains this offering, this Dharma discourse, should practice it as yoga in every way. Knowing the strength and weakness of all sentient beings, one should make it clearly known. And it is to be practiced by everyone in a clean place, not elsewhere. Whoever performs it should apply it in such a way that it does not reach those who have no longing for it, setting aside the attitudes of such beings, nor those who are disrespectful toward the Dharma and the one who teaches the Dharma.

"In this king of ritual manuals, for all practitioners, the mantra that serves as the vidyā king for protection, whether one has leftovers or no leftovers, once one has made oneself clean, is this: namo retnatrayāye nama ārya avalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvaya mahāsatvāya oṃ amṛta udbhava hūṃ phaṭ svāhā This is the vidyā king called Hayagrīva. By empowering ash with it seven times, one protects oneself; and to protect one's attendants one should perform the practice of knots.

"As for this king of ritual manuals, under the constellation Puṣya or Aśvinī, in a virtuous undertaking, one should make offerings and a vast offering of a mass of tormas, and give alms to the Dharma and to the one who compiles the Dharma, and fine food to the Great Vehicle, and above all, with a fee. Then one should bring it to completion. One should act in that way: one should recite the secret mantra of the vidyā of the king of ritual manuals just as the king of ritual manuals says, and in that way it will not decline. Thus it also swiftly bestows accomplishment."

When the Blessed One, the great bodhisattva, had spoken thus, the world with its gods rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.

Here ends the manual of the Blessed Lady, noble Tārā, from the king of ritual manuals called Ūrdhvajaṭā, of the greatly extensive Avataṃsaka, the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.

Then the Blessed One was dwelling on Potala, king of mountains. There the Blessed One called to the bodhisattva, noble Avalokiteśvara, and said this: "Great being, you have explained that great king of ritual manuals of Ūrdhvajaṭā. Now speak the applications of the very king of ritual manuals, Ūrdhvajaṭā: that secret later tantra together with the great secret later one, easy in method and accomplished with ease, set forth with its ritual procedures going first; of the nature of great compassion, for the benefit of many people, for the happiness of many people, and out of compassion for those tormented by suffering; rejoiced in by the buddhas of the past; the vidyā common to all the Tārās."

The great being said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if the Tathāgata permits it, and the other buddhas, the blessed ones, also rejoice in it, I shall explain it.

"First of all, the practitioner should for the present take up the three refuges, generate the mind set on awakening, see the maṇḍala as it is taught in the Ūrdhvajaṭā, and receive the pledges, the master's permission, and the means of accomplishment. Empowered with the empowerment, having offered a fee to the guru, and having received the vidyā within the maṇḍala, one should again take up the vidyā of any Tārā whatever, before a painted image or in the presence of a statue, and, beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight, recite it a hundred thousand times. Afterward, keeping a fast for three nights, on the full moon, before the statue or the painted image, one should perform the offering and the torma ritual, kindle the fire with kindling sticks from a milky tree, and make eight thousand fire offerings with sticks of khadira or black aloeswood measuring six finger-widths. At daybreak, having made a most vast night offering and the torma ritual as far as one's means allow, and having eaten food obtained by begging, one should have the accomplishment bestowed. Then the vidyā will be accomplished. Then one should perform all the rites.

Again, here there arises another rite of supremely secret accomplishment. One who wishes to accomplish the vidyā, having seen the great maṇḍala of the Blessed Lady, and having remained in that very maṇḍala in the pledges and the fire rite for as long as the ritual procedure prescribes, should draw three further maṇḍalas as taught in the rite of the means of accomplishment, the vidyā's thorough secret. Having offered a fee in full to the guru, and having received the vidyā in the center of the maṇḍala, one should kindle the fire with kindling sticks of a milky tree. First of all, one should make eight hundred fire offerings of gold powder in the measure of a tuṭi, smeared with ghee. Then one should make eight hundred fire offerings with sticks of black aloeswood about a span in length, together with ghee. One should make eight hundred fire offerings of sticks of white sandalwood smeared with ghee. Then once again one should make eight hundred fire offerings of gold powder smeared with ghee. Then one should make eight hundred fire offerings of silver powder smeared with honey. Then one should make eight hundred fire offerings of brass powder smeared with milk. Then one should make eight hundred fire offerings of copper powder smeared with curd. Then one should make eight hundred fire offerings with powder of pearls. Then one should make eight hundred fire offerings with powder of red sandalwood. Then one should make eight hundred fire offerings of sticks of red sandalwood smeared with curd, honey and ghee. Then one should make eight hundred fire offerings with all kinds of grain, food, provisions and the like. Then one should make eight hundred fire offerings of cloth made thoroughly white, well washed, sweet-smelling and free of hairs.

Having recited once over each one, one should then combine guggulu, śrīvāsa resin, gandharasa, kunduruka and camphor, and offer seven oblations of them smeared with ghee. Then one should make a fire offering of seven oblations of fruits and the like, whatever can be found. Then one should make a fire offering of seven oblations of fragrant flowers. Then one should make a fire offering of seven oblations of the finest food. Then one should make a fire offering of seven oblations of thread spun by a maiden, divided into portions and smeared with ghee. One should make a fire offering of seven oblations of karavīra flowers. Then one should make a fire offering of seven oblations of ghee. Then one should make a fire offering of seven oblations of ash. Then one should make a fire offering of seven oblations of stalked plants without fruit, smeared with ghee. Then one should make a fire offering of seven oblations of fresh butter. Then one should make a fire offering of seven oblations of kesara powder. Then one should make a fire offering of seven oblations of buttermilk. Then one should make a fire offering of seven oblations of turmeric powder smeared with ghee. Then one should make a fire offering of seven oblations of rock salt and salt smeared with ghee. Then one should make a fire offering of seven oblations of molasses. Then one should make a fire offering of seven oblations of powdered lac resin. Then one should make a fire offering of seven oblations of iron powder smeared with ghee. Then one should make a fire offering of seven oblations of cow dung that has not fallen to the ground, smeared with ghee. Then one should make a fire offering of seven oblations of bilva seeds smeared with curd, honey and ghee. Then one should make eight hundred fire offerings of black sesame together with parched rice, smeared with curd, honey and ghee, with gold and silver powder mixed together.

At this juncture all the gods look upon the practitioner. This, then, is my rite for employing the supremely secret, greatly secret practice of accomplishment. Rising, the practitioner should circumambulate the maṇḍala, bow to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, offer the finest fee to the guru, and make the request, either through someone or directly in his presence. Having seen the deities in the drawn maṇḍala and bowed to the guru, one should request the empowerment and also the permission for accomplishment. Then, by this rite of accomplished action, even one whose moral discipline is utterly broken will accomplish the Blessed Lady.

This rite for employing the means of accomplishment is supremely secret, an exceedingly great secret. In short, whatever action there may be, it will be performed by this. All its pacifying, enriching and beautifying rites: however one carries them out, in just that way accomplishment comes. And however the vidyā is applied, in just that way it will be well applied. However one carries it out, so one accomplishes; by this rite called Delight of All Vidyās, actions are supremely accomplished. In short, this lion's roar of mine: whoever delights in vidyā will perform the rites by it. It should be understood that the accomplishments rest, each one, in the palm of that very person's hand. This rite, too, should be understood by those who keep the poṣadha and have previously done the recitation, just as the noble one has taught. This is the rite of secret employment.

The rite of another means of accomplishment: one goes to the shore of the ocean and makes eight thousand stūpas of the Sugata, each a span in height. Before each one, one offers scents, flowers and so on, and recites eight thousand times. At the time of completion, one should eat begged food and offer a fee. Then the vidyā will be accomplished.

Another rite: on the bank of a river one should recite a hundred thousand times according to the ritual procedure, and it will be accomplished. There is also this other rite: one should recite a hundred thousand times on the summit of a mountain, and it will be accomplished. This is another rite: one should make a hundred thousand fire offerings with oblations of ghee, and it will be accomplished. This is another rite: one should make a hundred thousand fire offerings of black sesame smeared with curd, honey and ghee, and it will be accomplished. Another rite: one should make a hundred thousand fire offerings with sticks of black aloeswood, and it will be accomplished. Another rite: one should make a hundred thousand fire offerings with all kinds of flowers. This is another rite: one should make a hundred thousand fire offerings with all kinds of decoctions, and it will be accomplished.

Another rite: bowing down before the great stūpas, one should recite a hundred thousand times, and it will be accomplished. Likewise, these means of accomplishment then become effective for the rites. By merely calling it to mind, one protects oneself. By merely reciting it, one brings about pacification. A fire offering of white mustard seed brings about enrichment. With the dung of a donkey and of a she-camel it becomes a fierce rite.

Making an effigy of the king out of grains of mustard seed and flowers, and cutting it up again and again with a sharp blade, beginning from the right foot, one should make eight thousand fire offerings. Over that same effigy one should make eight hundred oblations of ghee in three sessions a day for seven days. In one session, or a fortnight, or a month, the king becomes like a subject and comes under one's power.

For a universal monarch as well, one should make a figure out of eighteen palas of salt and, in the fire for the king, make fire offerings, cutting it with a sharp sword, beginning from its left foot. Within one month the king comes under one's power.

This is another rite: gathering up dust pressed by the sole of an enemy's foot that has not yet scattered, and kindling a fire well with wood of the elephant tree, one takes it up with the hand other than the right, and makes a fire offering of eight thousand oblations, reciting once over each. Within one month the king comes under one's power.

This is another rite: kindling a fire with wood of the king of trees, one should make eight thousand fire offerings of royal mustard smeared with curd, honey and ghee. Within one month the lord of the earth comes under one's power.

This is another rite: first of all, kindling a fire with wood of the king of trees, if one makes one thousand and eight fire offerings of lac resin together with salt, mixed with ghee, the lord of the earth will act as he is commanded.

This is another rite: grinding red karavīra flowers that no one has taken, one should make an effigy and, cutting it again and again with a sword, beginning from the right foot, make eight thousand fire offerings in a fire of karavīra kindling sticks. For each month one should make an effigy of thirty-six palas. Then the king comes under one's power.

Another rite: mixing red flowers and salt together and grinding them, one should make an effigy of eight palas and make fire offerings, cutting it again and again with a sharp sword, beginning from the right foot. Then, if one does this with the wood prepared in the same way, every day for one month, the lord of the earth comes under one's power.

This is another rite: mixing mustard seed and blue utpala and grinding them, one makes an effigy of the person's form out of sixteen palas and presses it down. Kindling a fire well with wood of khadira and kovidāra, one should make eight thousand fire offerings for one month, every day, cutting it again and again with a sword, beginning from the head. Then the one represented by the effigy will serve one in every way, like a subject of the king.

Another rite arises: mixing salt from the ocean with salt, grinding it together with red karavīra flowers, one should complete an effigy. Kindling a fire well with kindling sticks of the king of trees, one should make eight thousand fire offerings, cutting it again and again with a sharp blade, beginning from the right foot. Each day there is one effigy, each one equal to the others. The king will obey commands like a tamed elephant.

Another rite: mixing aśoka flowers, white mustard seed and nāgakesara, and grinding them with ko me and nābhāsa, one makes an effigy of sixteen palas. Beginning from the head of the effigy, cutting it again and again with a sharp blade held in the left hand, and kindling a fire well with wood of that very tree, one should make eight hundred thousand fire offerings. The others are done with the right hand, every day, continuing for one month; at midday one swiftly brings the others under one's power, as one wishes, like subjects.

Another rite: grinding all the fragrant substances mixed with the fruit of somarāja, one makes an effigy of sixteen palas. Kindling a fire well with kindling sticks of a milky tree, one should make fire offerings, cutting it again and again with a sword from the navel down to the soles of the feet. Then, if one again makes fire offerings beginning from the head, every day for one month, the king will become like one who asks, "What shall I do?"

This is another, unsurpassed rite: grinding red sandalwood and salt in equal parts, one makes an effigy of twenty-five palas. Every day, in the morning hours, in a fire of red sandalwood wood, one should make eight thousand fire offerings, cutting it again and again with a sharp sword, beginning from the right foot. In this rite one offers the oblations with the right hand, and does the covering with it as well. In about one month the king will obey commands like a subject.

Another rite: one should mix cow dung that has not fallen to the ground thoroughly with salt and grind it. Then, making an effigy of twenty-five palas, the knowledgeable one should, in the afternoon hours, make eight hundred fire offerings, one effigy at a time, in a fire of palāśa wood, cutting each again and again with a sharp blade, beginning from the effigy's right foot. The rest of this rite is the same as the first; and it too, in about a month, makes the king carry out one's commands, like one who asks, "What shall I do?"

Another rite: with cow urine, dung, and earth from an anthill, together with honey in equal parts, one forms an effigy of twenty palas. For one month, every day, three times, at midday, in a fire laid with wood of the king of trees, one should make eight thousand fire offerings, cutting it again and again with a sharp sword, beginning from the effigy's right foot. He will become like a subject.

If these means of accomplishment are applied at all times, in the seasons of autumn, spring, summer and winter, one will always and without fail obtain these great and incomparable riches.

Next come the practices for summer. Combining curd and ghee of matching kind and color together with karavīra flowers and grinding them, one makes an effigy measuring thirty palas. In the morning or the afternoon, kindling a fire with palāśa kindling sticks, and placing the effigy with its head to the right, one should make eight thousand fire offerings, cutting it again and again with a sharp sword held in the right hand, beginning from the right foot. Within one month the king comes under one's power.

Another rite: mixing white mustard seed and saffron, grinding them well and making an effigy of ten palas, the rest of this is as before. The difference here is that one makes the fire offerings cutting it again and again with the left hand.

Another rite: grinding together ocean salt, barley and wheat, one makes an effigy of thirty palas and fills its mouth with the three hot spices. Having recited over a copper skewer in a fire of dustira, one pierces it from beneath the feet so that it comes out at the crown of the head. Then, placing the head to the right, cutting it up on palāśa leaves with the edge of one's own sword, one should make eight thousand fire offerings with the right hand in a fire of khadira, at whatever time one wishes. Within one month the king comes under one's power for as long as he lives. These are the means of accomplishment for the summer season.

Again, the rites of the rainy season arise here; these are to be carried out without fail in the rainy season. Combining pushel tsé, vālaka, sauvarcala and salt into one effigy, grinding them with rainwater, one makes an effigy of the king of twenty-five palas, and, cutting it again and again with a sharp sword held in the right hand, beginning from the right side, one should make eight thousand fire offerings in a fire of palāśa. This is done every day at whatever session one wishes, for one month. The king comes under one's power.

This is another rite: combining pushel tsé, priyaṅgu, ṭāṃpaṇa and fermenting agents, and grinding them with rainwater, one should make an effigy of the king of thirty palas. Cutting it again and again with a sharp sword held in the right hand, beginning from the head, and kindling a fire with dongka wood, one should make eight thousand fire offerings every day for one month, at whatever session one wishes. He will certainly serve one in every way, like a servant.

This is another rite: mixing together sarjikā, milk, barley ferment, sweet flag, māṣa beans and sesame, and grinding them with the water of the body, one makes an effigy of the lord of men of thirty palas. Kindling a fire well with mango wood, one should make eight thousand fire offerings every day for one month, at whatever session one wishes, cutting it again and again with the right hand, beginning from the head. The king comes under one's power.

This is another, supreme rite: combining ocean salt and cow dung that has not fallen to the ground, and grinding them with rainwater together with barley ferment, one makes an effigy of the king measuring thirty palas. If, every day for one month, at whatever session one wishes, one makes fire offerings in a fire of udumbara wood, cutting it again and again with a sharp sword held in the right hand, beginning from the right foot, the king comes under one's power. These are the means of accomplishment for the rainy season; for these alone accomplishment draws near.

Again, here another arises: the practice for late winter, in which one accomplishes in a single season. Grinding together husks of grain, barley stalks, gabina and sweet flag, one makes an effigy of the lord of the earth measuring fifty palas. Every day for one month, at whatever time one wishes, in a fire of nimba wood, with the effigy's head placed to the west and its feet facing east, one should make a thousand fire offerings, cutting it again and again with a sharp sword held in the right hand, beginning from the head. The king comes under one's power.

Another rite: grinding together chebulic myrobalan, the fruit of emblic myrobalan, śrīvāsaka, kunduruka and cow's ghee, one makes an effigy of the lord of men of thirty palas. Placing its head to the west, as before, in a fire of palāśa, one should make eight thousand fire offerings every day for one month, at whatever time one wishes. The king will always be under one's power, like a servant.

In the same manner: combining the fruit of beleric myrobalan, barley, tsikaseng with its leaves and roots, sesame and white mustard seed, and grinding them together with cow's ghee, one makes an effigy of the king of thirty palas. With its head pointing west, as before, in a fire of udumbara wood, one should make eight thousand fire offerings every day for one month. The lord of the earth will without doubt come under one's power.

Another rite: combining salt from the ocean, molasses, grains of emblic myrobalan and white mustard seed, and grinding them well, one makes an effigy of the king of thirty palas, with its head to the west. If, as before, in a fire of milky-tree wood, every day for one month, at whatever time one wishes, one makes eight thousand fire offerings in the fire, the king will carry out one's commands.

Another rite: combining sal ammoniac, ocean salt, barley, sesame and molasses, and grinding them thoroughly with cow's ghee, one makes an effigy of the king of fifty palas. Placing its head to the west, as before, at whatever time one desires, one should make eight thousand fire offerings every day for one month. He will always attend on one like a servant. These are what bring the practices of the winter season to accomplishment.

For that very purpose, these are supremely secret. Thus it is said; and may one again become a holder of the vidyā. In the secret practice, the accomplishment bound to the times for applying the practice is set in motion, the rites being performed in the fixed seasons as taught, summer and the rest. Then the king concerned will always be thoroughly bound. Nor is there any loss of accomplishment, for it is present together with the other rites.

Again, as for the other matter in the rite, the ways in which accomplishment slips away: these come from the particular nature of the beings, or from lacking the rite, or from the elements themselves, or from incomplete faculties; or from having no holy guru, so that one takes up one's own vidyā without the master's instruction and follows the Teacher's words piecemeal, without knowing much; or from lacking capacity, so that one has not seen the substances, has made no offering to the master of the maṇḍala of the ritual manual, and, toward the holy guru who is worthy of gifts, lacks the humility to say, "I myself do not know," and so, with neither realization nor vision, presumes to know the practices of the great rites. One who speaks what is without merit, one whose moral discipline is broken, whether monk or nun, layman or laywoman, one who has broken the bounds of his own training, who has fallen into a transgression of defeat, who is devoid of the awakening mind, who has committed a deed of immediate retribution, who has scorned the master, who has trampled the site of a stūpa with his feet, who steps on the master's shadow, who has scorned the Great Vehicle and come to hate the bodhisattvas, or who scorns all the gods: through these faults, any other rite such a person performs is not done properly but is done in some other way. That it is devoid of accomplishment is because it transgresses that very rite.

For whoever does these things, that accomplishment is destroyed in a single instant. The little recitation of the vidyā that was done remains for another time, and whatever is not an accomplishment bound to the time of practice comes about here.

Again, whatever holder of the vidyā, by the rite of secret practice, at this juncture makes a fire offering of eight hundred or five hundred oblations smeared with ghee, together with the king's footprint: the king, for whom all this is done in that very rite, comes under one's power for as long as he lives. For a universal monarch too, one who performs the practice at the times as taught will certainly not be without accomplishment, nor will the accomplishment decline.

Then again the eight thousand great beings remained without saying anything. Then again the bodhisattva, the great being Mahāsthāmaprāpta, as a small offering of virtuous conduct to the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, who had come down among many beings, rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and bowed down. He bowed to the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and said this to that great being, who was endowed with the samādhi of the equality of all beings: "Great being Avalokiteśvara, speak the king of samādhis of the great bodhisattvas called Beholding All Beings. Great being, speak it!"

When he had said this, that great being, meditating on the king of samādhis and smiling, free of obstructors, looked toward the Blessed One. The Blessed One gave his permission, and he said to the bodhisattva, the great being Mahāsthāmaprāpta: "Whoever follow you in great compassion, the ultimate, the supremely secret, and all the coemergent tantras: these will be worshipped by the world with its gods, and even one whose moral discipline is utterly broken will not go to the lower realms. Whoever obtains the ritual manual of the Blessed Lady, noble Tārā, knows it, recites it, copies it, practices it, worships it, writes it in a volume and keeps it in his home, and places it on his head at the time of lying down and at the time of rising from bed, will be the glory of all the gods, all the nāgas and all the yakṣas; he will be rid of all great misfortunes and will come to great wealth. He will also live long. In short, he will come to know the whole of my tantra. That great being will be known by all the gods, nāgas, yakṣas and the rest. Because he will overpower them by this, I shall explain it."

Then, in an instant, the great being meditated on the king of samādhis and took on a nature of broad smiling, and he was seen with his locks bound upward, three-eyed and four-armed, with the Blessed One Amitābha seated on his head, speaking evenly, holding a lotus in his hand, a great divine body, a form that cannot be fathomed by looking, the liberation of all beings, the very center of the tathāgatas, of whom one can conceive only a little. Keeping the Blessed Lady Tārā in mind, bowing deeply to all the buddhas, and seated upon a jewel lotus, he said:

"For the sake of the certain benefit and happiness of the conduct of all beings, their individual practices, the individual conduct of the bodhisattvas, and the sprouts of bodhisattvas, through whatever activity of skillful means the Buddha himself employs, for the sake of perfecting the perfection of generosity, for the sake of attaining the first ground, and for the sake of attaining unsurpassed buddhahood: just as the Buddha, the Blessed One, unsurpassed in the world with its gods, the charioteer who tames persons, continually generated a great accumulation of merit, in just that way, by the power of merit, one will be born as a universal monarch, adorned with the excellent marks praised above all beings.

"Then, by the deeds done before by one of the bodhisattva family, acting likewise, oneself always a universal monarch, one should bring that other universal monarch too under one's power, by just the rites described before. Through that one also becomes lord of the whole earth. Those who have no faith in the Buddha, the Blessed One, will through faith itself come within the circle as well. Or a governor of a province, by whatever merit he has, is made to rule as king above beings. Fully enjoying his enjoyments, he also carries out his duties. And if one applies just the rites stated earlier, he too becomes one's subject.

"Next comes the practice for bringing under one's power kings, ministers and other beings: one should carry it out without fail in the seasons of autumn, summer and the rains."

To bring a king's minister under one's power, mix equal parts of dust from his footprints and mustard seed, and for one month, at whatever hour one likes, at a single sitting, perform eight thousand fire offerings; he will come under one's power. Another rite: with jasmine flowers mixed with sesame he comes under one's power as before. Another rite: with mustard seed together with sprouts of dūrvā grass, perform eight thousand fire offerings for one month, and he comes under one's power as before. Another rite: mix neem seeds, pāśī, kaktukāma and powders with salt, and for one month, at whatever session one likes, perform eight thousand fire offerings; he will come under one's power. Another rite: by eight thousand fire offerings of sesame mixed with arjuna flowers and smeared with ghee, he comes under one's power. Another rite: perform eight thousand fire offerings of neem seeds smeared with pungent sesame oil, and he comes under one's power as before.

One who wishes to bring the king's purohita under his power should, for one month, perform eight thousand fire offerings of mustard seed smeared with curd, honey and ghee; beginning at whatever session one likes, if one performs eight thousand fire offerings at a single sitting, he will come under one's power. Another rite: perform eight thousand fire offerings of camedaka pulses smeared with ghee, and he comes under one's power as before. Another rite: perform fire offerings with iṅguda oil, and he comes under one's power as before. For all of these, kindle the fire with kindling sticks of cassia wood and make the fire offering, or else in a fire of palāśa wood.

To bring a brahmin under one's power, make fire offerings in a fire of milky-sapped wood for one month; beginning at whatever session one likes, if one performs eight thousand fire offerings at a single sitting, he will come under one's power. To bring a kṣatriya under one's power, if one makes fire offerings of white mustard seed smeared with pungent sesame oil in a fire of khadira wood, he comes under one's power as before. To bring a vaiśya under one's power, make fire offerings of śāli rice meal together with curd in a fire of mango wood, and he comes under one's power as before. To bring all the lowly under one's power, kindle the fire with thorny kindling sticks, and for one month, beginning at whatever session one likes, if one performs at a single sitting eight thousand fire offerings of mustard seed together with poison and neem, that one will come under one's power.

Further, what applies here in common to the rites that accomplish the supreme, the middling and the lesser is this: whoever is named when one performs a fire offering of eight thousand white mustard seeds comes under one's power. To bring a woman under one's power, perform eight thousand fire offerings of sesame, and she comes under one's power. On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should make a fire offering of seven oblations of white mustard seed smeared with ghee, curd and honey. Whoever is named comes under one's power within three days.

One who wishes to bring a maiden under his power should make an offering of eight thousand raṅgaṇa flowers to the noble Avalokiteśvara, and she comes under one's power. If one makes an effigy of wax, places it in one's own hand and recites eight thousand times, whoever is named comes under one's power. Before the painted image one should present eight hundred white flowers, and whoever one desires comes under one's power. Conch, musk, sweet flag, bezoar and costus should be put together and ground. Having consecrated it with eight thousand recitations, whoever drinks it, or whoever it is given to, comes under one's power. To bring a brahmin woman under one's power, if one makes eight thousand fire offerings of bilva sprouts before the painted image, she comes under one's power. By reciting seven times in a charnel ground, any woman before whom a man sits and recites eight thousand times comes under his power. Taking a stick one finger in length and consecrating it with eight thousand recitations, whoever and whatever one summons comes under one's power.

One should present eight thousand hundred-petalled flowers before the noble Avalokiteśvara. Taking one flower from among them, one should look at a woman and wave it around; she comes, and comes under one's power. Eating milk and barley gruel, one should recite in a solitary place.
