To bring śūdras under control, make eight thousand fire offerings of husks of black grain in a single day.

For three days, tie a tawny cow in the house, and one should have it eat green grass that has been empowered. Having empowered it, one should adorn it with that fine garland. Having empowered water, one should have it drink. A cowherd for whom protection has been made should milk it. Then place that milk in a completely secluded spot, and one should let it set into curd and churn it. Combine that butter with mālatī flowers, and one should make seven burnt offerings. Taking with both hands the pills wrapped in lotus petals, one should recite until they become warm. One who has first completed the approach recites over the pills until they give off smoke and blaze, until they blaze. When they grow warm, one brings under control. When they give off smoke, one becomes invisible. By their blazing one becomes a vidyādhara and lives for five thousand years. After death, too, one goes to Sukhāvatī.

Whoever's head one places white mustard seed upon, after empowering it seven times, will come under control. To bring a king under control, make an image, press it with the left hand, and recite a hundred thousand times: he will come under control together with a thousand. Make eight thousand fire offerings of white mustard seed mixed with ghee. Then one should take it up, and one becomes invisible.

At a stūpa containing relics, or at a river that flows to the ocean, make from sand or from a lump of earth a stūpa of the Sugata a span in size, containing the heart of dependent origination. Remaining pure and observing the poṣadha, make offerings as best one can, and, eating alms food or eating an oblation of boiled grain, recite a hundred thousand times. One will be capable of all rites. In the area of a great charnel ground, one should recite for binding the maṇḍala and so on, binding the directions, curing all poisons, sweeping clean, crushing grahas and fevers, and crossing great rivers, and one crosses them with ease. One will be honored and freed from tolls and customs. In debate, too, one will become the foremost of speakers. When one has gone to sleep, the semen will be held back.

By reciting a thousand times over a thread and reciting eight thousand times over a peg of acacia wood, one protects all crops; by setting it in the ground, the leaves of the willow grow even, and one makes the harvests of rice, śāli rice, and large grains abundant. With white mustard seed one overcomes all kings and ministers. By reciting eight hundred times over hail, thunderbolts, stones, and so on, one sends them wherever one wishes them to go. By reciting a thousand times over ash, in whichever direction it is scattered, in that direction one turns back thorns. By reciting eight hundred times, one removes all piercing pains.

Having done the preliminary practice, recite two million five hundred thousand times before the painted image. Then make a sword from a palm leaf cut with the fingernails, and draw on that leaf with saffron.

On the day of the eighth of the dark fortnight, or on the fourteenth of the dark fortnight, strictly observing the poṣadha, climb alone to the summit of a mountain. Having cleared a spot, smear a maṇḍala eight cubits or sixteen cubits across, make a stūpa of sand, make offerings to it as best one can, and face east. Taking the sword in the right hand and raising the arm upward, one should recite the secret mantra before the stūpa, until the letters of the mantra that are on the sword blaze. Taking it up, one goes wherever one wishes and becomes a vidyādhara, and no vidyādhara can harm one. No being can withstand one. Taking whatever form one desires, one lives for an eon, and one sees, hears, and smells across a thousand yojanas. One goes straight through mountains. One goes straight through walls. One goes straight through fences. One rises even above the ocean. One finds what has been hoarded.

If one wishes to accomplish orpiment and realgar, set up the painted image before an image containing relics, in that very place, and make offerings on the eighth day of the bright fortnight. In its center lay the corpse of a man with intact limbs, press it firmly on the chest with the left foot, make protection, and one should recite the mantra until it rises. Beforehand one should eat honey and milk porridge, and with a fist empowered seven times, one should melt the substances on its head. Then it makes them drip. By drinking that, one becomes invisible.

Entering a river teeming with fish that flows to the ocean, make eight thousand fire offerings of fragrant flowers. One obtains pairs of garments one after another. Having entered a village, one should recite eight hundred times, and one obtains fine food. By empowering salt and mixed water eight hundred times, one pacifies all stabbing pains. For a woman who cannot deliver her child, empower water eight hundred times and give it to her. She will give birth with ease.

Beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight and continuing until the fifteenth, one should recite, increasing by a thousand each day. At the end, fasting for three nights, accomplish the pills by the procedure for pills; if one puts them in the mouth, one becomes invisible. Take aśoka flowers, the bile of a kṛṣṇasāra antelope, the heart of dūrvā grass, and charcoal of sodriya in equal parts together, wrap them in iron obtained under Puṣya and again wrap them in the three metals, and one should accomplish them before the painted image. Placing them in the mouth, wherever one stays, one should first be freed from bonds.

Make an image of a man or a woman out of wax, kindle a fire in a completely secluded spot, empower the image eight hundred times, and one should melt it; one should pierce it with thorns of datura, and the person comes under control, and one obtains whatever one seeks.

On the full moon of the bright fortnight, fasting for a day and a night, one should offer eight thousand fragrant flowers before the painted image. One obtains five kārṣāpaṇas. On the fourteenth of the dark fortnight, fasting for a day and a night, kindle a fire with priyaṅgu wood before the image and make eight thousand fire offerings of kindling sticks of pekaṅkata. One obtains all kinds of wealth. On the eighth of the bright fortnight, fasting for a day and a night, one should recite eight thousand times before the painted image, until the crows take flight. One obtains ten coins.

Fasting for three nights, on the fourteenth of the dark fortnight, burn guggulu incense, kindle a fire of bāla wood, and one should make eight thousand fire offerings of oleander flowers mixed with curd, honey, and ghee. Then in the fire pit an oleander the size of a lotus springs up, and in the center of the oleander one sees realgar of its color; reciting the mantra, one should take it. Merely by taking it with the mind, one becomes a vidyādhara the color of the rising sun, in the form of a sixteen-year-old, with the swiftness of the wind, and vast desires come to be fulfilled. One lives for ten thousand years. One becomes pleasing to the minds of all beings and knows one's death, and if one performs the practice again, one's life becomes twice as long.

Enter an empty house, set up the painted image in a clean spot, and, keeping silent and eating milk and barley flour, one should recite in solitude. Then make vast offerings to the painted image, offer an exceedingly vast torma, sit with legs crossed, and one should recite until rays of light come forth. By seeing that, even the five acts of immediate retribution come to be exhausted. Then one will be accomplished and will obtain great kingship on every side. One will have no adversary.

Empower gorocanā eight thousand times, fumigate it with incense, and have it applied without interruption; if one then enters the king's palace, one becomes the foremost of speakers. Everyone, too, comes under one's control. If he has not come under control, then, to bring him under control, smear a maṇḍala in the house and with the left hand make a thousand burnt offerings of the abaabīya tree. He will come under control.

To bring an ordinary woman under control, make an image of salt and make fire offerings with the left hand. She will come under control. To bring a servant woman under control, combine punnāga filaments, barley, wheat, and meat, and make eight thousand fire offerings. She will come under control. Make an image of ground śāli rice and, cutting it piece by piece, make fire offerings. She will come under control.

Take antimony collyrium, wrap it together with a single stūpa inside an aśvattha leaf, empower it eight thousand times, and one should apply it to the eyes. Whoever one's glance falls on will come under control. Recite a hundred thousand times at the door of a cave. One makes its mechanical devices fall. At a cattle pen, set up a stūpa containing the heart of dependent origination and recite a hundred thousand times. One obtains a hundred thousand coins each time. At a nāga site, set up the painted image and perform the rite of protection; then kindle a fire with jambu wood, give a torma of the three sweet substances, and one should make eight thousand fire offerings of flowers of the nāga tree.

Then a nāga in the form of a brahmin comes, and he says, "What shall I do?" One should say, "Grant me seven coins every single day." He says, "So be it," and vanishes. Every day he grants seven coins. They should be used up entirely, with nothing left over; half is for the service of the Three Jewels.

One should recite for one month before the painted image. One obtains twelve thousand coins.

Beginning from the eighth day of the bright fortnight, one should recite for six months at a stūpa containing relics. It bestows kingship.

On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, keeping a fast day and night, before the image, one takes the heartwood of the śleṣmāntaka tree and winds it with red thread. Then, having kindled a fire with palāśa wood, one consecrates the peg eight thousand times, splits it into three pieces, recites twenty-one times over each piece, and puts them into the fire. At dawn one obtains three hundred coins each time.

On the eighth day of the bright fortnight, keeping a fast for one night, one should offer eight thousand atimuktaka flowers. Every seven days one obtains a thousand coins each time.

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, keeping a fast for one night, at night make eight thousand fire offerings into a fire mixed with the roots of the vatyaṭaka tree. One obtains a thousand silver coins each time.

On the seventh day of the bright fortnight, keeping a fast day and night, one should enter a river that flows into the ocean and offer ten thousand lotuses. One obtains a kingdom each time.

To bring a man under control: on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, keeping a fast day and night, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight keeping a fast for one night, one kindles a fire with the wood of the bodhi tree; then make eight thousand fire offerings of white water lilies smeared with curd, honey and ghee. He comes under control.

To bring a woman under control: on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, cast eight thousand saugandhika flowers at the noble Mañjuśrī. She comes under control.

For binding by means of medicine: one recites twenty-one times over the dung of elephants and of quadrupeds, and it should be placed at the waist. The semen is thereby bound.

If one recites seven times over the corner of a monastic robe and ties a knot, poison is bound. To cure poison, it is done with leaves. To open the seal, it is done with water.

For bringing down a spirit, one binds the graha with guggulu incense, or with water.

Having recited over one's finger, whoever one threatens with it comes under control.

One should recite eight hundred times before the painted image. It shows in a dream just how things will come about.

Having set the painted image in a stūpa containing relics and made vast offerings before it, one kindles a fire with bilva wood and should make a hundred thousand fire offerings of white apāmārga smeared with curd, honey and ghee. One obtains a kingdom each time. If that is not accomplished, one obtains a thousand townships each time.

Before the painted image, one consecrates gorocana or realgar eight thousand times and anoints oneself with it; then, on entering among enemies, one will not be afraid, and the enemies will do no harm.

For bringing down a spirit: one recites three times over warm water with white flowers, and recites three times over karavīra flowers, and one should strike the possessed one with them. It reveals the past and the future.

As for the binding, it is made auspicious with the finger-snapping mudrā.

One who wishes to accomplish the eye ointment should take one measure of sauvīra eye ointment, bought for a hero's price, and have it ground with the five products of the cow by a brahmin girl facing north. With the ring finger make four pills, raise them up to the eight directions, and by this same rite, burning ghee and lac resin, one should recite eight thousand times. One obtains ten of the finest villages.

By this same rite, having made a stūpa, one should offer eight thousand lotuses smeared with sandalwood. One obtains lordship of a region each time.

Having made a stūpa the size of a sugata-span, burn incense and offer eight thousand campaka flowers; one obtains a thousand pieces of gold each time. Having made a stūpa the size of a sugata-span, one should offer eight thousand flower filaments; one obtains a thousand garments each time. In the same way is the rite with any flower for whatever one desires.

Take ash from a corpse burned in a charnel ground, and on the day of the full moon, keeping a fast day and night, make a circle with blood from the ring finger and draw an effigy; press it down with the left foot and recite a thousand times. One brings the person under control together with his family line.

Having made a stūpa the size of a sugata-span, make eight thousand fire offerings into the fire of parched rice smeared with curd, honey and ghee. If one consecrates gorocana a thousand times and makes a mark on the forehead with it, whoever one sees, and all those who see one, one brings under control.

At dawn, consecrate turuṣka water seven times and wash the face; whoever one sees gives one gifts.

All in just the same way: eating sesame oil, consecrate a handful of water seven times and drink it. One obtains food without seeking it.

Entering a king's palace, take that monastic robe, recite twenty-one times, and if one ties a knot in it with the left hand, one becomes unhindered.

Among bandits, by bringing it to mind and reciting, one is freed from bonds.

For cutting, piercing, and the mantras of the hand: make an effigy from palāśa seeds, white karavīra and white mustard seed, and before the painted image press it down with the left hand and recite eight thousand times. The mantras will be roused.

One who wishes to destroy fever should make eight thousand fire offerings of girikarṇikā flowers. The fever will be destroyed.

Make a hundred and eight fire offerings with kindling sticks of khadira wood. One will be freed from all the grahas.

Reciting seven times over ash, one works upon the secret mantras of others. By reciting once over water, they are released.

If one writes it on cloth or birch bark and fastens it to the top of a banner, the opposing army will be paralyzed.

Living on water and flour, on the eighth or the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, keeping a fast for three nights, when a single night has passed, one should set the painted image at the right side of one's body and bind it. Having clenched the fist, one should recite until moisture comes forth. It binds. Thus on the third night the fist will be accomplished. When one makes the fist, one becomes invisible. One will live for seven hundred years. Even Maheśvara will ask, "What shall I do?"

Set the painted image in a clean place and, keeping a fast day and night, make an effigy before the painted image, worship it according to the rite, and make eight thousand fire offerings of bilva kindling sticks smeared with curd, honey and ghee. Rays of light come forth from the forehead of the Blessed Mañjuśrī. Then it is accomplished, and one obtains immeasurable wealth or gold.

Keeping a fast day and night, make eight thousand fire offerings of karavīra flowers before the painted image. Then take a single karavīra flower, go to a nāga abode, put the flower into the nāga lake, and one should recite the mantra. The nāga comes under control together with his nāginīs. One obtains whatever one seeks.

Keeping a fast day and night, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, make offerings at a crossroads and sit close by; make a pill of realgar the size of a pea, put it in the mouth, and one should recite until it splits open. The realgar will be accomplished, and by making a mark with it on the forehead one becomes invisible. Taking whatever form one wishes, one lives for five hundred years.

On the eighth day of the dark fortnight take bronze, and on the following eighth day have a trident made of the bronze. On the eighth day of the next dark fortnight, keeping a fast day and night, go to a charnel ground, make a great offering to the trident, sit in the cross-legged posture, take up the trident with the right hand, and one should recite until rays of light come forth from the trident. Then it is accomplished: at night a divine mansion appears without being built, and women appear adorned with every ornament. Many men of a retinue also attend, filling the whole place with laughter, playful charm and the like, and one obtains all that one thinks of. At dawn the Teacher sets it all aside.

Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, keeping a fast day and night, before the painted image recite eight hundred times over one measure of brāhmī juice and drink it. In seven days one will retain whatever one hears.

Before the painted image, make protection of various kinds, and one should recite over a dish of food until it turns into a meal. Then it is accomplished, and thereafter it keeps supplying food. So too with what grows from grain.

Having done the preliminary practice, make a wheel of the three metals, sixteen finger-breadths in size. On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, keeping a fast day and night, make vast offerings before the principal painted image, set the wheel on seven aśvattha leaves, sit in the cross-legged posture, and one should recite until it blazes. Then, merely by taking it up, one becomes a wheel-turning emperor of the vidyādharas, with hair curled and coiled and the color of the rising sun, and one flies together with all those who see one.

Taking the blazing Sudarśana wheel, press it with the hand and recite seven times; whatever one touches comes under control.

Make a wheel of kuśa grass, recite seven times over it, and put it into water. The nāgas rise up and say, "What shall we do?" One should say, "Give a hundred thousand coins."

Living on alms, climb to the summit of a mountain and one should recite a hundred thousand times. The body of the Tathāgata will appear. Having seen it, one achieves success.

Enter a river that flows into the ocean and make fire offerings of arka flowers. The Sun will grant a boon. Entering that same river up to the waist, scatter bilva flowers. The Grandfather (Brahmā) will grant a boon. Make fire offerings of mandārava flowers. Indra will grant a boon. In that same water, with mandārava flowers, Dhanada (Kubera) will grant a boon.

One should recite two hundred thousand times. It makes one a king. One should recite three hundred thousand times. It summons all sentient beings.

Entering a river that flows into the ocean, one should pour in a hundred thousand flowers of the aśoka tree. In seven nights it summons the yakṣiṇīs.

At a tree, keeping silence, one should recite for six months. One obtains each of the things one desires.

Make an effigy of a king, six finger-breadths tall, from arka wood, and have it painted in unmixed colors and adorned with every ornament. One will become the king of a realm, or else a vidyādhara.

Before the painted image, keeping silence for six months, consecrate the left hand and recite ten thousand times. A hundred thousand treasures that lie close by come to light.

Make ten thousand fire offerings of parched rice smeared with curd, honey and ghee, and ten thousand of apāmārga kindling sticks smeared with curd, honey and ghee. One obtains ten thousand pieces of gold each time.

Take gorocana, make it into a pill, and wrap it in the three metals. Then, wearing clean white clothes, go to a charnel ground, make offerings of scents, incense, flowers and the like, and give a torma to all the bhūtas; then place the pill between two skull cups joined face to face, and one should recite until a terrifying sound is heard. Without becoming afraid, share it with one's companions, and by putting it in the mouth again one becomes invisible. One will live for ten thousand years.

Take the eye of a pig and have it pounded together with cow products by the hand of a young girl. Make it into a pill, wrap it in the three metals, and hold it between the joined hands; then set it between two bowls joined face to face at the right side of the image of Maheśvara, press it with the right hand, and one should recite until the sound "śita" is heard. Reciting the vidyā, give some to one's companions as well, and by putting it in the mouth one becomes invisible. One makes all that is to be accomplished entirely joyful, and lives for thousands of years.

Lotus filaments, eye ointment, or realgar as well: make them into equal parts and have them pounded by the hand of a girl keeping the poṣadha vows. Wrap it in the three metals; then, having done the preliminary practice, at the conjunction of Puṣya, offer a torma to all the bhūtas at the right side of the image of Maheśvara, worship with scents, flowers and incense, place it between two bowls joined face to face, press it with the right hand, and one should recite until it cries out khaṭa khaṭa. Offer one portion to the Buddha, the Blessed One, share it with one's companions as well, and by putting it in the mouth one becomes invisible. One lives for a thousand years.

Having done the preliminary practice, living on milk and barley meal, set the painted image on the summit of a mountain and one should recite a hundred thousand times. Then one keeping the poṣadha vows should take earth from an anthill, mix it with milk and make it smooth, and should make a goose the size of a sugata-span. One should have a painter keeping the poṣadha vows paint it in unmixed colors. Then set the painted image in a secluded place, worship it with scents, flowers and incense, and give a torma to all the bhūtas; then, wearing clean clothes, one should recite before the painted image until the goose moves. Then the vidyādhara should offer as arghya the aparājitā flowers that were recited over beforehand. Again, one should recite eight hundred times. Everything comes; one should not be afraid. One should touch it with a peacock feather over which the mantra has been recited. It says, "What shall I do?" One should say, "Enter into my body." Then it vanishes into the body of the practitioner. In that very instant, with hair curled and coiled, sixteen years of age, appearing the color of the rising sun, one goes without hindrance. One flies together with whoever one sees and whoever looks on. All the vidyādharas come under this one's power; one lives for an eon, and when one dies one is born among the gods.

Having done the preliminary practice, set the painted image in a stūpa containing relics, and one should recite five hundred thousand times. One keeping the poṣadha vows, in silence, should take wood struck by lightning and put it into milk for seven days and nights. Then take it out and, rubbing it with white earth and sandalwood water, have the lightning-struck wood washed. Then the practitioner, keeping the poṣadha vows, should have a craftsman make a lion of it. Then, under the constellation Rohiṇī, having made vast offerings to the Three Jewels, one should eat alms food as directed by the Saṅgha. Having made vast offerings before the painted image, one should offer tormas of various kinds. Then the practitioner, pure and wearing clean clothes, sitting on a mat of kuśa grass, presses the lion with the right hand, and one should recite until the lion moves. When it has moved, signs of various kinds arise; one should not be afraid. Then the vidyādhara should pelt the lion with white mustard seeds consecrated seven times. The lion lets out a great roar. And the practitioner will not pass beyond the wilderness without having thought of it. Then the practitioner, having recited seven times, climbs onto the lion; all the vidyādharas too assemble, and riding on the lion, one flies together with the retinue. One goes like the wind by mere thought, with a retinue of many vidyādharas; one lives for an eon, and when one dies one is born wherever one wishes. This is the sādhana of the lion.

If one wishes to accomplish wealth, beginning from the full moon of the bright fortnight, in silence, living on milk and barley meal, one should recite a hundred thousand times before the painted image over the following three months. Then the painted image will move. And the image of the Tathāgata moves too. It becomes a great accomplishment of wealth.

Consecrate nīlāṭaka eight hundred times and one should tie a knot in it. One will be victorious in a wrestling match. If one recites twenty-one times over ash and places it on the crown of the head, one will be victorious in battle. This is the wrestler's accomplishment.

Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, place it with milk in a copper vessel, recite over it eight hundred times, and drink it. Likewise, in seven days one will retain whatever one hears. Rays of light come forth from the face of the noble Avalokiteśvara; the practitioner circumambulates, goes upward, and becomes a vidyādhara. Taking whatever form one wishes, one lives for three hundred thousand years.

On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, keeping a fast for one night, place gorocana before the image, and one should recite until it blazes. At that time one should take it up; merely by taking it up one gains the strength of Nārāyaṇa, and the weapons of others become powerless. Whoever has the garland, by keeping it, lives for three hundred years.

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, keeping a fast day and night, kindle a fire with bilva wood before the painted image and make a hundred thousand fire offerings of vikaṅkata kindling sticks smeared with pungent sesame oil. One obtains a coin.

On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, keeping a fast day and night, make a Kāmadeva of clay and make a hundred thousand fire offerings of thick rice gruel into its mouth. In seven days whatever girl one desires comes under control.

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, keeping a fast day and night, go to a charnel ground, smear a maṇḍala with the dung of a cow that has not fallen to the ground, take an intact skull, wash it with red sandalwood water, and worship it with red flowers, scents and flowers. Then sit close to the skull, and one should summon by reciting the secret mantra, until the skull moves. At that time it is accomplished. Then whoever one beckons with the fingernail comes and does whatever one says.

If one wishes to pacify, make eight thousand fire offerings of lotuses before the painted image; it will be pacified. Before the painted image, make eight thousand fire offerings of mālatī flowers smeared with curd, honey and ghee; it will be pacified.

One who has done the preliminary practice should, on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight, set the painted image in a stūpa containing relics, make a great offering, and offer a vast torma. Outside, give a torma to all the bhūtas, and then draw an image with nāgakesara powder. Having also bound the maṇḍala, sit on a mat of kuśa grass, and one should recite until a shooting star falls. Again, one should recite until the painted image moves. Other signs of accomplishment also appear; then, having paid homage to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, one becomes a flying vidyādhara. Taking whatever form one wishes, one sees and hears from a thousand yojanas away. None of the vidyādharas can harm one.

Having done the preliminary practice, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, keeping a fast day and night, make vast offerings, take an intact body, worship it with scents, flowers and incense, hold it with the right hand, and one should recite until it blazes. As soon as it blazes, surrounded by a thousand vidyādharas, one flies into the vault of the sky, in the form of one sixteen years of age, with hair curled and coiled, and none of the vidyādharas can harm one.

For bringing down a spirit, it is done by sitting. For destroying poison, it is done with a leafy twig. For protecting oneself, it is done by recitation.

Beginning from the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight and up to the fifteenth, one keeping the poṣadha vows, pure and wearing clean clothes, should recite before the image. One obtains whatever one desires.

Consecrate ghee eight hundred times and drink it. In seven days one will become sharp-witted.

Before the painted image, make eight thousand fire offerings of mallikā flowers. In seven nights wealth will arise.

On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, keeping a fast for three nights, kindle a fire with udumbara wood and make eight thousand fire offerings of udumbara kindling sticks smeared with curd, honey and ghee. One obtains five hundred coins.

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one keeping the poṣadha vows should light eight thousand butter lamps and make eight thousand fire offerings of coiled lamp wicks. Afterward one should offer the recitation. Then one obtains sight.

Set a volume of the Perfection of Wisdom in a stūpa containing relics, consecrate it eight thousand times, and pay homage to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas; then one should recite twelve times in each of three sessions in a single day. One obtains hearing in each ear.

For illness, according to the rite by which the samādhi of the noble Avalokiteśvara is sure to arise, one should have him painted with unmixed colors on cloth or on a panel. Make a great offering before it, and one should recite a hundred thousand times. Sitting on a seat of kuśa grass, living on milk and barley meal, bathing three times a day, wearing clean clothes, and keeping the eightfold poṣadha vows, one should offer recitation from the first day of the month until the first day comes round again. Then the illness will be completely pacified.

One who has done the preliminary practice, living on milk and barley meal or on cow's urine and barley meal, bathing three times a day, and keeping the poṣadha vows, should set the painted image in a stūpa containing relics, light eight lamps on each side, and worship with a thousand lotuses. One should recite during the dark fortnight. One should accomplish it from the first day of the bright fortnight. On the full moon, keeping a fast for three nights, make vast offerings and one should recite throughout the night. If one is to become a king, the practitioner's house blazes; and if the bunch of flowers moves, one will become the king of a realm.

Before the painted image, make a maṇḍala with white sandalwood, offer scents, flowers, incense and so forth, and a torma too; then take three hundred flower filaments, consecrate them eight hundred times, and light three ghee lamps. Kindle a fire with udumbara kindling sticks, consecrate each flower eight hundred times, smear it with ghee, and one should make the fire offering. Whatever one desires comes under one's control.

If one recites at the three times of day for seven nights, one's five deeds of immediate retribution will be diminished. If one recites eight hundred times each day, one's misdeeds will be diminished. Through constant recitation one obtains whatever village one wishes, and whatever one sees with one's eyes comes under control. One becomes victorious in debate and supreme among speakers. Make fire offerings of sesame and māṣa beans: it increases wealth. Make eight thousand fire offerings of vaṭa sprouts smeared with curd, honey and ghee: one will not die an untimely death. Before the painted image, with eight thousand flowers of the nāga tree, the lord of men comes under control.

Then Śākyamuni once more gazed over the whole circle of the assembly, complete in every respect, and said to the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, "Great being, through applying the fire-offering rite that is the special collection drawn from the arrangement of all the chapters of your vidyā mantras, there is a special procedure by which practitioners of vidyā work with fire, and when they are established in it, beings devoted to the practice of vidyā should apply it. What is that?" He spoke the words of the vidyā mantra for it:

tadyathā oṃ tiṣṭha hari sirgala lohitākṣa dehi dadāpaya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā

"This is the fire essence of Avalokiteśvara. It is regarded as the very nature that performs all rites and grants all wishes. With this the practitioner should make the fire offering: one should offer into the fire three oblations, reciting once for each. The fire will be invited. Likewise, in applying the rites of pacifying, enriching and fierce activity, the kindling sticks come in three kinds of wood. For pacifying, one should prepare sticks distinguished by being of aśoka wood that still holds its sap, a span or a cubit in length, or three finger-breadths, and smooth and supple; these are highly praised, and with them this rite should be accomplished. Without holes and not hollow, like the wing of a parrot, and likewise green, or with dried leaves, or black in color, should also be offered.

Rejecting those eaten by worms, one keeps only those without holes; rejecting those of other colors, both the best and the worst, and rejecting also those that are dry, one uses the rest for burning. One should use those that are not rotten and not crooked, and avoid the others.

Then make the fire pit square on every side and one should encircle it below; of the measure of a bow-length and a cubit, it is three cubits, or two cubits, or four cubits. Likewise, always free of living creatures, consecrate sand, and on it make the shape of a lotus. Then make the rim all around carefully in the shape of a square maṇḍala as well. Before the painted image, whether for pacifying or for enriching, these have been fully proclaimed.

For the fierce rite, as is taught,
one makes a vajra in the center,
both of its ends three-pronged.
Moreover, the fire pit is two cubits,
and straight across it is seven.
Likewise, behind a clean place,
or at a spot on a river's bank,
or a firm place, or a charnel ground,
or an empty house, one should duly begin the fire offering.
Likewise, on a mountain peak too,
in an empty temple of the gods,
and always in a great wilderness:
these three, likewise,
are declared the places of the practitioner.
These are the places of the supreme person.
Of all the fire-offering rites declared,
sitting on a mat of kuśa grass,
a cubit's measure from that place,
the fire-offering rites in particular
the knower of secret mantra should perform there.
Accomplishment comes swiftly indeed;
that it will remain, there is no doubt.
Facing east and facing north
are for pacifying and enriching;
for the fierce, facing south,
and that the mantra practitioner should shun.
Facing east, pacification increases;
for enriching, too, one faces north.
These the mantra practitioner, at the same time,
should duly begin with recitation of the vidyā.
With bilva, arka, plakṣa
and nyagrodha, one performs the enriching rite.
For the fierce rite, the woods
are milky, pungent, sour and sharp;
all of these are to be shunned:
they have been forbidden by the sages.
Always for pacifying and enriching rites
moist wood is highly praised;
likewise dry wood is for fierce rites,
which the sages have always shunned.
Where these are lacking, with kindling sticks
one should treat them as those woods.
Green, and as if glossy,
like the neck of a peacock,
likewise with kuśa grass of that kind,
always perform pacifying and enriching.
Like emerald,
and likewise with white grasses,
the sinful rites are always done:
these the supreme Victorious One has forbidden.
Here, with stainless water,
pure and free of insects,
one should always then thoroughly wash.
One should also encircle it all around,
or, with diligence, on the outside,
and touch it according to the rite.
The pure one should, with grass, make it the measure of a lamp.
Then, having made it the size of a fist,
one should carefully kindle the fire.
One should not blow on it with the breath of the mouth,
nor likewise with the hem of one's garment,
nor with a bundle of cloth or a lower robe;
avoiding coverings,
the sky's treasure and various winds,
whether harmful or pleasant,
and free from any lapse in purity,
likewise with a cloth or with a jewel
one should fan; with a good breeze
one should duly start the fire.
With this breeze that arises from it,
the knower of mantra should kindle the fire.
Well composed, for the sake of the fire offering,
having examined the other excellent fuel,
then at the end
three oblations of cow's ghee
should be offered there; of that,
whatever is fitting is to be the measure.
To all the buddhas, the protectors,
and to the lord, each with his own mantra,
then pay homage as one wishes,
and at that time make fire offerings into the fire.
By reciting the secret mantra seven times
one always invites the fire.
With fragrant flowers that one has gathered oneself,
with flowers alone, one always calls it.
The mantra practitioner skilled in the place
who offers a seat in that place
does so with that secret mantra and not otherwise.
With ghee mixed with curd,
three kindling sticks smeared with honey,
for enriching, one makes fire offerings into the fire.
In all the rites of mantra,
sitting upon a lotus seat,
one performs the fire offering of the pacifying rite.
For the enriching rite, these very things
are to be offered, with mantras of matching form.
For one engaged in the fierce rite,
one should view it in another form.
The stainless deities,
in due order, into the fire pit,
with flowers and scents as they are found,
reciting seven times,
are invoked; at that time,
those that are firmly set in their place
remain, just as they do in both.
Kindling sticks mixed with the substances,
well endowed with ghee and honey,
and likewise mixed with curd,
one should offer a thousand, or a hundred thousand,
or else always a hundred and eight.
Having taken up the mantra, likewise,
with the vidyā recited once,
into the garlanded fire with blazing eyes and crest,
a single tongue of flame.
In just the same way, the pacifying rite,
the fire offering that must be done,
and, for enriching, that and control as well.
The fierce rite is disparaged:
the Victorious One has rejected it. In fire-offering rites
the well-applied fire will be praised,
endowed with the strength of eighty Rāhus,
highly praised by the supreme Victorious One.
There one always accomplishes the secret mantra.
Make fire offerings into a white fire.
If the color is red, likewise,
it is always held as the accomplishment of enriching.
Black, smoky and pale yellow
are what is called "the left-handed."
The three kinds of color that appear
are the three kinds of accomplishment.
Mantra practitioner, other colors than these,
or colors of many kinds:
in that there is no accomplishment of mantra.
Again, here in the palm of the hand,
colors of many kinds:
there are such clear colors.
Having seen the fire blaze,
one should begin the rites again.
Having made the invitation, the form and color:
if accomplishment of mantra is to come,
engaging again in the fire offering,
by seeing the procedure of the rite,
inviting and requesting departure,
one should recite the mantra to the fire.
Even with what was set out before,
here in this maṇḍala, another way:
do it with that very supreme one.
In this fire offering, one who performs
the acts of inviting and requesting departure
should perform the rites with that very one.
There the rites of fire practice,
likewise before the image and the painted image,
are begun and accomplished.
For that, the mantra spoken before,
praised by the Tathāgata, the Victorious One:
with it all the rites are to be performed there.

Other rites are not to be performed,
especially sinful rites,
those censured by the supreme Victorious One,
and those censured as contrary to the world.
One rises to the state of a universal monarch (cakravartin);
then a bodhisattva, a lord of the earth,
likewise one who has gained the five superknowledges;
then one accomplishes divinity itself.
Here, one who always knows the application,
skilled in the rites of the painted image and the fire offering,
attains lordship of the underworld
and moves through the sky.
Then the gods above the earth,
yakṣas or yakṣiṇīs,
one summons; and always
lordship of a kingdom,
or else roaming here in this land,
or else knowledge and the state of a vidyādhara.
Asuras and all sentient beings
one brings under control, makes them follow, and summons them.
Genuine great beings,
great-souled bodhisattvas,
beings who abide on the ten grounds,
one summons by the rite of fire offering.
What need is there to mention humans on the earth?
Likewise lordship over the rest,
and especially sovereignty over the world,
truly and certainly over all bhūtas;
the state of a lord of men, and likewise,
for the purpose of subjugation, all sentient beings,
whether by that lord of men or by those men,
by all upon the earth alike:
likewise all the rites, in every way,
should always be performed by fire offering.
Relying properly and certainly on all the rites,
undertaking them oneself, one accomplishes them together.
For the sake of good fortune, its rites,
the supreme, the middling,
or else the lesser, should be accomplished.
Right there, in order to declare
the accomplishment of every substance, again
one should look for the accomplishments together.
One well engaged in the rites of fire offering
binds the mudrā for all the rites;
with self-protection, and with ghee,
one fully enters upon the rite of fire offering.
Then this secret mantra of the painted image,
recited seven times or recited eight times:
always conduct yourself by this rite.
namaḥ sarbba buddha bodhisatvānāna apratihatagatisatvānāna tadyathā auṃ jvala tiṣā hūṃ ruru biśva sambhabe svāhā
With this, applying it to the firewood, recite it;
then again, reciting it twice or seven times,
the knower of mantra makes a fire offering into the fire:
flowers, incense, or perfume as well.
For each and every one of them,
with this very sevenfold recitation
you should pronounce it.
In undertaking all the rites,
by the preceding procedure, the cause,
it is to be done with thorough application.
Having first bound, for all the rites,
the great mudrā Yaśovatī,
and likewise having performed the protection,
one skilled in the causes of accomplishment
should undertake all the rites.
If one sees signs of potency,
auspicious sounds,
and always that fruitful ground,
the secret mantra, just as one wishes,
will certainly grant this supreme thing.
First, the thorough application of the rite,
fully entered upon through the secret mantra as cause:
only those accomplishments
that bear fruit should be accomplished.
The sound of victory and the paṭaha drum,
the accomplishment of the great drum, is certain;
everywhere these are spoken of as censured.
For one who abides in the fire offering,
moreover, supreme auspicious signs,
birds, or auspicious sounds,
sounds of various kinds proclaimed by them:
any such sound is praised by the Victorious One.
Highly praised are gods appearing at the right time,
pleasing sounds of various kinds,
parasols, victory banners and flags,
women adorned with ornaments,
and likewise full vases;
if one sees an offering of water, these are causes of accomplishment.
Praised in this way, or
highly praised and honored by the world,
are monks and nuns:
if one sees them, it is the accomplishment
of the secret mantra in its various spheres.

Thus it was said.

This completes the eleventh chapter of the extensive collection, the rite of the thread of the counting rosary, from the Ūrdhvajaṭā Kalpa, a Great Vehicle sūtra of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, the Avataṃsaka.

Then, before the painted image, with eight thousand flowers of the nāga tree, the lord of men comes under one's control. For all diseases, for ailments of the legs, and for malignant wounds, if one gives a lump of earth empowered with seven recitations, they will be pacified.

Having done the preliminary practice, having purified the body with the five products of the cow, and bathing three times a day, one should drink milk. Before the principal painted image one should recite the mantra eight hundred times. Afterward, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, having made offerings before the painted image as far as one is able, sitting on a mat of kuśa grass, perform a fire offering of eight thousand bilva sticks smeared with ghee, curd and honey. Rays of light will issue from the crown of the head of noble Mañjuśrī. They circle around the practitioner and vanish in front of the image of the Blessed One, the Buddha. Then one sees noble Avalokiteśvara and obtains whatever of the three supreme things is to be obtained: the kingdom of the vidyādharas, and the words, "Just as you are, such a Blessed One am I." This accomplishment is achieved by honoring the guru, and by giving, with compassion and with a mind equal toward all sentient beings.

Fasting day and night, having made extensive offerings before the painted image, perform a fire offering of eight thousand arka sticks. Whatever one wishes, one summons in an instant.

Grind agaru, priyaṅgu and nāgakeśara in equal parts into a powder, place it in a pair of earthen bowls joined mouth to mouth, and empower it with eight thousand recitations. If one anoints the body with it and enters battle, one will be invincible to others.

By reciting it two million one hundred thousand times before Avalokiteśvara, one becomes a vidyādhara. Recite it one million one hundred thousand times: one sees noble Mañjuśrī. Recite it seven hundred thousand times before the painted image: fire will appear. For one stricken by disease, recite it one million five hundred thousand times before the painted image: it destroys the disease. Having done the preliminary practice, recite it one million two hundred thousand times: one obtains an elixir or a rejuvenating essence, each in turn. By eating it, wrinkles and grey hair are cast off, and one lives long with the appearance of a sixteen-year-old.

Having recited it three hundred thousand times, perform a fire offering of eight thousand royal mustard seeds: the king's queen comes under one's control. Within seven nights she will lavishly bestow wealth on this one, except for any approach of desire.

Before the painted image, perform a fire offering of a hundred thousand arka sticks: one obtains a hundred gold measures each time.

Perform a fire offering of eight thousand grains of parched rice: one will be free of obstructors. Perform a fire offering of a thousand sticks of piṇyāka wood: all people will be pleased. Recite it three hundred thousand times: one will be free of disease of the waist. For one stricken by fever, one should sweep him with kuśa grass. Having empowered a thread spun by a maiden with eight thousand recitations, one should tie it on: one will become fortunate. Perform a fire offering of a hundred thousand dongka flowers: one obtains a hundred and twenty million garments each time.

On a very beautiful bar made of iron obtained under the constellation Puṣya, make a wheel with ten petals. Having installed the painted image at a stūpa containing relics, fasting day and night, make extensive offerings, take up the wheel, and recite for as long as it takes for signs to appear. When it sends out sparks, and for as long as it blazes, one should recite. Then one becomes accomplished: one gathers all the vidyādharas, and flies together with one's retinue. One becomes a king of the vidyādharas, abides for a great eon, and travels without obstruction.

Rising early, one recites it for a year: it grants the supreme. By reciting it once in six months, one is freed from a great disease. Recite it for a month: even out of season, with the smoke of guggulu, one draws out the venom of fanged creatures. This applies to fevers of one day, of two days, of three days, of four days, and the like.

To bring a woman under one's control: before the painted image, for seven nights, in three sessions, perform twenty-one fire offerings of lāpana smeared with honey: she will come under control. This is also for a widow to use on a man. As for the king: before the painted image, perform a fire offering of eight thousand arka sticks smeared with curd, honey and ghee: he will come under control. For the king's ministers and the like: at night, in three sessions, perform a fire offering of salt twenty-one times: they will come under control. Having empowered one's head three or seven times, if one goes in at the king's gate, one will receive the king's great favor. If one sweeps with a peacock feather empowered eight hundred times, it destroys poison. Having wrapped realgar in aśvattha leaves, one should properly undertake the rite by empowering it eight thousand times: one will become fortunate.

Before the painted image, beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight, eating milk and barley flour, bathing three times a day and changing one's clothes three times, burning agaru, turuṣka and sandalwood, one should offer a torma of the three white substances. For the torma for all the bhūtas: fragrant flowers born in water or born on dry land, and three lamps of clarified butter. At the end, fasting for three nights, one should recite throughout the night. One obtains whatever one seeks. Between sessions, food too is given as far as one is able.

Having installed the painted image at a stūpa containing relics, fasting for three nights, perform a fire offering of eight thousand aśvattha sticks smeared with curd, honey and ghee. Then rays of light issue from the painted image, the earth shakes, the flames of the lamps grow, and the garlands sway: by these signs one becomes accomplished.

Having wrapped antimony eye-salve in aśvattha leaves and made burnt offerings to the full number of a thousand, sitting cross-legged, one should recite until the accomplishment occurs in its three forms.

On something bearing fruit, write the name of whatever substance one wishes, empower it eight thousand times, and throw it into a pond where a nāga dwells. That nāga accomplishes all the rites. Within seven days he gives garments just as one wishes.

On something bearing fruit, draw the substance one desires, and likewise place it in a well or a pond. Then have a man dive into the water. There too the man hears a great sound, and in such and such a direction the substances and so on are found. Then they should be taken up. One crosses to the far banks of rivers. At an assembly hall that is hard to approach, or even at the royal palace, having called the gods to mind, one becomes invincible to others. Wherever one wishes, one should bring it under control. Having also placed it in the mouth of the noble one, say, "Please speak a little, truly": before long it will come under control.

Having made a water vessel and visualized noble Avalokiteśvara in it, one should sprinkle the water empowered eight thousand times on one bitten by a fanged creature: he will be free of poison. For this, having fully entered the maṇḍala by the rite that has been described will not be in vain.

Having taken cow dung that has not fallen on the ground, eating caru, keeping silence, and making a maṇḍala, beginning from the full moon one should recite until the third, reciting a hundred thousand times. Practicing celibacy and this very discipline for six months, in one month there is accomplishment, and in six months one comes to see all beings directly. With one's very body one attains the supreme accomplishment. In a month one accomplishes all mantras.

Having drawn whatever nāga king one wishes, place one's left foot upon it and recite a hundred thousand times in a covered place. That nāga king comes and says, "What shall I do?" One should say, "Let me enter the abode of all the nāgas." He lets one enter there. Likewise, if one draws a yakṣa king and practices, he carries out one's commands.

Take a little dust from a clean place that bears all things and scatter it over a snake: the snake will be turned back. Again, if one wishes to release it, one should recite. Having made a seal from something white in color, empower it eight thousand times, have it placed upon the bite, and summon: it raises up even one who has died.

Substances such as realgar, and the sword, the axe, the wheel, the bhuṣuṇḍala and so on, are to be purified with the five products of the cow, and a burnt offering completing a thousand is to be made. Taking any one of these substances, with the rite going first, recite five hundred thousand times before the painted image. Afterward, having obtained realgar at whatever price is asked, kindle a fire with sticks of the bodhi tree and burn it until it turns the color of fire. Then make butter from the milk of a cow of pure strain, churned by a maiden, and put the ash into the butter. Do the same with a vessel filled with curd and with one filled with honey. Then take it out and place it in a saffron casket. Having protected oneself with this very Blessed Mother, at the time when the moon is seized by Rāhu, fasting for three nights, make extensive offerings to the painted image, wrap it all around with three aśvattha leaves, and cover it with four. Sitting on a mat of kuśa grass and pressing it with the right hand, one should recite until it grows warm, gives off smoke, and blazes. If one makes a tilaka with it while it is warm, one brings all beings under control. Through the smoke one becomes invisible. Through the blazing one travels through the sky. One lives for ten thousand years, and is unassailable by any being. This same rite applies to accomplishing eye-salve and orpiment, and to bezoar.

On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, place it on a lotus petal, make great offerings to the painted image, take it up in joined palms, and recite until it grows warm, gives off smoke, and blazes. In this too there are the three kinds of accomplishment.

Recite one million times before the painted image. Then have a craftsman whose faculties are complete and who keeps the poṣadha vows make, out of the three metals, a lotus of ten or of eight petals, adorned with a seat and ornaments. Put into the lotus saffron, bezoar and camphor ground with rainwater. On the eighth day of the bright fortnight, having made great offerings to the painted image, fasting for three nights, sit cross-legged, confess misdeeds, make supplications, and so on; then take the lotus in the right hand and recite until it blazes. Then through that lotus one, together with one's retinue, becomes joyful. One is unassailable by any being and lives for ten thousand years. It is said that the same holds for a bracelet, a crest ornament, an iron chain, a vajra, a battle-axe, and a wheel as well.

This is the special procedure for the wheel. Make a wheel of the five metals, sharp-edged, a wheel perfect in its characteristics, one span in size. Take earth from both banks of the Ganges and form it into a lump before the painted image. Set the wheel upon it, worship it with red sandalwood, and offer red karavīra flowers and garlands. On the eighth day of the bright fortnight, keeping the poṣadha vows and fasting, provide a feast for the Saṅgha from alms, and ask them to bestow accomplishment. Being clean and wearing clean clothes, one should apply oneself with a mind of compassion. Having made great offerings to the painted image, offering scents, flowers, incense and so on, and offering lamps as far as one's means allow, one should also offer four lamps at the four sides of the wheel, and guggulu incense. Sitting on a mat of kuśa grass, recite once over each of the flowers smeared with red sandalwood and strike the wheel with each one, up to eight thousand. Then the wheel makes a sound and sends out rays of light, and then it blazes. At the second sign the wheel will certainly move. Then the practitioner, having bowed to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, should recite the vidyā and take it up. As soon as he takes it, he, together with his retinue, becomes a vidyādhara: a great vidyādhara over ten thousand leagues, much sought after by all the vidyādharas of the nāgas and the yakṣas. He lives for five thousand years, and when he dies he is reborn in Sukhāvatī.

Then, if one wishes to accomplish pills: have saileṭaka, red sandalwood, lac, guggulu, the root of tārāvartaka, iron filings, girikarṇī, husks of grain, costus, spikenard, honey, long pepper and turuṣka combined and ground into a fine powder. Then take the milk of a tawny cow of pure strain, combine it with butter churned by a maiden, and with that powder have pills made the size of a juniper berry. Then, on the eighth or the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, fasting day and night and keeping the eightfold poṣadha vows, take about five pills and wrap them in aśvattha leaves. Before the painted image, one should give a rosary, sesame oil, flour and the like to others. Sitting on a mat of kuśa grass, having performed the rite of offering, press them with the right hand and recite for as long as they give off smoke. Divide them properly: by putting one in the mouth one becomes invisible. Beings in the form of gods come. All the siddhas come forth and one sees them. One lives for five hundred years. Then, when it blazes, one travels through the sky. These are the two kinds of accomplishment.

This too becomes a means of accomplishing the rites of the root vidyā of the Blessed Mother. In the third or the seventh practice, even one who has committed the five acts of immediate retribution will succeed. With the root essence mantra too these rites are accomplished; this is to be understood just as it is.

This completes the section called "All the Means of Accomplishment" in the root kalpa of the Blessed Mother.

Then again the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, having looked thoroughly with his buddha eye upon the world realm with all it contains, addressed the bodhisattva, the great being Avalokiteśvara, who had come into the center of the circle of the assembly:

"Out of love for the sentient beings
who dwell among humans and bhūtas,
all the maṇḍalas together with their rites,
great being, speak of them, speak!
The deities of Tārā's maṇḍala,
which make all excellence increase,
for the sake of benefiting practitioners,
O Guide, speak of them in full!
All the wondrous marvels:
the embodied beings of middling kind,
having heard your supreme words
that are yet to come,
swiftly, in accomplishing the deities,
wherever sentient beings have entered upon it,
right there, as was explained before,
by wise bodhisattvas
and by thousands of millions of buddhas
all of it is rejoiced in.
The maṇḍala that destroys all wrongdoing,
the virtue that brings about every accomplishment:
Protector of sentient beings, speak of it!
Tārā's maṇḍala, in your words,
will make the rites of sentient beings correct.
Having heard of this maṇḍala,
deep faith will arise in them.
It destroys misfortune and pacifies,
likewise it carries off disease and enemies;
the maṇḍala makes the splendor and strength
of all sentient beings increase.
Having seen it or heard of it,
they then give rise to deep faith.
Whoever they may be, I
prophesy them as well
to attain the awakening of all the buddhas.
The buddhas of the future who will appear,
the protectors of the world, too
will rejoice in it.
The maṇḍala that makes excellence increase,
that likewise gathers all good qualities,
the wondrous maṇḍala of Tārā:
great being, Protector of the World,
by true command speak of it, speak!"

When he had said this, the bodhisattva, the great being, noble Avalokiteśvara, rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, bowed with joined palms toward the Blessed One, and extolled the Blessed One Śākyamuni with words of praise in verses of one accord:

"King of the Śākyas, king of the gods,
possessed of many excellent qualities,
highly praised, your miraculous powers undiminished,
ever clothed in white garments,
pillar of offering, your face fragrant as a lotus,
of excellent intellect, the heart, holder of the teaching:
for you are excellence itself.
He who delights with joy
these beings here
is the protector of the gods;
through mindfulness of the intrinsic nature he shines everywhere.
His words are fully knowing;
that hero has exhausted attachment;
he holds the three fruits.
Otherwise, by him,
guarded all around by fair goddesses,
by eight, here, from the face of the lord,
the hero born of it, of great strength,
and the lord of stirring delight,
endowed all around with golden mountains,
the crest ornament and the seat together.
Of gods and asuras together with gods,
all the higher vehicles too,
the world, intermediate existence,
birth, your life, and so on,
arisen, beautiful, of their own nature:
his eyes are joy,
white as the moon,
the hare-marked one held by the gods,
of white kunda flowers and fine dukūla cloth
is the garment he wears, a cakora bird.
Śakra, with eyes like the hundred-petaled lotus,
the guardian of the earth goes at one shoulder, to one side;
the hare-marked moon upon the highest mountain;
Śakra, lord with a royal army,
hundred-eyed, through undiminished diligence,
number, and the ocean, the bringer of water,
the sound of the hosts, and joy,
and in the joy of stainless eyes,
the sublime rays of the Sun
in their forms circle with food and fragrance.
White vases filled, each one,
with those vases conferring empowerment,
sandalwood, the finest earth, the limbs declared,
the bezoar tilaka shining brightly,
the sublime limbs of the pārijāta tree,
the limbs of supreme joy,
made in order to vanquish the Bodiless One, the god of desire.
At the end of the limbs becoming attached,
the bath, dense, unchanging,
otherwise the excellent deathless one;
below that, with joined palms,
like one stricken by poison, reviled.
Proclaiming the supreme of the tathāgatas,
rain-laden, in your mouth:
from of old you are the head of the path,
having abandoned them like stains;
in the month of flowers,
fully completed, endowed with enjoyments;
these themselves, as though bound,
having been refined by an unprecedented rite,
on the tenth you are peace;
from endless beings without protector,
because existence is endless,
gods and asuras too, through stains,
his discipline, each in turn,
appear by the light of sublime eyes.
Coiled, wide-eyed, with supreme limbs,
the gods dwelling in the directions,
and humans fully awakened to awakening:
what is called 'will bring it about'
is the action by which humans arise and are gathered.
Therefore the lotus, the water-born,
has reached the sublime limbs of the god.
The hero's limbs are entwined, free of attachment;
as if dying, the body of earth is also set down;
wholly setting forth and wholly gathering in,
truly endowed with the grounds and the directions,
endowed with awakening, the four aspects in balance,
having won full victory
over the army of Māra at the foot of the bodhi tree,
and the unchanging state of a buddha.
At the root of the nāga tree,
through forests of harsh aversion,
for the fire of hollow stalks,
illuminating the stains of the darkness of delusion,
in the blazing fire of wrath,
unmoving, he gives completely;
he meditates on the vajra-like mudrā;
the measured creeper, the image steadfast;
the red fire blazing,
beautiful as a terrifying sun:
generating strength in my limbs, I bow and praise."

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Avalokiteśvara, having extolled the Blessed One with these verses, sat down on his own seat and entered into the absorption of the great bodhisattvas called All-Seeing. The very moment he entered it, many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of niyutas of light rays came forth from the mouth of the great being, and those light rays illuminated buddha fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. All the beings in the hells, too, in that instant and that moment, were freed from all suffering. In those buddha fields, those buddhas, the blessed ones, gave their approval to the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara: "Excellent, excellent!"

"Great being, speak! Great powerful one, speak of the empowerment of all sinful beings in the maṇḍala!" When in this way those buddhas, the blessed ones, in the endless and limitless ten directions, surrounded by their hosts of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, together gave their approval, "Excellent!", to the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, this great earth with its mountains, forests and caves shook violently.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Avalokiteśvara, arose from that absorption of the great bodhisattvas and began to explain the mantra of the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā.

"First of all, the master of the maṇḍala of the Blessed Mother is one who has seen the samaya and so obtained authorization equal to that of a master; who through faith has generated the mind set on awakening; who knows the strengths and weaknesses of sentient beings; who, being without avarice and without deceit, is free of darkness; who is neither too stout nor too thin; who is free of foul odor; whose faculties are complete; who is handsome; who, being endowed with courage, is fully possessed of generosity, moral discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom and compassion; who knows the intentions and the dispositions of sentient beings; who has clear faith in the Buddha, the Dharma and the Saṅgha; who is versed in many branches of learning; who is lucid and speaks lucidly; who is trained in the work of drawing maṇḍalas; who has previously completed the approach practice with a vidyā of any of the three families or the like; who knows the application of the mudrās and the maṇḍala; who has done the work of making stūpas; who is neither too old nor a child, and not born of low caste; who is young and in the bloom of youth; and who is of good conduct. Such a practitioner should draw the secret maṇḍala." So it is said.

Then a master such as this should begin the rite of the maṇḍala of the Blessed Mother:

To one who is neither incapable nor hard to discipline
the maṇḍala should properly be applied.
To those of deluded mind and full of attachment
the maṇḍala should not even be shown.
Whoever, even for a moment,
advances higher in the training,
that embodied one truly gains the higher realms and liberation,
and will attain mastery of mind.
For one whose mind of awakening has later collapsed,
accomplishment does not even come into view.
Having gained knowledge rooted in awakening,
from that mind one properly begins.
Then the master of the maṇḍala
should himself thoroughly examine
the beings who have deep faith
in the Buddha, the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
For them he draws the maṇḍala that is to be shown.
Then the master of the maṇḍala,
having first disciplined his body by strength,
in a fortnight of the month of miracles,
in villages, cities, market towns
and districts, in the northeastern
quarter, gives an offering of water.
On the surface of the ground, just as it is,
the site becomes mantra through the mantra:
smooth, with trees and fine flowers,
with many excellent fruits,
a place where water flows without ceasing,
on white and yellow ground,
free of potsherds, stones and gravel,
with the sound of great drums,
at crossroads and charnel grounds,
places held by other gods,
auspicious and wholly free of suffering,
where all around, within a range
of five krośas, there are rivers and ponds,
lakes and flowing streams,
trees, stūpas and temples,
and flowers at all times,
truly endowed in great abundance:
in either fortnight of the month of miracles,
then the master of the maṇḍala
of the Blessed Mother, going to that site
at midday,
should perform the rite of adornment
with the heart mantra of Ekajaṭī.
First, thoroughly purified, with love and compassion
for all sentient beings,
he focuses his mind on that site of the maṇḍala
and recites the virtuous vidyā.
The sublime heart mantra of Tārā,
and likewise the melody, he recites afterward.
Here, for the sake of worshiping the buddhas,
the maṇḍala is drawn by all embodied beings.
He stays in a place where beings go in the directions.
First having given the torma,
equipped with fragrant sticks,
staying in that place, having eaten everything,
in proper order, with the melody
of invitation, he should say these words:
"I, the master named so-and-so,
wish to draw the maṇḍala
of the Blessed One, noble Tārā.
For myself and for all sentient beings,
having to the end no harmful intent,
generating it and showing honor,
and for the sake of the beings
who have deep faith in the Buddha's teaching,
that again and again
they may have great faith,
I wish to draw the maṇḍala."

Thus he should say it twice and three times.
Then to those beings
the master of the maṇḍala
grants the seeing of signs by night.
Then, whether at the drawing place or having gone elsewhere,
at dawn he should examine the dreams.
Having gone to that site,
to a measure of a hundred cubits
he should make it square on every side.
Outside, going out by the measure
of the immeasurable Three Jewels,
whatever is in the ground, wood and chaff,
ash, charcoal and potsherds,
hair and nails, the black bricks
of sacrifice and the like,
and moreover every unwholesome thorn
of the auspicious maṇḍala,
having removed them all without remainder,
into that very pit of earth,
having further purified earth
from both banks of a great river,
he should put it in and pound it with a mallet,
and sprinkle it well with sandalwood water.
Having done so, mixing the cow products
that have not fallen to the ground with sandalwood water,
on the area of eight cubits,
and outside it too, to a measure of ten cubits,
on what has been thoroughly cleansed,
having given the restoration vows, he should have it smeared,
until that ground
has become very smooth
and very well perfected.
Thus for seven days.
Then, to a measure of four cubits,
at the four corners, eight pegs of khadira wood
should be made twelve finger-widths in measure.
A thread spun by a maiden,
of five colors, fine and smooth,
very strong, empowered with the root heart mantra
of the Blessed Lady seven times,
should be wound about the pegs;
making seven windings, he should drive them in at dusk.
Then the master of the maṇḍala,
wearing clean garments,
in the very center of the maṇḍala ground,
should take a vase without a black base,
filled with scented water,
flowers and lamps,
wind a garland of flowers about its neck,
and cover its mouth with sprigs of mango.
Kneeling firmly on his knees,
he should recite the root vidyā seven times,
or else twenty-one times.
Then, looking toward all ten directions,
he should proclaim this: "I, so-and-so,
in this place, in order to worship the buddhas,
contemplating the samādhi of all beings,
into this maṇḍala that has been drawn,
may all the buddhas who bring benefit
please come into the maṇḍala.
Having come here now,
please accept my offering water."
In its very center, as is to be visualized,
the Blessed One drawn in her place
should be invited, and having briefly shown
the abodes of the deities, he should declare:
"In Tuṣita heaven, the bodhisattvas;
whoever dwells in other worlds;
likewise in the abode of snows,
where the Lord of the Lotus (Padmeśvara) arises;
in Alakāvatī, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera);
on Kailāsa, Śaṅkara (Śiva), it is said."
With the vessel of offering water filled,
he should contemplate their abodes.
Then he should offer water for the face, attend on them and honor them.
In all the rites of the maṇḍala,
if the names and abodes are wholly lost,
it turns back the wrong way.
Thus for seven days,
each and every day, with sandalwood
water he should have it smeared,
and likewise in the session of the night.
In this interval all the requisites
are to be fully assembled.
On this the following is to be said:
With powder like pure crystal,
born of the nature of diamond,
and with powder like the jiba flower,
he should draw the whole maṇḍala.
With ruby and utpala,
it should be laid out with powders entirely;
like saffron water,
the maṇḍala of topaz;
and like the flower of flax,
likewise with emerald as well.
So many are the precious colors;
iron too is allowed, the five so named;
or else with powders ground with scents,
or whatever is found, transformed;
with jewel powders well gathered,
one who desires true accomplishment;
gems and lapis, whatever is unequalled,
and ruby in every way.
All the requisites of the maṇḍala
the master should have prepared
by the hands of a maiden:
one born of brahmin or kṣatriya family,
who has generated the mind of awakening,
born without fault, very beautiful,
not lacking in any faculty;
in short, born fully endowed
with the characteristics of a woman.
To one, two or three such maidens
he should give the restoration vows,
delight them with food of milk,
and, having them wear white garments,
have them make all the requisites of the maṇḍala.
All the requisites of the maṇḍala,
well gathered and examined one by one,
kept quite apart from water,
with the monks having done the discipline,
having done thorough purification,
preceded by conduct of cleanliness,
for the master's own preparatory consecration,
all the powders should be fumigated and the drawing made.
The tormas and the butter
he should have made by one versed in the rite.
Then the master, having gathered
all the requisites, should draw the maṇḍala himself.
He should take on disciples:
those with deep faith in the Buddha, the Dharma
and the Saṅgha of monks,
complete in all their limbs and parts,
speakers of truth, not coarse,
beautiful to see, and firm of complexion.
Not to be accepted are one, two, three,
eighteen, and another sixteen.
They should take up the three refuges,
generate the mind of awakening,
and eat a feast of milk.
Tooth sticks from a milky-sapped tree,
eight finger-widths in measure,
empowered with the root heart mantra of the Blessed Lady
twenty-seven times,
well steeped in cow's urine:
at the juncture of the night session,
outside the maṇḍala ground,
facing toward the east, seated in order
on mats of kuśa grass,
he should place the heart mantra into the hand of each.
He should recite the root heart mantra seven times,
and for tying the topknot also recite it seven times.
Then, having given those tooth sticks to them,
each should chew his own tooth stick.
With scented water empowered seven times
with the heart mantra of Ekajaṭī,
he should sprinkle the crowns of their heads.
Then he should say to them:
"The Blessed One, noble Avalokiteśvara,
the compassionate supreme Lord,
giver of the great and supreme,

who liberates those hard to liberate: keep him in mind.
And the Blessed Mother Tārā,
the great queen of knowledge-mantras,
who gives birth to all the buddhas
and bodhisattvas: keep her in mind."
After that, the master,
for all those disciples,
having made firm the Dharma
endowed with freedom from attachment,
should read the Perfection of Wisdom before them.
By a rite such as this,
women too are to be taken on.
Having risen, a thread spun by a girl,
of five colors,
twisted into an uneven number of strands,
washed with scented water,
for each one, with a lotus rosary,
having sprinkled it in purification,
he should empower it with the root heart mantra
twenty-one times,
and here he should say this over it:
"Because it is the ground of glory,
the mark on the feet of the buddhas,
the source of the bodhisattvas,
therefore the lotus rosary is praised."
Then the master himself
should tie it with a fine portion
onto the hands of the disciples.
Whatever is done for the disciples,
that same he should do for himself as a disciple.
Then the one in the preparatory consecration of the maṇḍala,
facing toward the east,
with his upper robe over one shoulder,
planting the cap of his right knee
firmly on the ground,
should bind the root mudrā
and recite the root knowledge-mantra.
Holding garlands of the scents
and flowers of gods and men,
to all the buddhas and those of awakening,
the pratyekabuddhas, the noble śrāvakas,
gods, nāgas, yakṣas and gandharvas,
to all of them he should make supplication:
"I, the master of the maṇḍala,
named so-and-so,
wish to draw the maṇḍala
of the Blessed noble Tārā;
so may you yourselves come:
all the buddhas, the blessed ones,
the bodhisattvas, the pratyekabuddhas,
the śrāvakas, gods, nāgas and yakṣas,
gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas,
kinnaras and great mahoragas,
surrounded by the hosts of your own knowledge-mantras;
out of compassion for all sentient beings,
having come, please grant me your permission."
Thus again twice and again three times.
Then the master of the maṇḍala
should recite the root knowledge-mantra,
and, looking at the maṇḍala ground,
throw a garland of flowers into the center.
If the flower garland moves,
then he should know that they have come.
Then to the buddhas and bodhisattvas
he should offer the offering water with scented water,
and flowers. Then,
on the ground outside the hundred cubits,
at a place thoroughly purified,
having kindled a fire well
with kindling of apāmārga,
facing east, with kuśa grass,
with the root heart mantra, he should offer
eight hundred oblations of honey, curd and butter.
Then to the buddhas and bodhisattvas
and to the deities too he should offer the offering water.
Then at the four sides of the maṇḍala
he should station men
who have taken up the restoration vows,
with protective garlands, and with all their faculties complete.
On this the following is said here:
Whoever does it any other way
will come to be without protection,
and the eight samayas of the maṇḍala
will not truly come about.
Therefore, by the performing of the rite,
the disciple will come to know the samaya.
Then whoever is master of the maṇḍala,
together with the consecrated disciples,
having gone and spread out kuśa grass,
recollecting all the hosts
of buddhas and bodhisattvas,
should lie down on his right side.
Then at dawn the master,
being clean and facing toward the east,
should examine the dreams.
On this the following is to be said:
Whoever sees sandalwood, bilva and the like,
udumbara and the like, and the nyagrodha,
covered with garlands of victory banners,
or a dream that inspires deep faith,
or some beautiful tongues of flame,
whoever sees thus, that is accomplishment
up to the supreme.
Geese and kāraṇḍavas, cranes,
peacocks and rohaṇas:
whoever comes to see such things,
that dream's middling accomplishment
will come about very swiftly indeed.
Or a mother, or a rahaṇa,
or likewise one holding a vīṇā,
or earrings and the like,
or likewise if one sees a, dhi and the like:
whatever dream is seen,
that is the lowest accomplishment for people,
as is definitely taught in the rite of Tārā.
Whoever comes to see caṇḍālas
and the hands of dogs,
