or sees donkeys, camels, carts and the like,
or knowledge itself and the like,
or being touched by lac and sesame oil,
whoever enters these in a dream,
his accomplishment surely remains,
and will come about only as the samaya.
Having examined with intelligence
dreams endowed with such qualities as these,
the one of keen mind, knowing thus,
should then explain
the meaning of the dream to that disciple.
Then the master of the maṇḍala,
if he is a householder,
or monks and nuns,
or laymen and laywomen,
those great ones, having taken
the restoration vows, afterward the disciples
should properly and respectfully keep the restoration.
For a disciple with an unwholesome dream,
before it is explained, a fire offering should be made.
Then the master of the maṇḍala
should have the earlier cloth,
and the painted cloth, and at the end the alāsa
made of copper, put in,
and have them properly set in place.
Then the ground of the maṇḍala
should be well smeared with sandalwood water.
All the disciples in one place,
having been protected with the heart mantra,
seated in one place outside the maṇḍala;
those who know the samaya
should be brought well inside.
Then at the time of the setting of the Sun,
the lines of the maṇḍala should be laid down.
A thread spun by a girl,
of five colors, empowered seven times
with the root heart mantra,
beginning from the direction of Īśāna,
he should bind those pegs with the thread.
All of them are a cubit in measure;
making three, he should wind them round with the thread.
Outside, all around, conches,
great drums and clay drums,
and staff drums of many kinds,
staffs and clappers,
he should have sounded on every side.
Parasols, victory banners, flags and the like
should be arrayed outside.
The maṇḍala is square, with four gates;
with a line cord of five colors,
making it a hundred cubits, the lines should be laid down.
That is the second maṇḍala.
Then, having all the colors,
binding the root mudrā,
he should recite the root knowledge-mantra eight hundred times.
Then the master of the maṇḍala,
having bowed to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas,
the pratyekabuddhas, and the noble
Saṅgha of śrāvakas,
all around the maṇḍala,
to five krośas, the great preparatory consecration:
with the heart mantra of Ekajaṭī,
the minds of all malicious beings
are to be bound.

And all the requisites
of the master of the maṇḍala,
having first made protection
with the heart mantra of Ekajaṭī itself,
beginning from the northeast,
he should lay down the Brahmā line.
Reciting the root knowledge-mantra all the while,
the skilled one draws all the maṇḍalas.
Fully marked off, and white in body,
the master, to the tathāgatas,
should pay homage with jewel powder.
Paying homage to the Lotus family,
with yellow powder the Blessed Lady,
noble Tārā; paying homage,
with green ones all the śrāvakas
and all the pratyekabuddhas;
and with black for the Vajra family.

Thus by the first, at the heart of the square maṇḍala with four gates. Outside, at the second, one enters to a measure of two cubits. The third is a span, double that. Having thus drawn everything in sequence, wishing to draw within the inner maṇḍala, one should request all the buddhas, the blessed ones, the bodhisattvas and the pratyekabuddhas to come there themselves. Filled with all grains, all jewels, all medicines, all scents and flowers, and sandalwood water, its mouth covered with sprigs of māṣa, its neck tied with white dukūla cloth, made of gold and silver, all the requisites of that maṇḍala: it is wound with a garland of flowers at the edge of the second section and empowered with the root knowledge-mantra. This is called the Fully Victorious vase, and it should be placed in the center of the heart maṇḍala. On this the following is to be said:

For the sake of the samaya, for the sake of merit,
to focus on each aim one desires,
having taken up the vows,
from wherever one dwells,
one should draw this supreme maṇḍala.
Aparājita, the Greatly Compassionate,
the Buddha, Maitreya, together with Locanā:
having invoked all these names,
one should draw the Tathāgata.
Trailokyavijayā, known as the White Lady,
and likewise Bhṛkuṭī,
who is known as the Wrathful Lady:
having recalled all these names,
one should draw Avalokiteśvara.
From the supreme knowledge-mantra, again the Terrifier,
Vajrapiṅgala, and Vajra,
held to be fierce, and the Lion,
and likewise Vajramuṣṭi itself:
with all these names,
one should draw Vajrapāṇi in full.

Then the master of the maṇḍala, in the center of the heart maṇḍala, with white powder mixed with white mustard seed, should first draw the Buddha, the Blessed One, seated on a jeweled lion throne, teaching the Dharma, with a maṇḍala of light, light radiating all around, rays of light coming forth from his uṣṇīṣa: the Blessed One endowed with every supreme aspect and adorned with the major marks of a great being. On the two sides above the Blessed One, with yellow powder mixed together with lotus pollen, the kings of the uṣṇīṣa, tumultuous with garlands of blazing flame, with the form, attire and shape of a great universal monarch, their bodies serene, facing toward the Tathāgata, full of seeds, and holding fruits in their hands, namely: the Blessed One Victor's Uṣṇīṣa, Cakravartin, the All-Blazing Uṣṇīṣa, the White Parasol (Sitātapatra), Mass of Splendor (Tejorāśi), Mass of Jewels, Mass of Gold, Mass of Renown, the All-Encompassing Mass, the Mass of Afflictions and Secondary Afflictions, the Mass of Unerring Suchness, the Mass of Permanence, the Mass of the Nature of Non-Entity, the Mass of All, the Mass of Melodious Sound, the Mass of the Three Worlds, the Infinite Mass, the Mass of Merit, and the Mass of the Gods: these are seated on the right side. On the left, namely: the Blessed One Victor's Uṣṇīṣa, the Exalted One, the Fully Victorious Uṣṇīṣa, the Lofty One, the Petal of the Earth, the Hundred-Petaled, the Thousand-Petaled, the Ray of Light, the Great Ray of Light, the Stainless Ray of Light, the Ray of Array, the White Ray of Light, the Lotus Ray of Light, the Uṣṇīṣa of Array, the Uṣṇīṣa Who Tames the Four Māras, the Exalted Uṣṇīṣa, and the Inconceivable Uṣṇīṣa: these, together with those called the Power of the Tathāgatas and the Prophecy, are the uṣṇīṣa kings who should be drawn on the upper left.

Beside the Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin, one should draw the eight great queens of knowledge-mantras resting on a single row: the Blessed Lady Locanā, Ūrṇā, the Moon, the Compassionate Lady, the Loving Lady, the Fearless Lady, the Lady of Prophecy, and the one called the Power of the Tathāgatas. These are seated on lotus thrones, tumultuous with garlands of flame, with serene bodies. The Stain of the Tathāgatas, the Net of Light of the Tathāgatas, the All-Illuminating One of the Tathāgatas, the Heart of the Tathāgatas, and the Near-Heart of the Tathāgatas: these are seated on lotus thrones, tumultuous with garlands of flame, their bodies serene, gazing intently a little toward the Tathāgata; one should draw their bodies shining forth from their own forms. Below the Uṣṇīṣa Cakravartin is the wrathful one of the Tathāgata, the Great Aparājita, in wrathful form, seated on a lotus throne, with a maṇḍala of light all around, his hands busy with a trident and a noose, looking a little toward the image of the Tathāgata. Elsewhere, beside the Victor's Uṣṇīṣa, the eight great queens of knowledge-mantras resting on a single row are these: the Blessed Lady Aparājitā, and then the Śramaṇā, the Beauty of the Tathāgatas, the White Buddha Lady, the Tathāgata Lady of Mind, and the Tathāgata Lady Who Summons with the Hook. These are seated on lotus thrones, with bodies of a maṇḍala of light, facing toward the Tathāgata.

Above these are the eight kings of secret mantra, namely: the Blessed One the End of the Tathāgatas, the All-Illuminating One of the Tathāgatas, the Knowledge of the Tathāgatas, the Three Worlds of the Tathāgatas, the Assembly of the Tathāgatas, the Body of the Tathāgatas, the Emanation of the Tathāgatas, and the World of the Tathāgatas. These are encircled all around by a maṇḍala of light, seated on lotus thrones, their bodies serene, gazing toward the image of the Tathāgata.

Below the Victor's Uṣṇīṣa is the king of knowledge-mantras called Endowed with the Limbs of the Tathāgata, with light all around, seated on a lotus throne, a lotus in his hand. All of them have the forms of deities, the right hand full of seeds and the left hand granting the supreme gift, and each remains in his own attire.

Above the uṣṇīṣa kings one should draw the eight pratyekabuddhas as one knows them, namely: the Blessed One, the pratyekabuddha called the Renowned, the Sage Above, the Great Sage, the Sage of the Gods, Mādara, the Heaped, the Well Heaped, and the Great Heap. These eight pratyekabuddhas are seated cross-legged on lotus thrones, absorbed in samādhi, tumultuous with garlands of flame, and wearing yellow upper robes. Below the Blessed One is the mudrā of the wish-fulfilling jewel; on the left, the outer monastic robe. Below, in front, is the wheel of Dharma with twelve spokes, tumultuous with garlands blazing all around, resting on an eight-petaled lotus. Beside that, one should draw the king of wrathful ones called Subdued by Tārā, wearing a crown of matted locks, seated on a lotus throne, receiving the command of the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā. Below him one should draw the queen of knowledge-mantras called Beauty of the Lotus Family, seated on a lotus throne, wearing a crown of matted locks, with lower and upper garments of silk and cotton, her palms joined, gazing a little toward the form of Tārā, receiving her command. Above that is the wrathful one called Great Lotus, red in color, tumultuous with garlands blazing all around, seated on a lotus throne, receiving the command of the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā. All these kings of wrathful ones should be made with a maṇḍala of light of great blazing all around, bearing transformed forms, with lower garments of silk and cotton, and with bodies fully adorned with every ornament.

On the left side of Tārā is the bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, white in body, wearing a crown of matted locks, fully adorned with every ornament, with an upper garment of fine silk and a lower garment of silk and cotton, seated on a lotus throne, paying homage to the Blessed One Śākyamuni. Below the lotus of Avalokiteśvara is the bodhisattva called Going Stainlessly, dark blue like the priyaṅgu, with a slightly smiling face, seated on a lotus throne, wearing a crown of matted locks, wearing a fluttering lower garment and an upper garment of fine silk, his body very serene, blazing with rays of light, paying homage to the Blessed One Śākyamuni. To the upper left of Going Stainlessly one should make the Blessed One Avalokiteśvara with a staff, a water pot, a rosary and a black antelope skin, his body serene and tumultuous with garlands of flame. Below him is the Fulfiller of Desires, seated on a lotus throne, white in body, his body entwined with lotus stalks, holding a lotus in his left hand and a wish-fulfilling jewel in his right, tumultuous with garlands of flame, with a slightly smiling face.

On a single panel to the right of Vajrapāṇi one should draw the great kings of knowledge-mantras, namely: the Blessed One Vidyottama, the Sleeper, Susiddhikara, Vajrasena, Subāhu, Ūrdhvajaṭā, Good Knowledge, Good Accomplishment, Good Army, Mahābala, the Destroyer, Kilīkila, the Supreme, Well Tamed, the Soarer, the Ancient, Jewel Kelī, Child Kelī, Good Kelī, the Well Filled, the Great Filled, the Ender of the Gods, the Great Vajra, and the Blazing One. These twenty-four are the great kings of mantra, tumultuous with garlands blazing all around, seated on peacocks, dark blue like the utpala, their faces slightly frowning in wrath, paying homage with the left hand to the Blessed One Śākyamuni.

Below these one should draw the great queens of knowledge-mantras, namely: the Blessed Lady Māmakī, the Vajra Hook Lady, the Vajra Chain Lady, the Vajra Victorious Lady, the Vajra Fully Victorious Lady, the Red Lady, Yaśovatī, Biśinī Vajralocanā, the Vajra Frowning Lady, the Vajra Fist Lady, the Vajra Fearless Lady, the Vajra Garland Lady, the Vajra Lady of Sound, the Vajra Auspicious Lady, the Vajra Holder Lady, the Vajra Mother, the Vajra Aparājitā, the Vajra Meteorite Lady, the Vajra Lady of Time, the Vajra Crest Lady, the Vajra Great Command, Vajra Light, the Victorious Lady, the Vajra Lady of Form, and Vajralocanā. These twenty-four are the great queens of knowledge-mantras of the Vajra family, seated on peacocks, dark blue like the utpala, tumultuous with garlands blazing all around, their faces made slightly frowning in wrath, wearing skirts of silk and cotton and upper garments of fine silk, holding a vajra in the left hand and with the right paying homage to the Blessed One Śākyamuni, bearing forms praised by the gods. They gaze toward the image of the Tathāgata, and should be drawn each according to her own form, attire and shape.

On the right side of the Blessed One is the noble Avalokiteśvara, white like an autumn cloud, wearing a crown of matted locks, with Amitābha seated in its center, with an upper garment of fine silk and a skirt of fine silk and cotton, fully adorned with every ornament, his left hand in the lotus mudrā and his right waving a yak-tail fan for the Blessed One, on a lotus throne, his body adorned with the marks of a great being, gazing a little toward the image of the Tathāgata. On the left of the Blessed One is the noble Vajrapāṇi, the color of the petal of a blue utpala, on a lotus throne, fully adorned with every ornament, his body serene, with a skirt of silk and cotton and wearing a red upper garment, his right hand paying homage to the Blessed One Śākyamuni, his left hand busy with a yak-tail fan, his eyes tumultuous with blazing, gazing a little toward the image of the Tathāgata.

To the right of Avalokiteśvara one should draw the Blessed Mother, the Great Tārā, dark blue like the priyaṅgu, tumultuous with garlands blazing all around, her body serene, seated on a lotus throne, slightly smiling, with a skirt of silk and cotton and wearing a red upper garment, holding an utpala in her left hand and with her right paying homage to the Blessed One Śākyamuni, her body bowing slightly, in the first bloom of youth, neither too stout nor too slender: so one should draw the Blessed Mother Tārā.

To the right of the noble Avalokiteśvara are the eighteen great kings of knowledge-mantras resting on a single row, namely: the Blessed One the Infinite-Armed, the Thousand-Armed, the Hundred-Armed, the Twelve-Armed, the Six-Armed, the Four-Armed, the Thousand-Footed, the Hundred-Footed, the Twelve-Footed, the Six-Footed, the Four-Footed, Hayagrīva, Amoghapāśa, the One Illuminating with a Thousand Rays, the White-Throated Victory over the Three Worlds, the Infinite Victor, the Great Victor, the End of the Gods, the Immeasurable End, the Chariot of the Mind, and the Giver of Fearlessness. These great kings of knowledge-mantras attend on the chief of the Lotus family, who enters into existence. They are tumultuous with garlands blazing all around, their bodies encircled by lotus forms, a lotus in the hand and the right hand granting the supreme gift, gazing a little toward Tārā.

Beside the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā, is Pāṇḍaravāsinī, seated on a lotus throne, her body serene, wearing a crown of matted locks, gazing toward the image of the Tathāgata, a fully opened lotus in her hand and holding a rosary in her right. To her right, again, one should draw the fourteen chief ladies of action of the Lotus family resting on a single row, namely: the Blessed Lady Bhṛkuṭī, the White Lady, the Great White Lady, the Glorious Lady in Front, the Lotus Go Bo Rig, Yaśovatī, the Buddha Hero Moon Lady, the Lady of Enjoyments, the Lady of Bliss, the Lady of Renown, the Lady Robed in Wisdom, the Lady of One Power, the Many Powers, the Lady of Ten Powers, the Mother of the Buddhas, and the Mother of the Limbs of Awakening. These are great queens of knowledge-mantras, tumultuous with garlands blazing all around, seated on lotus thrones, fully adorned with every ornament, wearing the attire of goddesses, their bodies serene, gazing a little toward the image of Tārā. Holding a lotus, and with the right hand granting the supreme gift, they should be drawn each in her own form.

Below Tārā is the one called What Shall I Do, the great wrathful one of the Blessed noble Tārā, four-faced and four-armed, seated on a lotus throne, his body firm, with the form of the black Antaka, frowning in wrath, baring his fangs, one face gaping with fierce laughter, the second gazing at the Tathāgata, the first looking at Tārā. With his first hand he is bringing forth a jewel to be seen, and with his first left he holds a noose, receiving the command of the Blessed Mother Tārā. To his right, again, one should draw the great wrathful one called Subdued by Tārā, seated upon the Great God (Śiva), his body entwined with lotus stalks, dark blue like the utpala, receiving the command of the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā. All the rites of entry and empowerment are just as stated before.

This is the rite of the great maṇḍala of the Later Tantra of Ūrdhvajaṭā.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Avalokiteśvara, said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, I shall give my own heart mantra for the great king of rites of Ūrdhvajaṭā. By merely reciting it, the samādhi of all the tathāgatas becomes manifest, and all fears, harms and epidemics are fully pacified."

Then the Blessed One gave his approval to the bodhisattva, the great being, the noble Avalokiteśvara, saying, "Excellent! Avalokiteśvara, excellent! Speak it."

Then the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara spoke this maṇḍala of his own heart mantra:

Then, greater than this, the maṇḍala
that truly holds the sublime:
in the form of a great maṇḍala,
draw the outer maṇḍala all around.
In its center, with an even thread,
surround it with a square.
At the second, the Destroyer goes,
and one should draw the sublime maṇḍala.
In the manner of eight maṇḍalas,
and the four lines as well,
one should draw an eight-petaled lotus.
On the anthers of the syllable of the lotus,
one should set the Protector of the World.
On the garlands of the lotus petals
one should draw images of the buddhas everywhere.
The master, seated well there,
with the supreme mudrā of the Great Lotus,
settled at the place of the maṇḍala,
in equipoise, sets it evenly.
Just as a lotus in water
is not stained even by
the many faults of its place, so here
one acts rightly through love for beings.
Having spoken this once as an example,
then with the supreme hooks,
having truly summoned, the Great Lotus,
Avalokiteśvara, is released.
For this, here is the great Lotus Hook:

oṃ mahāpadmo hūṃ ja hrī

Then the Blessed One, noble Avalokiteśvara, comes and grants the master a vision of himself, or else he sends forth rays of light. Then, with this very mudrā, the disciple should be led in. He should be clothed in white garments of white silk, and his head should be wrapped with a white turban. Having proclaimed this very thing to the world, one then says, "Speak!" Then, placing a lotus in his left hand and a water vessel in his right, one should say this:

"All the buddhas are the Great Lotus.
The sublime maṇḍala of the lotus
is noble Avalokiteśvara.
Examine that very thing together with him."

Then he should also be trained in binding the great mudrā and in the meditative absorption. This is the great maṇḍala called the Lotus of the Tathāgata.

Then comes the lotus maṇḍala. Having drawn the maṇḍala in the same way, one should sit close to the central pericarp and recite one hundred thousand times. The meditative absorption of all the tathāgatas, gazing upon that fully opened lotus petal, attains the very state of noble Avalokiteśvara. This is the lotus maṇḍala.

Then comes the pledge maṇḍala. Having arranged the maṇḍala in just the same way, one has a thousand lotuses laid out in the center. Then those thousand lotuses should be offered to the Blessed One, reciting once for each one. Then, having led the disciple in, one should declare the pledge:

"Even for the sake of a son or a disciple,
do not let the pledge decline.
Declare the pledge to me.
For through the form of the lotus,
all the attachment of desire is pure.
This is the pledge maṇḍala.
One should draw the action maṇḍala.
With the four kinds of offering,
with the mind one worships all the buddhas,
with the body the protector Avalokiteśvara,
with speech Vajrapāṇi,
and through action one is born into Ākāśagarbha.
Thus it becomes the rite of the means of accomplishment."

The Blessed One, noble Avalokiteśvara, is seated on the summit of Mount Meru, and from his whole body, which abides everywhere through his own meditative absorption, come eight bodies of tathāgatas. Then, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, reciting constantly and without interruption in the meditative absorption of total purity, one should recite until noble Avalokiteśvara becomes manifest. The bodies of the tathāgatas radiate out and settle in the center of the practitioner's lotus, and then again other bodies of the Buddha arise from there, and the practitioner's empowerment becomes established and firm. Then one's whole being becomes equal to Avalokiteśvara; in that instant one is endowed with bliss and flies wherever one wishes. All sentient beings come under one's power, and one's life becomes immeasurable.

Then come the other accomplishments and all the great actions. By reciting one hundred thousand times, all karmic obscurations are purified. By reciting two hundred thousand times, all evil deeds, such as the deeds of immediate retribution, are exhausted without remainder. By reciting three hundred thousand times, all merit becomes manifest. Then all the accomplishments of the yakṣas and all the excellences of the tathāgatas and so forth come about; by reciting three million five hundred thousand times, even the wisdom of omniscience becomes manifest.

Then, for the great mudrā, having made one hundred thousand stūpas, at the end one should recite through the whole night according to the rite. Then at dawn all the tathāgatas come and enter one's heart. Then one finds the bodhisattvas, each one. Then they enter one's mouth. Then one finds Avalokiteśvara himself. Even without the practice of accomplishment, it serves for all actions. By reciting it first, one protects the villages and towns of others, and having beautifully invited the deity, one may perform everything.

For bringing about possession, a graha is made to descend with sandalwood incense. With śirīṣa flowers one brings sentient beings under control. With fragrant flowers one immobilizes all sentient beings. With white clay, women. With sweet-smelling flowers, thieves are immobilized. With a fire offering of white mustard seed, wild animals and birds are immobilized. By scattering white mustard seed one displays magical illusions. With a peacock's breast one causes dreams to be shown. Reciting at the three times of day destroys bad dreams. With a fire offering of sesame one immobilizes all sentient beings. With a fire offering of crow's wings one brings a king under control. With a fire offering of king's-coil flowers one brings all desires under control.

Having made offerings to the Blessed One, noble Avalokiteśvara, one should recite while keeping a fast for eight nights. Then one will obtain everything one desires. To bring the chief queen of a king under control, a fire offering of a woman's pubic hair is used; likewise for bringing a maiden under control. For other aims as well, together with a fire offering, one should recite before Avalokiteśvara at the three times of each day.

In the later tantra of Ūrdhvajaṭā, the magic of all the great actions.

Then that great being, while meditating on that very meditative absorption, taught the secret maṇḍala of equipoise of the wrathful king Subdued by Tārā.

Five cubits in size, with four doors,
with door frames and porticos set firmly in place,
its outside should be made in the form of a lotus.
Then in all the corners as well,
having thought this through well,
one should draw the inner maṇḍala.
With this heart mantra spoken earlier,
reciting it, there is protection;
and with the fine powders
of the five colors, white, red, yellow,
black and green,
praised with the knowledge mantra of Tārā,
one should make the Blessed One who is to be accomplished.
The wrathful king is in front;
on the left one should make Ekajaṭī;
on the right, the lotus-born; in the outer
door frame, the heart mantra, accomplished as is fitting.
As one wishes, one may use kinds of stone;
it is purified with fragrant powder.
Vajramuṣṭi and Mahābala:
where the rite of the three worlds is,
through the wish of the great Vajradhara,
by passing beyond, it dissolves.
The fist, together with Vajramuṣṭi,
is in the right gatehouse;
having placed Mahābala there,
Mahābala with a fish at the throat
is to be made in the west.
In the outer gatehouse on the right
one should likewise make Maheśvara.
On him one should set the mudrā of the spear,
and one should draw Umā as she appears.
In the two southern corners are to be made
mudrās of various kinds.
In the western and northern corners,
the vajra, the mudrā of the vināyakas.
In the two northern corners
the wise should make the mudrā of the family.
In the single eastern corner
one should set the mudrā of the hosts of mātṛkās,
and Bhṛṅgiriṭi together with the vināyakas.
Then, as far as one's means allow,
one should worship the deities according to the rite.
By reciting the mantra of the wrathful one of great power, Subdued by Tārā,
one should protect oneself.
Having taken karavīra and tāla,
keeping the fast in one's own place,
the wise one, in the northern gatehouse,
in whatever place is clean, should lead the disciple in.
The intelligent one should invite the deities.
Through the wrathful king, on every side,
by the rite of the knowledge mantra as is fitting,
is the supreme subduing and caring.
The actions concerning grahas and the body
should be ascertained right there.
Having subdued them, ask about their pledge and their well-being.
Making grahas depart, devouring,
killing some, whoever they may be,
likewise purifying obscurations,
and for all sentient beings,
performing sādhanas and yantras,
activities of whatever kind,
the wise one's thousand actions,
summoning the grahas,
and the mudrās of one's own family and of other families,
should be indicated.
From all the maṇḍalas of this,
all the hosts of bhūtas and the rest
should then be worshipped extensively
with torma, incense and so on.
Through that one sees the graha; one should worship it.
Later, through the empowerment, it is tamed.
Drink given by people, fire offering
and the like should destroy it.
Having taken śiṣalāñcana,
one should make the graha that has seized depart.
Lips that rākṣasas have given,
seeing colors of that kind;
for piśācas, the hare-marked moon;
eyes that do not close and that drip;
if one sees terrors of various kinds,
one gazes all around.
Whatever the changes of the withering graha,
with power and relying on the arms,
against enemies everywhere,
the work of the deities and weapons.
The lotus-maker and the matted locks,
the staff, the rosary, the place of fear,
the water pot and flask, invincibility:
this mudrā is said to be the Brāhmī's.
The trident, the crescent moon,
the matted locks, the eye and so on,
the bull, the sound, the fierce one,
and the Īśānas: these are known as seven.
The śakti spear, the serpent hood, the banner,
the cock, and likewise the peacock's tail:
this mudrā is said to be Kaumārī's.
The wheel, the conch and the club,
the sword, the shield, the garuḍa,
and the head: this mudrā is said to be Vaiṣṇavī's.
The great cloud belongs to the Great God.
The vase and the pestle likewise,
and the first, the mudrā of the left side:
this mudrā is said to be Lahirikā's.
The Revatīs and the torma-eaters:
seeing an old, fierce man
is the seal of the white Revatīs.
Seeing one's own form
is the begging bowl of the stealers of vitality,
and lifting it is release.

Then comes the supremely secret maṇḍala. For all virtuous activities, having found a spot by a solitary tree, or a charnel ground, or a clean empty house without a window, the practitioner, in a wrathful frame of mind, should smear the maṇḍala with cow dung that has not fallen to the ground, and make three lines there. It is four cubits all around. The first line is of ash, the second of red ochre, and the third should be drawn with powder of blazing charcoal. One should have a single door made, in the north or in the west. In the middle of the door one should make the Great God holding a spear in his hand. Within the band one should make the Buddha, whose nature is truly wondrous. To the right side of the Buddha one should set out Subdued by Tārā. On the left one places the great heroine of great strength, Ekajaṭī. Those to be set behind the body of the Sugata are the nāga king Ananta, likewise Takṣaka, and the great hero Karkoṭa should also be set there. Likewise Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkhapāla, and Kulika are named among the mighty ones. Those deities, together with their retinues, should be arranged so as to fill the band. From all of this the host of mātṛkās should be left out; Śrīmatī is the band. At the door, a monkey and a goat, and the maidens too at the door, as watchers of the door.

On the eighth day of the dark fortnight one should properly worship the deities, not passing beyond the great mahoragas, and recite a thousand times. The wise one will accomplish the king of mantras. It drives out all fevers and grahas, and it also crushes disputes. The deities then return to their own abodes. Then, by constantly reciting this secret mantra too, with water of guggulu or with kuśa grass, the practices of Aparājita, of pacifying, of increasing, and of attraction, carried out as one wishes, are accomplished. That which destroys everything, Subdued by Tārā, is the maṇḍala of the secret means of accomplishment.

Then again the bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya, bowed to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha Śākyamuni, and said this:

"I know it directly, for I heard it in person from the Tathāgata Ratnaketu. Then, in the later tantra of Ūrdhvajaṭā, the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara taught the heart mantra called Halāhala. For the benefit of sentient beings, to show the power of Tārā, and out of compassion skilled in means, I shall explain it."

The Blessed One said, "Maitreya, speak!"

namaḥ sarbba tathāgatebhyo mahā buruṣa riṣabhebhyaḥ nma ārya avalokiteśvara mahāsthāma prāpta maitriya mañjuśrī bajra pāṇi prabhiti bhyo mahā satve bhyaḥ

Having paid homage to them: "Blessed One, noble Avalokiteśvara, I shall pronounce your heart mantra, which accomplishes every wish, which no sentient being can withstand, and which destroys the path of existence.

sādya thedaṃ he bodhisatvā mahāsatvā he hale ārya avalokiteśvarāya parama matri citta hita citta kāruṇi kāmāṃ gama biyati mahā biyati dhuru dhuru dhuru calentra bala nama stestu sarbba satvā bhaya prata hari hari hari bāha norbba ba bha bā na kha turu turu ghuru ghuru suru suru su pra śā si pā mala mūrti ārya avalokiteśvarāya kṛṣṇā jina jaṭā mukuṭā bala mutrā la mā la ba la ma la ma la kala kala nala hala hala hulu hulu he bodhisatvā priya bodhisatvā mahā bodhisatvā nama teru kuru kuru hṛdayaṃ manu smara idaṃ ca me kārya kuru svāhā"

This is the heart mantra of the bodhisattva, the great being, called Halāhala, given by the Blessed One, noble Avalokiteśvara. Each day, rising at dawn, one should make the maṇḍala of the Blessed One, lay out scents, flowers and so forth, and then recite it thirteen times. Then it pacifies every illness. By doing this for just six months, one brings the chariot of the mind, one's heart's desire, to complete fulfillment, just as one wishes.

Likewise the Blessed One, the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, said, "If even someone who has committed a deed of immediate retribution does not succeed with it, then may I myself be one who has committed a deed of immediate retribution, and may I have deceived all the tathāgatas!"

Then the Blessed One, the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, bowed to the Blessed One and said this: "Following the Blessed One, in the later tantra of the great ritual manual of the Blessed Mother, are the knowledge mantras against every fear: the four sisters, entering ever higher and higher, beheld by the buddhas, the blessed ones; born into four ritual manuals; of small form; traveling through the sky; going underground, invisibility, vetālas, combat, swift travel on foot, increase, fierce rites, subjugation, and the very bestowal of good fortune. They reverse what was taught by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara and the rest; through the character of their intrinsic nature they show birth into a superior house. For the sake of the power of the knowledge of the buddhas and bodhisattvas, even by a thousand, even by those hundred thousand, it is destroyed merely once; and, as a mere example, with regard to the domain of the bodhisattvas, which abides by its nature as the source of many worlds, these practices following the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā, have been taught in the later tantra of Ūrdhvajaṭā. The Blessed Mother, mastered by the mind, bestows the accomplishments.

tadyathā namo amitābhāya namo ārya avalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya oṃ jaye svāhā

This is the one called Jayā, the Victorious.

tadyathā namo amitābhāya nama ārya avalokiteśvarāya oṃ bijaya svāhā

This is the one called Fully Victorious.

tadyathā namo amitābhāya nama ārya avalokiteśvarāya oṃ ajite svāhā

This is the one called Ajitā, the Invincible.

namo amitābhāya nama ārya avalokiteśvarāya oṃ aparājite svāhā

This is the one called Aparājitā.

Such are the four sisters. The fifth is the brother:

namo amitābhāya tadyathā arhate nama ārya avalokiteśvarāya oṃ kini kini sarba tathāgatā utbhava śānte barade uttama tathāgatā utbhava hūṃ phaṭ svāhā

This is the brother called Tumburu.

The king of mantras has been fully proclaimed.
In brief, for the proud and conceited,
the actions of the later tantra,
in whatever way they are applied,
in just that way they accomplish."

Then the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, wishing to display his own miraculous power, rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One Śākyamuni three times, and entered into the meditative absorption called Fully Impelling One's Own Vajra. Then, arising from that meditative absorption, he said this to the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara:

"Bodhisattva, I too, in this later tantra, the king of ritual manuals, in order to show fully the power of the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā, shall bestow, through the stūpas of all worldly beings, the practice that follows the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā. Great being who rejoices in it, in the time to come, the supreme accomplishment, and even those of corrupt moral discipline who perform the supreme action, will succeed in a special way. These practices following noble Tārā, which have arisen from the one who is called, are the families and that which overpowers adversaries."

Then the bodhisattva, the great being, noble Avalokiteśvara, said this to the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi: "Vajrapāṇi, speak!"

Then Vajrapāṇi again entered into meditative absorption. The very moment Vajrapāṇi entered into absorption, this great trichiliocosm, this world system of a billion worlds, was entirely illuminated.

Then Vajrapāṇi stretched out the fingers of his hand. Those that came forth from his left hand, the one called Vajra Utter Destroyer, Vajramuṣṭi, Red Vajra, Vajra Gone to the End, and Black Vajra, are the brothers, the blessed Vajra Youths. Then they bowed to the Blessed One, and also to the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi and to Avalokiteśvara. Then the Blessed One said to the five youthful brothers, "Excellent! You are the source of merit for sentient beings, the bestowers of accomplishments, the givers of great benefit in the ritual manual of Tārā, arisen from the family of Vajrapāṇi, who have become lords over the lotus hand."

Then Vajrapāṇi taught the maṇḍala:

"One, two, three, four, five,
and so on up to eight cubits.
One who wants wealth uses one cubit;
one who wants a son, two cubits;
for ruining an enemy, three cubits;
for recitation alone, four cubits;
the fifth is for all accomplishments;
the eighth is for traveling through the sky,
for aims beneath the earth, for rivers,
for oceans, and for places of accomplishment.
It may be done in a house as well, or elsewhere
in a clean place that has been covered over;
with whatever is auspicious for the action,
one should lay out the lines of the maṇḍala with a cord.
It is square, with four corners,
with four doors, adorned with porticos and ornaments.
Having divided the maṇḍala into three parts,
in the upper part is the Blessed One,
the Buddha, seated on a lotus seat,
in the act of teaching the Dharma.
On the right is Avalokiteśvara,
holding Brahmā's staff and a flask in his hands;
on the left the noble Vajrapāṇi,
with a vajra in his hand; or at his side
is Viṣṇu, with conch and wheel,
holding a club and a wheel in his hands.
In the middle part, riding in a boat
with the boat's mast raised up,
first are Vajra Utter Destroyer,
Māyā and Tumburu;
second, Vajramuṣṭi
together with Jayā; in the third,
Red Body together with Fully Victorious;
in the fourth, Vajra End
together with Ajitā; in the fifth,
Black Belly together with Aparājitā.
Green, white, red,
yellow and black, in that order:
having set out the deities,
with white garments and white ornaments,
their hands holding weapons,
club, vajra, pestle,
bow and sword,
in the center, on lotus, moon and sun,
one should set out the deities as if present.
Beneath the boat one should place
fire and the treasure of the waters,
adorned with conches, fish and makaras.
In the east, south,
west and north are Indra,
Yama, Varuṇa and Kubera,
with their mounts and their mudrās.
Vases, well wrapped,
filled with scented water,
and beautified with leafy twigs,
should be set in the corners.
Here the fifth vase,
adorned with jewels, its neck
wrapped with soft cloth,
its mouth covered
with twigs of sahakāra,
with a parasol raised and garlands of flowers hanging,
should be set at the eastern door.
Outside the maṇḍala are four oceans,
made with conches, lotuses and so forth,
and with mountain peaks as well.
Banners flutter and a canopy is spread.
With powders of indranīla, of gold,
of silver, of copper and of iron,
one should draw the maṇḍala.
With divine flowers, and perfuming with incense,
one should worship with tormas of various kinds.
Flowers and fruits of the season,
wealth, gold and various jewels,
and food should be spread out in the outer courtyard.
One should lead the disciples onto the mountain.
With the later heart mantra, the invitation and the rest,
all the actions, and the request to depart are done.
Then whoever, through faith in the Three Jewels,
has given rise to the mind of awakening,
women, men and youths
who have kept the fast vow,
with their faces bound
with cloth, should be made to hear the pledge as well.
With flowers of precious metal and of gold
they should cast with their hand.
Wherever it falls,
that becomes their family. Then,
uncovering their faces, one should show them the deities,
and the mantras and mudrās too become theirs.
Or else, by drawing that maṇḍala
by day and by night, the deities become pleased."

Then come the images. Aśvattha, nyagrodha and udumbāra are for pacifying; cūta, campaka and nāgakesara for increasing; bilva, ariṣṭa and koṭha for fierce rites. For subjugation and for those of ill fortune: śleṣmāntaka, śasmali and dīrghabitta. For causing madness: sandalwood, the aśoka tree, honey and intoxicants. For good fortune itself: those made from asthidatta. For all actions: one made of gold. One who wants kingship uses one made of silver. Copper is for the sake of good fortune. One made of iron is for fierce rites. For causing ruin: campaka, nāgakesara, bakula and atimuktaka. One who wants wealth uses jasmine, yūthikā, mallikā, intoxicants, the golden tree and mālikā. One who wants good fortune uses lotus and kumuda. For pacifying: utpala and saugandhika. For increasing and for other aims as well: flowers that are fragrant. For whatever is for increasing: flowers of lesser fragrance. For fierce rites, causing ruin and the like: sandalwood and the like with their fragrance taken away. For pacifying, increasing, subjugation and good fortune itself, with incense of such kinds, joining the palms, one should perform the actions of these heart mantras.

namo ratna trayāya nama ścaṇḍa bajra pāṇaye mahā yakṣa senā pā ba taye namaśca turnāṃ bhaginīnāṃ namo deba tumburu sārtha kā ha ya jambhani jambhi karoti amitraṃ staṃbhani staṃbhi karotya mitraṃ mohani mohī karotya mitraṃ andhani indhi karotya mitraṃ jaye āgaccha bijaya āgaccha jambhani āgaccha stambhani āgaccha bali bali puṣpa dhūpa upahāraṃ prati gṛhṇa thā samāya yupālāyāthā suṭuṭu susla bajra bhañja nīya svāhā

This knowledge mantra extends to eighty-four thousand applications, namely: traveling through the sky, entering into caves, making treasures move, the state of a knowledge holder itself, accomplishing eye ointment with realgar, subjugation, causing ruin, utterly crushing others, protecting each one's own land, poison, messengers, contagious disease, abiding firmly with fangs bared, binding the maṇḍala of all sentient beings, and accomplishing Rājagṛha through wrath. Other actions such as these should likewise be accomplished as one wishes.

The heart mantra of the four sisters is complete.

Then he taught the maṇḍala again. It is four cubits, square, with four doors, adorned on all sides with porticos. One should have three door guardians made, Yama, Varuṇa and Kubera, with their mounts and their weapons. The north is to be taken as the entrance. Having divided it into three parts, in the upper part is the Blessed Mother Tārā. One should also draw noble Vajrapāṇi, holding a vajra in his left hand, his right hand in the gesture of granting the highest gift, blazing on every side. To the left of the vajra holder is Vajrāṅkuśa, holding a hook in his hand; elsewhere is Vajraśṛṅkhalā, holding a chain in his hand. All of them should be placed on mountain peaks. One should properly draw the Great God, who dwells in the direction of Īśāna, together with his consort and with his bull. The other three should be drawn in order, with their weapons and their abodes, as they are: Bhṛṅgiriṭi and the Mahākālas. In the west are Naradatta, Tumburu, Kāśyapa and Viśvāmitra, holding water pots, flasks and water vessels in their hands. One should draw a well, a raised mast, and tatasphu. He wears a green upper garment, holds a club in his hand, is adorned with a diadem, holds a crest-guard in his hand, and his ears are adorned with lac. The Victorious One is white and holds a vajra in her hand, wearing upper and lower garments. Fully Victorious has a red body and holds a pestle in her hand, wears an upper garment of red cloth, and holds a gold-colored bow in her hand. Aparājitā is black, wears an upper garment of variegated cloth and a skirt of black cloth, holds a sword in her hand, and rides in a boat. Then one should draw the moon, the sun and the deities, with lotuses scattered within. At the northern door is the great vināyaka; on the right side is the Vaitaraṇī river, and all around one should draw vajras, conches, lada and śrīvatsas everywhere.

Having drawn everything properly in this way, one should then offer, as far as one's means allow, tormas, five kinds each of soup, five kinds of food, plenty of kṭrañca, barley dough wrapped with food, jambulika, curd, molasses, butter and honey, as is fitting. There are four water vases, their mouths covered with leafy twigs as one wishes, and vases filled entirely with scented water, with all seeds and all medicines and leafy twigs, their necks wrapped with cloth, five each of vases adorned with precious metal, gold and jewels and with leafy twigs; and outside, jewels are laid out. Having done such auspicious things as these, one should afterward recite.

Then, first, one should lead the disciple in. The mantra that is different from this is:

namo ratna trayāya namaścaṇḍa bajra pāṇaye mahā yakṣa senā pataye namaśca turbha ginī nāṃ mama jayāya māheti svāhā

With this mantra one subjugates all sentient beings in eight ways: with flowers, white mustard seed, salt, water and ash, and also with an effigy that defiles even the stainless.

namo ratna trayāya namaśca ṇḍa bajra pāṇaye mahā yakṣa senā pataye namo bijayāya haha dhali kumārani piṣṇu mukhe raṭeśa svāhā

By reciting this knowledge mantra a hundred thousand times, the preliminary approach is accomplished. Then, taking wood struck by Śakra's thunderbolt, and having kept a fast for three nights, one should go to a place where there is a stūpa containing relics, and set out all four vases there, their mouths adorned with flowers and leafy twigs. Then, in the maṇḍala laid out on spread kuśa grass, pressing down the peg bound with three metals with the left foot or with the left hand, one should recite until the hand becomes invisible. One should not let go of the hand. Then that peg should be planted in a wilderness; the peg will appear in the house. Having planted it by this very rite, press the peg down firmly with the left foot and bring them under control! By squeezing the hand that destroys cities, it destroys all mudrās and also poisonings. It may also be planted among people, and it serves for everything. For other purposes too, it performs actions just as one wishes.

namo ratna trayāya namaścaṇḍa bajra pāṇaye mahā yakṣa senā pataye nama śca ta sṛ ṇāṃ bhaginīnāṃ nama stumburu sarbba bahasya mahā karṇasya pici pici amukāya bharga prapatāntu svāhā

On the eighth day of the dark fortnight or the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, keeping a fast for three nights, one should write this mantra in blood on a skull cup. Having consecrated it with eight thousand recitations, one should throw it into water. It becomes speech of every kind.

namo ratna trayāya namaścaṇḍa bajra pāṇaye mahā yakṣa senā pataye namaśca tasṛṇāṃ bhaginīnāṃ namo jambhani cāṭu cāṭu cāṭu cāṭu svāhā

With this knowledge mantra, in the month of Puṣya, beneath an aśoka tree, putting three black peppercorns in one's mouth, one should recite it eight thousand times.

Then, putting a single peppercorn into one's mouth, whoever one gazes at without blinking comes under one's power.

namo ratna trayāya namaścaṇḍa bajra pāṇaye mahā yakṣa senā pataye namaśca tisṛṇāṃ bhaginīnāṃ namastumburu mahā sārtha bāhāya namo jaye bijaye ajite aparājite svāhā

With this knowledge mantra, having first performed the approach recitation as one wishes, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight or the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, keeping a fast day and night and wearing clean clothes, one should offer lamps, banners, garlands and so forth, making an extensive offering. Drawing water oneself, one should place it in a copper vessel and recite over it for one session. Having drunk it and bathed, by that same rite, at dawn, having eaten the alms food designated by the Saṅgha, repeat this eight times. Then the fields of knowledge of the four directions enter one's mouth, and one retains whatever one hears.

namo ratna trayāya namaścaṇḍa bajra pāṇaye mahā yakṣa senā bataye namaśca tasṛṇāṃ bhaginīnāṃ tantri mili mili svāhā

With this knowledge mantra, entering a river that flows to the ocean and making a fist with the right hand, one should recite it for thirteen days. It raises up all who have died of poison or of fangs. With the fist one brings down the grahas.

namo ratna trayāya namaścaṇḍa bajra pāṇaye mahā yakṣa senā pataye namaśca tasṛṇāṃ bhaginīnā namastumburu sarbba mahāya suṭu suṭu bajra prabhañjanīye svāhā

With this mantra, make a maṇḍala of cow dung four cubits across, and there perform eight thousand fire offerings of vāsaka kindling sticks smeared with curd, honey and ghee, beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight and continuing until the fifteenth. It summons whomever one wishes.

With this too one should work upon the palace of an angered king. Having entered it as a wandering ascetic, one should draw him there with charcoal, press the drawing down with the left foot, and recite eight thousand times. Then he becomes free of anger.

Then the mudrās are well explained.
For every action of the virtuous hand,
whatever action is to be done,
for all of them the left hand is joined.
The mudrā held with the thumb
is proclaimed to be for the gods;
that with the index finger is for the yakṣas;
for the gandharvas, the middle finger;
for the bhūtas, the nameless finger;
for the nāgas, the little finger of the hand;
for the rākṣasas, the palm;
the staff mudrā is for the pretas.
The mudrās are explained as eightfold.
The thumb is Vajra Crusher;
the index finger is Vajramuṣṭi;
the crooked finger is Vajra Red Body;
the little finger is the Black-Limbed One;
and the thumb, this one is called Tumburu.
Each with its own form, for each one,
the five mudrās are to be set out.

Then once again the bodhisattva, the great being Mahāsthāmaprāpta, bowed his head to the Blessed One Śākyamuni and said this: "Blessed One, greatly compassionate one, who acts for the benefit of all sentient beings, please teach, by way of the later tantra of the great king of ritual manuals, Ūrdhvajaṭā, how one should act, Blessed One, in order to bring to complete fulfillment the perfection of skillful means in the conduct of knowledge mantras."

The Blessed One said: "Excellent, son of noble family! Those knowledge holders who call the knowledge mantra to mind while they are washing, who bathe without the knowledge mantra, and who perversely do so in a place that is not secluded, become rough of body and weak in strength. Those who recite mentally while walking on the road, or while sullied by sexual intercourse, will always be agitated in mind and suffer many illnesses. Those who again and again switch between knowledge mantras indiscriminately, who apply them to improper objects, and who recite without fire offerings, will always fail in their aims and lose their friends. Again, those knowledge holders who show contempt for their own knowledge mantra and who make use of what belongs to the deity are led astray and terrified by it. The world will never be pleased with them, and they will always be despised.

"The knowledge holder should always worship and honor, with flowers, incense and so forth, the knowledge mantras spoken by the buddhas, the bodhisattvas, the pratyekabuddhas and the noble śrāvakas.

"Those without samaya, those who take life, those who work sorcery with mantras, those who defile nuns, those who commit the acts of immediate retribution, those who improperly make use of the property of the Saṅgha, those who resort to grain liquor and brewed liquor, those who kill monks or nuns, those who tread on food with their feet, those without samaya who trample food in anger, those who scatter it, those without samaya who see a dead body and do not go, those who give mudrās and mantras to those without samaya and to those who have not entered the maṇḍala, and moreover those without samaya who tread on medicine with their feet, those who break samaya, those who step over the offering remnants of the buddhas and bodhisattvas and of other gods as well, those without samaya who step over a conch, a discus, a raised trident, a club, a spear, a vajra, a shield, a bow, a plough, a pestle, an arrow, a javelin, an elephant, a bull, a donkey, a pig, a śarabha, a lion, a goose, a peacock, a buffalo, a camel, a swan, a human being, the mounts of the gods, and the various weapons, and those who, seeing these various things being made, press them down with their feet: these the deity leads astray in other ways, and to them it does not grant accomplishment.

"As for the rules of eating here: sesame, meat, parpaṭa, jambulika, fish, many pūpalika cakes, sesame broth, food offered to the gods, and the offering remnants themselves should not be eaten. Stepping on the offering remnants of a deity, stepping on lotuses or on what lives in water, stepping on blue lotuses, cutting down the lords of the forest, and pulling up roots should also be avoided. By constantly recollecting the knowledge mantra and always wearing clean clothes, this is taught for all activities, and one makes offerings in all the other rites of knowledge mantras."

Then the Blessed One again addressed the assemblies of bodhisattvas: "Friends, listen! In the later tantra of Ūrdhvajaṭā, the words of the mantra accomplished by the mind, which together with their methods easily accomplish the knowledge syllables of the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā, and which benefit all sentient beings, are these:

namo ratna trayāya nama ārya abalokiteśvaraya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya ghuni ghuni la la la siddhe siddhe pārakrama svāhā amitābhāsuta svāhā sarbbaiśca ārya abalokite svāhā

"This is the one called noble Candrā, the sister of the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā, who performs all activities. The practitioner should always bind the topknot and also bind the mudrā. It utterly destroys all obstructors. With it, rising at dawn and having become pure, one should make a maṇḍala, scatter flowers and so forth, and, with fivefold diligence, recite it eight hundred times. It fulfills the aim one desires. Or else it brings whomever one wishes under one's power. Then, by scattering cetrājika in the maṇḍala, one drives away whomever one wishes. Whatever accomplishment comes through reading it should be understood just as it is. And here, in this treasury of enumerations, one recollects that which touches them as one.

"Then, if one wishes to rouse an executioner, one should go to a charnel ground, kindle a fire with charnel-ground wood, surround it with a great silk cloth, and perform a fire offering with blood, such as has been obtained. On the seventh day, at midnight, an executioner with a terrifying roar rises up. Praising it properly, one should also grant it consecration for the place one has named. Through the blessing of the Blessed Mother, it brings about whatever well-being one pleases. Then in some places people are seen dying, in some places fire is seen blazing, and in some places people are seen bound in iron chains. In this way that executioner roams about. To pacify it, one should offer eight thousand lotuses before the Blessed One. It becomes supremely pacified.

"If one wishes to rouse enemies, one should go to a charnel ground, kindle a fire of charnel-ground wood, and perform eight thousand fire offerings of white mustard seed smeared with the oil of black sesame. It makes them depart.

"Then, if one wishes someone to be seized by fever, one should perform eight thousand fire offerings of charnel-ground ash in a charnel-ground fire. He is seized by a great fever. To pacify it, one should recite one hundred and eight times over water and pour it on his head. He is freed from the fever.

"If one wishes his head to be seized by pain, one should recite eight thousand times over a peg of human bone and strike the peg into the head of an effigy made of cow dung. His head is seized by great pain. When the peg is pulled out, it is pacified. If it is struck into the sexual organ, he becomes impotent; when it is pulled out, he is freed. If it is struck into the heart, he suffers great stabbing pain; when it is pulled out, he is freed.

"A khadira peg smeared with flesh and blood and wound with thread, over which one has recited eight hundred times, should be struck onto the head of the human-bone peg. If it is planted at the enemy's door, he flees at dawn. As long as the peg has not been pulled out, he will not stay anywhere at all.

"If one wishes to rouse a king, one should go to a temple of the Great God (Śiva), smear the god with poison and blood, and offer incense of the great flesh. One should also worship with neem leaves. Then, combining poison, blood and salt, one should perform a fire offering eight hundred times. With the first eight hundred, his own flesh; with the second, flowers; with the third, the queen's retinue; with the fourth, great weapons; with the fifth, elephants; with the sixth, buffaloes. This is the action led by the great wrathful one.

"If one wishes to ruin someone's fine intellect, one should kindle a fire with neem wood and perform eight thousand fire offerings of oblations of neem leaves and charnel-ground ash mixed together. In an instant it is ruined.

"Then, if one wishes to make someone mute, one should make an effigy of kasamaya, recite eight hundred times over a copper peg, and, with the enemy in mind, strike the peg into its mouth. He becomes mute. If the peg is pulled out, he is freed. The section on fierce rites is complete.

"Activities come about even without having accomplished the mantra. Having recited it seven times over a tooth-stick, one should chew it: one obtains food without asking for it. Having recited it eight hundred times, by smearing it on one's head, all people are pleased. If one consecrates clothing seven times and puts it on, one becomes fortunate. If one consecrates eye ointment and applies it to the eyes, those who are gripped by anger are pleased when they see one. If one goes along the road while reciting it, bandits and thieves cannot overcome one. By reciting it seven times over one's finger, all fanged creatures are paralyzed. If one recites it eight hundred times over gravel and scatters it in water, it paralyzes all creatures that move in water. If one recites it for someone bound, or whose road is blocked, he is freed. Having recited it seven times over a karavīra twig, one should smear the maṇḍala with it and strike the ground with a weapon. It moves to wherever one wishes. One should consecrate a handful of water and scatter it upward: it stops untimely rain. If one recites it eight hundred times over ash, the ash becomes a fence. Iron filings become a fence of stone. Three lamps become a fence of lamps. Bilva leaves become a fence of bilva. Water over which it has been recited eight hundred times becomes a fence of water. In brief, in whatever way it is applied through the rites of the other ritual manuals of the Blessed One, the King of the Uṣṇīṣa, in just that way it performs those activities. By accomplishing the knowledge mantra, one is freed from the acts of immediate retribution and finds the awakening mind."

oṃ sarba tathāgata uṣṇiṣa anābalokite murdhani tejorāśi hūṃ jvāla jvāla dhaka dhaka dara bidar chinda chinda hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā

It is explained as splendor and as a mass: "It should be placed on the back of a small petal." So it is written in the smaller Tathāgatoṣṇīṣa Tantra, in order that it be completed on each of the petals.

Thread spun by a maiden should be made into cloth; or else cloth bought at the hero's price, obtained however it may be, with its edges uncut and free of hair, should be set on a frame by a painter who keeps the poṣadha, who is not lacking in faculties, and who faces east. Before it, one should invite all the buddhas, bodhisattvas and so forth, and especially the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā. Then one should kindle a fire with arka wood and, with the heart mantra of Ekajaṭī, perform eight thousand fire offerings of white mustard seed smeared with ghee, in a maṇḍala four cubits in size in front of the painting. While the painting is being drawn, there will be no obstructors.

Then, on an auspicious lunar day, karaṇa, constellation and moment, one should mix, with colored water, pigments placed in new vessels, unmixed in color and each ground very finely and separately, and with a brush of cow hair one should paint the Blessed One's tree of awakening: a place praised as manifold, where flocks of birds sing, like a wish-fulfilling tree. Here one should paint the Tathāgata Amitābha: teaching the Dharma, seated in the cross-legged posture, his form adorned with the marks of a great being, his body appearing beautiful, great golden rays of light radiating from his uṣṇīṣa, seated on a white lotus. At the Blessed One's left side is a white figure adorned with ornaments, wearing an upper garment of five colors and holding a yak-tail whisk in the hand.

Alternatively, under the lunar mansion of the Four Fires, one should paint here the bodhisattva called noble Vimalagati, at the Blessed One's right side: entirely white, adorned with golden ornaments, with a mass of matted locks, holding in the hand a water pot and a wooden staff, wearing the sacred cord hanging from the shoulder, dressed in white clothes, the supreme hand stretched out over the practitioner, four-armed, the measure of a sugata's span; noble Vimalagati is slightly raised up.

One should paint here noble Avalokiteśvara, slightly smaller than the Blessed One. At his right side one should paint Tārā: dark blue like the priyaṅgu, her body made brilliant with gold and jewels, adorned with a diadem, wearing a variegated garment, with an upper garment of jewels, her body slightly bowed, her palms joined toward the Blessed One, holding a blue utpala, her hand in the supreme gesture, gazing first upon the Blessed One. Below that, one should make a lotus pond.

Then, on the root lotus, at the Blessed One's right, one should make noble Avalokiteśvara, and at the left, noble Vimalagati. Further, at the right of the Blessed Mother Tārā, one should paint the nāga king Ananta, seven-headed, holding a lotus stalk, entirely white, adorned with variegated garments and all ornaments. At the left, one should paint the nāga king Sāgara, dark blue, holding a lotus stalk, in the same manner.

At the Blessed One's right side, near the root, one should paint a goddess, white, adorned with all ornaments, with an upper garment of jewels, holding a jewel and a caṅgaṭaka, kneeling with her knee on the ground. At the right side of the Blessed Mother Tārā, one should paint the Blissful One, seated near the root, entirely white, of youthful form, adorned with all ornaments, her palms joined, gazing intently upon the Blessed Mother and the Blessed One.

At the feet of noble Avalokiteśvara, one should make the practitioner, looking toward Avalokiteśvara, wearing white upper and lower garments, with whatever shape and features he has, kneeling on both knees, holding an incense burner in his hands. One should make a son of the gods beating a great drum. One should make clouds with lightning, in the four directions and the intermediate directions too. On the right, at the top of the painting, one should paint the sons of the gods of the Pure Abodes scattering flowers. Above, one should paint the moon and the sun, adorned with all ornaments. Above them, conches and great drums.

At the right of noble Avalokiteśvara, one should paint the great sister of noble Tārā: black, pot-bellied, wearing every ornament, baring her fangs, with a skirt of tiger skin, wrapped in a hide called go, a garland of skulls hanging from her topknot, seated on a rock, wearing a serpent as her sacred cord, four-armed, holding an axe in her right hand, and in her first left hand a vessel filled with blood, her body clad only in the directions, with eyebrows and hair, her palms joined toward the Blessed One, with long nails, her upper body covered with an elephant hide, receiving the command of the great bodhisattva.

Having thus painted the painting, it should be set in a clean spot that is free of faults in the factors of purity, protection and proper measure: on the bank of a river bearing jewels, or anywhere else, near a pure place. Then, by wafting smoke, one brings under one's power. That is whoever practices the secret mantra together.

One who wishes to make all the deities appear should begin the work, and the eighth day of the bright fortnight is suitable. In a clean piece of ground, one should smear an area the measure of a bow, and in its center place a brick. In the four directions one should set four vases of water, from the earth and without black roots, consecrated eight hundred times.

They are well wound with thread of five colors spun by a maiden. Having made a maṇḍala with fragrant powders, one should offer tormas without liquor or meat in the four directions. One should make an offering of fragrant flowers. One offers guggulu incense. One should set a copper vessel filled with ghee close beside the powders, at the edge. Facing east, outside, in a maṇḍala, one should make offerings and offer a torma to Ekajaṭī.

Then, taking green kuśa grass and wearing a single white garment, one should make it as long as the space between the two feet. Then one should cast it with that kuśa onto the vessel of ghee. Then, if one sees dirt, a nail or a hair in that small amount of ghee, one should gather each of them together into one, until one's own wishes and speech have arisen in abundance. Then one should take up each vase in turn and set it down while reciting. Having made the purified vessel stand firm, one has the person prostrate to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas. One should also give him a massage with it. Having combined priyaṅgu, nāgakesara, madhuka and turuṣka, and consecrated them seven times, one should anoint him. He should eat excellent food mixed with cow's ghee. He becomes free of illness.

Thread spun by a maiden and dyed blue should be consecrated seven times and tied on: eye disease is pacified. If it is tied at the throat, it cures vomiting. One should have cloth woven from this same thread. Consecrated eight thousand times, it should be tied on the body of a wrestler: he becomes invincible in battle.

Having smeared a maṇḍala four cubits in size and worshiped the Blessed Mother with fragrant flowers, one should offer lamps of cow's ghee. Then, kindling a fire of wood from the tree of awakening and sitting on a mat of kuśa grass, one should perform eight thousand fire offerings, in three sessions, of oblations of lac and resin consecrated seven times. In seven days it pacifies even long-standing illness in whomever one wishes.

One who wishes to pacify all obstructors should take earth from one bank of a river that flows to the ocean and make one hundred and twenty-one obstructors of various forms, colored like lions and tigers. Then, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, keeping a fast for three nights, one should begin the work in a clean place, having brought what is needed for the blood rite. Below that, one should set the obstructors, according to their directions, sitting on leaves of the lac tree. In the midst of the obstructors one should set the great obstructor, the vināyaka. First one should make seven maṇḍalas with the powders of five colors, consecrated once. One should worship them with red flowers and red scents. One should offer butter lamps in the four directions. One should scatter lac juice in the four directions. Then, with a red thread consecrated eight thousand times, or eight hundred times, with the mantra of the Blessed Mother, one should wind it clockwise around all the obstructors.

Then one should bind the great king of obstructors. In their midst, kindling a fire with udumbara kindling sticks, one says, "Bind the obstructors!", and with the syllables svāhā one should perform at night eight thousand fire offerings of calf dung smeared with curd, honey and ghee. Then all the obstructors and vināyakas of that practitioner become bound. When he is accomplishing any knowledge mantra, there will be no obstructors.

As for those, according to what they are to do, having set the great vināyaka apart, one offers every kind of flower to all the obstructors, and every protection as well. As incense, one offers red karavīra and red sandalwood to the great vināyakas. One offers water for welcome to all the obstructors and all harmers. To those together with the vināyaka, one offers water for welcome mixed with guggulu and ghee. Then one should dig a pit to the depth of the navel. Having placed each of them in it separately, one should make the ground level once again. In this way all the obstructors of the knowledge holder will cease to be.

At a stūpa containing relics, having smeared a maṇḍala with cow dung that has not fallen to the ground, and having worshiped with scents, flowers and so forth, one should kindle a fire with udumbara kindling sticks and perform eight thousand fire offerings of palāśa kindling sticks in three sessions. By eating caru for one hundred days or for two hundred days, one's mind becomes keen.

Having smeared a maṇḍala four cubits in size and kindled a fire with kindling sticks from a milky tree, one should perform a fire offering of milk: brahmins come under one's power. One should make oblations of caru: kṣatriyas come under one's power. One should make oblations of curd: vaiśyas come under one's power. One should make oblations of barley: śūdras come under one's power. In every case, to accomplish what is to be accomplished, it is one hundred days.

One should recite while looking at an enemy: he becomes paralyzed. One should perform eight thousand fire offerings, in three sessions, of māṣaka kindling sticks smeared with curd, honey and ghee: whoever one looks at while reciting becomes incapable of acting. Water consecrated seven times removes all poisons. For every poison one should do as one wishes. Having consecrated a smelter's pellet seven times, one should cleanse the eyes with it: it pacifies eye disease. For a child seized by a graha, one should consecrate a thread seven times and tie it on: it frees him. One should tie it on a sick person: all grahas become powerless. Reciting seven times over ash binds the maṇḍala. For a child who will not come out, one should recite over sesame oil and give it: the birth will be easy. For a woman who is barren, at the time of her fertile season, having had her bathe with water over which the mantra has been recited, one should consecrate seven times ghee from a cow of matching lineage and give it to her to drink. She should eat excellent food. It causes a son to be born.

Then a woman who has many daughters should perform eight thousand fire offerings of kindling sticks. Having filled four vases with water and that ash and consecrated them eight hundred times, one should set three of them in the maṇḍala. She becomes fortunate. Her sons will not die.

If one recites eight hundred times over birch bark and ties it on the left arm, one becomes the foremost of all speakers. One should perform a thousand fire offerings of aparājitā flowers in three sessions: in one direction one becomes invincible in battle. One should consecrate thread spun by a maiden eight hundred times and tie seven knots in it. When it is tied on the hand, poisons both stationary and moving become powerless.

Then, for the fang venom of a fearsome snake, one should take a handful of water, consecrate it eight hundred times with the mantra up to the syllables svāhā, and give it to drink. It raises up even one whom the poison has laid low. Then, if he does not rise, one should consecrate it in the four directions and give it to drink. It raises up even one struck by the fang venom of Takṣaka.

For a swelling of the breast, one should give an ointment consecrated seven times. Even without binding, it dries it up right there. It makes it painless.

For those afflicted by an epidemic, at midnight in the center of the village or town one should smear an area the size of a cowhide, give a torma of the three white substances, give scents, flowers and a torma from the hand, kindle a fire with leafy wood, and perform eight thousand fire offerings of oblations of milk. In three days it pacifies the epidemic of three villages, and in seven days an epidemic within. Then, if it is not pacified, one should here, for seven days, kindle a fire with kindling sticks of phlegm-ender wood and perform eight thousand fire offerings of parched rice smeared with akṣa oil. In three days it pacifies a sudden epidemic.

Having bound the boundary with ash, whoever one sees while reciting is pleased. Even what one has not accomplished comes about in front of the painting of the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā.

Another rite: at a stūpa containing relics, before an image, at the full moon, first, in the dark fortnight, one should make a great offering to the image, kindle a fire with arka kindling sticks, and perform eight thousand fire offerings, in three sessions, of finger-length sticks smeared with curd, honey and ghee, up to the fifteenth day. Then it becomes accomplished. By such an application one should recite it three thousand times. Having recited it three thousand times, it serves for other activities. When the approach has first been done with this, it becomes accomplished.

Then, if one wishes to bring a king or a king's minister under one's power, one should make offerings to the Blessed Mother and perform eight thousand fire offerings, in three sessions, of kindling sticks from the tree of awakening smeared with iṅguda oil. In seven days he comes under one's power. By this same rite kumbhāṇḍas come under one's power. One should perform eight thousand fire offerings of sesame-smeared sticks: bhūtas come under one's power. One should perform eight thousand fire offerings of pieces of a corpse burned in a charnel ground: piśācas come under one's power. One should perform eight thousand fire offerings of kindling sticks of vaṭa wood: yakṣas come under one's power. One should perform eight thousand fire offerings of oblations of wool. One should perform fire offerings of milk porridge, caru and sesame porridge: it brings the four castes under control, and they come under one's power. One should perform eight thousand fire offerings of pellets of guggulu: the grahas who follow the Great God (Śiva) come under one's power.

Rising at night in purity, one should perform eight thousand fire offerings and recitations: in one fortnight one is freed from bondage. In a month it frees one from great bondage. A fire offering of sesame and piṇḍyaka pacifies anger, or else a fire offering of sesame alone. One who wants clothing should perform a fire offering of dūrvā sprouts: one obtains a hundred pairs of garments. To bring an ordinary person under one's power, one should perform a fire offering of gobetraṃ. To bind the mouths of bees and wasps, one should perform a fire offering of sāla leaves. To bind the power of a tiger, one should perform a fire offering of girikarṇikā. To bind the mouth of a lion, one should perform a fire offering of siṃhakarṇikā. For snakes, one should perform a fire offering of nāgakesara. For pacification, and for every aim one desires, one should perform fire offerings, in three sessions, for seven days or half a month, with sāla leaves and kindling sticks from a milky tree smeared with curd, honey and ghee.

Having made offerings to the bodies of the buddhas, the blessed ones, and to the bodhisattvas, one should recite it a hundred thousand times. It accomplishes what has not been accomplished. It also destroys what others have accomplished. For the grahas of the nāgas and so forth, binding the directions, binding the maṇḍala and so forth are done by recitation alone.

For seven nights, in three sessions, one should perform fire offerings of thorns: it destroys enemies. One should perform eight thousand fire offerings of neem kindling sticks smeared with pungent sesame oil: in seven nights it arises. Especially to bring ruin, one should perform eight thousand fire offerings of ariṣṭa kindling sticks, from the hair onward. For flesh that has grown and for madness one should constantly recite: none of it will turn back.

Having recited twenty-one times over bezoar, one should make a mark on the forehead with it and go to the king's gate; and having consecrated birch bark eight thousand times and tied it on the hand, one obtains whatever one asks for. To make grahas flee, one should take a human bone, make it eight fingers long, consecrate it eight hundred times and plant it in the place of the graha: it makes the graha flee. Having consecrated flowers, scents, fruits and so forth eight hundred times, whoever one gives them to comes under one's power. To destroy obstructors by means of the knowledge mantra, one should perform eight thousand fire offerings of khadira kindling sticks. From the third day there will be no obstructors. In this way it performs all methods of this kind.

In every case, one who keeps the poṣadha fast should practice before the painted scroll, reciting just as prescribed. Having taken a thousand of them, one should set them on one's right side, consecrate each one seven times, and offer them into the fire as a fire offering. In the course of this, the painted scroll will shake violently, the tip of the lamp flame will grow taller, the sound of great divine drums will resound in the sky, a fragrant wind will rise, and the earth will quake. Then noble Avalokiteśvara, possessed of great compassion, surrounded by many hosts of bodhisattvas and of knowledge mantras, holding a water pot, a wooden staff and a black antelope skin, his crown of matted locks hanging down, will come. Rays of light issue from the body of noble Avalokiteśvara, and by those radiating rays all the sentient beings in the hells, the animals and the hungry ghosts are freed from their painful feelings in an instant. One then sees noble Avalokiteśvara himself, possessed of great compassion, who loves all sentient beings. The practitioner, kneeling on both knees, offers him water for welcome from the Fully Victorious vase that was placed in the east.

Then noble Avalokiteśvara says, "I grant whatever boon you wish." Whatever one asks for, that one obtains: being a universal monarch of the knowledge holders (vidyādharas), great kingship, long life, the retention of all one has heard, or a body lacking none of its faculties, the destruction of diseases hard to cure, or the moving of treasures, entering into caverns, or the accomplishment of all knowledge mantras, invisibility, or lordship over the great earth; whatever one asks for, that one obtains. The blessed noble Avalokiteśvara also goes to wherever one wishes. Through this one's life lasts for an eon. At that time, one who practices the Blessed Mother gains universal sovereignty over all knowledge mantras, is much sought after, is unobstructed, and is longed for by all the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas and kiṃnaras. On the seventh day of practice, even one who has committed the deeds of immediate retribution will succeed. It should be understood in every respect by just such means as these.

This completes the rite of the first great accomplishment, extracted from the first root text of the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā.

Having set up the painted scroll facing east, one should then begin the rite on the eighth day of the bright half of the fortnight of the Miracles, or on the tenth of the fortnight of the Miracles. Living on leaves, barley gruel, flowers, fruits, caru porridge, marsh plants, curd, milk, flour, the food of gandharvas, or else food obtained by begging, one who keeps the poṣadha fast, endowed with loving-kindness and great compassion, should generate the supreme mind set on awakening and, keeping in mind the welfare of sentient beings, should make offerings that increase day by day.
