Using a bed strewn with kuśa grass, bathing three times and changing one's clothes three times, sitting on a mat of kuśa grass, and increasing the offerings each day as far as one's means allow, one should eat food obtained by begging. Setting out with the left foot when walking and so forth, one should recite the mantra one million six hundred thousand times. Having thus first completed the approach, one should begin the accomplishment on the eighth or the fourteenth day of the bright half. A saṅgha of like-minded monks should be sought out.

Then, in the four directions of the painted scroll, one should place earthen vases free of cracks and blackening, forty in all, covered with sprigs of mango and filled with all kinds of seeds. Before the painted scroll one should place a great vase four cubits in size, made of copper, gold or silver, or else of earth, adorned with leaves and creepers of every kind and filled with pure water, holding all the things already spoken of, all medicines, flavors, scents and precious essences, its mouth covered with a cluster of flowers and its neck tied with a matched pair of dukūla cloths: this vase is called Fully Victorious. On the left side of the painted scroll one should place the Blessed Mother Prajñāpāramitā. Then one should offer sixteen garlands of fragrant flowers to the painted scroll. In front there should be those eight vessels, filled with water of fragrant sandalwood and filled with milk. One should offer eight lamps of cow's butter. Having filled bowls with caru porridge, milk porridge, sesame porridge, warm gruel, paṇḍaka cakes and other foods to be chewed, one should offer them in the four directions of the painted scroll. In every case one should offer to the deities painted on the scroll tormas of the three white substances and food for the deities, and outside one should offer torma. Then one should offer as torma, in the four directions of the painted scroll, all the grains and all the fruits one can obtain. One should offer incense of black aloeswood. Then, sitting on a mat of kuśa grass, with one-pointed mind, one should begin the rite toward that direction. Having kindled a fire with kindling sticks of a milky tree, perform eight thousand fire offerings of kindling sticks of black aloeswood smeared with curd, honey and butter.

He entered into equipoise in the meditative absorption called Surveying All Sentient Beings. Then, rising from that meditative absorption and surveying with his divine eye the world-system with all it contains, he said to the bodhisattva, the great being Mahāsthāmaprāpta: "Listen, son of noble family! Even without having accomplished the great queen of knowledge mantras, all rites take effect merely by recollecting her. To protect oneself, reciting her once binds the crown knot; reciting twice gives the great protection; reciting three times binds the maṇḍala; reciting four times binds water; reciting five times protects bipeds and quadrupeds and brings them under one's power; reciting six times one may enter a charnel ground; reciting seven times one brings all sentient beings under one's power.

"One who wishes to perform pacification should, before the painted scroll, in the presence of Avalokiteśvara, kindle a fire with kindling sticks of ariṣṭa and of a milky tree, and perform eight thousand fire offerings of parched rice as oblations in three sessions. In three days one person is pacified; in seven days a great multitude of people, the villages of the region and those of the city; and in a month a great kingdom is pacified."

If one wishes for increase, one should, before the painted scroll, kindle a fire with kindling sticks of a milky tree and perform eight thousand fire offerings of grain and thick rice porridge in three sessions. In three weeks there will be increase. In seven days there will be increase. In seven days there will be great increase.

Having kindled a fire with kindling sticks of mango, perform eight thousand fire offerings of shoots of dūrvā grass: one becomes the foremost of speakers among speakers. From sunrise until sunset, into a fire of arka wood, uttering the person's name, perform a fire offering of husks with the left hand seven times: that person comes under one's power.

Having kindled a fire with kindling sticks of the bodhi tree, perform fire offerings of śatapuṣpa, śatāvarī, white sweet flag, white mustard seed and barley in three sessions, eight thousand, twenty-one times over: in seven days one brings a great man under one's power. By a fire offering of butter one brings bipeds and quadrupeds under one's power.

Having kindled a fire with kindling sticks of royal arka, perform eight thousand fire offerings of leaves of the lac tree smeared with hot sesame oil: in seven days it destroys an army. Having kindled a fire with kindling sticks of khadira, perform eight thousand fire offerings of green kuśa grass: it cuts off the movements of enemies in every direction.

Having kindled a fire with kindling sticks of a milky tree, perform eight thousand fire offerings of kindling sticks of devadāru at the three times of day: in one month one brings the goddesses of the regions below under one's power. Living on caru porridge, kindle a fire with wood of the nāga tree and perform eight thousand fire offerings of nāgakesara smeared with butter in three sessions, making offerings that increase day by day: in seven days or in one month one brings the goddesses who move above under one's power.

Living on caru porridge, kindle a fire with kindling sticks of the bodhi tree and perform eight thousand fire offerings of white mustard seed and royal mustard as oblations, smeared with curd, honey and butter: in three days one brings the king's queen under one's power. She fulfills everything one says, except what is proposed out of lust.

Having kindled a fire with kindling sticks of the bodhi tree, perform eight thousand fire offerings of mango leaves in three sessions: it pacifies harms that come near the house.

Before the painted scroll, smear a ground the size of an arrow's flight. Having made an effigy out of eight thousand barley pellets, cutting and cutting it with a sharp blade consecrated seven times, one should perform eight thousand fire offerings of oblations. Uttering the person's name all the way down to the feet, one should sit with the fist clenched and offer with the hand from above. Then one should visualize him appearing as one without a home. Before him one should open the fist, and he becomes calm and comes under one's power. Thus in seven days he will attend upon one as a subject.

Having kindled a fire with kindling sticks of ariṣṭa, perform eight thousand fire offerings in three sessions of splinters of tārabarta wood, reciting over each seven times: food arises without interruption in that region.

Having kindled a fire of palāśa kindling sticks, uttering the person's name, perform eight thousand fire offerings of anointed apāmārga kindling sticks in three sessions: in seven days whoever one wishes comes under one's power.

Having made an effigy of cow dung, cut it from the head down to the feet with a sharp blade consecrated seven times and perform eight thousand fire offerings: in seven days one who is greatly proud comes under one's power.

On the fifteenth day of the bright half of the month, with cow dung that has not fallen to the ground, smear a ground the size of a cowhide. Having set up the painted scroll at a stūpa containing relics, take, in a vessel of gold, silver or copper, butter churned by a young girl from the milk of a tawny cow whose calf is of the same color. Sitting on a mat of kuśa grass, make a vessel within leaves of the aśvattha tree, set four of them out in a clockwise circle, press down on it with the left hand, and recite eight thousand times in three sessions. On the eighth day one should stir it with the ring finger of the right hand and recite until it becomes warm. Then one should drink it, and the binding of the armor should be done with the Blessed Mother herself. One's mind becomes keen.

This is the application of the lunar rite in the later tantra of Ūrdhvajaṭā.

For all the knowledge mantras of the sādhanas of Tārā, one should make a square maṇḍala in a clean place with dung from a tawny cow that has not fallen to the ground. One should complete it entirely with that cow dung, and in that maṇḍala one should place an image of the Buddha. Then, having made leaves from the tips of the bilva tree, with foods of sesame, sesame porridge, sesame oil, the intoxicant, milk porridge, molasses, filled cakes and barley gruel, or, if these are not to be had, one burns incense of aloeswood. Likewise to the south and to the west, and so in all four directions, one should recite, uttering the names of the yakṣiṇīs mentioned before. One recites a knowledge mantra with words such as these: "Come, and accept, each of you, scent, flowers, incense and torma." There one should also place molasses, filled cakes and milk porridge in the eastern direction. For the gandharvas one should place in the southern direction torma, sesame, sesame porridge and a vessel filled with beer. For the yakṣas and kumbhāṇḍas one should place in the western direction torma filled with milk, and milk porridge. For the nāgas and garuḍas one should also place in the northern direction torma filled with parched flour, a vessel filled with curd, and gruel. For the yakṣiṇīs there should be torma filled with buttermilk and mixed with water. Having offered to the Blessed Mother a torma of the three white substances, one should also worship her with every kind of flower. In her four directions one offers incense of guggulu. One should place in the four directions torma of aloeswood, turuṣka, camphor or fragrant sarja resin, or warm gruel and flour. If one does not have these, one should offer torma according to one's means and whatever one has. To the Blessed Mother one also offers a lamp of butter. Then one should quickly place the water pot on one's right side. Taking a cloth, or seven blades, or kuśa grass, one should consecrate it a hundred times and, facing east, cast it twenty-one times with the four knowledge mantras.

With eight hundred, one becomes victorious over weapons. One should recite at the three times of day, uttering that person's very name. Then, having done the casting away in the same manner, one should remove whatever flowers, incense and lamps were offered to the Blessed One, take up all the tormas of the other kinds, and throw them away. They should be put into a dry pond or a well. Or else another clean place that has a covering will also do; there one should dispose of them, where crows, jackals and dogs will not eat them. Nor should they be trodden on by feet. Or else they should be thoroughly burned in fire. This is also the rite for sending off the torma in all maṇḍala practices.

Afterwards, on what is called the maṇḍala arising from the moon, made fivefold in the directions, which has not been smeared, one should make an image of the Buddha and set it in its own place. These are the means of clearing away. In accordance with the rite, in every case, with the complete knowledge mantra and with the heart mantra, for all the great rites, for as long as they last, one should in just this way make the maṇḍala with the dung of a tawny cow that has not fallen to the ground, by the rite described before, and in just this way set out the torma. Having offered incense and flowers as prescribed, one should clear them away. One should tie the cord. One should protect oneself. Whoever wishes to extend this into great rites should accomplish them by that same rite, with only the preceding procedure, for that long.

On whatever cloth one can obtain, free of hair, one should have an image of the Buddha painted with unmixed colors. With the image facing west, on its left side one should have the Blessed One, noble Avalokiteśvara, painted. He should be made four-armed, with the śrīvatsa mark in gorocanā. The knowledge mantra one is to accomplish should be written with saffron in its center, appearing the color of lac. Or it may be on the forehead; one should make a golden silk band. To the right of the bodhisattva is the Blessed Mother Tārā, golden and blue-green, wearing white garments, holding offerings, holding a blue utpala in her hand, and with her right hand granting the supreme boon. To her right is the queen of knowledge mantras, Mahāmāyūrī, four-armed. Within the space of Mahāmāyūrī one should paint the king of peacocks called Suvarṇāvabhāsa, with golden wings, adorned with every jeweled ornament. The knowledge queen Mahāmāyūrī should be painted white and pure.

To the right of this is Jambudvīpa, three-pointed, in the shape of the front of a chariot. In the west one should paint the western continent Godānīya, round. In the northern direction one should make the northern continent Uttarakuru, square and even. In the east, at Pūrvavideha, one should paint the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of the gandharvas, with his retinue. Beside Jambudvīpa one should make the great king Virūḍhaka, lord of the kumbhāṇḍas. Beside western Godānīya, above the image of the Buddha, one should make the great king Virūpākṣa, lord of the nāgas, on a golden seat, wearing white garments, with eyes like an ox. The noble Ānanda, beside the Blessed One, should be made with palms joined and both knees set on the ground. Behind him, on the right side, Vajrapāṇi should be made holding a yak-tail fan in his hand. All around the image of the Buddha are flowers and small fruits. East of the Buddha is the eastern continent Pūrvavideha. Beside northern Uttarakuru one should paint the great king Vaiśravaṇa, great lord of the yakṣas, with his retinue.

Then, beginning from the first day of the bright half of the month, keeping celibacy and the eightfold upavāsa vow, living on milk and gruel, burning incense of kunduru at the three times of day, one should recite the knowledge mantra twenty-one times before that painted scroll. One should say this: "May the accomplishment of the knowledge mantra come to me!" By abiding in the poṣadha fast for the last three days, on the fifteenth there will be delight.

One should take a cord prepared by a householder from seed sown in the bright half of the month, spun by a young brahmin and made by a maiden, and place it at the feet of the image of the Buddha. The five metals, in pieces the size of a juniper berry, gold, silver, copper, tin and black iron, should be placed at the feet of the image of the Buddha. When the knowledge mantra is accomplished, one should offer those metals. Or else they serve for acts of worship to the Buddha.

Then, with dung from a tawny cow that has not fallen to the ground, one should smear a ground in the shape of a cow, with its head pointing east, and at the root of its mouth one should make the round eastern continent Pūrvavideha. At its two southern feet is triangular Jambudvīpa; in the southwest, before the painted scroll, one should make the round western continent Godānīya. Before the western feet is the northern continent Uttarakuru, square and even. In the direction of Vāgdāna one should set an image of the Buddha facing west. On its left side one should have the Blessed Mother Tārā painted; one should set up one that is painted or one made of clay.

Then, with reverence for the Buddha, one should offer scents, flowers and the like, yellow in color as is fitting, and countless lamps of butter. Before the Blessed Mother one should offer a lamp of butter. On the continents one should offer vessels filled with honey, and lamps of butter or lamps of sesame oil. In the eastern direction one should offer incense of sandalwood paste to the gandharvas. In the southern direction one should offer to the kumbhāṇḍas vessels filled with molasses, flour paste, milk porridge, incense, parched rice, white mustard seed, sesame and thick rice porridge mixed together, sesame porridge, and a vessel filled with beer. In the western direction one should offer incense of butter and guggulu, and also vessels filled with milk and milk porridge, to the nāgas and garuḍas. In the northern direction one should also offer incense of kunduru, parched flour and curd gruel to the yakṣas.

If kunduru cannot be found, sandalwood paste, or even resin incense, will do. Vessels of flour paste and vessels filled with honey are also to be set in the four directions, well known and determined by one who knows the foods of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the others, as has been stated. One should offer vases, one for each, filled with water from a river's eddy, along with grain, juniper as one can find it, udumbara, walnuts, grapes and the like. All the seeds as well should be offered a little at a time, keeping some back.

Then, if, while one is accomplishing the knowledge mantra, the howl of a female jackal sounds in the east, one should go from that place and set a torma with the remainder in whatever is the eastern direction, and should scatter it always. If it is in the south, the one who has set out the torma with the remainder should scatter it in that place out of fear of danger. Likewise one should scatter it in the west and the north; this is to be done by the attendant. The practitioner of the knowledge mantra should apply himself wholly to accomplishing the knowledge mantra.

At the base of the former image of the knowledge holder, facing east, having taken kuśa grass, one sits down; having sat down, the knowledge holder should make, outside the four continents, in the four directions, on the four faces of the encircling mountains, a circle with that same tawny cow dung. On the seat where one sits down having taken it, between oneself and the image of the Buddha, one should set charcoal, cow dung and things made of palāśa. Leaving no remainder or the like, one should perform eight thousand fire offerings. Having meditated on what is to be accomplished, one should first place the weapon, and then insert the offering at the svāhā at the end of the complete recitation. Kindling sticks of śāli rice and arka; if these cannot be found, one may put udumbara, palāśa, apāmārga or anything else into the fire to burn.

Then, over whatever thread has been spun by a maiden, one should name it with this mantra: namo ratnatrayāya nama ārya avalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya avalokite svāhā. Reciting this mantra eight hundred times, one should make eight knots, saying rakṣa svāhā. Those threads should be tied on one's own hand in order to protect oneself. When it is accomplished at that time with that Buddha, the attendant should take the remaining threads, seeds and so forth and place them high up in the temple. The temple priest should worship them. Then one should offer to the sick bowls of food and drink and the like. The remainder, apportioned in the mind, should be poured into a river. One should bury it in the ground in a dry pond, or a well, or a covered place. One should burn it thoroughly in fire.

Whoever wishes to practice the Blessed Mother Tārā should, in keeping with this meaning taught by the Blessed One, at the very outset generate the mind of awakening along with it. Everything the Blessed One has taught is the ground of the supreme accomplishment of great awakening. Here, what is called the Buddha is the cessation of knowledge mantra and the arising of knowledge mantra; therefore one should accomplish the knowledge mantra before him, and obstructors cannot hinder it.

First of all, the times for accomplishing knowledge mantras in other ways are the full moon on the fifteenth of the month of Vaiśākha, or of Phālguna, or of Āṣāḍha, or the fifteenth of the bright half of Kārttika; any of these will do. Whoever wishes to accomplish a fierce rite should, in this manner, undertake it from the first day of the dark half of the month, and on the fourteenth of the dark half, with this mantra: namo ratnatrayāya nama ārya avalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya mahākāruṇikāya oṃ vedavid svāhā. With this mantra one should first tie a red thread, then in a charnel ground smear a ground in the shape of a cowhide with tawny cow dung, and in just the same way, by the rite of torma, make various tormas for the other bhūtas. Four attendants bearing weapons should put kindling sticks into the fire. Making eight hundred knots in the thread, one should tie it on for the sake of protecting oneself. Through that Buddha, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, brahmarākṣasas and the like come under one's power. When the knowledge mantra is accomplished, one requests them to depart in just the same way, by the rite of torma.

For all practices of knowledge mantras, whoever wishes to accomplish a knowledge mantra should, at night, being clean and wearing clothes that are clean, perform the practice himself. Burning incense of kunduru or black aloeswood and facing east, one should recite ten times. One should also say this: "Blessed Mother, come yourself, accept the flowers and the tormas, each of them, and do this task of mine!" Likewise one should say it facing southeast, southwest, northwest and northeast, and toward the zenith and the nadir: "Come yourself, accept the incense, the flowers and so forth, and the lamps, each of them, and do my task as well!" Again at dawn, too, seven or ten times, one should invite her in the same way in the ten directions. When she has come, one should offer incense and the like. Again, at midday, having performed all the torma rites, wishing to take kuśa grass and sit down, one should invite her in the same way in the ten directions: "Blessed Mother, come, accept the scents, the flowers and so forth, and do my task as well!" Then, taking kuśa grass and sitting down, one should perform the accomplishment as explained.

When one accomplishes a knowledge mantra, these signs appear. The dreams seen on account of the knowledge mantra are seeing elephants, horses, temples and palaces, and climbing them. And as for the marks of accomplishment of the knowledge mantra, by seeing a horse one gains the accomplishment of the activity of the wind. Likewise, seeing one's mother, father, grandfather, great-grandfather, a great king, a girl adorned with ornaments; wearing white clothes; food, cattle, a young brahmin, gold, moisture, a peacock, meat, fish, milk, curd, and the performance of rites of butter torma and the like; people speaking pleasantly; and if one sees flowers, fruits and the like, it is in accordance with success.

Then, if one sees barley and wheat standing in moisture, not seen in spring and summer, it portends rain out of season. As for one who wishes for pacification as it has been praised, if one sees a full vase, milk, curd, butter, flowers and fruits, these are the best signs for proceeding. Having seen cows, brahmins, youths, gold, peacocks and the like, and having regarded them as accomplishment, one should begin the rites in all the tasks of accomplishing knowledge mantras.

If one sees these adverse things, one does not sleep: if in a dream one sees scorpions, donkeys, camels, pigs, monkeys, crows, owls, vultures of every kind, rats, cats, a club, naked people, sitarukṣa, empty vessels, dry wood, charcoal from a charnel ground, dried-up rivers, and those who lead one astray, which are inauspicious, the knowledge mantra will not be accomplished. Obstructors will arise in all one's activities. Then one should apply this mantra against all the obstructors: oṃ vajra khuru vikritānana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This mantra belongs to the king of wrathful ones called Hayagrīva. When one has protected oneself by consecrating with this mantra, no fear arises in accomplishing any rite.

Then, for fevers and for children seized by grahas, one should perform the sweeping and tie a thread; the wiping away of poison too is accomplished just by reciting the knowledge mantra once. For this, one should have a vase painted; with the principal mantra one should make eight hundred knots in thread spun by a maiden and tie it on that vase. That procedure shows whether there is accomplishment or no accomplishment. On the second day one should untie all the knots. Otherwise, if what is bound by the knowledge mantra is left untied, it renders things fruitless; effects of this kind and others arise eighteenfold from that mantra.

This is the means of accomplishment for all consecrations and all mantras. Now the particular application of the knowledge mantras should be stated. Wherever the practice is being done, it grants a vision to that person: the person perceives the higher deity as present close by. That mantra grants a vision to whoever is accomplishing it, and he perceives the higher deity as present close by. This is the distinctive feature of the knowledge mantras.

The rite of the means of accomplishing this mantra is as follows. Smear a square maṇḍala; in its center set an image of the Buddha facing west, and on its right side one should place the Blessed Mother. On the left is the king of wrathful ones, Hayagrīva. Then quickly, abiding facing east, take kuśa grass; make offerings of scent, lamps and the like to the image of the Blessed One, burn incense of aloeswood and turuṣka, and also offer whatever torma has been obtained in the four hidden directions. Then, having taken kuśa grass before the image of the Buddha, one sits down and should sweep away every disease in particular. All diseases dissolve and one is freed from them, at dawn on the seventh day, or within three nights.

One upholds the rite of that entire tantra of Tārā together with its retinue. Any other nun who dwells apart by the ocean, in the mountains or in charnel grounds should offer recitation in order to protect herself. Then no fear arises from whatever piśācas, yakṣas and the like there may be.

Then, one who wishes to go in the eastern direction should make a square maṇḍala, offer scent, flowers, incense and so forth there, and offer recitation twenty-seven times in order to protect oneself. Likewise, when the time of night comes, one should offer recitation on the road. One should keep it constantly in mind. One should also tie a thread on oneself. By what was stated before, these too, consecrated seven times, will be inscribed. Likewise, with the heart mantra, one should sweep the grahas with kuśa grass by the rite stated before, with those stated before, with those seven knowledge mantras. Likewise, one who wishes to go in the southern direction should offer incense and flowers and offer recitation twenty-one times. Likewise one should sweep away the grahas of the kumbhāṇḍas by the rite stated before. One should also tie a thread, and they will be pacified. Likewise, one who wishes to go in the western direction should likewise sweep away the grahas of the nāgas and garuḍas by what was stated before, by the rite stated before. Likewise, one who wishes to go in the northern direction should likewise treat the grahas of the yakṣas by the rite stated before. And likewise in the intermediate directions.

Then Avalokiteśvara again spoke to the gods, the yakṣas and the others: "Friends, listen! Having seen the body of the Tathāgata, complete with all the marks of a tathāgata's form, granting the supreme boon with the right hand, teaching the Dharma, and bestowing fearlessness, there one should accomplish the knowledge mantra. One engaged in fierce rites should not practice there; one should accomplish it together with the wrathful one subdued by Tārā. As long as it is before Ekajaṭī, it is close to Vajrapāṇi. He also bears the characteristics of a wrathful one. Before a figure of peaceful form, with all the characteristics perfectly complete, glossy and blue-green, of the kind described before, one should also accomplish other knowledge mantras. For one engaged in fierce rites it should be made in a transformed form. For one engaged in pacification and one engaged in increase it is of peaceful form. Wherever the practitioner faces and looks, there one should practice.

"As for the permission for the rites of the means of accomplishment of all the knowledge mantras taught in the Ūrdhvajaṭā: whatever female deity it is, one should give her that female's characteristics, form and attire. If it is a male, one should make him endowed with the characteristics of a male, adorned with male ornaments, with his implements, just as he is or just as described before. With a mistaken form, accomplishment does not arise. For as long as it lasts, one should place the Tathāgata beside that fierce deity.

a stūpa, or again one that contains the heart of dependent origination and is not cracked or broken into pieces, bestows accomplishment.

Now, this maṇḍala of the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā, is the maṇḍala called Generating All Commitments. It is called the Fully Victorious Consecration. It performs all auspicious and meritorious activities and increases harvests, life, and health, and even those whose commitments have lapsed come to generate commitment.

This maṇḍala should be drawn on the bank of a river of any kind, or on the bank of a lotus lake. Having made a plot of ground well cleansed with water, free of hair, chaff, charcoal, ash, wood, bricks, gravel, skulls, and skeletons, to the depth of a neck or to the level of water, in a place where there is water nearby, on the right side, or in the west where there are trees bearing flowers and fruit, in a direction that is pleasing to the mind and where there is wealth, one should draw the maṇḍala, square, with four doors, in rice powder of five colors. The lines should be laid out with a thread of five colors, and with pegs of udumbara wood as well. On a day of the bright fortnight when the lunar day, the karaṇa, the moment, the constellation, and the yoga are auspicious, with those colors: first white, second red, third yellow, fourth blue, and fifth black. For the rest, the deities should be drawn in the middle of the east.

In the center of the lotus one should set up a vase filled completely with all grains, jewels, medicines, and flowers. To its east, the Buddha, the Blessed One. To his right, noble Avalokiteśvara. To his left, Stainless Goer. Beside noble Avalokiteśvara, the seven Tārās. To the left, the seven women of Stainless Goer. Beside Śrīdevī, Pāṇḍaravāsinī. Beside the Tārās one should place Candrā. Beginning from Candrā, Śrī, Yaśasvinī, and also Śvetā. Beside them, Mahāśvetā and Bhṛkuṭī. Toward the door, the Courageous Lady and Śakti. Inside the maṇḍala, on both sides, Brahmā and also Rudra. Beside Rudra, the goddess Umā; beside Brahmā, Sarasvatī. Inside the door, a staff and a water pot. On one side, Prajñāpāramitā; on the other, She Who Has Attained Peace. At the door one should place the wrathful one called Hayagrīva, facing inward. Beside him one should set the rākṣasī called Ekajaṭī.

This is the arrangement of the maṇḍala of the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā. One should draw a maṇḍala of four cubits, or eight cubits, or twelve cubits, or sixteen cubits.

In setting out the forms and the mudrās: everywhere, the Blessed One's lotus is a fully opened lotus mudrā. For the bodhisattvas, the emblems of their excellent families. For noble Tārā, the blue lotus. For Śrī, an opened flower and a white lotus. For Pāṇḍaravāsinī, that same, with its stalk, fully opened. For noble Yaśasvinī, a flower with its stalk. At all the doors and at all the corners, set ten mango twigs on each bundle of kuśa grass, and raise banners above.

Then one should invite each deity with its own mantra, and also request it to depart. Or else, do so with the complete heart knowledge mantra of noble Avalokiteśvara. Or else, invite with white flowers using the heart mantra of noble Tārā, and request departure.

At night, having made offerings of scent, flowers, incense, and lamps, one should make offering with torma: auspicious dishes, ullopika cakes, peas, oily fried foods and the like, laḍḍus of lentils, sesame porridge, milk porridge, rice with curd, buttermilk, broth, other oily foods for the spirits, molasses cakes, and also curd. This is the rite of the torma.

Then, having again made offerings of fragrant scents and of flowers, water-born flowers in particular, one should recite each mantra seven times. Or else one should recite the mantra of noble Tārā eight hundred times. Over the inner vase one should recite the five-syllable heart mantra one thousand eight hundred times. Then, having taken up fire in the fire place, one should perform the fire offering with butter, sesame oil, and food, according to the rite, in its proper form and without limit of number.

Afterward, the practitioner should lead in the student, who has been well examined and is a fit vessel. Covering his face with a cloth, having led him in with his joined palms filled with flowers, one should have him cast them. Wherever they fall, that will be his family. When he has thus been led into the maṇḍala, the student will come to know the commitments. Having given whatever empowerment is desired, facing east from the south and the west, one should fumigate him with incense of sarja resin and bdellium mixed with ghee. At midday, with the vase. One should offer oblations into the fire, reciting each mantra seven times. Having offered the oblations, then, by the great activity of the Blessed Mother, one should place the student on the left side, and then have him circumambulate the maṇḍala. One also gives him the heart mantra. He should bind this mudrā of noble Tārā and recite. In this way he is consecrated.

If all these things are done in every respect, this will quickly bring pacification, and one greatly pleases the Blessed Mother. One who desires kingship should be consecrated as if seated on a lion throne. One who desires wealth, seated on palāśa leaves. One who would cast out wrongful contamination, seated upon bricks. One who desires long life, seated on the essence of the earth that moves upon ten short ones. One who desires to flourish as a master should be consecrated drawn out with ariṣṭa and seated upon a skull. By consecrating seven times, misfortune is pacified. By consecrating twelve times, one becomes a king. By consecrating five times, the poor become wealthy. Afterward one should again make offerings and request departure.

This is the maṇḍala rite of noble Tārā called the Fully Victorious Consecration.

When this maṇḍala has been drawn, before long one greatly pleases the Blessed Mother.

Then again the bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta said to the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi: "Out of compassion for the buddhafield, in order to protect and guard fully the teaching of the whole vajra family, this Ūrdhvajaṭā together with its subsequent tantra brings accomplishment to the whole vajra family itself, and so that all the ways of the Dharma may remain even in this age afflicted by the five degenerations, it performs activities equal to the subjugation by Tārā." And in order to establish the path of this subsequent tantra, at that time he also said this:

"Blessed One, I shall establish it, and I shall utter an aspiration. May this conduct of mantra become for beings a cause of the perfection of wisdom. I shall dispel for them every fear of strife, dispute, famine, disease, enemy armies, untimely rain, people who rain down threats, non-humans, and animals; and also inauspiciousness, bad dreams, evil omens, malevolent yakṣas, hostile persons, loss of taste, cold, heat, foul smells, harsh contact, and poison. As the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā, in a woman's form and attire, I shall dispel for them thieves, floods, famine, and violence. I shall completely pacify every fear of kings, lions, tigers, buffalo, wolves, poison, thieves, humans, and non-humans. I shall make all beings skilled in the rite of accomplishing mantra, and I shall bring to completion their enjoyment of fruits of many kinds, medicines, flowers, the taste of fruits to eat, drink, clothing, dwellings, bedding, and seats. I shall make all beings long for the Dharma and set them to the practice of virtuous dharmas.

"This is my ultimate aspiration in the presence of all the buddhas. May all the buddhas, the blessed ones, grant me their permission! May the accomplishment of the activity of the buddhas, the blessed ones, the chariot of the mind, be perfected in me. And in order surely to liberate myself and persons of this kind, I in such a form, and Vajrapāṇi in a woman's form, shall ripen beings with forms and attire of many kinds."

Then again the buddhas, the blessed ones, out of compassion for Avalokiteśvara, summoned Śakra, Brahmā, the other world protectors, the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and the rest, and he would act in the manner of a great being in such a form. Then all those buddhas, the blessed ones, declared: "The bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara will be accomplished."

Then Śākyamuni said to the great bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara: "Son of noble family, this makes Māra, Śakra, Brahmā, the other world protectors, the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and humans of great splendor, of very great splendor, come; it is fully embraced and blessed by all the buddhas. Your knowledge mantras and mantra words are made in such forms and in the manner of such persons as you are able to assume.

"Son of noble family, you too, in an instant, in the guise of Brahmā, rightly join beings to the way of the Dharma of all the buddhas. In a moment, in the guise of a monk; in an instant, in the form of medicine and elixir; in a moment, in the form of Śakra, you lead them onto the noble path. In an instant, in the form of Māra, you emanate the forms of others: the lord of the gods of Vaśavartin, Tuṣita, Yāma, Akaniṣṭha, the Four Great Kings, all the bhūtas, the charnel ground, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva, Kubera, Maheśvara, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, kṣatriyas, brahmins, vaiśyas, śūdras, lions, elephants, buffalo, monkeys, pigs, birds of many forms, mountains, trees, fruits, garments, Dharma robes, mounts, bedding and seats, paṭaha drums, conches, and many kinds of jewels, adorned with forms decked in ornaments; and you become like the form of a buddha. Son of noble family, this becomes like the form of the eighty-four colors, forms, signs, and shapes."

Then the Tathāgata Amitābha said to the Lord of Secrets, Vajrapāṇi: "Son of noble family, this has come here through the great power of the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. In the domain of Māra and his army, all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and wherever they dwell in the domain of Māra and his army, through the means of the conduct of the knowledge mantras and mantras of the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, he cares for beings. Beings of every kind, measureless and countless, in the ten directions, in pure and impure buddhafields, he will behold with the unobscured eye of wisdom. With forms that accord with their dispositions, he establishes himself and the beings to be tamed, in whatever way they are to be tamed, in the third state, that of irreversibility. For as long as is needed, in the form of a buddha, he overcomes whatever attachment beings have, and for those who long for necessities and enjoyments of many kinds, in order that they may give up their clinging, he gives them those necessities and then establishes them in irreversibility itself."

Then again, surely, with that commitment, the bodhisattva noble Avalokiteśvara spoke to the whole assembly: "Sons of noble family, I take great delight in what you, Śakra, Brahmā, the world protectors, the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and the rest, have expressed in your minds. And may what I, the great king of wrathful ones called Hayagrīva, have spoken become, together with the Blessed One, of mutual benefit and of gentle mind. This secret mantra of mine has great fruit and great splendor and accomplishes every aim of activity. Here it is:

namo ratnatrayāya namo amitābhāya tathāgatāya arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya nama ārya abalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya mahākāruṇikāya sarbasatvāya anukaṃpakāya sarbbasatvābyasanaghīteni sarbasatvāmakṣakarāya sarbbabīryarāja adhibhikrāṃtāya mahārājāprokte

Having paid homage to these, I shall recite the mantra spoken by noble Avalokiteśvara, which accomplishes the aims of all beings, slays all obstructors, and conquers all:

oṃ hu hu hu tarule bitarule sarbbabiṣa ghātaka jvalitabiphuliṅka trihāsa keśarāṭepa bajrakhurnirghāta kacalita basudhātala niśvāsa mārutitkṣipti dharaṇīdhara bhīṣaṇā trihasa aparimitabālākramabhītabhutagani bughna bughna hayagrība khāda khāda paramantraṃ siddhi medina ābeśāya jvalarapiśācagraheṣu apratihato bhaba bajrakiñcarāyasi imaṃ duṣṭagraha duṣṭa sarbbaṃ bā dhuna dhuna paṭa paṭa pandha bandha buddha ddharmma saṃgha anujñākāra śīghraṃ hayagrība phaṭ bajragatrāya phaṭ bajranetrāya phaṭ bajradaṃṣṭāya phaṭ bajrakhurāya phaṭ bajra ārya khurānighātanāya phaṭ paramantrabināśānāya phaṭ trailokyabhayaṃkārāya phaṭ sarbbakarmmeṣu apratihatāya phaṭ bajrakulotrasanāya phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā

The mantra from the mouth of Hayagrīva, resting on fourteen, increased by eighteen with the three hūṃ syllables and the four phaṭ syllables, is complete.

oṃ bajrakhura bikṛtānana hūṃ phaṭ

This is the near-heart mantra.

oṃ hayagrība hṛdaya mābartayiṣyami ehi ehi mahābāla bajranakha bajraroma bajrakoṭa bajrakoṣa bajrakhura bajradaṃṣṭa hana hana daña daha paca paca gṛhṇa gṛhṇa bandha bandha raṅga raṅga saha saha jalpa jalpa turu turu ruṭu ruṭu dhuna dhuna bidhuna bidhuna matha matha kampa kampa kaṭ kaṭ sarbbadebāṃ sarbbayakṣa sarbbabiheṭhakā sarbbabiṣīprabi prabe prabiśa hayagrība priyajvāla abiśa ābiśa bajrakhur mābilamba buddhadharmmasaṃghabacana manusmara jatimanusmara hṛdayam nusmar pikir pikira gaja gaja nanda nanda gulu gulu mulu mulu nihana nihana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā

This is the heart mantra.

nama ārya abalokiteśvarāya

This too is the great king of knowledge mantras, of immeasurable strength and power to overcome others, which destroys the splendor of the supreme body; it is followed by all the tathāgatas and permitted for worship; it subdues all violence; it is worshipped by every host of knowledge mantras; it is truly praised by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, and worshipped by pretas, piśācas, and kumbhāṇḍas; greatly transformed, baring its fangs. This will be the rite of Hayagrīva the king.

Having purified one's wrongdoing, one recites it three hundred thousand times at a stūpa. Then one should begin the practice. On the fifteenth of the bright fortnight, having kept a fast for three nights, one should have a painter who observes the poṣadha paint, on a cloth free of hair whose fringe has not been cut off, with colors that are not mixed and with a clean new brush, an image of the Blessed One seated on a lotus seat, in the act of teaching the Dharma.

On his left side, noble Avalokiteśvara, wearing a white sacred thread, white like an autumn cloud, with a lotus body, wearing a crown of matted locks in the middle of which is a white Amitābha dwelling within a purified vessel; with his right hand bestowing fearlessness, his left hand occupied in bestowing a lotus. The practitioner too is gazing intently. Below noble Avalokiteśvara, on the left, one should draw Hayagrīva, king of knowledge mantras, white like an autumn cloud, with a wrathful face, red eyes, and tawny hair, his great hand holding an antelope skin, wrapped in a length of cloth, fierce, with a hanging belly, wearing a snake as his sacred thread, gazing intently at Avalokiteśvara, his face blazing, his head adorned with a garland of sixty lotuses. Beside him, a diligent vidyādhara, his hand occupied with an incense bowl, kneeling on both knees.

Then on the left side of the Blessed One, one gazing intently at the wrathful one, his face slightly smiling, stroking a vajra, wreathed in garlands of flame. Below the Blessed One, on both sides of a Dharma wheel, figures seated upon lotuses, and those lotuses are held by young nāgas.

Then, when the vidyādhara has completed the work of painting and has made vast offerings, having kept a fast for three nights, he sets down the rosary and offers large butter lamps and white torma. Then the vidyādhara, having done the preliminary practice, should place it within and leave it for one night. Then, having taken it out, he should have a wheel made of iron under the constellation Puṣya by a craftsman who observes the poṣadha, who is clean and not lacking in any faculty: eight finger-widths across, broad, fully closed, wreathed in garlands of blazing vajras. Then the vidyādhara should place that wheel too in the five products of the cow and leave it for one night.

Then, having taken it out and bathed it in the proper way, and having wrapped it all around with white cloth, one should set up the painting facing west. Taking incense, torma, and a vessel of guest water, one should invite all the deities. Having offered the guest water and then requested them to depart again into oneself, one makes a fence of ash with ash over which the root mantra has been recited seven times, and a fence of lamps with a lamp over which it has been recited seven times. Then, having performed the rite of protection, one binds the ground with white mustard seed over which it has been recited seven times, and binds the sky with water consecrated seven times.

Then the vidyādhara, with a vessel filled with scented water together with white flowers, kneeling on both knees, should invite his own deity with the root mantra, offer the guest water, and satisfy the deities on that seat. One should make a fire offering of seven oblations of butter, honey, and milk. Then the vidyādhara should take up the wheel in both hands and recite until it blazes.

There will be the sound of a great drum heard, thunder rumbling "golu golu" from the clouds, the tips of the lamp flames growing, the painting moving, the sound of a conch heard, the sound of bells ringing out, the sound "haha" resounding, and the words: "Son of noble family, these are accomplished. Excellent, excellent! This wheel travels the path of the bodhisattvas and carries one across the great ocean of existence."

Then the vidyādhara should recite quickly, quickly, until noble Avalokiteśvara comes. When he has come, one should offer him guest water. Then, when the practitioner has offered the guest water, noble Avalokiteśvara says to the practitioner: "Son, you have surely subdued those of Māra's side and traveled those paths of the bodhisattvas. What is to be done?"

Then the Blessed One, noble Avalokiteśvara, strokes the crown of the practitioner's head with his right hand. In that very instant of stroking there appears a canopy a thousand leagues wide, hung with nets of little bells and dangling with golden leaves, bound with Tārā, adorned and richly adorned with vajra power by sapphires, rubies, saugandhika gems, and other special ornaments. And with other auspicious things too: daughters of the vidyādharas, of fine form and beautiful, singing and sending forth sweet melodious voices, accompanied by lutes, clay drums, flutes, and cymbals. This canopy of the practitioner of noble Avalokiteśvara, by the power of that king of knowledge mantras itself, sports together with its retinue for as long as the moon, the sun, and the stars endure; and by the power of this king of knowledge mantras he is the sovereign of the universal monarchs of all vidyādharas.

Then, having paid homage to noble Avalokiteśvara, he ascends the celestial palace together with those who share in his enjoyment, and departs. That wheel too, blazing at the summit of the celestial palace, the universal monarch of all knowledge mantras, with a mind that travels where it will, goes to Sukhāvatī. There, where the Tathāgata Amitābha dwells, praised by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and vidyādharas, amid showers of falling flowers, he remains for an eon as the sovereign of the universal monarchs of all vidyādharas.

When he dies, he is born among brahmins, and he has recollection of his births, all the marks complete, superknowledge of all times, great wealth, great enjoyments, the power to overcome others with great diligence; he is a delight for all beings to see, compassionate, of deep faith in the Buddha, of upright mind, retentive of what he hears, and skilled in every craft, in letters, and in drawing; whatever inconceivable thing he thinks of, he understands with his mind. He is born into a brahmin family, free of every illness. So it is said.

Consecrating seven times, one binds the crown knot. With the syllable hūṃ, increase, suppression, and bewildering. With the syllable ja, one requests departure. With the syllable gha, killing. With the syllable svāhā, the aim of pacification and sustaining life. In brief, it teaches this: the vidyādhara who wishes to accomplish the supreme great secret should perform here cutting, killing, splitting, destroying, threatening, and every other act of killing as well. All of it is to be done with a nature of compassion, never with fierceness. One must never apply the king of knowledge mantras where it should not be applied; whoever does apply it so will not achieve the supreme accomplishment, and will also be without knowledge of the commitment. This accomplishment holds in all sādhanas and in all tantras.

Having consecrated a finger seven times, one suppresses the clouds. Having touched the head, one wins at dice, and likewise in every dispute. Having consecrated white mustard seed seven times and struck with it, one brings ruin. Having consecrated mālatī flowers seven times, if one gives them to a woman to hold, or pours them on her head, she comes under one's control.

Costus, cinnamon, black aloeswood, sandalwood, saffron, sahakāra blossom spikes, leaves of the three pungent spices, black pepper, bakula flowers, and priyaṅgu flowers should be ground to a fine powder, mixed with honey, and made into pills on chickpea leaves. When these have been recited over five times and given, that person comes under one's control. With the root mantra, a woman together with her husband comes under one's control. One who has entered upon the practice, wherever he stays, should carefully undertake it with that very powder, and vināyakas will not overpower him. By this same means, neither will rākṣasas, pretas, and the like.

Kuṭaja seeds, nāgakesara, lotus petals, śirīṣa flowers, spikenard, tagara, costus, the seeds of the plant called hand-born, red sandalwood, and white aparājitā flowers: having combined these seeds, one should have them ground with the urine of a tawny cow by a maiden's hand. Then, having made pills, one should perfume them in the shade with white mālatī flowers. If one anoints the body with these, one will not be overpowered by anyone, whether vināyakas, pretas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, or the like. If one does not give them, then, having consecrated cow's urine seven times, one completely destroys illness.

Guggulu, picumarda seeds, sandalwood, turuṣka, and śrīvāsaka: grind these to powder and fumigate your clothes with them. You will not be overpowered by anyone.

Realgar, bezoar, the hand-born plant, belleric myrobalan, kadamba flowers, licorice, śephālikā flowers, cinnamon, the seeds of white pepper, the two kinds of turmeric, and sweet flag: one should have these ground with the urine of a tawny cow by the hand of a brahmin maiden who observes the poṣadha. Having made pills, one should perfume them with blue lotuses. One should perfume them with atimuktaka, śāla, and blue flowers. One will not be overpowered by anyone, whether vināyakas or others, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, rākṣasas, or the like.

The chapter on freedom from illness is complete.

Next comes the accomplishment of the vetāla. On the fifteenth of the bright fortnight, take the corpse of a man, undamaged and very handsome, and anoint it. Having placed it in a purified vessel, the one who observes the poṣadha lets its hair hang loose, ties a garland of flowers about its neck, and goes down into a dry well. Having placed it in the well at a stūpa that contains relics, with the products of a tawny cow, one should make vast offerings and torma, bind it with four pegs of khadira wood, and set up the guardians of the directions. Mixing puffed rice and flour with the milk of a tawny cow, make oblations into the mouth of that corpse until its tongue comes out. Having cut it off, one becomes a sword vidyādhara. One becomes a great hero who overcomes others. One becomes like the rising sun, of equal radiance. One lives for five thousand years.

Next comes the second accomplishment of the vetāla. Having drawn a vetāla with ash from the charnel ground and made vast offerings and torma, sitting before it on a mat of kuśa grass, one should perform the fire offering with sticks of khadira wood smeared with pungent sesame oil until the vetāla rises. Whatever one thinks of in one's mind, it quickly summons. It bestows the elixir of rejuvenation. Riding upon it, one travels by means of the fire offering, and one lives for thirteen thousand years.

Next comes the third accomplishment of the vetāla. Having anointed a maṇḍala with the products of a tawny cow, drawn a vetāla with the ash of a fire offering made in the fire, made vast offerings, and set it up properly in the same way, one performs the fire offering with oblations of vikaṅkata, and the vidyādhara should strike it all over with vikaṅkata. Remembering the root mantra, one should say: "Rise! Rise!" It gives off smoke, and when one releases it with fierce laughter, it becomes terrifying. If one strikes it until one's own task is done, it follows one, and it quickly summons even the wife of Indra. It becomes an elixir of rejuvenation. Having eaten it, one lives for thirteen thousand years. When one dies, one is born into a family of great wealth, and one also remembers one's births. This is the accomplishment of the vetāla.

On the fifteenth of the bright fortnight, having kneaded well a peacock, a garuḍa, an elephant, and a horse out of anthill earth and milk, and having recited the root mantra over the three separated waters, one should give them to a tawny cow to consume. Then the vidyādhara, with the products of a secluded cow, observing the poṣadha, takes the milk of that tawny cow and kneads that lump of earth. Then, having made any one of a peacock, a garuḍa, an elephant, or a horse, as a drawing or in any other way, one should have a painter who observes the poṣadha paint it. Having set up the painting facing west, made vast offerings and lamps, and performed the rite of protection, one should perform a fire offering of seven oblations with sticks of udumbara wood. Having invited the deities with scented water and again opened it out, one offers guest water, places the peacock in front of the painting, and should recite until it blazes.

Then the vidyādhara should recite quickly, quickly. If one is accomplishing the peacock, the signs of its accomplishment are these: the peacock cries out, the elephant trumpets "gula gula," the horse neighs, and the garuḍa beats its wings. When these signs of accomplishment occur, one becomes a king of peacocks, a second Kārttika, and with great diligence one gains strength and overcomes others. One subdues the pride of the gods. One lives for an intermediate eon. When one dies, one is born into a brahmin family. This is the accomplishment.

Then the one who fashions the vajra accomplishes a wheel, a hook, an axe, a short spear, a vajra, and a trident with a serpent hood, made of aguru, of sandalwood, of devadāru, of khadira, of fragrant wood, of neem wood, of iron made under Puṣya, of anthill earth, of crystal, or of clay. Having had a four-pronged vajra sixteen finger-widths long made, complete in every part, by a craftsman who observes the poṣadha, and having washed it thoroughly with the five products of a tawny cow, on the fifteenth of the bright fortnight, in front of the painting, one makes torma, lamps, and vast offerings. Having bathed the vajra in scented water and made an image arranging all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, one recites over the scented water with the root mantra.

Having invited one's own deities, one offers the welcoming water again and again; then, having requested them to depart, one should perform a fire offering of oblations of ghee. Then the vidyādhara, holding the vajra in his right hand, should recite for as long as it blazes and gives forth a crackling sound, "ciṭi ciṭi."

Then the vidyādhara should recite swiftly, until he sees in the eastern direction Avalokiteśvara, the one of great compassion, the deliverer of bodhisattvas, surrounded by all the perfections; Hayagrīva, the king, surrounded by ten million vidyās; the noble Bhṛkuṭī, Tārā, Pāṇḍaravāsinī, and Parṇaśabarī; and the heart essences of the bodhisattvas, each surrounded by fifty million, coming as they follow behind the Blessed One.

Then the gods worship the noble Avalokiteśvara by letting fall a rain of flowers. The noble Avalokiteśvara holds a water pot and a staff, and with his right hand he comforts the practitioner. He is white like an autumn cloud, steadfast as a pure white vessel, and wears a black antelope skin. In the middle of his crown of matted locks is the Tathāgata Amitābha, blazing like the sun, bearing a golden rod for worship. With words deep as the sound of a great drum, he comforts the practitioner.

Then the practitioner offers welcoming water and seats to all who have come, makes aspirations, and says: "Out of loving kindness, take the Blessed One's loving kindness upon me, and speak! Blessed One, with great compassion toward all sentient beings, toward the evildoer, and toward merit and the other accomplishments, great bodhisattva of great compassion, you whose very nature is great compassion, speak! For the evil I have done, the accomplishment of wealth." Having made aspirations thirteen times, the practitioner should request accomplishment from the Blessed One.

Then the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara touches the crown of the practitioner's head with his right hand and says, "Son, what shall be done?" Then, having offered welcoming water and a bouquet of flowers, kneeling on both knees, one should say this: "Blessed One, grant me the vajra accomplishment! Through your great diligence in activity and your great power, make my body like that of Vajrapāṇi, king of vidyādharas and lord of all vidyādharas!"

Then the Blessed One says: "Son, these are accomplished. This vajra is the power of great diligence and the subduer of adversaries; yours is a body like that of Vajrapāṇi, king of vidyādharas, who moves without obstruction and has great might."

Then the vidyādhara takes the vajra, circumambulates the Blessed One, and becomes a king of vidyās. Surrounded by fifty million vidyādharas, he sports together with vidyādhara maidens. With a fine form, utterly beautiful, perfect in all the major marks, he lives for an intermediate eon. When he dies, he is born into a brahmin family, and he remembers his former births. This is the accomplishment.

Then, if one wishes to accomplish the eye salve, at noon one should obtain antimony (srotoñjana) at the hero's price, have it washed seven times with the milk of a tawny cow, and likewise with the five products of that same tawny cow. After that, one should put the eye salve into a copper vessel and grind it. Then, having taken it from the fire, one makes vast offerings and torma before the painting and places the eye salve in the mouth. On the eighth day of the bright fortnight, or when the moon is seized by Rāhu, fasting for three nights, one should recite until it becomes warm, gives off smoke, and blazes. When it has become warm, one brings others under one's power. When it gives off smoke, one becomes invisible. When it blazes, one travels through the sky. By anointing one's eyes with it, one lives for five thousand years. When one dies, one is born into a rich family of great wealth, and remembers one's former births.

Then, if one wishes to accomplish a yakṣiṇī, on a cloth free of hair a painter who observes the poṣadha should draw, with colors that are not mixed, an image of the Blessed One one sugata-span in size, adorned with all ornaments, with a slightly smiling face, holding an aśoka in his right hand. On the eighth day of the bright fortnight the vidyādhara, setting up the painting before the image of the Blessed One, makes torma and vast offerings. Fasting for three nights, he invites his own deity, offers welcoming water and a seat, offers the water of requesting departure, and then, with the root mantra, should perform a fire offering of eight oblations of milk. Then the vidyādhara, seated on a mat of kuśa grass, should recite until the yakṣiṇī herself comes.

When she has come, having offered welcoming water, one should say this: "Accept it, accept it, and be seated!" With a broadly smiling face she says, "Excellent!" and, "What command shall I carry out?" Then the practitioner should say, "Be my wife." If he says, "Sister," then the practitioner will be parted from life. If he says, "Wife," then she takes the practitioner by the hand and, with a smiling face, goes to her own abode. She gives him an elixir. By eating it, in that very instant he becomes curly haired, with the appearance of one sixteen years old, colored like the rising sun, a divine image, with a fine form, utterly beautiful, and he lives for five thousand years. He sports together with her. When he dies, he is born into a great family, and he remembers his former births.

By that same rite, on a cloth with uncut fringe, a painter who observes the poṣadha should draw, with colors that are not mixed, a yakṣiṇī one sugata-span in size, hanging from a camphor priyaṅgu tree, wearing a single garment, resembling a sesame flower.

Then, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, the practitioner, fasting through the night and wearing clean clothes, makes offerings, torma, and lamps at a stūpa containing relics. Having invited his own deity, he offers welcoming water and a seat and then requests it to depart; then he should perform a fire offering of eight oblations of priyaṅgu kindling sticks smeared with the ghee of a tawny cow. Then the vidyādhara should recite until the yakṣiṇī herself comes. When she has come, he should offer her welcoming water. She speaks thus: "What command shall I carry out?" Then the practitioner should say this: "Be my wife." When the practitioner has said this, she replies with a broadly smiling face, "Just as you command." The practitioner takes her by the hand and goes to his own dwelling. She gives him an elixir. In that very instant he comes to have a fine form, utterly beautiful. He lives for five thousand years.

By that same rite, on a cloth with uncut fringe, a painter who observes the poṣadha should draw a yakṣiṇī: yellow like gold, wearing a single garment, her hair loose, gazing intently at the practitioner with a mind wholly filled with desire, hanging from an atimukta tree, with a slightly smiling face, threatening the practitioner with a finger of her right hand.

Then the practitioner installs the painting at a stūpa containing relics. Wearing clean clothes, he fasts for three nights before the painting and makes vast offerings. Having offered welcoming water and made the drawings, and having again offered welcoming water, he requests departure; then he should perform a fire offering of twenty-eight oblations of milk. Then the practitioner should strike the yakṣiṇī with mālatī flowers, one at a time, each enchanted seven times with the root mantra, until she herself comes. Taking the practitioner by the hand, she goes to her own dwelling. Having gone to her dwelling, she gives him an elixir. In that very instant he comes to have a fine form, and he sports together with her. He lives for five thousand years. When he dies, he is born into a family of great wealth, and he remembers his former births.

By this same rite, one should combine sandalwood, tagara, costus, cinnamon, paripālapā, saffron, realgar, bezoar, lotus petals, and lotus seeds, and with scented water and water from the sky have them placed in the hands of a brahmin girl who observes the poṣadha. Having made a white, fragrant image, one makes offerings at a stūpa containing relics on the eighth day of the bright fortnight. Fasting for three nights, one sets that image before the stūpa, invites one's own deity with the root mantra, offers welcoming water and a seat, and offers the water of requesting departure. Then, seated on a mat of kuśa grass, one should perform a fire offering of seven oblations of lotus filaments smeared with the ghee of a tawny cow. Right there, seated on the kuśa mat, one should recite until the yakṣiṇī herself comes. When she has come, one should offer her welcoming water. Then she says, "What command shall I carry out?" One should say this: "Be my wife." Then she says, "So I shall do," and taking the practitioner by the hand she goes to her own dwelling and gives him an elixir. He comes to have a divine form. He lives for five thousand years. When he dies, he is born into a brahmin family, and he also remembers his former births.

By that same rite, one should make an image out of fresh ghee of a tawny cow and, before the painting, cut it piece by piece and offer it into the fire, until the yakṣiṇī appears.

By this same rite, one should make an image of red sandalwood, recite the root mantra over it twenty-one times, and place it in a river. In that very instant a beautiful yakṣiṇī comes and grants every wish.

Having had a yakṣiṇī made of neem wood, one sugata-span in size, one should have a painter who observes the poṣadha paint it with colors that are not mixed. At a stūpa containing relics, one makes torma and vast offerings of lamps according to the rite. Then the practitioner, in complete seclusion, with a purified vessel and clothes, should invite the deities with the root mantra, offer worship and a seat, and request them to depart. For as long as it takes the yakṣiṇī herself to come, making her form manifest and bearing a garland of flowers, for that long one should recite. When she speaks, the practitioner should say, "Be my wife." Then, with a broadly smiling face, she gives the practitioner the garland of flowers. Taking him by her own hand, she goes into the presence of the Blessed One. She gives him an elixir. In that very instant he comes to have a divine form, with a fine form, utterly beautiful. He sports together with her and fully enjoys delight and pleasure. He lives for five thousand years, the lifespan of a god. When he dies, he is born into a family of great wealth: utterly beautiful, a joy to all sentient beings who see him, with great enjoyments, great wealth, great pleasures, compassionate, giving everything, of great diligence, and remembering his former births.

The chapter on the yakṣiṇīs is complete.

Having gone to a lotus lake, the practitioner should perform the fire offering until Śrī comes. Costus, tagara, lotus seeds, lotus filaments, and sandalwood should be ground together with honey. Whoever it is given to comes under one's power. Having recited the root mantra over a garland of flowers, whoever it is given to comes under one's power.

Then one who wishes to gain prowess should make stūpas containing the heart of dependent origination, until the last stūpa trembles strongly. Then, the obscurations of karma being exhausted, success comes even to one who has committed the five deeds of immediate retribution, and not otherwise. Such is the magnificent display of the bodhisattva.

Then, if one wishes to accomplish the noble Avalokiteśvara, on a cloth with uncut fringe and free of hair, a painter who observes the poṣadha should draw with a new brush, using colors that are not mixed, the Blessed One, the noble Avalokiteśvara, yellow like gold, with hanging locks, bearing Amitābha on his head, surrounded by all the perfections. Below, the practitioner should be shown holding a censer in his hand, kneeling on both knees, contemplating awakening intently.

Then the vidyādhara, beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight, should make uninterrupted offerings, torma, and lamps before the painting every single day, until the full moon. On the full moon, having made vast offerings, torma, and lamps, he should also make aspirations. Having paid homage to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, he takes up with both hands a vessel of scented water filled with mālatī flowers, kneels on both knees, recites the root mantra seven times, and invites his own deities. Having offered welcoming water and seats, and having again dismissed them, he should perform a fire offering with mālatī flowers smeared with the ghee of a tawny cow.

Having satisfied the deities and made protection, he sits on a mat of kuśa grass, free of pride, silent, rid of all guile, and, fixing his attention with supreme mindfulness, he should recite until the noble Avalokiteśvara himself arrives, surrounded by all the perfections.

When the great being arrives, the earth trembles, the mountain peaks shake, all the illnesses of all sentient beings are completely pacified, all the gods let fall a rain of flowers, all the vidyādharas let fall a rain of sandalwood powder, the gods of the Pure Abodes let fall a rain of great jewels, and all the asuras let fall a rain of utpalas. All the Rudras become free of anger. Even the hell beings in that instant feel happiness and speak of their supreme fear. The gandharvas make the sound of sweet songs heard. All the vidyādharas too, each surrounded by his own vidyā, come into the presence of the bodhisattva of miraculous display. All the vināyakas, all the obstructing spirits, all the rākṣasas, all the pretas, and every kind of fierce being, seeing the bodhisattva arrive, turn to peaceful minds. From the clouds comes a rumbling sound, "gulu gulu," the earth quakes in six ways, and the guardians of the four directions come into the presence of the bodhisattva. All the vināyakas and all the obstructing spirits come, and the four directions become fully at peace. The wind blows, and blows strongly. The trees burst into flower out of season. All the worldly vidyādharas come, and wherever the vidyādhara performs the practice, there they all gather for the festival of the great being.

The practitioner, on seeing the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, should offer welcoming water and pay homage. He offers welcoming water and seats to all the gods and all the vidyādharas. Then all the gods and all the vidyādharas give their "Excellent!" to the practitioner and to the bodhisattva. Those whom he has ferried across the great river of the three realms of existence are surely sealed by the all-illuminating Victor and live together with the path of the bodhisattva.

Then the noble Avalokiteśvara gives his "Excellent!" to all the gods, and the bodhisattva strokes the crown of the practitioner's head with his right hand. Then whatever essence the practitioner holds in mind, that he becomes: a vidyādhara cakravartin, a vidyādhara king, divinity itself; whatever he wishes appears, and more besides. He should then say this: "Blessed One, noble Avalokiteśvara, I wish to see Potalaka today."

The bodhisattva, the great being, took him by the right hand and entrusted him to Hayagrīva, king of vidyās, saying: "Go to Potalaka. Whatever is wished for will be given."

Then the king of vidyās, surrounded by a host of vidyā kings, takes the practitioner by the right hand and goes to Potalaka, in the midst of the ocean, while gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and others let fall a rain of flowers on the practitioner's host of vidyās, and great drums, paṭaha drums, drums, single-headed clay drums, and clay drums resound. There, upon the ocean, the great Ocean sees the king of vidyās and that holy person, and, surrounded by all the rivers, presents an offering of welcoming water made of jewels. He also grants his "Excellent!": "Son of noble family, excellent! This is the abode of the Blessed One, the noble Avalokiteśvara, who lives well and is endowed with splendor."

Then, having crossed the great ocean, he goes to Potalaka. As soon as he sees it, all who are there, the vidyādhara gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, come to welcome the practitioner with welcoming water, vessels, and a great rain of flowers. Then he sees Potalaka, anointed with various gems and medicines, hung with pearl necklaces, with stairways made of gold, of crystal, of beryl, of sapphire, and of great sapphire, and with cloth hangings beautified by various flowers. They consecrate the king of vidyās and the practitioner, and say to the practitioner: "This abode is the abode of the Blessed One, the noble Avalokiteśvara, made of four kinds of jewels. In the central chamber, until awakening, enjoy it and dwell as though in your own abode." Then, having consecrated the vidyādhara king, the king of vidyās departed.

This is the accomplishment: through the magnificent display of this Blessed One's might, even one who has committed the deeds of immediate retribution accomplishes it.

King Hayagrīva said to all the kings of vidyās: "In the central chamber of the abode of the Blessed Mother and the noble Avalokiteśvara, made of four kinds of jewels, dwelling on its ground as though in their own abode, are the vidyās Tārā and Bhṛkuṭī and all the other vidyās, the great subduers of adversaries."

This king of vidyās performs its actions even without being accomplished: it cuts through bolts; with the syllable hūṃ it dries up the ocean; with the threatening gesture of the finger it paralyzes all; with the syllable oṃ it summons; with the syllable phaṭ it shatters even the Meru mountains; by mental recitation it brings all sentient beings under its power. With the syllable oṃ the deities are invited, with the syllable hūṃ they are requested to depart, with the syllable phaṭ one kills, and with the syllable svāhā one restores life. In short, whatever rites of the vidyās there are, all of them should be accomplished, in a way that transcends the world, by this very vidyā.

This is the rite common to all mantras: one who has no rite, and even one who does evil, should recite it three times. This Hayagrīva, king of vidyās, of great diligence, authorized by all the buddhas, of great power and a great subduer of adversaries, brings accomplishment through three recitations even to one who has committed the deeds of immediate retribution. For one who has faith, who has embraced the awakening mind, who has great aspiration, whose nature is compassion, who is without avarice, who is grateful, who has deep faith in the Buddha and the Dharma, who honors mother and father, who is quick to be patient, who keeps moral discipline, and who gives gifts, it brings accomplishment even without practice.

In short, it serves for every action: one who wishes to cut through a vidyā, or wishes to remove one, should recite this. This serves for every action.

This is a special samādhi of the bodhisattva, a perfection of giving bestowed by another, namely: the king of vidyās, for the sake of perfecting the happiness of all sentient beings, at the neck of King Hayagrīva.

The chapter called The Magnificent Display of the Bodhisattva's Might is complete.

Then, if one wishes to see Amitābha, on a cloth with uncut fringe and free of hair, a painter who observes the poṣadha should draw, with colors that are not mixed, the noble Amitābha in the world realm of Sukhāvatī, yellow like gold, seated on a lotus. Below, on the left side of the wheel of Dharma, one should draw King Hayagrīva seated on a lotus, his face distorted and terrifying, his belly hanging down, radiating blazing red and yellow fire, bearing a garland of jewels as an offering, adorned with ornaments of snakes, bearing Amitābha in his locks, threatening the vināyakas with his finger, while behind him the vināyakas flee. On the right side is the noble Avalokiteśvara, adorned, with a purified vessel and garments, comforting the practitioner with his right hand, yellow like gold, bearing on his head Amitābha in the middle of his crown of matted locks, subduer of adversaries. On the cloud above Amitābha, one should draw the gods of the Pure Abodes scattering flowers from among the clouds. The lotus of the Blessed One is held up by young nāgas. Below is the practitioner holding a censer in his hand, kneeling on both knees, gazing at Amitābha.

When the work of drawing is complete, the practitioner makes torma, lamps, and vast offerings, and on the full moon, fasting for three nights, with this same purified vessel and garments, he summons Hayagrīva, king of vidyās, offers welcoming water, performs the practice, and requests him to depart again. Then, having combined the ghee of a tawny cow, lotus seeds, and nāgakesara, he should perform a fire offering for seven days. Then the vidyādhara, having satisfied the deities and seated on a mat of kuśa grass, should make aspirations, and he should recite until the earth quakes in six ways, the tips of the lamp flames grow, a rumbling sound, "gulu gulu," comes from the clouds, a rain of flowers falls, a rain of sandalwood powder falls, and the sound of bells is heard. Then the vidyādhara should recite more and more swiftly, until Hayagrīva, king of vidyās, of great diligence, subduer of adversaries, comes with all the vidyās to the place of practice.

Then the practitioner offers welcoming water from a vessel filled with white flowers and scented water and makes aspirations. He spoke thus: "You are welcome! Welcome again, for the sake of the noble Avalokiteśvara together with the perfections." This Hayagrīva is of great diligence, power, and subduer of adversaries, worshipped by all the hosts of vidyās.

Then the vidyādhara should circumambulate Avalokiteśvara three times, kneel, and say this: "Whatever has appeared to you, I ask for all of it together." Then the Blessed One, the noble Avalokiteśvara, stroked the crown of the practitioner's head with his right hand and said this: "Holy being, of great diligence, power, and subduer of adversaries, you who through great diligence and the subduing of adversaries have accomplished the king of vidyās: excellent, excellent! Speak what you desire. I shall grant you a boon." One should say this: "Blessed One, I wish to go to Sukhāvatī." Then to the Blessed One, the noble Amitābha, with the bodhisattvas, in that world realm. Then the Blessed One, the noble Avalokiteśvara, stretched out his right hand, took the practitioner by the right hand, and entrusted him to King Hayagrīva.

"Great king of vidyās, take this holy being and go to the world realm of Sukhāvatī, where a rain of flowers falls. There, where the Tathāgata Amitābha, the Blessed One, dwells with the maṇḍala of his assembly, have him offer praise, and then come back again to where Potalaka is."

Then Hayagrīva, king of vidyās, took the practitioner and went to the world realm of Sukhāvatī, where a rain of flowers falls, and the practitioner said: "Holy being, look, look at the Tathāgata Amitābha teaching the Dharma to the bodhisattvas!" Then the king of vidyās, having had him offer praise, brought him back again to the Potalaka of the noble Avalokiteśvara. Then the practitioner listens to the Dharma in the presence of the noble Amitābha in that world realm.
