This accomplishment must not be applied to those who are unfit vessels; whoever does so transgresses the samaya. Having declared this, among the supreme practices this is not to be applied to those who are unfit vessels, for they have no samaya for it.

All these actions should be performed with the root mantra. With ash, a fence of ash. With three lamps, a fence of fire. By enchanting water seven times, the sky is bound. With white mustard seed, the ground is bound. By a fire offering of sesame, all the vināyakas come under one's power. By a fire offering of mustard, all the pretas and piśācas come under one's power. A fire offering of karavīra flowers accomplishes all the wrathful ones. By a fire offering of all kinds of flowers smeared with pungent sesame oil, all the worldly kings of vidyās come under one's power. By a fire offering of dhudhu, Maheśvara comes under one's power. If one performs a fire offering of priyaṅgu flowers, mālatī, saugandhi, and guggulu combined with the ghee of a tawny cow, one brings under one's power all the vidyās, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kinnaras, and all bipeds and quadrupeds. Having enchanted bezoar seven times and made a tilaka with it, one makes fanged creatures eat apart, and one is victorious in disputes. Taking the ghee of a tawny cow according to the rite described before and smearing it over the body, one enters into fire.

Taking a vajra made of khadira wood, together with the syllable hūṃ, at the entrance of a cave, an asura maiden comes forth; and when one has entered, the danger of the wheel does not arise. If the wheel is set in motion, by remembering the samaya, with the syllable hūṃ the wheel is ground to powder.

Next comes the practice of the pills. The vidyādhara who accomplishes the pills should combine red sandalwood, the five flowers, lotus filaments, the husks of red śāli rice, katnika sprouts, ṇūka seeds, grain, māṣa sprouts, costus, tagara, and turuṣka sesame oil, mixing them in equal parts. One who observes the poṣadha, in seclusion, should recite the root mantra over a tawny cow with a calf of the same kind and tether her at home; having enchanted well-strained water, she should be tended for seven days, either at home or in a secluded place. Then a cowherd for whom protection has been made should milk the cow. Then one should recite over that milk in a vase in a clean, secluded place. Then the vidyādhara should have a brahmin girl churn it. With that butter the ingredients are kneaded, and the pills are wrapped all around with the three metals; then they should be placed in the five products of a tawny cow and left for one night. Then, taking them out, one should place them in scented water. Having washed them, one should smear lotus petals with bezoar and set them on these.

Then, setting up the painting facing west and performing the rite of protection, one performs the vast rite of torma, lamps, and offerings. Then the vidyādhara takes up with both hands the eight pills on the lotus petals, holds them in his hands joined in the shape of a lotus, and, combining that same ghee of a tawny cow with mālatī flowers, should perform a fire offering of seven oblations. Then, having invited his own deity with the root mantra, he should recite before the noble Avalokiteśvara until they give off smoke and blaze. While they give off smoke, he becomes a vidyādhara who is invisible, who brings others under his power, and who travels through the sky. With a radiance like the rising sun, the vidyādhara, perfect in all the major marks, sports and delights together with the vidyādhara maidens. He lives for five thousand years. When he dies, he is born into a kṣatriya household, and he also remembers his former births.

With this same rite, lotus seeds, paṇḍītakara seeds, turuṣka, black aguru, red sandalwood, saugandhika, mālā flowers, saffron, realgar, and bezoar should be ground with the five products of a tawny cow by a maiden who observes the poṣadha and is not deficient in her faculties. Then the vidyādhara takes priyaṅgu wood and, in a clean multistoried house, has a casket made by the hands of a carpenter who observes the poṣadha, has generated the mind set on awakening, and is not deficient in his faculties. Having placed twenty-one pills in that casket, he makes vast offerings before the painting and also offers torma; then, taking up the casket, he covers it with a clean cloth and, fasting for three nights, invites the deities of the vidyā and should recite until it grows warm, gives off smoke, and blazes. When it grows warm, he brings others under his power, and he becomes invisible. When it gives off smoke, he becomes the one supreme youthful vidyādhara. When it blazes, he goes together with six vidyādharas and, surrounded by vidyādhara maidens, sports and delights on the summit of Meru and fully enjoys delight and pleasure. He lives for five thousand years.

When he dies, he is born among those of great wealth, and he also remembers his former births.

With this very mantra one accomplishes an eye ointment of realgar. On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, one takes gorocana bought at a hero's price, without haggling, and keeps a fast for one night. At midday a brahmin maiden who keeps the poṣadha vow should grind it with lotus petals and the milk of a tawny cow. Having made vast offerings to the painting, with the painting set facing west, one performs the rite of protection and invites one's own deities. Having offered them welcoming water and seats, make a fire offering of seven oblations of priyaṅgu flowers and tawny cow's milk. Having satisfied the deities, again, before those deities, one places the pellet inside two lotuses joined face to face, and one should recite until it gives off smoke, grows warm, and blazes. If, while it is warm, one makes a forehead mark with it, all people become pleased. While it gives off smoke, one becomes invisible. Making a forehead mark with it as it blazes, one sports together with vidyādhara maidens, surrounded by six vidyādharas. When he dies, he is born into a house of great wealth, and he also remembers his former births.

Make a fire offering of sesame, and the nāgas come under one's power. Make a fire offering of fish and meat, and the pretas come under one's power. If one makes a fire offering of mālatī flowers, the goddess Born of the Waters comes under one's power. Make a fire offering of priyaṅgu flowers, and the gods come under one's power. If one makes a fire offering of saugandhika lilies, the yakṣas come under one's power. With white mustard seed empowered by mantra seven times, whoever's crown it is placed upon comes under one's power. Before someone seized by a graha, struck by fever, or seized by a rākṣasa, if one makes a fire offering of mustard seed empowered by mantra seven times and smears him with its ash, he will be freed.

This detailed rite of King Hayagrīva is also complete.

There arises the magnificent power of noble Avalokiteśvara that extends to everything worldly and beyond the world. Those vidyā kings that have no rite of their own are accomplished by this very rite, and everything is done by that very king of ritual manuals. In short, even one who has committed the five acts of immediate retribution will succeed by doing it three times. Any son of good family who has faith, who is without stinginess, without deceit and without slander, who is respectful toward the vidyā king, who honors the one who keeps this ritual manual, reads it, recites it and praises it to others, being free of stinginess, will remember his former births. He will be cared for by spiritual friends and will have deep faith in the Buddha, the Dharma and the Saṅgha.

The detailed rite of King Hayagrīva in the Later Tantra of Ūrdhvajaṭā.

Then again, at that time, from the eastern direction, from the world realm Abhirati, the tathāgata called Tārā Akṣobhya, together with bodhisattva great beings in numbers to be measured and counted, through the power of the blessing of the miraculous display of the domain of all the buddhas, came in a single instant to this buddhafield where the secret mantra is obtained, to this very middle world of four continents where the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha Śākyamuni dwells. They remained on lotus seats as these arose, and those bodhisattva great beings too sat upon those lotus seats according to the power of their growth and their practice. In the same way, as many buddhas, blessed ones, as dwell, equal in number to the finest atoms of immeasurable and countless buddhafields, all came in an instant, a moment, a second, to the buddhafield of the middle world of four continents.

Then those tathāgatas, Akṣobhya and the rest, in order each to rejoice in the conduct by mantra of the Blessed Avalokiteśvara in this Later Tantra of the great king of ritual manuals, for the sake of protection, defense and safeguarding, for the sake of exhausting all karmic obscurations, and for the sake of the accomplishment of the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā, spoke these words of the dhāraṇī mantra, accomplished by the power of merit:

namo ratnatrayāya nama akṣobhyāya tathāgatāya arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya tadyathā kaṃkani kaṃkani rocani rocani troṭani troṭani trāsani trāsani pratihana pratihana sarvva karmma paraṃ parāṇi svāhā

namo ratnatrayāya namaścaṇḍasūryāya tathāgatāya arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya tadyathā candre mati candre karṇe milā milā buddha adhiṣṭhite sili sili dharmma adhiṣṭhite kili kili saṃgha adhiṣṭhite svāhā

Any son or daughter of good family who holds the name of this tathāgata, and who always, without interruption, recites it for an eon and keeps it in mind, will always live for forty thousand eons. He will remember his former births, and he will attain the unforgetting awakening mind.

namo ratnatrayāya namaḥ puṣpe ketave tathāgatāya arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya tadyathā puṣpe puṣpe puṣpe puṣpe puṣpe puṣpe supuṣpe svāhā

Having recited this dhāraṇī twenty-one times over flowers, and having acted in accordance with the rite and with the proper perception, one should scatter them upon a stūpa of the Tathāgata. All one's wishes will be completely fulfilled, and all karmic obscurations will be exhausted.

namo ratnatrayāya namaḥ sarva nivarṇa viṣkaṃbhine tathāgatāya arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya tadyathā sphuṭa sphuṭa sphuṭandu me sarva pāpāni sarva buddha satye dharma satyena saṃgha satyena indra satyena varuṇa satyena ye loka satyena virṇa satyena satya sacanena sphuṭantu sarva pāpāni sarva buddha adhiṣṭhānena svāhā

In twenty-one nights one exhausts all karma. Doing it for three days and nights, applying it six times, one will certainly exhaust the acts of immediate retribution.

namo ratnatrayāya namo vairocanāya tathāgatāya arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya nama ākāśagarbhāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya mahākāruṇikāya kala kala kili kili huru huru vairocana rasmi sañcodide āgaccha ārya ākāśagarbha mahākāruṇika pūrāya śubaṃ darśaya buddha piṣaya racaracara ciri ciri svāhā

This is the dhāraṇī called the Heart of Vairocana, which is accomplished simply by reciting it. It subdues fears, adversities, poison, persistent poison, sorcery, kings, bandits and the like. Wherever it is kept written down, or for whoever wears it on the head or on the arm, no harms and no contagious diseases will arise. By reciting it constantly, one attains the stainless samādhi.

name ratnatrayāya namo varocanāya tathāgatāya nama ākāśagarbhāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā vajrambu vajrambu vajradhvaje śūnyatāpradeśe vairocanagarbhe sañca indriya śodhane svāhā

The rite: by reciting it constantly, one attains the state of the noble Perfection of Wisdom. One becomes hard to overcome for all māras, all opponents, all enemies, obstructors, and all who lead astray. Likewise, whoever writes it down and wears it on the arm also has these qualities.

namo ratnatrayāya namaḥ sarva durgati pariśodhāya tathāgatāya arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya tadyathā śodhane śodhane sarva pāpaṃ viśodhane śuddhe viśuddhe sarva karmma āvaraṇi viśuddhe svāhā

This is the rite of this dhāraṇī: by reciting it constantly, one is freed from all evil deeds. Through the blessing of the buddhas, one will remember one's former births for four lifetimes. Until one finally reaches the seat of awakening, one's roots of virtue will never be used up.

namo ratnatrayāya namo bhagavati āryaprajñāpāramitāyai oṃ śruti smṛti vijaye svāhā

By retaining this, one retains the Perfection of Wisdom. Its rite is this: set out a volume of the noble Perfection of Wisdom, and before it smear a maṇḍala with the dung of a tawny cow that has not fallen to the ground. Fasting for a day and a night, make vast offerings in that place, offer lamps of cow's butter, and, keeping in mind the task to be done, one should recite it. Having spread kuśa grass right there, one sees the golden-colored body of the Tathāgata, and he teaches this person in accordance with the right view. One should recite it aloud at dawn, or else during the night itself. One should cultivate the recollection of the Buddha.

namo ratnatrayāya nama ārya avalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā jaye jaye mahājaye jayavāhīni jala uttare kala kala mala mala cala cala hulu hulu kṣiṇi kṣiṇi sarva karmma āvaraṇāni me viśvadhāya bhagavate sahasra āvarta sarvva buddha avalokite cakṣu śrotra ghrāṇa jihvā kāya manovijñāna śodhani suru suru prasura prasura sarvva buddha adhiṣṭhite svāhā dharmadhātugarbhe svāhā abhāva sarva dharma avibhedani svāhā

This is the rite of this dhāraṇī: keeping it in mind for one night and reciting it constantly, even obscurations accumulated over a thousand eons will be exhausted. It becomes a root of virtue gathered by a thousand buddhas. One turns back from a thousand eons of saṃsāra. Changing one's birth, one is born among the gods. One is born into kingship among humans, or in pure buddhafields. By reciting it for twenty-one days, one sees whatever dream one wishes. This is the dhāraṇī called the Thousand Turnings. It is of great benefit. One should read the sūtra that the bodhisattva proclaimed, and always keep it in mind.

namo ratnatrayāya namo buddhāya namo dharmāya nama saṃghāya namaḥ ārya avalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya svetāya svetābhujāya dvādaśabhujāya ehi ehi bhagavāna ārya avalokiteśvarāya buddha buddha buddha ārya manusmara buddha manusmara dharmma satya manusmara saṃgha satya manusmara tadyathā natu natu kiṇi kiṇi turu turu bhyo bhyo kuru kuru sarva sarvaṃ me sādhayaṃ hiri miri ṭiṭi nini mama sabarivārasya sidhyantu mantra padā svāhā

Then the Tathāgata Amitābha, having spoken this dhāraṇī, said this to the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara: This root vidyā dhāraṇī of the bodhisattvas is accomplished simply by reciting it; even without prior practice, its rites take effect. On the day of the full moon, one who keeps the poṣadha may also fast for a day and a night. In the presence of Avalokiteśvara, kindle a fire with wood of the bodhi tree and make a fire offering of eight thousand black sesame seeds. If one does likewise for seven days, once a day or in three sessions, a king or a king's minister comes under one's power. Fasting for three nights, make a fire offering of eight thousand white mustard seeds. For a fortnight or a month, for the sake of the land, one should go to the tops of seven anthills, climb each one in turn, and recite from morning until afternoon. One is freed from the acts of immediate retribution. If one wants a son, make a fire offering of milk, and a boy endowed with all the marks in perfect completeness will be born. With this very dhāraṇī one protects oneself and puts harmful grahas to flight, whether by performing the rite or by binding it into substances as an amulet. Or else all bandits come under one's power. One who recites it constantly and without interruption will amass wealth and will also be victorious over enemies.

Then the Tathāgata Amitābha again spoke, in the Later Tantra of Ūrdhvajaṭā, these words of the secret mantra of the dhāraṇī:

namo budadhāya namo dharmāya namaḥ saṃghāya tadyathā hulu hulu vimale nirmale śodhani kācati mirpaṭala sarvva nirogaḥ vinaśanicchadani cchadani vātasamutṭhitaṃ vātasamutiṣṭhitaṃ śleṣma sannipātasamutṭhitaṃ sarvva nāśāni ārya avalokiteśvarasya tejana nasyantu akṣirogaḥ svāhā

This is the rite of this dhāraṇī: having made a maṇḍala in the presence of the Blessed One and remaining out of sight, one should consecrate one's hand or kuśa grass with eight hundred recitations and stroke the eyes with it. Even the blind will regain their sight. If one keeps it constantly in mind for six months, eye disease will not arise.

Then the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, having looked well upon the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara and the great assembly dwelling on Potalaka, said to the bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta: Son of good family, these words of the accomplished dhāraṇī mantra, declared in this Later Tantra by the king of ritual manuals, were spoken by the buddhas of the past. The practitioner of the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā, whether monk, nun, layman or laywoman, should always tie a knot in the corner of the Dharma robe or in the hem of the garment. Whoever practices the Blessed Mother Tārā, having recited it once, wears it on the garment with three knots, whether wishing that enemies come under power, wishing that all the vicious be kept far off, wishing to realize all siddhis, wishing to fulfill all aims, wishing to enter the king's palace, or wishing to vanquish the hostile, for whatever reason it may be; and likewise one of the bodhisattva family, engaged in accomplishing all aims, keeps it. Here the words of the dhāraṇī mantra accomplished in the mind are these:

namo ratnatrayāya namo amitābhāya tathāgatāya arhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya namaḥ ārya avalokiteśvarāya bodhisatvāya mahāsatvāya nama ārya mahāsthāmapraptāya bodhisatvā vāmanetrānnama syāmitānnamaḥ syāmivāmane piśāci parṇaśavari parṇaśavari piśāca bhagavati pāśahasta parśudharaṇi yāni kāni chchata bhayani utpatyante yakṣaśca ritāyo yākaścita mahāvādyo ye kocita upadravī ye kecita ārya vakśa ye kecita upasarga a uvasarga sambhadhava atpatyante sarvvaṇitāne sarvvāṃstaṃ sarvete vālatadhana utpatyantane paṇḍita anena satyena satyavākena ibhiḥ paṇḍita adhiṣṭhatairmantravarairmama rakṣiṃ kuru paritraṇaṃ kuru parigrahaṃ kuru paripālanaṃ kuru svasti yanaṃ kuru daṇḍapariharaṃ kuru viṣapariharaṃ kuru viṣadbuṣaṇaṃ kuru viṣanāśanaṃ kuru tadyathā amrite asvatargemā mara mara sama prasama upasama tunu vitunu tule tumule mama sarva satvānāñca rakṣaṃ kuru svāhā

This is the dhāraṇī called Parṇaśabarī. Through recitation and fire offering, it destroys all diseases, all grahas and all harms. For instance, when people are afflicted by an epidemic, kindle a fire of śamī wood kindling and make a fire offering of eight thousand full oblations in three sessions, as far as one is able. Having made offerings to the Blessed One, noble Avalokiteśvara, one should do so to Parṇaśabarī as well. By performing the rite in this way, all harms are destroyed.

For an affliction of cattle, make a fire offering with cattle hair and bones, and it will be pacified. For all diseases of buffaloes, make a fire offering with their hair and bones for seven days, and it will be pacified. For harm from the lunar mansions, make a fire offering of milk for seven days. One who wishes to realize all siddhis, and for harms, for seven days: a fire offering of khadira powder. For headache, recite over fragrant flowers, take them up, and put them into the fire, and one returns to one's natural state. For fever, tie on a cord, and one returns to one's natural state; one should also eat it and make a fire offering. For a graha, make an effigy of dough and recite seven times, and after seven days one will be freed. For pain in the eyes, make a fire offering with eye ointment, and in seven days one is freed.

One who wishes for pacification should make a fire offering of dūrvā grass, and pacification will come. One who wishes for increase should make a fire offering of mustard seed, and there will be increase. For victory, make a fire offering of sweet flag, and one will be victorious. Make an effigy of salt and make a fire offering, and it comes under one's power. For one seized by a snake's fangs, there is the rite with leafy twigs. For what arises from snakes, in seven days one brings it under control. For an affliction by bhūtas and piśācas, strike with mustard seed recited over twenty times, and they go back to their own place. By constant recitation, all people become pleased. On entering the king's palace, if one recites it twenty-one times over one's face, whoever one sees comes under one's power. For all rites of fire offering, perform the fire offering for seven days. In short, all harms will be destroyed. By a fire offering of jasmine flowers one performs all rites. For all rites, first make a fire offering of full oblations. For all rites, it is said, perform this very rite. It is to be done by one who keeps the poṣadha.

Holding all beings in mind, one should consecrate an earthen bowl and a sellaka with eight hundred recitations, and a young girl should tie eight hundred knots. Then, having washed it with scented water, place it on a stick and tie it to the person's head. Likewise, when buffaloes, goats and livestock are harmed by thieves, tie it to their horns. Fill a vase with water, have one who is pure consecrate it with eight hundred recitations, and tie it to the sick person's waist, and he will return to his natural state. For houses afflicted by brahmarākṣasas and piśācas, make a fire offering and offer torma as far as one is able.

Thus it was spoken. This is the dhāraṇī called Parṇaśabarī, spoken in the Later Tantra of Ūrdhvajaṭā, and it is also the sūtra proclaimed by the bodhisattva.

Again, at that time, all the buddhas, the blessed ones, stretched out their right hands, stroked the crown of the head of the bodhisattva great being, noble Avalokiteśvara, and said this: Son of good family, there is a dhāraṇī called the Jewel Garland. All the buddhas, rejoicing, have declared that it is accomplished by reciting it. For protection and defense in that later great king of ritual manuals, and for the sake of proclaiming it, we set it, in the Later Tantra of Ūrdhvajaṭā, always to bring about the siddhi of the practitioner of the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā. The wise one does so having written it on any auspicious date.

Then the Tathāgata Śākyamuni spoke these words of mantra:

namo buddhāya namo dharmāya namaḥ saṃghāya namaḥ saptānāṃ samyaksaṃbuddhākoṭīnāṃ namo metreya pramukhānāṃ sarva buddha bodhisatvānāṃ namaḥ samyaggatānāṃ namaḥ samyakpratipannānāṃ namo arhatāṃ namo nāgāmīnāṃ namaḥ sakridāgāmīnāṃ namaḥ śrotāpanmānāṃ namo arhate mardhvatu aparājetahṛdayaṃ mavartayiṣyami samyaksaṃbuddha bhāṣita manumodataṃ devaganai sarva karma karaṃ śubhaṃ papitrañca vā maṃgalyaṃ dhanyaṃ śubhya karaṃ śubhaṃ rākṣo ghna sarva satvānāṃ devañca aparājitā hṛdayaṃ māvartami sarva pāpa praśamānāṃ sarva artha sādhanāṃ dhanyaṃ sarva graha vināśanāṃ nityaṃ jaya kari hyeṣa śakrasye va aparājita paṣa kritye nāśane ceva rājā agni ripu nāśanī kritya karmāṇi vetaḍo duḥsvapha duḥsvapnā vi atha sputana deva dānava gandharva yakṣa rākṣasa pannāga rakṣaṃ kurvantu me nityaṃ samānta ca tejanaṃ ehikā dritīyaka jvarā tritīyakṣa caturthakebhyo rakṣayaṃ viṣama jvara karmāṇi viṣabhuktaṃ garaṃ caiva bhyojye varjayiṣyati yasya vānabhavata garbho hayante yasya dākaraka ratnamāla iyaṃ teṣāṃ kṣipra mamavahate jāyamartha kāmo lavatarthe śrīkāmo labhate śrīyaṃ vithate raṇa saṃgrahe kṣipramāvāte japaṃ atra vityaṃ pravakṣāmi ratnamālati viprutaṃ tavatā lokanātha hri driṣṭa satvānupadrutāṃ tadyathā oṃ dhanakari vipulakari yaśakari viddhakari ayuntati alakṣiprasamani dhaṃnarvānyavinyavivardhani vaśrīkari sarva graha nakṣatra vaśa vartinime thājanani sutrajanani varivāra vadhyani āyundani prītikāri jambhani stambhani amoha śakti kāñcanamāla graha saumya karaṇi sarva kālikālāhā vigraha vivāda praśamani parcatra nivāraṇi parasainya stambhāni citta nirmalīkarṇi sarva pāpraśamani sarva kilbiṣa nāśani svāhā cuṭu cuṭu tuṭu tuṭu muṭu muṭu svāhā sarva deva anujñvāte svāhā sarva nāgasaṃrakṣite svāhā oṃ niri phaṭ hana hana phaṭ daha daha phaṭ paca paca phaṭ yeṣāṃ vidhvaṣanti viśama cittāyanti hahani kakhorda kurvanti karayanti kṛtañca abhayānumodenarthava phaṭ svāhā agniṃ stambhayāmi viṣaṃ śasta udaka cauri sarva duṣṭa sarva vyādhita cantraṃ janayāmi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā

Having bathed with leaves of the aparājitā plant, adorned with the Jewel Garland, this, which accomplishes all rites, always gives protection. Likewise, written on birch bark, or anywhere at all, it guards some against obstructors, grants supreme merit, destroys evil and defilement, gives victory in battle, in disputes, or in anything, and is auspicious. For whoever keeps this, having written down the fourfold vidyā, and for the man who always recites it, no fear will arise. It always protects all who recite it and keep it. The secret ones guard them. One who always carries this king of rites through to completion holds the vidyā, which is like the splendor blazing upon a garland adorned with jewels. Through it the grahas are destroyed, diseases do not arise, children and grandchildren increase, and one lives with a good retinue. This vidyā was given by the tathāgatas of every quarter for the sake of benefiting beings, and especially for the protection of children. The gods, kings and bodhisattvas, and likewise that Tathāgata, look upon such a one from every side in the ten directions. Wholesome aims increase, all evil deeds are utterly exhausted, and one is freed from bad dreams and from misdeeds; of this there is no doubt.

This is the dhāraṇī of the Later Tantra of Ūrdhvajaṭā.

Then, in this tantra, the characteristics of the mudrās of the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara were taught. They are of five kinds, namely: the crest, the armor, the enclosure, the heart, and the near-heart. For the root vidyā, sixty are taught. For the one that accomplishes all aims, first of all there are ravita, viṇika, and those that culminate in the Buddha. It is explained as the middle fingers and thumbs pressed firmly together, with the little fingers in the shape of a needle. This is renowned as the full mudrā of noble Tārā, and it accomplishes all aims. To satisfy the vidyā, strike the two little fingers together, and it will be satisfied. For the empowerment, move both thumbs apart in the shape of a needle; this should be known as the heart. It goes by the name of praise alone. For the near-heart, the two thumbs are held thus: in a fist, inside it. The little fingers joined like the links of a chain, and the index fingers opened and made into a needle: this is the characteristic of the armor, which one should always apply to oneself. Pressing the two index fingers firmly together, winding the middle fingers around them, and making the threatening gesture in the shape of a needle: this is the sign of the crest mudrā, which one should apply when binding one's own crest.

Again, binding a fist, with the index finger opened in the shape of a needle: this is the characteristic of the recitation mudrā. Turning that very same one around, with the index finger in the shape of a needle, one should make the enclosure mudrā. Binding a fist, with the two index fingers in the shape of a chain: this sign is the mudrā that guards the samaya. Standing with the feet even, set the right foot forward and turn around with the movement of a dance; having turned the other way, apply with both hands the action of the root mudrā. At the forehead, too, it becomes the samaya mudrā of all rites. Then it should be applied when binding mudrās, at the time of recitation, at the time of lying down to sleep, and in other ways as well. For rites against grahas and for all rites, the root mudrā should be applied.

Then again the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, out of affection for Avalokiteśvara, taught in the Later Tantra of Ūrdhvajaṭā the binding of mudrās for the sake of practicing the Blessed Mother, noble Tārā:

Here these are to be properly applied:
for easing epidemics, and the homage of the wise;
and the mudrā common to the three families.
The homage mudrā that invites them is this:
on the joints of the right fingers, joint to joint, all the tips;
bind the mudrā itself in this way.
For constant supplication, the pure one's supplication
mudrā is just the same: of the right-hand fingers
make the joints into points, and then rejoice.
For all offerings, the pure one, always,
constantly rejoicing in the offering,
joins all the nectar of the fingers fully,
the tips of the joints fully joined to the thumb at the heart.
These become the mudrās of the Victor.
The fingertips properly joined, the middle fingers and
both thumbs, with the mudrā that changes nowhere,
recitation grants the supreme; with mental recitation it is the mudrā.

Then again all those blessed ones, while showing the signs of departing to their own buddhafields, made the sign of rising once more. Then the entire assembly, those on the ground and those dwelling in the sky, their minds deeply stirred, were frightened as this whole earth shook of itself; a rain of flowers fell, and ten million bhūtas moving through the sky thoroughly tamed the vicious ones who roam everywhere.

Then again the bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta asked the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, "Blessed One, what is the name of this Dharma discourse?"

The Blessed One said, "Son of good family, therefore keep it as Ūrdhvajaṭā. Keep it also as The King of Ritual Manuals. Keep it also as The Questions of Avalokiteśvara. Keep it also as The Sūtra on the Conduct of Vidyā and Secret Mantra. Keep it also as The Vast Chapters of the Great King of Ritual Manuals. Keep it also as The Conduct of Skillful Means."

Then the bodhisattva Maitreya said this: "Blessed One, with how many roots of virtue will they be endowed? By how many qualities are they blessed?"

"Maitreya, therefore, whoever merely sees such a text has ten qualities: they will be protected on every side by all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, and by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, mahoragas, garuḍas, kinnaras, pretas and the rest; they will be endowed with the profound forbearance of a mind equal to the dhāraṇī; as long as they remain on the ground of abiding in wholesome qualities, they will copy it; having written it, they will keep it; having made it into a volume, they will worship it; they will have long life and freedom from illness, sovereignty, and perfect happiness; and they will go to the good destinies. With its many benefits and its great benefits, this Dharma discourse, blessed together with the gods, this gathering of vidyās and great mantras that has gone beyond saṃsāra, which I too have blessed, will bring rebirth in the higher realms, for happiness through the lunar mansions, the nights and days, the months and years. The ten courses of wholesome action and renown will increase and be perfected. This holds for those who keep the Ūrdhvajaṭā, whether they stay in a household or have gone forth."

When he had spoken thus, the entire assembly, and the world with its gods, humans, asuras and gandharvas, rejoiced in the Blessed One with their minds as well, and delighted in what the Blessed One had said.

The Later Tantra of Ūrdhvajaṭā is complete.

This text, the personal copy of the great Lord Atiśa, was brought from Radreng with great hardship, and the Śākya monk Rinchen Drup completed its translation on the fifteenth day of the Horse month, the month of the Great Miracle, in an intercalary year. The scribe was the Śākya monk Sönam Drup, who lived in close attendance on this great translator.

Since I did not consult a paṇḍita
and found no authoritative copy or commentary,
if word or meaning may have gone astray,
I ask the learned to correct it.

Translator's notes

"Tārā's ship" renders སྒྲོལ་མའི་གྲུ literally; the image may reflect a Sanskrit play on tārā as "she who ferries across," and the exact locale intended is uncertain. "Wisdom crown" renders ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་སྤྱི་བོ literally. The text names the buddha of Sukhāvatī both Amitāyus and Amitābha within this passage; both are kept as written. The clause rendered "at its limit laid open by spreading fragrance" (དྲི་རྒྱས་པས་རྣམ་པར་ཕྱེ་བའི་མཐར) is obscure, and its exact sense is uncertain. The long opening sentence of Amitābha's speech is loosely constructed in the Tibetan; the structure given here is an interpretation. "With loving-kindness" renders བྱམས་པ་དང་བཅས་པ; it could also be read as "together with Maitreya," but the parallel phrase that follows ("a mind whose very nature is loving-kindness") favors the reading adopted. "Fully Blossomed" translates the name of Amitāyus's buddhafield (ཀུན་ནས་མེ་ཏོག་ཅན / ཀུན་ནས་མེ་ཏོག་ལྡན); its Sanskrit form could not be identified with confidence. The sentence beginning "Whatever the tathāgatas accomplish" is syntactically loose in the Tibetan, and its rendering is interpretive. Kalaviṅka is a bird famed for its sweet voice; "kutara" and "vitara" are left as transliterated in the Tibetan, as their identity (apparently makers of drums or kinds of drum) is uncertain. "The extensive Great Ritual Manual" renders ཕལ་པོ་ཆེ་རྟོག་པ་ཆེན་པོ; ཕལ་པོ་ཆེ may instead be a title element (Avataṃsaka). Several tathāgata names are translated into English because their Sanskrit forms could not be identified with confidence. The sentence structure of the long list in Śākyamuni's speech, and of the final sentence, is loose in the Tibetan and is rendered interpretively. Most of the names in these two lists are translated into English because their Sanskrit forms cannot be identified with confidence; Sanskrit is given only for well-attested figures (for example the past buddhas Vipaśyin through Kāśyapa, and bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra and Kṣitigarbha). "Imikimi" and "Viṣatesvara" are transliterations kept as the Tibetan spells them. "Healing Moon" (སོ་བའི་ཟླ་བ) and "Near Portent of Death" (ཉེ་བའི་འཆི་ལྟས) are uncertain renderings. The names of the female bodhisattvas, uṣṇīṣa kings and vidyā kings are given in Sanskrit only where the identification is secure (Abhyudgatoṣṇīṣa, Sitātapatra, Jayoṣṇīṣa, Tejorāśi, Ūrṇā); the rest are translated from the Tibetan, since their Sanskrit forms cannot be confirmed. "In the guise of medicines" renders སྨན་གྱི་ཆ་བྱད, which may refer to herb deities (oṣadhī). དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་མཥྛ appears to transliterate Sanskrit oṣṭha, "lip", and is translated so. "Stain" (དྲི་མ) is kept as written, though its sense in a list of the Tathāgata's attributes is unclear. Most names in these lists cannot be matched with confidence to Sanskrit forms and are translated from the Tibetan; Sanskrit is used only for secure identifications (Amoghapāśa, Hayagrīva, Nīlakaṇṭha, Avalokiteśvara, Padmapāṇi, Trailokyavijaya, Bhṛkuṭī, Parṇaśabarī). Anuttāṭī, Lauṭī, Urṇūkā and Ṣalūkā are transliterated in the Tibetan and are given as spelled. "Great Thousandfold" renders the obscure སྟོང་བུ་ཆེན་མོ. The syntax of the closing sentence is compressed in the Tibetan and is rendered by sense. Most of these names cannot be matched with confidence to Sanskrit forms and are translated from the Tibetan; Sanskrit is used only for secure identifications (Pūrṇabhadra, Maheśvara, Bhṛṅgiriṭi, Māmakī, Jayā, Vijayā, Aparājitā; Hiṇḍanī and Sālabirṭī are transliterated in the Tibetan). The opening "you who gathered here" (ཁྱེད་རྣམས) is kept as in the Tibetan, which has no closing quotation mark; it may be the words of Vajrapāṇi's summons. "Acting as a father" renders ཕ་དང, which is unexpected in a list of ritual acts. The names of the dhāraṇī goddesses and of the pratyekabuddhas are translated from the Tibetan, since most cannot be matched to Sanskrit forms with confidence; Sanskrit is kept where the identification is secure (Candana, Mahendra, Śakra, Upendra). "Gadan" is the Tibetan ག་དན as written; it may stand for དགའ་ལྡན (Tuṣita). "Who Keeps Far from Kin" renders གཉེན་ལས་ཐག་རིང་བྱེད་པ literally. Many of these names cannot be matched to Sanskrit forms with confidence and are translated from the Tibetan; Sanskrit is given for well-attested disciples and nuns. "Kapphiṇa" renders the Tibetan transliteration ཀ་པི་ན. Ruru, Kuru and Kurukulle are transliterated in the Tibetan. The name of the wrathful mantra, sgrol mas gnon pa, is rendered literally as "Tārā's Subjugator"; its Sanskrit form is not identified with confidence. In the list of rites, ltung ba is taken in its ritual sense of "felling" (causing to fall) rather than "transgression," and nyams dgang 'chos pa as "restoring what has declined." The syntax of the closing sentence is loose; the long list is read as the things the buddhas and bodhisattvas have taught. Many names in these lists cannot be identified with confidence and are translated by meaning, among them the spirit classes rendered "suckers," "oppressors," "child-spirits," "wailers," "shadow-oppressors" and "vomit-bringers," the gods "the Thunderer," "the Paralysis-Holder," "the Kuṣma-Holder," "the Green One," "the Joy-Maker" and "the Wealth-Maker," most of the rākṣasa, piśāca and nāga names given in English, and the sages "son of the Stream-Knower," "Mountain Mouse," "Side-Born" and "Māra's Arrow." The class written bram pa is unidentified and is given as "brampas." Kampoja, Amasti, Sulasti and Traṃḥgiras are given as the Tibetan spells them. "Paraśu" renders dgra sta, "axe," likely the sage Paraśurāma. Many of the names in these lists cannot be identified with confidence and are given by their meaning, among them most of the garuḍa, kinnara, asura and planetary names given in English, the god realms "Light of Joy," "Light of Merit," "Fine Below," "Fine Emanation" and "Total Emanation," and the later, non-standard items in the list of lunar mansions. Bheraṇḍa, Bhuruṇḍa, Maruṇḍa, Danadhāta, Māṣṭi, Riṣṭi, Biśīta, Lubha, Rotra and Adgirasā are given as the Tibetan spells them. "Upasdugu" renders nye bar sdu gu, which is unclear. In the list of lunar mansions, chu stod is the mansion Pūrvāṣāḍhā, not the earlier "Upper Waters." "Maitra" renders byams pa as the name of a celestial body. Many names in these lists of houses, yakṣiṇīs and piśācīs cannot be identified with confidence and are translated by meaning; Elā and Talala are given as the Tibetan spells them. The "houses" are the astrological mansions, beginning with the twelve signs of the zodiac. The arjaka is a plant whose blossom splits into pieces; it is the stock simile for a head bursting as punishment for breaking a pledge. Several items in the lists of seven and eight qualities run together in the Tibetan, and the count of items is not cleanly marked; they are translated as they stand. The phrase "overpowering the continuum of awakening" (byang chub kyi rgyud gnon par byed pa) is unclear. The phrase rendered "they should also be practiced as a cause for the awakening of experience" (nyams sad pa'i rgyur) is uncertain; nyams sad can also mean testing or examining one's practice. In "we shall regard as equal to ourselves" (mtshungs par brtag par bgyi), the sense of the promise to the kings is not fully clear; it may mean that the assembled beings will look after them impartially. The chapter colophon is rendered with its nested titles in English order. The text introducing the sandalwood, saffron and camphor offering reads gdug pa'i rig sngags ("malicious vidyā-mantra"); the context of an incense offering makes the reading bdug pa'i ("incense") evident, and it has been translated so. The sentence on applying the mudrā to the root vidyā-mantra is terse and its exact construction is uncertain. "Fragrant herbs" renders rgya spos, an aromatic plant whose identification is unsure. The final sentence calls the preceding flower mantra an "incense mantra," as the Tibetan has it. The verse beginning "My son, for your benefit, the utmost of the fierce" is obscure in its syntax; the rendering follows the Tibetan word by word as far as possible. The "Six-Faced One, a limb of Tārā" (zhal drug pa) could not be securely identified with a Sanskrit name. The text reads dpang du byed ("makes witnesses") of the bhūtas; the common phrase dbang du byed ("brings under control") fits the context and has been translated. The sentence on constant recitation ("they will not turn to loving-kindness ... neither release nor binding") is terse and its subject is uncertain. Keśinī renders skra can ma; the second name, nye bar spyod pa'i skra can ma, may correspond to Upakeśinī but is rendered literally. "She of the Stalk" (sdong bu can) could not be identified and is translated literally. Several names of vidyās here are Tibetan descriptive renderings that could not be confidently matched to Sanskrit forms and are translated literally: Tārā Endowed with Intention, the Radiant One, Great Diligence, the Manifold One, the Great Glorious Lady. "The Eye" (spyan) may refer to the goddess Locanā. The lines "That very protection on which beings rely / is well marked with the signs of the world" render an obscure couplet (srung ba ltos 'gro). The "Veda of the Guardian of Existence" (srid srung gi rig byed) is unidentified. The verse names "the Four Sisters," while the following mantra invokes three names. "Śiva tantra" renders zhi ba'i rgyud, taking zhi ba as the standard rendering of Śiva, since the preceding mantra invokes Maheśvara. The name of the maṇḍala, rendered "the Array of Ornaments of the Jewel Essence in the Hand" (phyag na rin po che'i snying po rgyan bkod pa), is uncertain in its construction. The opening sentence of that paragraph has no main verb in the Tibetan; "there appeared" is supplied from the sense. "The tantra that names the garuḍa" renders mkha' lding mngon par brjod rgyud, which may refer to a garuḍa Abhidhāna tantra. The vocative "O being, O great being" is followed by a sentence in the indicative ("Avalokiteśvara spoke the maṇḍala rite"); it may stand for a request ("please speak") in the underlying Sanskrit, but it is rendered as written. "ས་གཅན" (Rāhu) in the list of months is read as ས་ག་ཅན, the month of Vaiśākha, which the context of month names requires. "རྟ་བབས་བཞེས་བརྒྱན་པ" is read as རྟ་བབས་བཞིས་བརྒྱན་པ, "adorned with four gateways." "Coarse grain" renders ཐུག་པོ་ཆེ, literally "great broth," whose exact sense here is uncertain. "Barley" renders ཆང་པ་ནས, perhaps barley of the kind used for beer; uncertain. The goddess བརྟན་པ ("the Steadfast One") paired with Bhṛkuṭī could not be identified with confidence, nor could several of the bodhisattva names (ནད་ཐམས་ཅད་གསོ་བར་བྱེད་པ, ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་དབང་ཕྱུག་རྒྱལ་པོ, འཇིག་རྟེན་འགྲོ་བ, མངོན་པར་འཛིན་པ) or གཙུག་ཏོར་རྒྱལ་མོ; these are translated literally. "Two or three" in the first sentence is taken as the number of painters. The pratyekabuddha names ནམ་མཁའ and ཡོངས་སུ are given as Gagana and, literally, "Completely," since the second could not be identified. The door guardians འཇིག་རྟེན་ལས་འདས་པར་འགྲོ་བ ("Going Beyond the World") and མ་རྒྱལ་བ་ལས་རྒྱལ་བ ("Victor over the Unvanquished"), and the five Pure Abode bodhisattvas, could not be identified with confidence and are translated literally. ཁྲོ་བོའི་རྒྱལ་པོར་གྱུར་པ is read as ཁྲོ་བོའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་ལ་ ("gazing at the king of wrathful ones"), which the following phrase requires. "The Lord of Flower Kings" (མེ་ཏོག་གི་རྒྱལ་པོའི་དབང་པོ) is probably the same Tathāgata later called Saṃkusumitarāja. "With a vajra in his hand" for Mahābrahmā (ཕྱག་ན་རྡོ་རྗེའོ) is rendered literally; it is an unusual attribute and might instead be a stray mention of Vajrapāṇi. Among the Four Great Kings' gods, པི་ཝང་གཉིས་པ ("the Two-Lute ones") could not be identified and is translated literally. The god "who holds a noose in his hand" in the west is presumably Varuṇa. The closing "These are the Blessed One's" (འདི་རྣམས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་སོ) is terse and rendered as it stands. "The bull among the naked tīrthikas" is presumably the Jain founder (Ṛṣabha or Mahāvīra); the text gives no name. The "lord of the rākṣasas of Laṅkā" is likewise left unnamed in the Tibetan. In the east the text names a triangular maṇḍala but no emblem within it. "The ways of the village" renders the Tibetan for grāmyadharma, that is, sexual intercourse; the young disciples are to be those not yet sexually experienced. "Aśoka coils," "filled pastries" and "garbhatkvā cakes" render names of Indian confections whose exact identity is uncertain; garbhatkvā is kept as the Tibetan spells it. "Tagara" for rgya spos is a probable identification. "With their minds set on the Victor" renders rgyal bar dgongs pa, which could also mean "intent on victory." "The practitioner should first lead them in before the Blessed Lady" renders bcom ldan 'das ma sgrub pa pos, which is compressed; the Blessed Lady is the goddess of this tantra, Tārā. "Deeds of immediate retribution" are the five inexpiable acts (ānantarya). "Regarding it just like the consecration of a king" renders sems bzhin pas, which is terse. "The master's three accomplishments" renders slob dpon gyi sgrub pa gsum, which is not explained here. Kaṭake is a fierce-rite substance not identified with certainty, possibly a pungent plant (kaṭuka); kept as spelled. The sentence on low-caste entrants is compressed and its construction is uncertain in detail. "Who later perform the fire rite" renders phyi nas me'i bya ba mdzad pa literally. Several trees named here cannot be identified with confidence and are kept as the Tibetan spells them: the haḍpya tree and the bodeci tree. Pa ṭa is taken as vaṭa, the banyan. "A place protected by Brahmā" and "a nāga tree" are literal renderings of tshangs pas bskyangs pa and klu shing. "In the west, apart from the order of entry" renders a terse phrase, presumably meaning that the western gate, used for entry, receives no emblem. The verse's 'phan is read as phan, "benefit." The "hero's price" (Skt. likely vīrakraya) is explained in the verses: paying the craftsman's first asking price without haggling. "Seize it!" renders 'dzin du chu gcig, which is obscure as written. "The fortnight of miracles" is the bright fortnight of the month commemorating the Buddha's miracles at Śrāvastī. Dog pa is taken as the cotton thread. "The accomplishment of the ritual dagger" renders ཕུར་པའི་དངོས་གྲུབ as written; since ཕུར་བ can also mean "to fly," the line may instead refer to the accomplishment of flight (sky-travel), which would suit the highest grade of cloth painting. In "even Śakra and the other lords of bliss," the phrase "lords of bliss" (བདེ་སོགས་བདག་པོ) is uncertain and may name a further deity. "Even" (མཉམས་པ) is read as མཉམ་པ. The bodhisattva on the eighth lotus of the left side, སྤྱན་བཟང, could not be identified with confidence and is translated by meaning as "Fair Eyes." The object Vajrapāṇi holds in his right hand, ཉེ་བར་འགོག་པ་འབྲས་བུ་དང་བཅས་པ, is unclear; it seems to be a plant or fruit name and is translated literally. The flower names in the verse are romanized as the Tibetan spells them. Several names could not be identified with confidence and are translated by meaning: the eighth tathāgata (here "Lord Who Utterly Pacifies All Suffering"), and the pratyekabuddhas "Fragrant One" and "White One"; "Sika" is kept as spelled. The phrase ཕན་པ in the description of the second mountain is unclear and is taken as "likewise." The figure kneeling below the first mountain with a censer is not named in the Tibetan; it is presumably the practitioner or donor. "Using the colors taught before" reads the unclear དོག་པ as ཁ་དོག ("color"). The epithet in the closing title, རལ་པ་གྱེན་དུ་བརྫེས་པ, is rendered "of the Upswept Locks" (Skt. Ūrdhvajaṭā, as in the Sanskrit title of the text). "With a crown bearing an auspicious emblem at its center" renders བདེ་ལེགས་དབུས་མའི་ཅོད་པན, which may refer to a svastika. The text announces eight buddhas but names only seven. The first, མེ་ཏོག་རབ་ཏུ་རྒྱས་པའི་རྒྱལ་པོ, is identified as Saṃkusumitarāja; it may be the same buddha called Saṃkusumitarājendra in the first painting. "Stainless," among the gods of the form realm, is translated by meaning because the Sanskrit name could not be fixed with confidence. Here ཉེ་བར་འཁོར means Avalokiteśvara's "close retinue," not the name Upāli. The text reads "right covering" (gyogs) where the parallel "left side" (zhogs) plainly calls for "right side"; translated accordingly. The verse lists both Kubera (lus ngan) and Dhanada, normally two names for the same god; both are kept as the text has them. "The Lion, the Seizer" (seng ge 'phrog byed) is uncertain: it may name two classes of beings or a single figure, and has been rendered literally. After the request, the Tibetan has no explicit verb of speaking for the Blessed One; "said" is supplied from context. The name "Ārya Tārā shin tu rgyas pa" has been translated by meaning ("the Fully Flourishing"), as its Sanskrit form cannot be identified with confidence. The six Tārā names (dbus legs ma, legs spyod ma, mtshan legs ma, lho chung ma, legs gnas ma, nye bar 'dud pa) are translated by meaning, as their Sanskrit forms cannot be identified with confidence. "At a hero's price" (dpa' bo'i rin) translates the Tibetan literally; it is likely a stock expression for buying the material at whatever price is asked, without bargaining. The word rendered "material" (dog pa) is uncertain; the following weight measure suggests yarn to be woven. The description of Samantabhadra holds both a jewel and a lotus in the left hand, and the text places him on the right here though on the left in the previous rite; translated as it stands. In the verse, "all the deities" reads lha for the written lta ("views"), which makes little sense in context and is evidently a scribal slip. The phrase rendered "bowing with body and knees" (lus dang pus mo'i lha nga 'dud pa) is somewhat obscure in the Tibetan. "Ūrdhvajaṭā" (ral pa gyen brdzes, "with upswept locks") follows the Sanskrit of the text's own title. The buddha of Sukhāvatī is named here me tog yang dag par skyes pa'i dbang gis rgyal po, not Amitābha; its Sanskrit form cannot be identified with confidence, so it is translated by meaning ("King Mighty through Perfectly Arisen Flowers"). Several plant names are given in Tibetan transliteration of Sanskrit; chidhrika and kabuka could not be identified with confidence and are given as written. The description of the chidhrika as coming "from the back of an elephant" and appearing when thunder roars is translated literally; it may refer to a mushroom. "The substances of accomplishment they hold out" renders ཉེ་བར་བཅིངས་པའི་དངོས་གྲུབ་ཀྱི་རྫས, literally "closely bound substances of accomplishment"; the sense appears to be that the nāgas proffer such substances as a distraction, but the phrase is not entirely clear. "Lamp bearers" (མར་མེ་འཛིན་པ) appear to be the vidyādharīs described in the following sentence. The "far-following attendant" renders རིང་དུ་རྗེས་སུ་འབྲང་བ, one in a list of mantra types; its exact identity is unclear. In the closing verses, which concern bodily purification with earth, the lines "at the village outskirts, for the four acts" (བས་མཐའི་གྲོང་གི་ཆོས་བཞི་ལ), "for the body, at the abode of the gods" (ལུས་ལ་ལྷ་གནས), and "for touching, soft earths are wanted" (རེག་ན་གཞོན་ཤ་ཅན་རྣམས་འདོད) are obscure and have been translated tentatively. Several lines of the verse are obscure and are rendered tentatively, in particular "the excellent town that brings prosperity" (གྲོང་མཆོག་འཕེལ་བར་བྱེད་པ, possibly a place name such as a Vardhana, not identified), "the lowlands where this excellent one flows" (དམའ་བ་གང་དུ་འདི་འགྲོ་མཆོག), and "the best of beings, of vast intelligence" (སྐྱེས་མཆོག་བློ་གྲོས་རྒྱུ་ངན་པ, where རྒྱུ་ངན་པ "bad cause" makes no sense in a line praising the Buddha and is read as a slip for a word meaning "vast"). "The Venomous River" (དུག་ཅན) is a river meeting the Ganges that I cannot identify with confidence. "Pushel tsé" (པུ་ཤེལ་ཙེ) is a substance of the Tibetan pharmacopoeia whose Sanskrit equivalent is uncertain. "The ways of the village" (གྲོང་གི་ཆོས, grāmyadharma) refers to sexual intercourse. "Fine iron" renders རྒྱལ་གྱི་ལྕགས (literally "royal iron" or "victor's iron"); the metal intended is uncertain. "An implement carried for worship" renders མཆོད་ཕྱིར་ཐོགས, whose precise referent is unclear. "The lineage of the true limit" renders ཡང་དག་པའི་མཐའི་རིགས (bhūtakoṭi), translated literally. "Not overly tall" renders a line that literally reads "not long of end" and is uncertain; it may instead mean "not far from the goal" or "not long-winded." The lines on the eye "that increases the affection of embodied beings" and on "seeing the guru and the mantras" are also obscure in the Tibetan and are rendered literally. "When he is to go far from that father" renders a line that literally says "when the father has gone to the far side"; it may instead refer to the master's death, after which the disciple is free to go where he wishes. The lines on cleansing with "the pure earth set down beforehand, clean, seven times" render a passage whose Tibetan reads "eating" (bza') where washing or rubbing is evidently meant; the sense of the hygiene sequence is somewhat uncertain. The Tibetan of this piece appears to have been displaced in transmission: the sentence "In accordance with one's intention ... one should take it up and wash" sits inside the narrative of the food clouds, and the verse on eating breaks off at "All food and," after which the prose resumes the story of the food raining down. The translation keeps the order of the Tibetan as it stands. "Scented water" renders dri chu; in some tantric rites the term means urine, but here it is mixed with jasmine flowers as water for the feet. "The lordship of the three bodhisattvas" is a literal rendering of an unclear phrase. In the verse, "food without leavings" renders the obscure sgum med. The plant names are given as transliterated in the Tibetan; pāṭī and sāṭala may stand for pāṭalī and pāṭala, but are left as written. "A hut of leaves of the Sage" renders thub pa'i lo ma'i spyil po literally; thub pa'i lo ma may instead be a plant name (the "muni" tree). "The Victor's followers and Śiva's followers" renders rgyal ba can and zhi ba can, which seem to mean devotees of the Jina and Śaivas; this is uncertain. In "the sage should recite this mantra," thub pa seems to refer to the practitioner as an ascetic rather than to the Buddha. In the list of dangers, ltung ba is taken as "falling," not "transgression," and sdug bsngal nye bar 'gags pa as "choked by suffering." "Watch" renders thun as a period of time, not ritual substances. Two of the eight pratyekabuddha names ('dod pa and nye ba'i 'dod pa) could not be identified with confidence and are translated literally as Desire and Near Desire; the Tibetan also gives mu khyud (Nemi) twice, which is kept as written. The flower names dhānuskārika, parṣika and indravara, and the jewel madaka, are given as transliterated in the Tibetan. "The seventh supreme Sage" refers to Śākyamuni as the seventh of the buddhas of the past. The line rendered "Having gone, by night or at other times" (rab sngags 'gro ba mtshan sogs kyi) is obscure, and the rendering is tentative. The closing verses on cleansing with earth after relieving oneself are terse, and the counts are given as the Tibetan states them. Several place names are identified from their Tibetan renderings: skal ldan shing rta as the Bhagīrathī (Ganges), zla ba'i cha as the Candrabhāgā, dpal gyi ri as Śrīparvata, 'bras phung as Dhānyakaṭaka, me tog as Kusuma(pura), bcom brlag as Mathurā, and 'phags rgyal as Ujjayinī. Rgya yul is taken as China and mang yul is kept as the Tibetan place name Mangyul; both identifications are uncertain. Sāpakṣe and Vakṣu follow the Tibetan spelling, and Sāpakṣe probably stands for Sāṃkāśya, the site of the descent from the gods. "Where the twice-born castes have left" renders gnyis skyes rigs kyis dor ba literally, and its sense is unclear. The verses on action and fruit are very terse and are rendered closely. In the last couplet 'dud pa ("bowing") is read as 'dod pa ("eagerness"), which fits the context. "The aim of the feet" renders rkang pa'i don literally; it may refer to the siddhi of swift-footedness, but this is uncertain. The trees for rosary beads are given as the text names them: dbang po'i shing is rendered "the Indra tree," and bo de tse, which may stand for a bodhi-seed tree, is kept as transliterated, "bodetse." The verbs in the list of rosary rites (sbyang ba, dbugs pa, blang ba, rgyu ba) are technical and are rendered as purifying, enlivening, taking and setting in motion. "With three or two marker beads" renders phyi mo gsum mam gnyis, whose exact sense in stringing the rosary is uncertain. Intrakṣa and musāra follow the Tibetan spelling. "Those like the rhinoceros" refers to pratyekabuddhas. "The seventh Sage" is Śākyamuni, as the seventh buddha of the past. The line "Likewise both will go" (de bzhin gnyis ka 'gro bar 'gyur) is terse and is rendered as written. "Of minerals" renders khams as mineral substances. The term rendered "pacifying" (ཞི་བ་ཅན) is here clearly the class of pacifying rites, paired with increasing and fierce rites, not a name. The line about the sticks (སྣམ་པའི་རྣམ་པ) is obscure; "the proper form of the sticks" is a contextual rendering. "By a solitary tree" reads བསྟན་པ་གཅིག as an evident slip for ལྗོན་པ་གཅིག, since "a single teaching" makes no sense in a list of ritual sites. སླཀྵ is taken as the plakṣa fig tree. Several verse lines on fanning and kindling the fire are terse; the renderings follow the most natural sense of the ritual sequence. Several verse lines are terse and their sense is reconstructed from the ritual context, notably "by firm establishment both remain" and "the other rites that are done", where a negative ("are not to be done") may be intended. "The one with tresses" (སྐྲ་ཅན་མ) is taken as the name of a mudrā taught earlier in the text. "Rising aloft" (ལྡང) is uncertain; it may refer to the power of flight. The phrase rendered "free of discursive thought" (མ་བརྟགས་པ) is uncertain in this context, as is "giving away one's goods in full measure" (རྫས་ཡོངས་སུ་འཇལ་བ, literally "fully weighing out substances"), taken here as an antidote to avarice. "Sauvīra eye ointment" reads དཔའ་བོ་བཟང་པོ as a calque of sauvīra (antimony); "bought at the hero's price" renders the ritual stipulation that materials be bought without haggling. "The vināyakas" interprets རྣམ་པར་འདྲེན་པ, which could also mean "the Guide" (a buddha). Several phrases are obscure: "seizes six shares" (སྐལ་བ་དྲུག་འཕྲོག), "a one-year-old" (ལོར་སྐྱེས་པ), "the gesture of teaching" (རིག་བྱ་སྟོན་པས), and "if he wishes for release" (གྲོལ་བར་འདོད་ན), which context might suggest is a slip for a summoning or subjugating rite. ཙནྡན here is sandalwood, not a name. The passage on obstructors, the thumb at the heart, and the mudrā is repeated in the Tibetan and is translated as it stands. Several items are uncertain: "adhibalaja" and "kāba" are transliterated plant names not identified with confidence; "for all the rites in which flowers of every kind are desired" and "water carried at will" render obscure phrases literally. རྒྱལ་པོའི་ཁབ is taken here in its general sense, "the royal palace", rather than the city Rājagṛha, since the rite concerns success in speech at court. The request of Avalokiteśvara (བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་མ་སྒྲུབ་པའི་དོན་དུ) could also be read "for the sake of practice, Blessed One". "Mahāśvetā" renders དཀར་མོ་ཆེན་མོ, "the Great White One". "Milk in thirty-two portions" renders a terse phrase (literally "milk should be made to go into thirty-two"); the exact measure intended is unclear. The phrase "holding it up for the sake of worship" in the description of the painting is equally terse, and the object held is not named. The names of the samādhi and mantra ("Endowed with Vastness") and of the vidyā king ("One-Footed") are translated by meaning. The weights for the fragrances are given as "zho or srang," Tibetan units of weight, rendered here as "measures." "Indian incense" renders rgya spos, and "leafy rumru" renders a plant name that I cannot identify with confidence. The meaning of the sign that the vidyādhara "will move about in three ways" is unclear. Several ingredients are hard to identify: "bushel-tsé" is a Tibetan plant name kept in phonetics; "śrīveṣṭaka" and "sarjarasa resin" are interpretations of dpal btags pa and sra rtsi, and "gum" renders pog. The phrase about the twelve bowls is terse; it seems to mean twelve bowls in all, of curd and honey together with ten of milk porridge. "With a brush" renders the obscure gnur bas. "Basket" renders the Sanskrit word caṃgauṭaka (caṅgoṭaka) written in Tibetan letters. "Padmāvataṃsaka" interprets "the Tathāgata, the lotus Avataṃsaka"; the identification of this buddha is uncertain. "Keeps all beings from going to ruin" renders a terse phrase, literally "makes all beings not go." "Wearing a white sacred thread" takes mchod phyir thogs as the brahmanical cord (yajñopavīta). "Remaining wholly absorbed even outside the proper times" renders an obscure phrase (dus ma yin par gzhol long la gnas pas); its exact sense is uncertain. The vidyā king's name here (Who Causes All Beings to Follow) differs from the name given when it was introduced in the previous piece (Who Follows All Kings of Vidyās); both are rendered as the Tibetan has them. The "fortnight of miracles" is the waxing half of the first month of the year, associated with the Buddha's miracles at Śrāvastī. The list of buddhas to be drawn above Avalokiteśvara contains thirteen names although the text says twelve; it is translated as it stands. The buddha rendered "Ever Melodious" could not be identified with confidence and is translated literally. "Having had such a painting made" reads the written "drir bcug" as "bris su bcug" or "bri ru bcug". The substances "cekata" (tse ka ta) and "resin incense" (sra rtsi pog) are uncertain identifications. A volume marker of the Kangyur edition ("Here is volume Tsha of the Collection of Tantras") stands after the first colophon; it belongs to the printed edition, not the text, and is not read out. "Divine Flower" and "Moon herself" may be the names of yakṣiṇīs; they are translated literally. Several yakṣa generals could not be identified with confidence and are translated literally: the Son of the Secret One, the Son of Fair Gait, the Son of the Loving One, the Son of the Noble Hero, Mindful of Water, End of Victory, Trunk and Attainer of Victory. Here རྒྱལ་བ is the yakṣa Jaya, paired with Vijaya, not the epithet of a buddha. The phrase "phyed phyed" ("each doing your share") is obscure. The repeated "'drir gzhug" is read as "have it drawn" ("bris su gzhug"). "Five resins" (thang chu lnga) is an uncertain identification. The paragraph addressed to the deities ("For the hundred million ... protect them!") is syntactically loose; its sense is given as closely as the Tibetan allows. ཕྱུགས་བདག ("lords of cattle") is taken as the Pāśupatas, the Śaiva ascetics devoted to Paśupati, which fits the offering of ash; it could also be read literally as cattle owners. ཆད་པ in "bringing ཆད་པ under one's power" is read as "the agents of punishment" (Skt. daṇḍa); this is uncertain. The phrase "he is three-eyed" (gang gi tshe mig gsum pa) is elliptical and is taken to describe Īśāna. Several of the birds are uncertain identifications: ཀུ་ར་བ is taken as the osprey (kurara), ངུར་པ as the ruddy shelduck, and ཤང་ཤང་ཏེའུ as a partridge. The phrase "spoke to the Blessed One" (bcom ldan 'das la) may instead mean "within the Blessed Lady's" ritual manual. Some numbers in the lotus offerings (a million lotuses for one town, thirty thousand for five towns) are odd, but they are translated as they stand. The vidyā introduced as "Characterized by Light" (od dang ldan pa'i mtshan nyid) is called "Endowed with Rays" (od zer dang ldan pa) in the lines that follow and in its colophon; both titles are kept as the text gives them. In that introduction Avalokiteśvara is said to have "spoken of" (gsungs nas) the samādhi, where the parallel passages have "meditating on" it. "For twelve months" renders zla ba bcu gnyis su; it may mean twelve lunar days or twelve portions. The Tibetan reads literally "an effigy of an effigy of salt," apparently a dittography; it is rendered as a single salt effigy. In the rite for a woman, "in an open field" renders thang gi phyogs su, which is terse and slightly uncertain. The coins (dong tse) are given as "a thousand at a time" for stong stong; the interval (per day or per recitation) is not stated. In the rite of Endowed with Heroism, the painting instruction contains the unclear syllable "wang gis" (perhaps a slip for a pigment or for "in the proper manner"); it is left implicit in "one should have ... painted." "On a panel" renders 'bras bu can, evidently a calque of Sanskrit phalaka, which means both "fruit" and "board, panel." "Cow bezoar" for ba bla (gorocanā, a yellow pigment) is a probable identification. "Resin incense" renders sra rtsi pog, an uncertain compound. In the eye-salve rite the Tibetan reads rna ba'i mig sman, literally "eye salve of the ear"; the qualifier is obscure and is not rendered. Pālika, mixed with the nāgakesara powder, is unidentified and kept as written. "On a frame of paṭa wood ... each figure separately" renders pa Ta'i shing la so so so sor bzhag, which is unclear. The colophon of the Eleven-Syllable section names it "the great king of vidyās that bestows what one desires and seeks" rather than repeating its title. "Mixed with other meat" renders gzhan sha la dang bsres te literally; the sense (perhaps food given to another) is unclear. "A discharge from the private parts" for mtshan mar gdol pa is a tentative reading of an obscure phrase. In the powder recipe, pu shel tse and, in the last rite, le brgan rtsi (a dye) are unidentified and given in phonetics. The text gives eight thousand flowers and then speaks of "those one thousand and eight lotuses"; both numbers are kept as written. "Except for what has been set up out of mere desire" renders 'dod pas nye bar gzhag pa ma gtogs so, whose exact scope is uncertain. The opening speech after the chapter colophon is syntactically loose in the Tibetan; "I shall teach" supplies the verb implied for "the great king of vidyās called Bhṛkuṭī" (khro gnyer can). Bestowal of Fearlessness (mi 'jigs pa sbyin pa) is distinct in the Tibetan from the earlier Perfect Bestowal of Fearlessness (mi 'jigs pa rab tu sbyin pa). The sentence identifying Ratnaśrī with the goddess Pāṇḍaravāsinī and describing the "going and coming" of the vidyā in Amitābha's buddha field is syntactically loose in the Tibetan; the rendering follows the most plausible construal as the answer to Vajrapāṇi's question. The buddha names gser kun tu snang ba, lus mdzes and rin chen rab snang could not be identified with confidence and are translated literally (All-Illuminating Gold, Beautiful Body, Jewel Radiance). The samādhi name mtha' kun tu snang ba is likewise translated by meaning. "The heart of the Tathāgata" (de bzhin gshegs pa'i snying po) here refers to the Tathāgata's heart mantra just proclaimed, not to the doctrine of buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha). The rākṣasas' cry "truṭatatara" is rendered as an onomatopoeic sound as the Tibetan gives it; its sense is unclear. "sgyu" in the garuḍa clause is read as their swiftness. The text announces eighteen vidyādhara kings but names only fourteen; the list is translated as it stands. Their names are translated by meaning, since Sanskrit equivalents could not be identified with confidence; "Sumeru" follows the standard rendering of ri rab lhun po. In the opening list, gnon po is rendered "oppressing spirits" and sman chen po "great medicine deities," both uncertain; "the gods of the earth" reads sgra ("sound") as a slip for sa ("earth"). The cloth "of no fixed size" renders tshad med, whose exact sense here is unclear. The plant names bhūtakeśī, gajāhva, śatrughnī and priyaṅgu are given in their usual Sanskrit forms. Several retinue figures could not be identified with certainty: gser ldan ma is rendered "the Golden One," gnam lcags ma "the Goddess of Meteoric Iron," and lha skrag pa "the Terrifier of the Gods"; rdo rje blo gros rdo rje ma is taken as two figures, Vajramati and Vajrī. The vidyādhara king lus med ("Bodiless") is given as Anaṅga, its usual Sanskrit equivalent. jambulika and svatika are left as the Tibetan transcribes them. Several terms are uncertain. The vidyādhara king rnam par gnon pa is translated by meaning ("Overpowerer"). "She Who Goes in Equality" renders snying po mnyam par 'gro ma, apparently the name of a heart-mantra goddess. The implement kurba (perhaps kūrca, a bundle of grass) and the "pankan" fruit (pan kan mthar byed) are left uncertain. "Cow of like stock" renders rgyud mtshungs pa'i ba, and "maṇḍalaka" renders maṇḍal dang bcas pa bza', both tentatively. The clause "and to all the bhūtas on the ground" is elliptical in the Tibetan; an offering to them is implied. The sentence on the second eye of the Victor and the spear of Maheśvara is loosely constructed; "the great lords of the earth" reads sa dbang phyug chen po, which could also be taken as "Maheśvaras of the earth." "The soot of the great fat" refers to lampblack from human fat, a standard ingredient in such rites. "As the Blessed Lady has commended" renders an instrumental construction whose sense is not fully clear. Several ritual items are uncertain. "Burn a measure of it" renders srang, a unit of weight, whose object is unstated. "The fire of the vajra" and the vidyādharas' "eight right hands" are literal renderings of unclear phrases. "Lord over the twelve lands" renders sa bcu gnyis, which may mean twelve regions or grounds; compare "lord of sixty vidyādharas" below. Phushel tsé and kyibung (skyi bung) are unidentified materials, given in phonetics. Rgya spos is taken as tagara. The thread "twisted under Puṣya" renders rgyu skar rgyal. The elephant king's name, Phurbu Sumpa, is translated as "Three Pegs" because no Sanskrit form could be identified with confidence. "Limb-born part" renders yan lag las skyes pa, which probably stands for Sanskrit aṅgaja and may mean the hair. Kharusta (kha ru sta) and svatika (swa ti ka) are unidentified and are given as written. Svatika may be a form of "svastika". "Rise up!" renders stod cig, which is uncertain. "Unspoiled cloth" reads mnyams pa'i ras as ma nyams pa'i ras, as in parallel passages. Several passages are uncertain. The subject of "they will come all together from the directions" is not stated. "Other practitioners will surely take heed" renders an obscure line, sgrub pa po can gzhan gyis nges par bsam par 'gyur. "Except for birth and the exhaustion of the defilements" is one reading of a sentence that may also mean "except for taking birth as whatever he thinks of." The repeated instruction to eat milk and barley meal and recite three hundred thousand times is translated as it stands. The ingredients in the medicine verse (zla bcas, lto ba, byams pa, stag 'joms pa, lag bzhi, phag gi rna ba, glang po 'bod, spyod ral) seem to be coded names of plants. They could not be identified with confidence, so they are translated literally. "Glancing in dread" renders the obscure lta ngan phyogs bzhin. "Kuñjika" is given as the Tibetan spells it. The chapter numbering moves from the sixth chapter to "the eighth" without a numbered seventh chapter. Īśāna's chapter, which closes at the start of this piece, is presumably the seventh. Some phrases are uncertain. "The six portions of the earth" is a literal rendering of sa'i cha drug. "A bamboo that has not been touched" renders 'od ma lhags pa. "Free of stain" reads dri mnams pas as dri ma med pas. "A cow whose calf is of the same color" renders rgyud mtshungs pa'i ba, taken in its usual ritual sense. The subject of "it will be accomplished" and "puts it in his mouth" at the end of the garuḍa chapter is not stated in the Tibetan. The opening clause (yi dgas dri med nyid kyi ming nas smos pa) is obscure; "Stainless" (dri med) is taken as the preta's name, but it may be an epithet or a scribal slip. "Lāñja" is unidentified, and the sentence about becoming "a king of Lāñja or a minister" is uncertain; it may instead mean that kings and ministers are affected by the rite. The cry "stod cig stong cig" makes little sense as written; it is read as "sdod cig", "Stay!". "dga' ba" in the list of dream signs is taken as the name Nanda rather than "joy". In "then he sees them" (for the ancestors) the Tibetan gives no object. The plant and substance names boḍḍaka, kāmāja and nīmala are given as spelled, since they could not be identified with confidence. Several lines in the opening list of minor rites are obscure: "bsud pa" is taken as "bewitched"; the line about the vulture, the "cutting water knife" and "making the fangs go in" is translated literally; "ser mo" is rendered as "a yellow substance". "pānāya", "veda" and "paṭṭaka" are given as spelled, since they could not be identified with confidence. "mchod phyir thogs" is rendered "an implement carried for worship". In the cave rite, "gtogs" is taken as "touch". "The three" (gsum po) is left as the text has it; its referent is not stated. Thags zangs ris is taken as a variant of Thags bzang ris, the asura lord Vemacitrin. "Varṇata" (brṇa ta) is given as spelled; its meaning here is unclear. The "month of miracles" (cho 'phrul gyi phyogs) is the month of the Buddha's great miracle at Śrāvastī, the first month in the Tibetan reckoning. "The Blessed One" is masculine in the Tibetan in the vision passage, though the Blessed Lady is probably meant. "Warm" and "smokes" are the standard signs of the effigy's success (heat, smoke, blaze); the third sign is only implied by "blazes forth". "Kindling sticks as before" renders snga gyi nas yam shing, read as barley and kindling sticks as in the earlier rite. The "heart of dependent origination" is the verse on dependent origination placed in stūpas. "Nandyāvarta" takes dga' ba 'khyil pa as the Tibetan rendering of that flower's name. In the eye-salve rite the Tibetan says four leaves with the fourth pressing down; this is translated as written. "White water pot" renders mchod phyir thogs, the ascetic's water vessel held by Avalokiteśvara. "Srotāñjana" takes rna ba'i mig sman ("ear eye salve") as a rendering of srotāñjana, in which srotas, "stream", seems to have been read as śrotra, "ear". "Hakamika" is given as spelled and is unidentified; the syllable bar before it is read as "in the interval". The phrase "This is the second. In this second" renders an abrupt and unclear transition in the Tibetan (bsgrubs pa gnyis pa'o / zhes pa gnyis pa). "Without end" renders mnyams ma zad par, which may be corrupt. "The binding of the liquid" renders khu ba bcing ba literally; the term is unusual, and it may stand for a protective binding such as the binding of the boundary or of the topknot (śikhābandha). "The immeasurable recitation of the rite" and "one's aims are achieved even when distracted" render terse phrases whose exact sense is uncertain. Twice the Tibetan has "the Blessed One" without the feminine ending ("one sees the Blessed One", "where the Blessed One is to be accomplished"); it is kept as written, though the second may refer to Tārā. "The remains of the offerings" interprets dri med, which here seems to correspond to nirmālya, the used offerings that are cleared away (the word appears in the mantra). The fire-offering substance is given in the Tibetan only as a transcribed Sanskrit word, nūlakavarti, which I cannot identify with confidence; varti suggests wicks, possibly cotton wicks. "The binding of the liquid" again renders khu ba 'ching ba literally, as in the previous passage. In the words to be spoken to Ekajaṭī, the second clause reads literally "and make obstructors for me"; it is taken as a request that she deal with the obstructors, most likely an abbreviated "make me free of obstructors". "At the time when the moon is seized by Rāhu" renders the Tibetan for a lunar eclipse. In the passage on Avalokiteśvara's vidyā, "three months or one month" reads mam (a slip for "or") where the text has ma. At the start, the Tibetan does not name what is placed in the aśvattha leaves; "the substance" supplies the evident object. "Seizes a sixth share" renders cha drug 'phrog literally; its exact reference is unclear. The plant names kumbhira, vāraṇi, ananta, betaśi, brihati, yutika, karṇikara and somarāja are given in the Tibetan as transcribed Sanskrit and are kept as written; brāhmī and sweet flag render the Tibetan tshangs ma and shu dag. Manakara is taken as makara, a crocodile-like water creature. The three named forms of Tārā (She Who Is Endowed with Eloquence, Bestower of Twofold Light, Accomplisher of All Great Rites) are translated from the Tibetan because their Sanskrit forms cannot be identified with confidence. Patsalaṇḍika and iguta are given in the Tibetan as transcribed Sanskrit plant names and are kept as written; iguta may stand for iṅguda. "The fortnight of miracles" renders cho 'phrul gyi phyogs, the fortnight of the Buddha's miracles at the start of the year. "The Blessed One binds the painted cloth" renders the sentence literally; its sense in context is unclear. In the gold-vessel rite, the words for the second sign (lci ba, "heavy") are taken as the ghee thickening. "Bring down a divinatory vision" renders pra dbab pa, the prasena rite of divination through a child seer. Several clauses are terse and their sense uncertain: the bathing of a boy and girl "until young are born in a crow's nest"; "it wears through seven layers of hide" (lpags bdun nyams par byed), apparently a further power of the recitation alongside freeing from bonds; and "likewise with a thread, with sesame and with charcoal" (srad bu can dang til dang sol ba nyid do). "Bahuputrā plant" renders bu mang po can, whose identification is not certain. "Lac and resin" renders sra rtsi pog, whose exact identification is uncertain. "She reveals herself, and by means of white mustard seed one becomes free" is a terse clause whose sense is uncertain. "Having placed jewels inside them" reads bcug nas for the written bcu gnas, which makes no sense here. The phrase rendered "curd rice together with the first portion" (zho zan sngon ma can) is obscure. "Four lumps of earth for a site seven cubits wide" interprets an elliptical phrase. In the healing rite the text says "the four" but names only three ingredients. "Royal tree" renders rgyal po'i yam shing, perhaps the rājavṛkṣa. "Curd" reads zho for the written zhe, which makes no sense in this list of offering substances. Several clauses are terse and their sense uncertain: "water empowered seven times brings everything down and brings wealth"; "a pill of refined collyrium" (zhun mkhan gyi ril bu); the closing instruction about liquor dregs given "in the case of a death, if the child does not come forth", read as referring to a stillbirth; "having gone downstream seven times" (lan bdun du mar rjes su song nas); and the sign "until the words 'I breathe out' are spoken". The "brahma tree" (tshangs ma'i yam shing) is probably the palāśa. The sentence about one who "expounds the Piṭaka and has been placed under guard" (sde snod smra ba yang sgo ba'i las byas pa) is obscure, and its rendering is tentative. "Dhālan" is left as written because the plant cannot be identified with confidence. The "measures" obtained in the Supreme Tārā rite translate tshal, an unclear unit.
